numbersAllowed.111: UK NHS 111, the non-emergency advice line

turns.text: Hello, I'm the dentist who'll be looking after you today. Before we go any further, thank you for telling the nurse how you feel about X-rays. That's really helpful to know. Can I ask what's made you decide against them?
I just think I've had far too many. My last dentist took them almost every time I went. It felt like a routine, not a choice.

That's a fair point, and I understand why you'd question it. Let me explain what I've found, and then you can decide. On the lower left, between two of your back teeth, there's the spot where food keeps catching. The edge of one tooth feels slightly rough there, so I suspect there may be some decay.
Can't you just look and see?

That's the difficulty. Decay very often starts between the teeth, right where they touch. Neither my eyes nor the small instrument I use can reach that surface, so a tooth can look perfectly healthy from above while a cavity is growing underneath.
So what exactly would you take?

Two small pictures called bitewings, one on each side. You bite gently on a little holder, and each one takes about a second. The picture shows the surfaces between your back teeth and how deep any decay goes, so I'd know whether it needs a filling or just careful watching.
And how much radiation is that?

Very little. Two bitewings give roughly the same as a day or two of the natural radiation we all receive from the ground, the air and even our food. I don't want to brush your worry aside, though. Any radiation should have a good reason, which is why I'd only take them if they would change what we do.
Hmm. It's not really about the amount, if I'm honest.
Would you like to tell me what's on your mind? Take your time.
My sister had thyroid cancer last year. She's fine now, but I keep wondering whether all those X-rays I've had could have done something to me too.
I'm so sorry about your sister. That must have been a frightening year, and it's completely understandable that it's made you think about this. Thank you for telling me.
I haven't told anyone that, actually.

I'm glad you felt able to. Two things may help. First, for these pictures the beam is aimed at the back teeth, well away from your neck, and the dose is tiny. Second, if you're worried about your own thyroid, your GP is the right person to talk to, and they can check you properly.
That does help. So would you be taking them every time I come?

No. X-rays should only be taken when there's a clinical reason. How often depends on your risk of decay. Someone at low risk might need them only every couple of years. I'll decide that for you individually, and I'll always tell you why.
And if I said no today?

That's your right. The risk is that if there is decay, it keeps growing quietly. Small decay can be treated with a simple filling. If it reaches the nerve, it can cause pain or an abscess, and then you might need root canal treatment or even lose the tooth.
That doesn't sound great.

It's not inevitable, but it's why finding it early matters. The decision is still entirely yours. If you'd rather not today, we could take extra care cleaning that area, I could prescribe a stronger fluoride toothpaste, and we'd look again in a few months. We can revisit X-rays then.
I think, knowing it's just two and they're nowhere near my neck, I'm happy to have them.
Thank you. I'll note in your records that you'd like X-rays kept to a minimum and always explained first, so whoever sees you knows. Could you tell me in your own words what we've agreed?
Two small X-rays today for the teeth on the left, only when there's a real reason in future, and I'll speak to my GP about my thyroid.
Exactly. And in the meantime, if that tooth starts to ache, stays sensitive to hot or cold for more than a moment, or you notice any swelling, please contact us so we can see you sooner.
I will. Thanks for not making me feel silly about it.
Not at all. It was a very sensible question to ask.

coverage.how: Thanks her for telling the nurse and asks what has made her decide against X-rays.
Describes the food trap on the lower left and the rough contact edge that raises suspicion of decay.
Explains that decay starts where teeth touch and that neither eye nor probe can reach it.
Describes bitewings, how they are taken and what the picture shows.
Compares the dose with a day or two of natural background radiation and says every exposure needs a reason.
Invites the worry behind the refusal, acknowledges the sister's illness and answers the thyroid fear directly.
Explains that X-rays are taken for a clinical reason at a frequency set by her individual risk.
Explains how undetected decay can progress to pain, abscess, root treatment or loss of the tooth.
States the decision is hers and offers preventive care and a review in a few months instead.
Records her preference, checks understanding by teach-back and safety-nets for symptoms.

concern.how: She hints that the dose is not the real issue, is invited to say more, reveals her sister's thyroid cancer and is reassured about the beam direction and directed to her GP.

safety.point: Any personal worry about her thyroid should be assessed by her GP.
Toothache, lingering sensitivity or swelling means contacting the practice sooner.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination finding beyond a food trap and healthy other teeth; the script adds a slightly rough contact edge, which is benign. The dose comparison of two bitewings with roughly a day or two of UK natural background radiation is approximate. The X-ray frequency for low risk is given only loosely as every couple of years.

turns.text: Your own check-up is all done, and everything looks healthy. I'd be very happy to look at your daughter. Before I do, could you tell me how she's feeding and drinking, both during the day and at night?
She's still having formula, and some baby food now. Mostly bottles, a few in the day.
That sounds good. And what goes into her bottle or cup, apart from milk?
In the day it's just milk, and water sometimes.

Lovely. Let's have a gentle look. If you sit facing me and lay her back with her head on my knees, you can hold her hands. That's it. She has two healthy lower front teeth coming through nicely, and her gums and the rest of her mouth look healthy too.
Oh, good. When should I start brushing them?

Now, as soon as teeth appear. Brush twice a day, and make one of those times last thing at night before bed. Use a soft baby brush and just a smear of fluoride toothpaste, no bigger than a grain of rice. Don't rinse afterwards, so the fluoride keeps working.
A family toothpaste, not a baby one?
Yes. Some children's toothpastes have less fluoride than she needs, so a family-strength one is a good choice. With only a smear, she swallows very little, so it's safe.
Right, that's easy.

The other big thing that protects teeth is what she drinks. When sugary drinks, including fruit juice, sit around the teeth, they cause decay very quickly, especially overnight, when there's less saliva to wash them. So milk or water only in the bottle, and nothing sugary at bedtime.
Even if it's watered down?
Even watered down, I'm afraid. It's still sugar, just spread over a longer time. Is that something that happens at the moment? You won't be told off, I promise.
Honestly, yes. Diluted apple juice at night. It's the only thing that settles her. After what happened to my son, I know I should know better.

Thank you for telling me. I know that wasn't easy. You're clearly a caring mum doing what works, and nobody here is judging you. The good news is that her teeth are healthy now, so changing this protects them.
But how do I get her to sleep without it?

Many parents make it a little weaker each night until it's just water, or switch to water straight away. Some give the last milk before the bedtime routine rather than in the cot, then brush her teeth, have a cuddle and a song, and settle her. It may take a few unsettled nights, but it does pass.
I'll try making it weaker bit by bit. She'd scream otherwise.

That's a sensible start. It also helps to give her a free-flowing cup, one without a valve, for drinks in the day. She can practise now, and the aim is to stop bottles at around her first birthday. Sipping from a cup keeps drinks away from the teeth.
OK. She's been grizzly and dribbly lately, too. Is that her teeth?

Very likely. A chilled teething ring helps, or rubbing her gums gently with a clean finger. But teething doesn't cause a high temperature, diarrhoea, or a baby who is floppy or very unwell. If she has any of those, speak to your GP or call 111, and if she seems seriously ill, call 999.
Good to know. I just don't want her going through what my son did.

Of course. That must have been a very hard time. Most early decay can be prevented, so with brushing twice a day, no sugary drinks at night and regular check-ups, your daughter has every chance of keeping her teeth healthy.
Does she need her own appointment?

Yes, please register her with us. NHS dental care is free for children, and we'd like to see her regularly, ideally when you come, so she gets used to us. When she's a bit older, we can also paint fluoride varnish on her teeth.
That's easy enough.
So, what will you do first when you get home?
Start brushing tonight with a family toothpaste, make her bedtime juice weaker until it's water, and buy a free-flowing cup.
Perfect. Let's book you both in together for your next check-up. And if you notice any white or brown marks on her teeth before then, ring us and we'll see her sooner.
Thank you. That's a weight off my mind.

coverage.how: Asks about feeding and drinking day and night and what goes into the bottle or cup.
Positions the baby knee to knee with the mother's help and reports healthy teeth and gums.
Gives brushing advice: twice daily, last thing at night, soft brush, a smear of family-strength fluoride toothpaste, no rinsing.
Explains why sugary drinks in a bottle at night cause decay and recommends milk or water only.
Invites disclosure without blame, thanks her, and suggests gradual dilution and a changed bedtime routine.
Advises a free-flowing cup now and stopping bottles at about one year.
Gives teething comfort measures and names fever, diarrhoea and a floppy or unwell baby as reasons for GP, 111 or 999.
Acknowledges the son's experience and explains that early decay is largely preventable.
Explains free NHS dental care for children, registration, regular visits and later fluoride varnish.
Asks what she will do first and books a joint check-up with a safety-net for marks on the teeth.

concern.how: Gently asked whether sugary drinks are given now, she admits the bedtime juice and her guilt about her son; the dentist thanks her, removes blame and helps her change the routine.

safety.point: High temperature, diarrhoea or a floppy, unwell baby is not teething and needs the GP, 111 or 999.
White or brown marks on the teeth mean booking an earlier dental visit.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination finding; the script finds healthy teeth and gums, which is benign. Advice follows NHS and Delivering Better Oral Health guidance: a smear of fluoride toothpaste for under-threes, a free-flowing cup from about six months, bottles discouraged from one year, and varnish from age three.

turns.text: Good morning, I'm one of the dentists here. I've had a quick look at the tooth, but first I'd like to hear from you. What happened?
What happened is I paid for a filling a month ago, and it fell out yesterday eating a sandwich. A sandwich! I want my money back, and I'm not seeing that dentist again.
Go on. Tell me the rest.
I've lost a morning's work to come here. I'm self-employed; if I'm not on site, I don't get paid. It's just not good enough.
I can hear how frustrating this is, and you're right to expect a filling to last far longer than a month. I'm sorry it's failed, and I'm sorry you've had to take time off work to come back.
Well, at least someone's saying it.

Let me tell you what I've found. The filling has come out in one piece. The tooth itself isn't broken, there's no new decay, and it isn't sore. So the tooth is in good condition, and it can simply be filled again.
So why did it come out, then?

There are a few possible reasons, and often it's a combination. White fillings bond to the tooth, and that bond is very sensitive to moisture while it's being placed. The shape of the cavity matters too, and so does how much force the tooth takes when you bite. It isn't something you've done wrong, and I can't say it was anyone's fault without more information.
Hmm. And who pays for the new one?
No one. Under NHS rules, if a filling fails within 12 months of your treatment, we replace it free of charge. I can do it now, if you'd like, so you don't need another morning off.
Today? Right. That's something, at least.

This time I'll place a thin rubber sheet around the tooth to keep it completely dry, prepare the surface carefully so the filling bonds well, and check your bite carefully, so the filling isn't taking extra pressure.
And what if it comes out again?

Then you'd come straight back, and it would still be covered. But I'll do everything I can to make sure it doesn't. You seem quite worried about this tooth, beyond the inconvenience. Is there something else on your mind?
My dad lost all his teeth by the time he was my age. I keep thinking this is how it starts with me.

That's a very understandable worry, and thank you for telling me. From what I've seen today, your teeth are in good shape. A filling coming out isn't a sign of your teeth failing. Adults mostly lose teeth through decay and gum disease, and both can largely be prevented now, much more than in your dad's day.
So I'm not going the same way?
There's no sign of it. Your gums looked healthy when I checked. If you'd like, at your next check-up we can go through your gums in more detail, so you know exactly where you stand.
Yes, I'd like that. But I still don't want to see that dentist.

That's absolutely fine. You can choose who you see, and I'll note it on your records. If you'd like to make a complaint, or ask about the charge, our practice manager handles that, and I can give you our complaints leaflet. If you're not happy with our response, it explains how to take it further with the NHS.
I'll think about it. Let's just get it done.

Of course. Afterwards, you can eat once the numbness wears off; just take care not to bite your cheek. Avoid very hard or sticky foods on that side for a day or so, and keep brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between your teeth.
Fine.

A little sensitivity to cold for a few days is normal. But if the tooth aches constantly, keeps you awake, or feels high when you bite, or you notice swelling, call us and we'll see you quickly. If a swelling spreads towards your eye or neck, or you struggle to swallow or breathe, go to A&E straight away.
Right. Got it.
So, are you happy with the plan: a free replacement now, a different dentist from now on, and the complaints information if you want it?
Yes. That's fair. Thanks for actually listening.
Thank you for being so honest with me. Let's get you sorted so you can get back to work.

coverage.how: Opens by asking what happened and invites him to continue without interrupting.
Acknowledges his frustration as reasonable and apologises for the failure and the lost time.
Reports the examination: filling lost whole, tooth intact, no decay, no pain, so it can be refilled.
Gives moisture control, cavity shape and biting force as possible reasons and blames no one.
States the NHS 12-month free replacement rule and offers to do it today.
Describes rubber dam isolation, careful surface preparation for bonding and bite checking.
Notices the worry beyond the inconvenience, invites it, and answers the fear of tooth loss honestly.
Agrees to a different dentist, records it and explains the practice complaints route and escalation.
Gives aftercare: numbness care, avoiding hard or sticky food briefly, brushing and interdental cleaning.
Safety-nets for persistent pain, a high bite and swelling, and checks he is satisfied with the plan.

concern.how: Asked whether something else is on his mind, he reveals his father's tooth loss; the dentist reassures him from today's findings and offers a fuller gum assessment.

safety.point: Constant ache, pain at night, a high bite or swelling means calling the practice.
Swelling spreading towards the eye or neck, or difficulty swallowing or breathing, means A&E.

scripts.notes: The free replacement within 12 months follows the NHS England rule for courses of treatment in Band 2 or 3, which applies to his filling.

turns.text: Good morning. I'm the dentist who'll be taking out your broken tooth next week. Before we plan the day, I'd like to check how you take your warfarin, and whether you're planning to change anything beforehand.
Morning. Yes, I've got that sorted. I'll stop the warfarin three days before, so I don't bleed. My mate did that when he had a tooth out.
I'm glad you mentioned it. Do you know why your friend was told to do that, or whether he takes it for the same reason as you?
No idea, really. He just said it worked for him.
Well, the advice for you is clear: please don't stop or change your warfarin before the extraction, unless your anticoagulation clinic tells you to. Keep taking it exactly as usual.
But surely it's safer to stop it? It's a blood thinner.

It's a fair question. You take warfarin because of your atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that can let clots form in the heart. If a clot travels to the brain, it causes a stroke. Stopping warfarin, even for a few days, raises that risk, and a stroke is far more serious than bleeding from a tooth socket, which we can control.
I didn't know it could happen that quickly.

It can. So instead, we check how thin your blood is. I'll arrange an INR blood test within 24 hours before the extraction. Yours is usually between 2 and 3, and if it's below 4 on the day, it's safe for us to go ahead here in the practice.
And if it's higher?

Then we'd postpone and speak to your clinic. On the day, I'll take out just that one tooth, place a dissolvable pack in the socket to help a clot form, put in a couple of stitches and have you bite firmly on gauze. I'll also book you early in the morning, so there's the whole day to deal with anything.
Right. That's more careful than I expected.
We take it very seriously. You still look a little worried, though. What concerns you most about the bleeding?
Honestly? I've lived on my own since my wife died. Last year I had a nosebleed that took an hour to stop. I keep picturing bleeding in the night with nobody there.

I'm very sorry about your wife. That nosebleed must have been frightening, and it makes complete sense that you're thinking about this. A socket is different from a nose: I can see it, pack it and stitch it, and pressure works very well there. Before you leave, I'll make sure the bleeding has stopped.
That helps. Should someone be with me, though?

If a family member or friend could stay with you for the first evening, that would be reassuring. I'll also give you a leaflet with our number and the out-of-hours number, so you're never left wondering who to call.
My daughter could come round.

Good. For pain afterwards, paracetamol is the one to use, at the dose on the packet. Please avoid ibuprofen and aspirin, as they increase bleeding with warfarin. And if anyone prescribes you a new medicine, including antibiotics, tell your anticoagulation clinic, because some affect warfarin.
Paracetamol only. Got it.
For the first day, don't rinse your mouth, avoid hot drinks and chewing on that side, and keep your tongue and fingers away from the socket.
And if it starts bleeding at home?

Roll up a clean piece of gauze from the pack, place it over the socket and bite down firmly for twenty minutes without checking. Most bleeding stops with that. If it doesn't, do it once more with fresh gauze.
And if it still won't stop?

Then call us in practice hours, or the out-of-hours dental number on the leaflet, or NHS 111 at night. If the bleeding is heavy, you feel faint, or you're swallowing a lot of blood, go to A&E or call 999.
OK. I feel a lot better about it now.
I'm glad. Can you tell me the plan in your own words, so I know I've explained it well?
Keep taking my warfarin, have the blood test within 24 hours of it, early appointment, paracetamol not ibuprofen, press on it for twenty minutes, and call if it won't stop.
That's exactly right. I'll book the INR test and the early appointment now, and I'll write it all down for you to take home.

coverage.how: Asks what he plans to do with his warfarin and where the idea came from.
States plainly that he should keep taking warfarin unless his anticoagulation clinic advises otherwise.
Explains atrial fibrillation, clot and stroke risk, and why that outweighs controllable socket bleeding.
Arranges an INR within 24 hours and states the practice proceeds if it is below 4.
Describes single extraction, dissolvable pack, sutures, pressure and an early appointment.
Asks what worries him most and responds to his fear of bleeding alone at night.
Advises paracetamol, avoiding ibuprofen and aspirin, and telling the clinic about new medicines.
Gives first-day socket care and the gauze pressure method for bleeding at home.
Gives the escalation path: practice, out-of-hours dental line, 111, then A&E or 999.
Checks understanding by teach-back and agrees the INR test and early appointment.

concern.how: Asked what concerns him most, he describes living alone and the long nosebleed; the dentist acknowledges his loss, explains why a socket is controllable, suggests someone stays and gives him contact numbers.

safety.point: Use paracetamol and avoid ibuprofen and aspirin; tell the anticoagulation clinic about any new medicine.
Bleeding at home: bite on gauze firmly for twenty minutes, then repeat once.
Persistent bleeding needs the practice, out-of-hours or 111; heavy bleeding or faintness needs A&E or 999.

scripts.notes: Follows SDCEP guidance on anticoagulants: do not interrupt warfarin, INR within 24 hours (up to 72 if stable), treat in primary care if below 4, local haemostatic measures, avoid NSAIDs. The card gives the INR range and threshold. The twenty-minute pressure advice is standard post-extraction advice.

turns.text: Hello, good to see you again. Today is about making sure you're fully informed before you decide anything. Could you tell me what you understand about the implant, and what you're hoping it'll do for you?
Basically a screw in the jaw with a tooth on top. I want to chew properly on the right again. I've read the plan, so I'm happy to sign.
That's a good summary, and I'm glad you've read it. I'd still like to go through the key points, because signing should come after we've talked, not before. Is that all right?
Sure, go ahead.

There are three stages. First, I place the implant in the bone under local anaesthetic. Then there's a healing period of a few months while the bone grows onto it. Finally, we take a mould and fit the crown on top.
A few months? I thought it would be quicker.

It varies, but the bone needs time to fuse properly. It's also worth knowing the alternatives. A bridge fixes a false tooth to the teeth on either side, but those healthy teeth would need trimming. A partial denture is cheaper and removable, though many people find it less comfortable. Or you could leave the gap; some people manage well, but the neighbouring teeth can drift.
No, I'd rather have the implant.

That's a reasonable choice. After the placement, it's normal to have some discomfort, swelling and sometimes bruising for a few days. Most people manage with ordinary painkillers and are back at work within a day or two.
That's fine.

Less commonly, the area can become infected, which we'd treat. Occasionally the implant doesn't fuse with the bone and has to be removed, and we can often try again after healing. And rarely, the nerve in the lower jaw can be bruised or damaged, causing numbness or tingling of the lip or chin. That's usually temporary, but it can be permanent.
Permanent. My brother had that. His lip's still numb after a wisdom tooth.
I'm sorry to hear that. It must be worrying, having seen what he lives with. Is that something that's been on your mind?
If I'm honest, yes. I didn't want to make a fuss.

It's not a fuss at all; it's exactly what we should talk about. Your scan shows the nerve canal lies well below where the implant will go, so there's a good safety margin. I plan the depth from the scan and stay well short of it. Wisdom teeth often sit right against the nerve, which is why your brother's situation was different.
That's reassuring. But it's not impossible.

No, I can't promise there's no risk. It's rare, but not impossible. If you noticed numbness lasting beyond the time the anaesthetic should have worn off, you'd contact me the same day, because early assessment matters.
OK. Anything else?
One thing I do need to ask: do you smoke at all?
Now and then. A few a day, really.

Thank you for being honest. Smoking reduces blood flow to the gums and bone, so it slows healing and makes an implant more likely to fail, both early on and over the years. Stopping, ideally before the placement, makes a real difference. Your local stop smoking service can help, and I can give you the details.
I've been meaning to stop. Maybe this is the push I need.

That would be great. Long term, an implant needs as much care as a natural tooth: brushing twice a day, cleaning around it with small interdental brushes, and regular reviews here. If it isn't kept clean, the gum around it can become inflamed and the bone can shrink away, rather like gum disease.
So it's not fit and forget.
Exactly. And you don't need to sign today. You can take the consent form home, think it over, ask me anything, and even change your mind after signing, right up to the procedure.
I think I'd like to try stopping smoking first, then come back and sign.

That sounds a very sensible plan. So, to recap: three stages, a few days of discomfort, a small chance of infection or failure, and a rare risk of numbness that your scan makes very unlikely. Could you tell me what you'll do next?
Get help to stop smoking, think about the form, and book another appointment to sign when I'm ready.
Perfect. I'll write to you summarising today, and please call with any questions in the meantime.

coverage.how: Asks what he understands and hopes for, and explains that discussion comes before signing.
Outlines placement, a healing period of a few months and fitting of the crown.
Compares a bridge, a partial denture and leaving the gap fairly.
Describes a few days of discomfort, swelling and bruising.
Explains infection, failure to integrate and nerve injury with lip or chin numbness, temporary or permanent.
Invites his worry about his brother and explains the scan's safety margin honestly, without promising zero risk.
Asks directly about smoking and explains its effect on healing and long-term failure, offering support.
Explains lifelong home care, interdental cleaning, reviews and the risk of inflammation around the implant.
Tells him he need not sign today and may change his mind after signing.
Summarises the risks, asks him to state the next steps and agrees a written summary.

concern.how: The nerve risk prompts his brother's story; the dentist explores it and uses the scan to explain the margin. Asked directly, he admits smoking, which is explained and supported.

safety.point: Numbness lasting beyond the anaesthetic needs same-day contact with the dentist.
Poor cleaning can cause inflammation and bone loss around the implant, so lifelong care and reviews are needed.

scripts.notes: No failure rates or costs are given, deliberately.

turns.text: Hello, come in and take a seat. I'm sorry you're in pain. Can you tell me how things have been since I took the tooth out?
The first day was fine, but since yesterday it's been throbbing, right up to my ear. And there's a horrible taste. I think you've left a bit of tooth in there.
That sounds really unpleasant. What have you been taking for the pain, and how have you been looking after the area?
Paracetamol, but it barely touches it. I've been brushing round it and rinsing with mouthwash.

Thank you. Let me explain what I've seen. The socket, where the tooth was, is empty. The blood clot that normally fills it and protects the bone has broken down or come away, so the bone underneath is exposed, and some food has collected there. That's called a dry socket.
Dry socket? I've heard of that. So there isn't a bit of tooth left?
No. The tooth came out whole, and I checked it at the time. Today I can see the whole socket clearly, and there's no fragment there. The pain is coming from the exposed bone, which is very sensitive.
Is it infected, though? Do I need antibiotics?

That's a very common worry, but a dry socket isn't an infection. You have no swelling and no temperature, and you can open your mouth normally, which all fits. Antibiotics wouldn't help it and could give you side effects, so I won't prescribe them.
So what can you do?

Today I'd like to gently wash out the socket with salt water to clear the food, and then place a soft medicated dressing in it. It soothes the bone, and most people feel much better within hours. I can numb the area first if you need it. Is that all right?
Yes, please. Anything. Why did it happen, though?
Sometimes it happens for no clear reason, especially with lower back teeth. Some things make it more likely, such as rinsing too soon or smoking. Do you think anything might have disturbed the clot?
I did smoke a couple of cigarettes that evening. I know you told me not to. I feel so stupid.
Please don't. Thank you for being honest with me. You're far from the first, and we can't be sure that's what caused it. What matters now is helping it heal.
I'm also worried it's got into the bone. I can't take time off; it's a busy term.
That's understandable, but this isn't a bone infection. With the dressing and good pain relief, most people manage at work. It usually settles over a week or so.
That's a relief. What should I take for the pain?

If you have no stomach ulcers, no asthma that ibuprofen makes worse, and no kidney problems, you can take ibuprofen and paracetamol together, each as directed on the packet. They work better in combination. Is that suitable for you?
Yes, I've taken both before.
Good. From tomorrow, rinse gently with warm salty water after meals to keep the socket clean. It's gentle and helps it heal. Keep brushing your other teeth normally, just carefully around that area.
OK.

The other important thing is to avoid smoking while it heals, because it reduces the blood supply and slows healing. It may also be a good moment to think about stopping altogether. The NHS stop smoking service can help, and I can give you the details.
Maybe. I've been meaning to.
I'd like to see you again in two or three days, to check the socket and change the dressing if needed.
Fine, after school if possible.

We'll find a time. Meanwhile, contact us if the pain isn't easing after the dressing. Swelling of your face or jaw, a fever, or feeling generally unwell would suggest infection rather than a dry socket, so ring us that day, or NHS 111 if we're closed. If you have difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a swelling spreads quickly to your neck or eye, go to A&E or call 999.
OK. So it's not infected now, but if I get swollen or feverish, I call.
Exactly right. Shall we put the dressing in now and get you more comfortable?
Yes, please.

coverage.how: Asks about the pain course, the painkillers taken and how she has cared for the socket.
Explains the lost clot, exposed bone and debris as a dry socket.
States the tooth came out whole and that the socket is clearly visible with no fragment.
Explains that a dry socket is not an infection, lists the reassuring findings and declines antibiotics.
Describes saline irrigation and a medicated dressing, with anaesthetic if needed, and asks consent.
Asks what may have disturbed the clot and responds to her smoking without judgement.
Advises combined ibuprofen and paracetamol after checking suitability, and warm salt-water rinses.
Explains why to avoid smoking while it heals and offers stop smoking support.
Arranges review in two or three days to check and redress the socket.
Lists swelling, fever, feeling unwell and airway symptoms as signs of something else, with actions.

concern.how: Asked what might have disturbed the clot, she admits smoking and her shame; the dentist removes blame, then answers her fear of bone infection and time off work.

safety.point: Facial or jaw swelling, fever or feeling unwell suggests infection and needs same-day contact.
Difficulty swallowing or breathing, or rapidly spreading swelling, needs A&E or 999.

scripts.notes: The card gives the examination findings. Combined ibuprofen and paracetamol follows SDCEP dental pain guidance, after checking contraindications. A medicated dressing such as an iodoform-based paste is mainstream UK practice; no product is named in the script.

turns.text: Thank you for waiting. I have the result of your daughter's X-ray. It isn't an emergency, but it does show something we'll need to deal with. Is now a good time to go through it?
Oh. I thought you'd say everything was fine. Go on.

Her teeth and gums are healthy, which is good news. But the X-ray shows that one of her adult teeth, on the upper right, is lying sideways in the roof of her mouth, behind her front teeth, instead of coming down into place.
Lying sideways? Is that serious?

It's quite common, and it can be treated. The tooth is a canine, sometimes called an eye tooth: the pointed one at the corner of the smile. It usually comes through at about her age, but this one has developed in the wrong position and can't find its way down on its own. Her baby canine is still there because nothing is pushing it out.
Can't we just leave it and see what happens?

I'm afraid that isn't the safest option. Where it's lying, it can press on the roots of the front teeth beside it and slowly damage them. That's why it's best to have it assessed now, while there's plenty that can be done.
So what happens next?

I'll refer her to a specialist orthodontist, a dentist trained in straightening teeth. At the first appointment, they'll examine her, probably take another X-ray or a scan to see exactly where the tooth is, and then talk through the options with you both.
What sort of options?

I can't promise a particular treatment, because the specialist will decide. They may suggest taking out the baby tooth to see whether the adult one moves down. Often, a small operation is needed to uncover the adult tooth, and then a brace gently guides it into place over time.
An operation and a brace? Oh no.
That's a lot to take in. How do you think your daughter will feel about it?
That's my worry. She's just started secondary school, and some girls are already teasing her about her teeth. A brace will make it worse. And I couldn't afford private treatment.

I'm sorry she's having a hard time; that's really tough at a new school. Lots of children her age have braces, so she's very unlikely to be the only one, and in the end treatment should improve her smile. The specialist team are used to supporting children through this, and she can talk to them about her worries too.
I hope so. And the cost?
NHS orthodontic treatment is free for children who meet the criteria, and a tooth stuck like this usually qualifies, so I'd expect her to be treated on the NHS.
That's a relief. How soon would she be seen?
I'll be honest: there can be a wait for the first specialist appointment, sometimes several months. I'll send the referral today and make the reason clear.
And in the meantime?

Carry on as normal. Keep up her brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, keep sugary snacks and drinks to mealtimes, and keep coming for check-ups. Healthy teeth matter, because brace treatment usually only starts when the mouth is free of decay.
She's quite good with brushing, actually.

That's great. If she has pain or swelling in the roof of her mouth, or any of her front teeth start to feel loose, please contact us so we can see her sooner. And if you haven't heard from the specialist within a couple of months, ring us and we'll chase it.
OK. Should I tell her, or will you?
I'm happy to explain it to her now, if you'd like, and she can ask me anything she wants. Sometimes it helps to hear it from the dentist.
Yes, I think that would help her.
Before I call her in, could you tell me what you'll say if she asks you about it later?
That one of her eye teeth is stuck in the roof of her mouth, she'll see a specialist, probably on the NHS, and she might need a small operation and a brace.
That's exactly it. I'll ask her to come in now, and we'll go through it together.

coverage.how: Gives a warning shot, asks permission, then states the X-ray finding simply.
Explains what a canine is and that this one developed in the wrong position.
Explains the risk of root damage to the neighbouring front teeth if it is left.
Explains the referral to a specialist orthodontist and what the first visit involves.
Describes possible removal of the baby tooth, surgical exposure and a brace without promising any.
Asks how her daughter will feel and responds to the teasing with empathy and realistic reassurance.
Explains free NHS orthodontics for children who meet the criteria and that this usually qualifies.
States honestly that the wait can be several months and sends the referral today.
Advises on brushing, sugar and check-ups, with safety-netting for pain, swelling or loose teeth.
Offers to explain to the daughter, checks the mother's understanding and agrees to call her in.

concern.how: Her shock at the treatment is explored by asking how her daughter will feel, revealing the teasing and the cost worry; both are answered.

safety.point: Pain or swelling in the palate, or loosening front teeth, means contacting the practice sooner.
If no specialist appointment arrives within a couple of months, the practice will chase the referral.

scripts.notes: The card does not state root resorption; the script says only that it can happen, which is true of palatally displaced canines. An impeded canine normally scores high enough on the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need for NHS treatment, so 'usually qualifies' is appropriate.

turns.text: Hello, you must be his dad. Thank you for coming so quickly. He's been very brave. Shall I explain what's happened and what I've done?
Yes, please. Is it bad?

He's chipped one of his upper front adult teeth. The chip goes through the hard outer layer into the layer underneath, called dentine, but not as far as the nerve. The tooth isn't loose, the X-ray looks normal, and there are no other injuries in his mouth. I've covered the chip with a white filling to protect it, and it looks quite natural.
Thank goodness. The school just said he'd had a fall.
Do you know how he fell, and whether he banged his head?
I don't, actually. They rang to say he'd fallen and broken his tooth, that's all. It's been bothering me.

Let's check, then. He told me he tripped and landed on his hands and his mouth, and I can't see any bumps or grazes on his head. Since you collected him, has he been sick, drowsy or confused, or complained of a headache?
No, he's been chatty, and he wants to go back to school this afternoon.

That's reassuring. It's still worth asking his teacher what she saw. Keep an eye on him today. If he vomits, becomes very sleepy or confused, has a worsening headache or any problem with his eyesight, take him to A&E. If he passes out or has a fit, call 999.
Right. I'll ring the school and tell them, too.
Good idea. Over the next few days, the tooth may feel a little tender when he bites, or sensitive to cold. That's normal and should settle.
Will it be all right in the long run, though? I've heard teeth can die and go grey. Will he end up with a false tooth?
That's a very natural worry. Most teeth with this kind of chip do well, especially when the nerve isn't exposed and the tooth isn't loose. A false tooth would be very unlikely.
But it can happen.

I'll be honest: yes, sometimes. The knock can bruise the nerve, and it can slowly stop working, even when the tooth looks fine at first. So watch for the tooth turning darker or grey, a small spot or swelling on the gum above it, or pain that starts later. If you notice any of those, contact us, because it can usually be treated if it's caught early.
OK. And if the filling comes off?

Bring him back, and we'll replace it. For the next few days, give him soft food and avoid biting into hard things, like apples or crusty bread, with his front teeth. Brush gently but thoroughly with a soft brush, and if he's sore, children's paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed on the packet.
Fine. Does he need to come back?

Yes. I'd like to see him in a couple of months for a check and another X-ray, and again in about a year. Nerve problems can develop slowly without any pain, and the X-ray shows changes we can't see by looking.
That makes sense.
Does he play any contact sports, like rugby or hockey?
Football and rugby at the weekends.

Then a mouthguard for rugby is well worth having. A custom-made one, made from a mould of his teeth, fits best, but a good shop-bought one that you shape in hot water is much better than nothing. It protects his teeth if he has another knock.
I'll look into that.
So, could you tell me what you'll look out for?
Head injury signs today, so being sick, sleepy or confused. And for the tooth, it going grey, a lump on the gum, or pain.
Perfect. For the tooth, call us, or NHS 111 if we're closed. For any head injury signs, it's A&E. He can go back to school this afternoon if he feels well.
Brilliant. Thanks, you've been great with him.
My pleasure. I'll see him for his check in a couple of months.

coverage.how: Explains the enamel-dentine chip, the normal findings and the white filling placed today.
Asks how he fell and checks for head injury symptoms since collection.
Lists head injury red flags needing A&E, and collapse or a fit needing 999.
Explains that tenderness on biting and cold sensitivity for a few days are normal.
Answers the fear of a grey tooth and a false tooth with a realistic, mostly good outlook.
Explains delayed loss of the nerve and lists discolouration, a gum spot or swelling and later pain.
Advises soft food, avoiding front-tooth biting, gentle brushing and children's painkillers as directed.
Arranges reviews with X-rays at about two months and one year, and explains why.
Asks about contact sports and recommends a mouthguard, ideally custom-made.
Checks the father can repeat the warning signs and agrees who to contact for each.

concern.how: He admits not knowing whether his son hit his head, which is checked and safety-netted; he then voices the fear of a dead grey tooth and a false tooth, answered honestly.

safety.point: Vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, worsening headache or visual problems needs A&E; collapse or a fit needs 999.
A darkening tooth, a gum spot or swelling, or later pain may mean the nerve has died and needs review.

scripts.notes: The card does not say whether he hit his head; the script has the boy report landing on his hands and mouth with no head bumps or grazes, which is benign. Follow-up at about two months and one year follows IADT guidance for an uncomplicated crown fracture.

turns.text: Hello, nice to see you. I've finished your check-up. Before I tell you what I found, the nurse mentioned you'd like to talk about your fillings. What have you read, and what's made you want them removed?
I've read a lot online saying the mercury in silver fillings leaks out and poisons you. I want all of them out and replaced with white ones.

Thank you for telling me. It's clearly important to you, so let's go through it properly. First, what I found: you have six silver fillings in your back teeth, and all of them are intact. There are no cracks and no decay around them, and nothing needs treatment today.
But they're still mercury, aren't they?

They do contain mercury, bound with silver, tin and copper into a stable filling material. A tiny amount of vapour can be released when you chew, but UK health bodies have reviewed the evidence carefully, and it hasn't shown that intact amalgam fillings harm the general health of the people who have them.
So why is it being phased out, then?

Mainly for environmental reasons, to reduce mercury waste. As a precaution, we also avoid using it for children and for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. But that isn't because existing fillings were found to cause illness.
I'd still rather have them out.

I understand, and it's your decision. I'd just like you to know the downsides first. Drilling out a sound filling always removes some healthy tooth as well, which weakens it, and the more often a tooth is worked on, the more likely it is to need root canal treatment later. Removing amalgam also releases more mercury vapour in the short term than leaving it alone.
I hadn't thought of that.
Can I ask, has something been happening with your health that's made you look into this?
I've been exhausted for months, and my joints ache all the time. My GP did blood tests, but nothing showed up. I thought maybe it's the fillings.
That sounds really hard, feeling that tired for so long without an answer. No wonder you've been searching for a cause.
I'm worried they're missing something serious.

That's a completely understandable worry. I don't think your fillings explain your symptoms, and I'd hate for removing them to delay finding the real cause. Tiredness and joint pain that carry on for months do need following up, so please go back to your GP, tell them it hasn't improved, and say how worried you are.
I suppose I gave up a bit after the first tests.
That's understandable, but it's worth going back. And if you notice anything new, such as weight loss, night sweats, or joints that become swollen or hot, see your GP sooner.
OK. I'll book an appointment this week.

Good. As for the fillings, we'd replace one if it cracked, if decay developed around it, or if part of it broke away. At that point we'd discuss the material, and often a white filling would be suitable.
Couldn't I just have them all done in white on the NHS anyway?

The NHS covers fillings when they're clinically needed, but not replacing sound fillings, and white fillings in back teeth aren't always available on the NHS. If you'd still like them replaced, for appearance or peace of mind, it can be done privately, and I can give you a written estimate.
That makes sense. I don't really mind how they look.
Then there's no need to rush into anything. Whatever you decide, I'll respect it, and I won't push you either way. If you'd like more information, I can point you to the NHS pages about amalgam.
No, I think I'll leave them for now, and see my GP.

That sounds a sensible decision. So, to sum up: your fillings are intact and need nothing today, you'll see your GP about the tiredness and joint pain, and we'll keep an eye on the fillings at your check-ups. Shall I book your next check-up for the usual time?
Yes, please. And thank you for not brushing me off.
Not at all. Thank you for telling me what's been going on. I hope your GP gets to the bottom of it.

coverage.how: Asks what she has read and why she wants the fillings removed.
Reports six intact fillings with no cracks or decay and nothing needing treatment.
Explains amalgam's composition, the UK evidence on intact fillings and why it is being phased down.
Explains loss of healthy tooth, later root treatment risk and extra vapour during removal.
Asks about her health and acknowledges months of unexplained tiredness and joint pain.
Urges her back to the GP, explains why the fillings should not take the blame and gives red flags.
Explains replacement for cracks, decay or fracture, and that white material is often suitable then.
Explains NHS limits and offers a private option with a written estimate.
States she may decide freely, offers information and applies no pressure.
Summarises the agreement and books the next check-up.

concern.how: Asked about her health, she reveals months of unexplained tiredness and joint pain and her fear that something is being missed; the dentist empathises and redirects her firmly to her GP.

safety.point: Months of tiredness and joint pain need GP follow-up, not attribution to fillings.
New weight loss, night sweats, or swollen or hot joints mean seeing the GP sooner.

scripts.notes: Reflects the UK position: no evidence that intact amalgam harms general health, except rare allergy; the phase-down under the Minamata Convention is environmental, with alternatives used in under-15s and pregnant or breastfeeding women. The script does not mention rare amalgam allergy.

turns.text: Good morning, and thank you for coming in. Before we plan the extraction, the receptionist said you'd read something about your osteoporosis tablets. What have you read?
That they can make your jawbone die if you have a tooth out. So I'm stopping them, from today.
I can see why that would alarm you. What did the article say about how likely it is?
It made it sound very common. There were photos.

Those photos are usually of the most severe cases. Let me explain where you stand, and then we can decide together. First, the tooth. It has broken down below the gum, so there isn't enough left to hold a filling or a crown. If it's left, it's likely to decay further and become infected, which is painful and could make things harder for your jaw later.
So it really has to come out.

I'd recommend it, yes. Now, the condition you read about. Very rarely, in people taking certain bone medicines, the jawbone where a tooth was removed doesn't heal properly and stays exposed in the mouth. It's called osteonecrosis of the jaw, which simply means an area of bone that doesn't heal.
That's exactly what frightens me.

It's an understandable fear. But it's rare, and your risk is low. You take alendronic acid as a tablet, for osteoporosis, you've taken it for 3 years, and you don't take steroid tablets. That puts you in the low-risk group, and the great majority of people like you heal completely normally.
But surely stopping the tablets would make it even safer?

Please don't stop them without speaking to the doctor who prescribes them. These medicines build up in the bone and stay there for years, so stopping now wouldn't remove the risk quickly. What it would do is leave your bones less protected.
That's the other thing. My mum broke her hip at seventy-five, and she never walked again.
I'm very sorry. That must have been hard to watch, and it explains why you take your bones so seriously. Is that what worries you most?
Both, really. I'm frightened for my jaw, but I'm just as frightened of breaking a bone. I feel stuck.

That's a hard position to be in, and you're right to weigh both. The good news is that you don't have to choose. Your tablets are protecting you against fractures, and the jaw risk is low, so the safest plan is to keep taking them and have the tooth out carefully. If you'd like, I'll write to your GP so they know the plan.
Yes, I'd like that.
I can do the extraction here in the practice, under local anaesthetic. I'll be as gentle as possible with the bone and gum, and if it helps, I'll put in a stitch so the gum closes over the socket.
And afterwards?

For the first day, avoid rinsing, hot drinks and chewing on that side. From the next day, rinse gently with warm salty water after meals, and keep brushing your other teeth carefully. Paracetamol at the dose on the packet is fine for any discomfort.
That sounds manageable.
I'd like to see you a few weeks afterwards, and again at about eight weeks, to make sure it has healed fully. If it hasn't, I'd refer you to a specialist team at the hospital, who see this regularly.
What should I look out for?

Contact me if you can see or feel bare bone in the socket, if it's still painful after the first week, or if you notice swelling, discharge or a persistent bad taste. Those would mean we should look sooner rather than wait.
Bone, pain after a week, swelling or a bad taste. Got it.
Exactly. And keeping up regular check-ups will help us avoid more extractions in future. Could you tell me what we've agreed, so I'm sure I've been clear?
I keep taking my tablets, you'll write to my GP, the tooth comes out here, and you'll check it heals properly.
That's perfect. Let's book the extraction, and please bring any questions with you on the day.

coverage.how: Asks what she has read and what she understood about how likely the problem is.
Explains the tooth is unrestorable and that leaving it risks infection that could harm the jaw.
Explains osteonecrosis of the jaw in plain words as bone that does not heal.
Places her in the low-risk group from drug, indication, duration and no steroids.
Advises not stopping without her prescriber, explains the drug stays in bone, and offers to write to the GP.
Explores her mother's hip fracture and names her two competing fears, then reconciles them.
Describes a gentle extraction under local anaesthetic in the practice with a stitch if helpful.
Gives socket aftercare and arranges review at a few weeks and about eight weeks, with referral if unhealed.
Lists exposed bone, persisting pain, swelling, discharge and bad taste as reasons to make contact.
Checks understanding by teach-back, which includes the agreed letter to her GP, and books the extraction.

concern.how: Her mother's hip fracture comes out when stopping the tablets is discussed; the dentist names both fears and shows that keeping the tablets and extracting carefully answers both.

safety.point: Healing is checked at about eight weeks, with referral if not healed.
Exposed bone, pain beyond the first week, swelling, discharge or a bad taste means contacting the dentist sooner.

scripts.notes: Follows SDCEP guidance on medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw: oral bisphosphonate for osteoporosis under five years without systemic steroids is low risk; extract in primary care, no drug holiday, review healing, refer if not healed at eight weeks.

turns.text: Good morning. I'm Sam, one of the hospital dietitians, a specialist in food and nutrition. My job is to help people eat well enough to get better. Is now a good time for a chat?
Now's fine. Though why is a dietitian bothering with me? I'm not fat, am I?

Quite the opposite, and that's why I've come. Everyone admitted has a short check called the malnutrition screening tool. It looks at three things: your weight for your height, weight lost without trying, and whether illness has stopped you eating.
And I failed it, did I?

It isn't pass or fail; it shows who needs extra help. Your score is 3, which means high risk. Four months ago you weighed 68 kilos; now you're 61. That's over a tenth of your body weight, lost without trying.
That much? I knew my trousers were loose. But you lose a bit at my age, don't you?

Losing that much isn't just age. Your body needs energy and protein to fight this infection, keep your muscles strong and keep you steady on your feet. When you're underweight, recovery is slower. The doctors found no other cause, so food is where we can help.
Right. Well, I don't eat much these days, that's true.
Can you talk me through a normal day at home, from getting up to bed? And who does the shopping and cooking?
Tea and biscuits in the morning, maybe toast. More tea, more biscuits. My wife did all the cooking. She died last spring.
I'm so sorry. That's a huge loss, and it sounds as though meals changed completely. How have you been managing since, honestly?
Not well. I can't cook, never could. I'd rather not say so, though. If I tell people I can't cope, they'll put me in a home.

Thank you for telling me; that can't have been easy. Not being able to cook isn't the same as not coping, and nobody will move you into a care home for it. There's practical help, like delivered meals or someone popping in at mealtimes. It's your choice. Shall I ask the ward team to talk through options?
If it's my choice, then yes. I'd like to stay in my own house.

That's what we'll aim for. Here, there are three things. A fortified diet, where the kitchen adds butter, cream or cheese so small portions give more energy. Snacks between meals, like a pudding or cheese and crackers. And a nourishing drink, like a milkshake with added protein and vitamins.
I'm not having those milkshakes instead of proper dinners.
And you shouldn't. The drink tops up your food rather than replacing it, so have it between meals. What do you actually enjoy? If you hate something, you won't eat it.
Proper food. Fish and chips, steak pie, rice pudding. Strawberry, if it must be a drink.
Strawberry I can do, and the menu usually has fish, a pie and rice pudding. I'll note your favourites for the staff.
And when I get home? I still can't cook a pie.

You don't need to. Try beans on toast with grated cheese, a microwave ready meal, scrambled eggs, porridge with full-fat milk, yoghurts, cake instead of plain biscuits, and milk at bedtime. Little and often is fine.
Full-fat milk? I thought that was bad for you.
For many people cutting fat is sensible, but your priority now is regaining weight, so full-fat is better for you. We'll weigh you again before you go home, and I'll write to your GP with the plan.
And if I keep losing it?

Please don't wait. If your clothes keep getting looser, you're eating less, or you feel weaker or unsteady, contact your GP surgery to be weighed. If you fall or suddenly feel very unwell, call 111, or 999 in an emergency.
Righto. I can do that.
To make sure I've explained it well, could you tell me in your own words what we've agreed?
Extra butter, puddings, a strawberry drink between meals, help at home if I want it, and the GP if I keep shrinking.
Exactly. The ward team will talk about help at home today or tomorrow. Anything else on your mind?
No. Thank you, love. It helps to say it out loud.
I'm glad. I'll pop back tomorrow to see how the food's going.

coverage.how: Introduces self, explains the dietitian's role simply and asks if it is a good time.
Names the screening tool in words and lists weight for height, unplanned weight loss and illness stopping eating.
States the score of 3 as high risk, uses 68 and 61 kilos, and links weight to fighting infection, muscle and steadiness.
Asks for a normal day at home and who shops and cooks.
Offers condolence for his wife's death and asks how he has been managing.
Describes fortified meals, between-meal snacks and a nourishing drink.
Explains the drink tops up rather than replaces food and asks his preferences, then records them.
Separates not cooking from not coping, lists practical help and offers the ward team.
Gives no-cook or low-cook ideas and explains why full-fat versions suit him now.
Says he will be weighed before discharge and his GP will receive the plan.
Safety-nets further weight loss to the GP, gives 111 and 999, and checks understanding by teach-back.

concern.how: He reveals his wife's death and that he cannot cook; the dietitian acknowledges the loss, then answers his fear of a care home honestly and offers choices.

safety.point: Continued weight loss, eating less or feeling weaker means contacting the GP to be weighed.
A fall or sudden illness at home means calling 111, or 999 in an emergency.

scripts.notes: The dietitian's name is invented. The card gives no ward menu; the script assumes the menu usually offers fish, a pie and rice pudding. The no-cook food ideas are general first-line food-first advice.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the dietitians. I hear you're going home tomorrow, so I'd like to talk about eating and drinking with your new stoma. First, what have you been told so far, and what have you managed to eat since the operation?
The stoma nurse said something about chewing. I've had soup, toast, a bit of chicken and mash. It's been fine.

That's a good start. Your large bowel used to soak up much of the water and salt from what passed through. Without it, output is looser and you lose more fluid and salt, so we replace them by drinking well and adding a little salt.
More salt? We're always told that's bad for you.

For most people, yes, but you're different now. A little salt on food, or salty snacks like crisps or crackers, helps your body hold on to fluid. Drink regularly through the day; if your urine is pale, you're drinking enough.
Okay. What about food generally?

For the first few weeks, eat regular small meals, sit down to eat, and chew everything really thoroughly. Go easy on tough, stringy or high-fibre foods while everything settles. After that, you can bring foods back one at a time.
Which foods are the problem ones?

The usual ones are sweetcorn, nuts, mushrooms, dried fruit, the pith of oranges, celery, and skins on fruit or potatoes. They can clump together and block the stoma if they're not chewed well. Most people enjoy them again later, introduced slowly, a small portion at a time.
Fine. That's manageable.
Good. You're back at school in six weeks. How do you picture eating on a working day?
Honestly? I wasn't going to eat until I got home. I'm not emptying a bag in the staff toilet with colleagues queuing outside.

Thank you for being honest; that's a very understandable worry. But it might backfire. When the gut is empty, output often becomes more watery, windy and unpredictable. Regular small meals tend to make it thicker and easier to manage.
Really? I assumed less in, less out.

It's a common assumption, but going all day without food or drink also risks dehydration, especially on your feet in a classroom. Could you plan to empty the bag at break and lunch, and ask the stoma nurse about arranging a private toilet at school?
Maybe. I hadn't thought of asking the school. I suppose there's an accessible toilet.
Most schools have one, and employers are generally supportive. Many teachers with a stoma work without colleagues knowing. Keep easy snacks with you too, like crackers or a banana.
Bananas are okay?

Yes, and white bread, rice, pasta, potatoes without skins and smooth peanut butter can help thicken output. Now, two sets of warning signs. First, dehydration: feeling very thirsty, a dry mouth, dark urine or not much of it, dizziness, headaches or muscle cramps.
And how would I know the output's too much?

If you're emptying the bag much more often than usual and it's watery, more like water than porridge, for more than a day, contact the stoma nurse or your GP the same day. They may suggest a special rehydration drink. If you feel faint or confused, call 111 or go to A&E.
And the blockage thing?

Signs of a blockage are no output for several hours with cramping tummy pain, a swollen stoma or tummy, and feeling or being sick. Stop solid food and call the ward or the stoma nurse straight away. If the pain is severe or you keep vomiting, go to A&E or call 999.
That sounds scary.
It's uncommon, especially if you chew well, and acting early is what matters. Could you tell me back the main points, so I know I've explained it clearly?
Small regular meals, chew loads, extra salt and drinks, go easy on sweetcorn and nuts, and don't starve myself at school. Watch for thirst and dark wee, watery output, or no output with pain.
Perfect. I'll phone you in two weeks, and see you in clinic before you go back to work. Here's a card with my number and the stoma nurse's, so you can call before then.
Thanks. I feel better about going back to work now.
I'm glad. You'll find what works for you, and we're here if you need us.

coverage.how: Asks what he has been told and what he has eaten since surgery.
Explains the large bowel absorbs water and salt, so output is looser and losses must be replaced.
Gives regular small meals, chewing well and easing off tough fibrous foods for the first weeks.
Lists sweetcorn, nuts, mushrooms, dried fruit, pith, celery and skins, and says most return gradually.
Explains extra salt and regular drinks, with pale urine as the sign of enough fluid.
Asks about the school day, acknowledges the worry and plans emptying times and a private toilet.
Explains an empty gut gives watery, windy, unpredictable output and raises dehydration risk.
Lists dehydration signs and high-output signs with same-day contact, 111 or A&E.
Lists blockage signs, says to stop solids and call the ward or stoma nurse, and A&E or 999 if severe.
Arranges a phone review in two weeks and a clinic visit, and gives contact numbers.

concern.how: He admits he will not eat at school to avoid emptying the bag; the dietitian validates it, explains why it backfires and plans practical solutions.

safety.point: Dehydration signs: thirst, dry mouth, dark or little urine, dizziness, headaches, cramps.
Frequent watery output for over a day needs same-day contact; faintness or confusion needs 111 or A&E.
Blockage signs need an immediate call to the ward or stoma nurse; severe pain or vomiting needs A&E or 999.

scripts.notes: The card gives no review timings; the script invents a phone review in two weeks and a clinic visit before he returns to work. Food lists are standard UK ileostomy diet sheet advice; local leaflets may differ slightly.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the ward dietitians. The nurse in charge asked me to come and see you. I understand you're worried about your mum's eating. Please tell me what you've seen.
Worried? I'm furious. Two days running her lunch was sitting there, cold, lid still on. Nobody had even opened it. She's had a broken hip, she's skin and bone, and you're starving her.
That must have been really upsetting, and I'd be angry too. I'm sorry. A tray left unopened beside someone who needs help to eat shouldn't happen, and I won't make excuses for it.
Well, at least someone's admitting it.

Can I tell you honestly what her records show? Over eight days she's eaten about a quarter of most meals and lost 3 kilos. After a broken hip, the body needs extra energy and protein to heal, rebuild muscle and walk again, so this matters.
So you knew, and nothing's been done.
The chart flagged it, which is why I'm here, and I'd rather it had been sooner. What's she like with food normally? What does she enjoy, and how was she eating at home before the fall?
She loves a boiled egg, soup, anything with custard. At home, I don't know. I'd pop in at weekends. Her fridge was pretty empty, now I think about it.
That's useful. Is anything making eating harder for her now? Her teeth, glasses, pain, feeling sick, or tiredness after physio?
Her dentures are loose. And she can't reach the table properly. I've seen that.

That explains a lot. From today she'll be on the red tray system, which tells all staff she needs help and her tray mustn't be removed until someone checks what she's eaten. A healthcare assistant will sit with her at meals, and I'll ask for her dentures to be looked at.
And when I'm not here? I work twelve-hour shifts and can't come at lunch. That's what scares me.

I understand. You shouldn't have to be here for her to be fed; that's our job. Everything she eats and drinks goes on a food chart, so poor intake is seen the same day, and I'll review it too. Ask to see it whenever you visit.
I should have noticed at home. That empty fridge. Some son I am.
Older people often hide it, especially from busy family; many relatives tell me the same. You've noticed now and spoken up, which is what helps her most.
Okay. So what's she actually going to eat?

I'm recommending a fortified diet, with extra butter, cheese or cream added, so small portions give more energy. She'll be offered snacks like custard or yoghurt between meals, and a nourishing milkshake-style drink twice a day to top up her food, not replace it.
Can I bring things in? She'd eat my wife's soup.

Please do. Homemade soup, custard pots, her favourite biscuits; just label them with her name and the date. If you or your wife can ever come at a mealtime, even at weekends, you're very welcome to help her eat.
And if she still doesn't eat?

Then I'll review her with the medical team and look at why, whether mood, pain or swallowing, and we'd discuss other options with her and you. I can't promise she'll suddenly eat everything, but I can promise she won't be left without help.
Fine. But if I find another tray like that, who do I tell?

Tell the nurse in charge straight away, or ask for me. If you feel it hasn't been dealt with, the Patient Advice and Liaison Service, called PALS, will follow it up. Raising a concern won't affect your mum's care.
Right. I'll hold you to that.
Please do. I'll ring you on Friday after reviewing her chart and weight, and tell you honestly how she's doing. Does that suit you, and is there anything in the plan you're unhappy with?
Friday's fine. No, it sounds better. I just want her looked after.
So do we. To check: red tray, help at every meal, a food chart, extra snacks and drinks, her dentures checked, and soup from you when you can. Anything missed?
Her glasses. She can't see what's on the plate without them.
Good point; I'll add that to her care plan. Thank you for raising all this.
Thank you for listening. That's all I wanted.

coverage.how: Introduces self, invites his account without interrupting and acknowledges his anger.
Apologises plainly for the untouched trays and declines to make excuses or blame staff.
Gives a quarter of most meals and 3 kilos lost, and explains energy and protein needs after a hip fracture.
Asks her favourite foods, intake at home and barriers such as teeth, glasses, pain and tiredness.
Puts her on the red tray system with a healthcare assistant at meals and a denture review.
Explains the food chart and same-day review, and that feeding her is the ward's job when he is absent.
Normalises hidden poor intake in older people and reframes his speaking up as helpful.
Describes fortified meals, between-meal snacks and a nourishing drink twice a day.
Invites labelled home food and family help at mealtimes.
Explains review with the medical team and discussion of options, with no promise of full intake.
Names the nurse in charge, the dietitian and PALS, and says raising concerns will not affect her care.
Agrees a Friday call, invites objections and summarises the plan, adding his point about her glasses.

concern.how: He reveals his fear about the times he cannot visit and his guilt about missing poor intake at home; the dietitian explains the safeguards that work in his absence and responds to the guilt directly.

safety.point: Red tray flag and mealtime assistance so trays are not removed unchecked.
Poor intake triggers review with the medical team, including mood, pain and swallowing.
Concerns go to the nurse in charge or PALS without affecting care.

scripts.notes: The red tray system and food charts are common UK ward practice, though names vary by trust. The card gives no barriers to eating; loose dentures, reach and glasses are invented and benign. The Friday call is invented.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the gastro dietitians. I understand the enzyme capsules aren't helping yet. How have you been taking them, what does a usual day's eating look like, and what are your stools like now?
I take them after my tea, once a day. Stools are still pale and greasy, they float and won't flush. And I'm still losing weight.

Thanks, that's helpful. Your pancreas normally makes juices that break down fat, protein and starch so your gut can absorb them. With chronic pancreatitis it doesn't make enough, so food passes through undigested. That's why the stools are oily and you're losing weight.
So the capsules do the pancreas's job?

Exactly. They contain the same enzymes, but they only work when they're mixed with food in your stomach. If you take them after you've eaten, much of the food has already moved on. So the key is to take them with your first mouthful.
Nobody told me that. I thought after was fine.

It's a really common mix-up, and it could explain a lot. You'll also need them with every meal and snack that has fat or protein in it, not just your evening meal. That includes a milky coffee, a sandwich, or a biscuit with your tea.
Every snack? That's a lot of tablets.

It is more, I know. You don't need them with fruit, vegetables on their own, fizzy drinks or black tea. For a long meal, take some at the start and the rest halfway through. Swallow them whole with a cold drink, and keep them away from heat, so not on the van dashboard.
Ha, that's exactly where they live. Fine.
Has your eating changed because of the symptoms?
Yeah. I've cut out fat completely. No butter, no cheese, nothing fried. And I skip lunch on my round, because there are no toilets. I thought that was the sensible thing.

That makes sense from where you're sitting; nobody wants to be caught short in a van. But fat is the richest source of energy, so cutting it out and skipping lunch means far fewer calories, and that's likely to make the weight loss worse, not better.
But fat's what sends me running to the toilet.

Without enough enzyme, yes. With the capsules taken properly, most people can eat normal amounts of fat comfortably. So rather than cutting fat, we want the capsules working. The team and I will adjust the dose to suit your symptoms, so please don't stop them, even on a bad day.
Okay. So what do I do on my round?

Could you take a packed lunch, like a cheese or ham sandwich and a yoghurt, with capsules in your pocket? Take them with the first bite. Lunch at a regular time, near a toilet you know, can help while things settle.
There's a supermarket I stop at most days. That works.
Perfect. Could you keep a short diary for the next couple of weeks: what you eat, when you take the capsules, and what your stools are like? That will help us get the dose right.
Yeah, can do. What should I watch out for?

If your stools stay oily or you keep losing weight even when you take them properly, let us know, because the dose may need increasing. Also, pancreatitis can affect blood sugar, so if you're very thirsty, passing urine a lot or unusually tired, see your GP for a blood test.
Diabetes, you mean?

It can happen with chronic pancreatitis, which is why we check regularly. And if you get severe tummy pain, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or you're vomiting and can't keep anything down, go to A&E or call 111 straight away.
Right. That's clear.
Can you tell me back how you'll take the capsules from now on?
With the first mouthful, every meal and snack with fat or protein, split for a long meal, swallow whole, keep them off the dashboard. Eat lunch, don't cut fat.
Spot on. Let's see you in four weeks with your diary, and I'll ring you in between. Anything you'd like to ask?
Just one. Will I always need these?
Most people with chronic pancreatitis do need them long term, but once the dose is right, it becomes routine. Hopefully you'll feel much better for it.
Then it's worth it. Thanks.

coverage.how: Asks how the capsules are taken, what he eats and what his stools are like.
Explains the pancreas makes digestive juices and the capsules replace them.
Explains the enzymes must mix with food, so they go with the first mouthful, and that this could explain his symptoms.
Lists meals, snacks and milky drinks with fat or protein, and what needs no capsules.
Explains splitting doses over a long meal, swallowing whole with a cold drink and keeping them from heat.
Asks about diet changes and responds to his complete fat cut-out.
Explains less fat and skipped meals mean fewer calories and more weight loss.
Suggests a packed lunch, pocket capsules, a regular stop with a toilet and a diary.
Says the team will adjust the dose and he must not stop the capsules.
Gives contacts for ongoing oily stools, diabetes symptoms, and severe pain, jaundice or vomiting.
Checks understanding by teach-back and books a review in four weeks with a call in between.

concern.how: He reveals he has cut out fat and skips lunch because of toilet access; the dietitian accepts his reasoning, then explains why it worsens weight loss and offers a working alternative.

safety.point: Do not stop the capsules; the dose is adjusted by the team.
Thirst, frequent urination or tiredness may be diabetes and needs a GP blood test.
Severe tummy pain, yellow skin or eyes, or vomiting with nothing kept down needs A&E or 111.

scripts.notes: No doses are given; the card leaves dose changes to the team. The diary and review timing are invented. Which foods need no capsules follows common UK enzyme leaflets; local guidance may differ.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the head and neck team's dietitian. I'd like to talk about eating during treatment and the feeding tube the team mentioned. First, what have you been told, and how do you feel about it?
Six weeks of radiotherapy and chemo, starting in a fortnight. Then they said a tube in my stomach. I haven't said yes.

That's completely reasonable. Radiotherapy to the throat makes the lining sore, like a very bad sore throat, and it builds up, so by the later weeks swallowing can become really painful. Many people can't eat enough by mouth then.
And the tube's for then?

Yes. You've already lost 4 kilos, and keeping your weight steady helps you get through treatment and keep your strength. A gastrostomy is a thin, soft tube through the skin of your tummy into your stomach. The team who'd place it will explain how it's done.
Is there another way?

You could wait, and if swallowing becomes too difficult, have a thin tube passed through your nose into your stomach then. That avoids a procedure you might not need. But it goes in when your throat's already sore, it's visible, and it can come out.
And the stomach one?

It's ready before you need it, hidden under clothes and usually more comfortable over weeks. But it's a procedure, with small risks like infection or leaking at the site, and some people never use it. Both are reasonable choices.
Can I ask you something straight? If they want a tube, does that mean it's worse than they've told me?

I'm glad you asked. A tube is suggested because of the treatment's effect on swallowing, not because of how advanced a cancer is. We offer it to many people having this treatment. Your oncologist is the right person to discuss the cancer itself, and I can ask them to see you.
Please. I've been lying awake over it. And the other thing: once it's in, I'll never eat properly again, will I?

That's a common fear, and for most people it doesn't happen. The aim is to keep eating and drinking by mouth as much as you safely can throughout. The tube tops up what you can't manage. Using your swallow keeps the muscles working, which is why the speech and language therapist's exercises matter.
So I'd still eat?

Yes, even sips count, if the team say your swallow is safe. Day to day, a liquid feed goes through the tube, from a pump, often overnight, or a large syringe. We'd teach you and your family to look after it.
And afterwards?
Once treatment's over and you're eating enough, the tube is taken out, usually quickly, and the hole closes on its own. Most people have it out within a few months of finishing.
That's better than I thought. I pictured it forever.
