I can see why. This is your decision, with no pressure today. If you choose the tube, the team placing it will go through the risks and take your formal consent, and you can change your mind until then.
Thank you. I'd like to talk to my husband.

Of course. Meanwhile, if you can't swallow enough food or drink, you're losing more weight, or you're coughing or choking on food, don't wait. Ring the team or me, and if you can't keep fluids down or feel very unwell, call 111.
Even before treatment starts?

Yes, any time. During treatment, if your mouth is too sore to drink, you have a temperature, or, with a tube, the site becomes red, painful or leaks, contact the team the same day. Out of hours, the oncology helpline is always open.
Okay.
Here's a leaflet on both options. Shall we meet again next week, perhaps with your husband, before the team needs your answer?
Yes, I'd like that. He'll have more questions than me.
He's very welcome. Could you tell me what you understand the choice to be?
A stomach tube now, ready for when it gets sore, or wait and maybe have a nose tube. Either way I keep eating, do my exercises, and it comes out after. And it's not because it's worse.
That's exactly right. I'll ask your oncologist to talk to you about the cancer itself. Is there anything else worrying you today?
No. I feel like I can actually think about it now.

coverage.how: Asks what she has been told and how she feels before giving information.
Explains cumulative soreness from throat radiotherapy and why keeping her weight matters.
Describes a gastrostomy simply and leaves procedural detail to the placing team.
Compares waiting with a nasogastric tube against a planned gastrostomy, with pros and cons of each.
Answers the cancer question honestly, refers it to the oncologist, and addresses her fear of never eating.
Explains continued eating by mouth and the role of swallowing exercises.
Describes pump or syringe feeding at home and removal after treatment.
States the decision is hers, without time pressure, and that the placing team takes consent.
Gives contacts for poor intake, choking, being unable to keep fluids down, and problems during treatment.
Offers a leaflet and a joint appointment next week, and checks understanding by teach-back.

concern.how: She asks whether the tube means her cancer is worse and fears never eating again; the dietitian answers both honestly and refers the cancer question to the oncologist.

safety.point: Poor intake, further weight loss, coughing or choking on food needs a call to the team; being unable to keep fluids down or feeling very unwell needs 111.
A sore mouth preventing drinking, a temperature or a red, painful or leaking tube site needs same-day contact or the oncology helpline.

scripts.notes: The card does not say which gastrostomy method the unit uses, so the script leaves placement detail to that team. Removal timing is described generally. The 24-hour oncology helpline is assumed to exist, as in most UK cancer centres.

turns.text: Good morning. I'm one of the bariatric dietitians, and I hear you're going home today. What do you remember from the sessions before your operation, and how are you feeling about going home?
Excited, a bit nervous. I remember something about stages. Liquids first? It's all a blur now.

That's normal after an operation, so let's go through it. Your new stomach is much smaller, roughly banana-shaped, and the staple line needs time to heal. So we build up gently: fluids only for two weeks, then puréed food for two weeks, then soft food for two weeks, then normal textures.
What counts as fluids? Just water?

Anything smooth enough to pour: water, milk, sugar-free squash, smooth soups, runny yoghurt, and the protein shakes on your list. Sip slowly, a small mouthful at a time, steadily through the day; you won't be able to gulp. Avoid fizzy drinks, as the gas can stretch the stomach and hurt.
And then food?

From the puréed stage, keep drinks separate from food. Stop drinking about half an hour before a meal and wait half an hour after. Otherwise the drink fills that small space and pushes food through, so you're uncomfortable or hungry sooner.
How much food will I actually manage?

At first, just a few tablespoons. Your body will tell you when you're full, perhaps a feeling of pressure under your ribs, a hiccup or a runny nose. When you notice it, stop, even if there's food left. Eating past that point can cause pain, vomiting or food getting stuck.
Okay. What should I eat first?

Protein first, every time. It helps you heal and protects your muscles while you lose weight. At the fluid stage, that's milk and the protein shakes. Later, puréed fish, eggs, lentils, chicken, cottage cheese or Greek yoghurt, then vegetables, and only a little starch.
Got it.

You'll also need a vitamin and mineral supplement every day for life, because you'll eat much less and absorb some nutrients less well, and we'll check your blood regularly. Is anything coming up in the next few weeks that might make this hard?
Actually, yes. My niece's wedding, in four weeks. In my family, if you don't clear your plate, it's an insult. My aunties will be piling food on me. I'm dreading it.

That sounds stressful, and it's good you're thinking about it now. At four weeks you'll still be on puréed food, so a full plate isn't safe yet. Would it help to tell the family beforehand that you've had surgery and are following medical advice?
Maybe my sister. She'd tell the aunties. But I don't want everyone knowing.

That's your choice; you don't owe anyone details. You could just say you've had a stomach operation. On the day, take a small plate, choose something smooth like a well-blended dal, eat slowly, and leave what you can't manage. Saying it's delicious but you're full is perfectly polite.
Smooth dal. My mum makes that. That works.

Perfect. Now, warning signs. If you're vomiting repeatedly or can't keep fluids down, have increasing tummy, chest or shoulder pain, a fever, a racing heartbeat, or breathlessness, ring the unit's helpline straight away, day or night.
And if it's really bad?
If you have severe pain, collapse or struggle to breathe, call 999 and tell them you've just had a sleeve gastrectomy. A painful, swollen calf can mean a clot, so ring us urgently about that too.
That sounds frightening.

Problems are uncommon, but acting quickly matters. A common reason people come back in is dehydration, so keep sipping all day, even when not thirsty. Signs are dark urine, passing very little, dizziness and headaches.
Sip, sip, sip. Okay.
Exactly. Your first follow-up is my phone call in two weeks, before you move to purée, then clinic with the whole team. Could you tell me the main points, so I know I've been clear?
Fluids for two weeks, no fizzy drinks, no drinking with meals later, protein first, stop when I'm full, vitamins forever. Ring if I'm vomiting or in pain, 999 if it's serious.
Brilliant. And the wedding?
Small plate, smooth dal, tell my sister, and say I'm just full.
Exactly right; you've planned that well. Anything else before you go?
Just that I hope I can dance at it.
Gentle dancing should be fine by then; check with the surgical team about anything more strenuous. Enjoy the wedding.

coverage.how: Asks what she remembers from pre-operative education and how she feels about going home.
Explains the small, healing stomach and lists the unit's stage plan.
Lists pourable fluids, slow sipping through the day and avoiding fizzy drinks.
Explains separating drinks from meals by half an hour and why.
Describes fullness signals and the pain, vomiting or blockage that follow overeating.
Puts protein first and gives examples for each stage.
Explains a lifelong daily vitamin and mineral supplement and regular blood tests.
Asks about events, then plans the wedding with a small plate, smooth dal and a polite phrase.
Lists urgent signs for the helpline, 999 for severe signs, and calf pain as a possible clot.
Explains steady sipping to prevent dehydration and lists its signs.
Books a phone review in two weeks and clinic, and checks understanding by teach-back.

concern.how: She reveals the family pressure to clear her plate at the wedding; the dietitian explains why it is unsafe at that stage and helps her rehearse a plan she is comfortable with.

safety.point: Repeated vomiting, not keeping fluids down, worsening pain, fever, racing heart or breathlessness means calling the unit's helpline at once.
Severe pain, collapse or breathing difficulty means 999; a painful swollen calf needs urgent contact.
Dehydration signs and steady sipping all day.

scripts.notes: The stage plan is on the card and follows common UK practice; units vary. The follow-up timing is invented. Satiety signals such as hiccups or a runny nose are commonly described by bariatric teams and are harmless. The script assumes the unit gives a 24-hour helpline.

turns.text: Hello, lovely to see you both again. He looks really well. How did you find starting the first step of the milk ladder, and can you tell me exactly what happened afterwards?

I gave him the biscuit every day, like the sheet said. By the second day his eczema was terrible, red patches all over his cheeks and legs, so I stopped. He still had loose nappies for three days. It's settled now.

Thank you, that's really clear, and it sounds like a horrible few days for you both. I'm afraid those symptoms do suggest his body isn't quite ready to cope with milk yet, even baked into a biscuit. So we won't move up the ladder for now.
I knew it. I shouldn't have started. I've made it worse, haven't I?

No, you haven't, and I want to be really clear about that. Trying the ladder doesn't make the allergy worse or make it last longer. It's simply how we find out whether he's ready. You followed the plan, noticed the signs and stopped, which is exactly right.
Really? I've been beating myself up all week.

Really. Reacting at the first step is very common at this age. The good news is that most children grow out of this type of allergy over time, usually in early childhood. For most, it's a question of when, not whether.
So what now?

Back to a fully milk-free diet, as before, which you've been doing really well. We'll try the first step again in about six months, and I'll talk you through it then. Keep a note of what happened this time, for comparison.
Six more months. I was hoping he'd be on normal milk by now.

I know that's disappointing. Until then, carry on with his prescribed formula. It gives him the calcium, protein and vitamins cow's milk would, so his bones and growth stay on track. I'd also like to check how much he drinks, because if it's below a certain amount, he'll need daily vitamin drops.
About three bottles a day, I think.
That may well be enough, but let's check the exact amount together before you leave. How are you finding food labels at the moment?
Mostly okay. I look for milk on the back.

That's the right place. By law, milk has to be highlighted, usually in bold, in the ingredients list. Also watch for words like whey, casein, butter, cream, cheese, yoghurt and milk powder. If you're unsure about a product, leave it and bring the label to show me.
Okay. The other thing is I go back to work next month. He's starting nursery. What if they give him a yoghurt by mistake?

That's a really understandable worry. Most nurseries manage allergies very well. I can write a letter for them explaining his allergy and which foods are safe, and you could meet the nursery cook before he starts. Would that help?
Yes, so much. I was going to write something myself.

I'll do it this week. His allergy is the delayed type, so reactions are usually like this one, slow and in the skin or gut. But know the signs of a rare, immediate reaction: swelling of the lips, face or tongue, a widespread itchy rash, noisy breathing, wheezing, coughing, or going floppy or pale. If that happens, call 999 straight away.
Okay. I hope I never see that.

It's unlikely, but it's best to know. Also contact me or your GP if his eczema doesn't settle, he has blood in his nappy, he vomits repeatedly, refuses feeds or starts losing weight before his next review.
Got it.
I'll see you both in three months to check his growth and how nursery's going, and then we'll plan the next attempt. Could you tell me the main points, so I know I've explained everything properly?

Stay off the biscuit, back to milk-free, keep his formula, check labels for words like whey. Try again in six months. Letter for nursery. 999 if his face swells or he's struggling to breathe, GP if his eczema's bad or he stops feeding.
Perfect. And remember, this setback is common, and you've done nothing wrong.
Thank you. I needed to hear that.
You're doing a great job. He's growing beautifully, which shows the milk-free diet is working. Any other questions?
No, I think that's everything.

coverage.how: Asks how the first step went and exactly what happened.
Explains gently that the eczema flare and loose stools mean he is not ready yet.
Answers her self-blame directly: the ladder does not worsen or prolong the allergy.
Says early reactions are common and most children outgrow it in early childhood.
Gives the plan: fully milk-free, retry the first step in about six months, keep a note.
Explains the formula's nutritional role and checks his intake for vitamin drops.
Asks about label reading and adds the highlighted allergen rule and milk ingredient words.
Responds to the return to work and nursery with a letter and a meeting with the cook.
Lists signs of an immediate reaction and says to call 999.
Lists eczema not settling, blood in the nappy, vomiting, feed refusal and weight loss as reasons to contact.
Books a review in three months and checks understanding by teach-back.

concern.how: She blames herself for making the allergy worse and later raises the nursery worry; the dietitian removes the blame clearly and offers a letter and a meeting with the nursery.

safety.point: Lip, face or tongue swelling, widespread rash, noisy breathing, wheeze, or floppiness or pallor means calling 999.
Eczema not settling, blood in the nappy, repeated vomiting, refusing feeds or weight loss means contacting the dietitian or GP.

scripts.notes: The card gives no formula volume; the script has the mother estimate three bottles and defers the vitamin drop decision to an exact check, in line with NHS advice that formula-fed children taking enough formula do not need drops. A retry after about six months and a three-month review follow common UK milk ladder practice.

turns.text: Hi, come in. I'm one of the diabetes dietitians. It's been about a month since you started carb counting. How are you finding it, and what's been going well?
Better than I expected. The app helps. My readings after dinner are more even than they used to be.
That's great to hear. Can we go through one meal together? Tell me something you ate recently and how you worked out your dose.
Last night: pasta, a jar sauce and garlic bread. I weighed the cooked pasta, got the carbs from the app, added the carbs from the bread label, then used my ratio.
That's exactly right; weighing it cooked with a cooked value is accurate. Remember the sauce too, as some jar sauces contain sugar, so check the label. Have you had any hypos recently?
One or two small ones at home. And a bad one at a party a few weeks ago, before I started this.
Can you tell me what happened at the party?
I went wobbly, slurring, couldn't walk straight. My mates thought I was just drunk and laughed. Someone eventually gave me a cola. It was mortifying.

That sounds frightening and embarrassing, and I'm sorry. It shows why hypos get missed. Early signs are shaking, sweating, hunger, and feeling irritable or anxious. Then you might become confused, slur your words or be unsteady, which people easily mistake for drunkenness.
Yeah. That was me.

So, the team's advice: if you're below 4, or you feel hypo and can't check, take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting sugar, like glucose tablets or a small glass of fruit juice. Recheck after 15 minutes, and repeat if you're still below 4. Once you're back up, have a starchy snack if a meal isn't due. Always carry glucose tablets.
I do keep them on me. Usually.
Good. How do you manage your insulin and food on a night out these days?
Honestly? Since that party, I don't take my dinner insulin if I'm going out. Or I take half. I'd rather be high than have that happen again. Please don't tell me off.

I'm not going to tell you off. Thank you for trusting me; it's an understandable reaction after something so embarrassing. Can I ask, is it only about avoiding hypos, or is your weight part of it at all?
No, it's just the hypos. I'm not bothered about my weight.

That's helpful. The trouble with running high on purpose is that missing insulin can let ketones build up, making you seriously ill quickly; that's diabetic ketoacidosis. Over years, high glucose damages the eyes, kidneys and nerves. So it swaps one risk for a bigger one.
I didn't think skipping one dose could do that.

It can, especially with alcohol. Alcohol lowers your glucose, sometimes hours later, overnight or the next morning. So eat carbohydrate while drinking, have a starchy snack before bed, check before sleeping, and set an alarm to check in the morning. Never skip food to save insulin.
What about the insulin, then? Do I take less?

That's a question for the diabetes team, as they may suggest adjusting your dose on drinking nights. Please don't change your ratio or skip doses yourself. Would you be happy for me to tell them about this today, so they can plan it with you?
Yeah, okay. As long as I'm not in trouble.

You're not. One more thing: tell a close friend about hypos. If you ever become too drowsy to swallow, they mustn't put food or drink in your mouth. They should put you on your side and call 999. Wearing a medical ID helps too.
My flatmate would do it. I'll tell her.
Brilliant. Could you tell me in your own words what you'll do differently now?

Treat a hypo with 15 to 20 grams and check again after 15 minutes. Take my insulin on nights out, eat while drinking, snack before bed, check in the morning. My flatmate knows to call 999. The team sorts out any dose changes.
Perfect. I'll see you in six weeks to review carb counting and nights out. Meanwhile, if you're having frequent hypos, or high readings with ketones, ring the team straight away.
Will do. Thanks for not lecturing me.
Thanks for being honest. That's what makes this work.

coverage.how: Asks how carb counting is going and what has gone well.
Talks through a recent pasta meal and confirms cooked-weight counting, adding the sauce.
Asks about recent hypos and what happened at the party.
Lists early hypo signs and later ones that can look like drunkenness.
Gives the team's treatment and recheck steps, a follow-up starchy snack, and carrying glucose tablets.
Asks about nights out, responds without judgement and checks gently whether weight is a factor.
Explains ketones and diabetic ketoacidosis in the short term and complications over years.
Explains delayed hypos after alcohol and gives eating, bedtime and morning checks.
Says not to change the ratio or skip doses and asks consent to inform the team.
Explains friends must not give food by mouth if he is drowsy, should use the recovery position and call 999.
Checks understanding by teach-back, books a review in six weeks and gives interim contact rules.

concern.how: He admits skipping or halving insulin on nights out after the embarrassing hypo; the dietitian responds without blame, screens for weight-related omission and explains the risk.

safety.point: Hypo treatment as per the team: 15 to 20 g fast-acting sugar, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if still below 4.
Missing insulin risks ketones and diabetic ketoacidosis.
If too drowsy to swallow, nothing by mouth, recovery position and 999.
Frequent hypos or high readings with ketones means ringing the team at once.

scripts.notes: The hypo threshold and treatment are on the card and match common UK guidance. The patient's meal is invented and benign. Glucagon is not mentioned because the card does not say he has been prescribed it.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the clinic's dietitian. The nurse mentioned you're thinking about losing weight, so let's chat about food and your warfarin. Lots of people change what they eat. Has anything changed in your eating or drinking lately?
Oh, not much. My daughter's keen on these green smoothies. She says they'll help me shift a few pounds.

They're very popular. First, can I explain warfarin? It slows how quickly your blood clots, lowering the chance of a clot causing a stroke with your irregular heartbeat. The INR test shows how long your blood takes to clot, so the clinic can keep your dose right.
And mine's low today, the nurse said.

That's right, so your blood is clotting a bit faster than we'd like. One thing that affects warfarin is vitamin K, which helps blood clot. It's mostly in leafy greens, like spinach, kale, broccoli, cabbage and sprouts. A sudden increase can make warfarin work less well.
Oh dear. Then I'd better confess. I've been having a big spinach and kale smoothie every morning for a fortnight. Please don't be cross, and don't blame my daughter. She was only trying to help.

I'm not cross at all, and I'm really glad you told me. Your daughter meant well, and smoothies aren't bad in themselves. They quite likely explain your lower INR, which is useful: we have an explanation rather than a mystery.
So I have to stop them?

Not necessarily. You don't need to avoid green vegetables; they're good for you. What matters is keeping the amount steady from week to week, so the clinic can set your dose around it. Big swings up or down are the problem.
So I could keep having them?
You could, if you'd like one every day and keep it roughly the same size. Or you could go back to how you ate before. Which would suit you better?
To be honest, I don't love them. Maybe a smaller one, on the same three mornings each week?

That can work, if it's the same pattern every week. The clinic must know whichever you choose, as they may adjust your dose and check your INR more often while it settles. Please tell the nurse before you leave.
I'll tell her. What else should I watch?

A few things, briefly. Avoid cranberry juice and grapefruit juice, as they can affect warfarin. Keep alcohol within the usual limits and avoid drinking a lot in one go. And check with the clinic or a pharmacist before taking any herbal remedies or supplements, including fish oils.
Oh, I take cod liver oil. Is that all right?

Mention it to the nurse today. Now, losing weight is a sensible goal. Go gradually, with smaller portions, fewer biscuits and cakes, steady amounts of vegetables, and regular walking. Avoid crash diets or juice cleanses, as big changes in eating can throw your INR off.
That's fair. I was eyeing a soup diet in a magazine.

I'd skip that. While your INR is low, the main risk is a clot. Sudden weakness or drooping on one side of your face or body, slurred speech, chest pain or sudden breathlessness means 999. A painful, swollen leg needs medical advice the same day.
Goodness. And the other way?

If your INR goes too high, the risk is bleeding. Seek advice the same day for unusual bruising, nosebleeds or gums that keep bleeding, blood in your urine or black stools. A severe headache, coughing or vomiting blood, or any head injury needs 999 or A&E straight away.
Right. I'll write that down.
I'll give you a leaflet too. Any dose change will be decided by the clinic, so please don't change your tablets yourself. Could you tell me what you've decided, so I know I've been clear?
A smaller smoothie, the same three mornings every week, tell the nurse today, and about the cod liver oil. No cranberry or grapefruit. Lose weight slowly. And 999 for a stroke or bad bleeding.
That's perfect. The nurse will arrange your next INR check. Is there anything else on your mind?
Only that I was dreading this. I thought I'd get a telling off.
Not at all. Telling us what's changed is exactly what keeps you safe. Thank you for being so honest.
Thank you. I'll tell my daughter she didn't get me into trouble.

coverage.how: Normalises dietary change and asks openly about recent changes.
Explains warfarin slows clotting to prevent stroke and the INR measures clotting time.
Explains vitamin K counteracts warfarin and lists leafy green sources.
Thanks her without blame, absolves the daughter and links the smoothies to the low INR.
Says greens need not be avoided; steady intake is what matters.
Offers choices, supports her chosen pattern and explains the clinic must know.
Mentions cranberry and grapefruit juice, alcohol limits, herbal remedies and fish oils.
Advises gradual weight loss and avoiding crash diets that destabilise the INR.
Gives stroke and clot signs with 999, and bleeding signs with same-day or emergency care.
States the clinic decides dose changes, checks understanding and confirms the INR check.

concern.how: She confesses the daily smoothies and fears blame for herself and her daughter; the dietitian thanks her, removes the blame and frames the news as useful.

safety.point: Stroke or clot signs mean 999; a painful swollen leg needs same-day advice.
Bleeding signs need same-day advice; severe headache, coughing or vomiting blood or head injury needs 999 or A&E.
Do not change warfarin doses; the clinic decides.

scripts.notes: The advice on cranberry and grapefruit juice, alcohol and herbal remedies follows NHS warfarin patient information. Cod liver oil is invented and the script only asks her to tell the nurse.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the oncology dietitians. The nurse said eating's been hard since the chemotherapy started. Could you tell me how things have changed, and what you manage on a typical day now?
Everything tastes like I've been sucking coins. Breakfast is a bit of porridge made with water. I skip lunch. Tea's a chicken salad, if I'm not feeling sick.

That sounds really tough. You've lost 5 kilos since starting. Keeping your weight steady matters, because it helps you cope with side effects, keep your strength and recover between cycles, and can help you stay on schedule.
I hadn't thought of it like that.

Let's start with the metallic taste. Try plastic cutlery instead of metal, and cold or room-temperature foods, which have less taste. Strong flavours like lemon, herbs or a marinade can cover the metal taste, as long as your mouth isn't sore. Chicken, fish, eggs or beans often taste better than red meat.
Plastic forks. I'd never have thought of that.
It helps lots of people. On the days you feel sick, are you taking the anti-sickness tablets you were given?
Only when I'm really bad. I don't like taking more pills.

That's understandable, but they work best taken as prescribed, rather than waiting until you're really sick. If they're not helping, the team can change them. Small, frequent snacks help too, as do dry foods like crackers, cold foods, ginger biscuits, and keeping away from cooking smells.
And my mouth is like sandpaper half the time.

Sip water through the day, try sugar-free gum, and choose moist foods with sauces or gravy. Brush gently with a soft toothbrush after meals, and use the mouthwash the team recommends. If your mouth becomes sore or ulcerated, tell the team.
Okay.
You mentioned porridge with water. Have you cut out any foods on purpose?
Yes. I read online that sugar feeds cancer. So no sugar, no bread, no potatoes, hardly any pasta. I'm not going to feed the thing.

I can really see why that would worry you; you want to fight it in every way you can. Can I tell you what we know? All the cells in your body, healthy ones too, use glucose for energy, and your body keeps your blood sugar steady whatever you eat. Cutting out sugar and starchy foods doesn't starve the cancer.
So the article was wrong?

There's no good evidence that eating sugar or starchy foods makes cancer grow. What we do know is that losing weight and muscle during treatment can leave you weaker and less able to cope. So right now, energy is what your body needs most. Does that make sense?
It does. I've felt so weak. It's a relief, honestly.

Then let's add energy and protein back in. Porridge made with full-fat milk and a spoonful of honey, toast with peanut butter, yoghurts, cheese and crackers, rice pudding and milky drinks. If you're still struggling, I can recommend nourishing supplement drinks to have between meals.
I could manage a milkshake more easily than a meal some days.

Then that's a good option at home. While your immunity is lower, food safety matters too: wash your hands, cook meat and eggs thoroughly, stick to use-by dates, and avoid unpasteurised milk and cheese.
That's common sense.

It is. Now, this is important. Ring the chemotherapy helpline straight away, day or night, if you have a temperature, feel shivery or suddenly unwell, can't keep fluids down, have diarrhoea several times a day, or can't eat or drink because of mouth sores. Don't wait until your next appointment.
The number's on my card, isn't it?

Yes, the helpline number on your alert card. So, the plan: plastic cutlery and sharp flavours, anti-sickness tablets as prescribed, mouth care, and bringing sugar and starchy foods back, with snacks between meals. Could you tell me what you'll do?

Plastic forks, lemon, cold food. Take the sickness pills properly. Gum and water for my mouth. Bread and potatoes again, full-fat milk in my porridge. Ring the helpline if I've got a temperature or can't keep fluids down.
Spot on. I'll see you here at your next cycle, and we'll weigh you to see how it's going. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No. Thanks. I feel like I'm doing something useful now.
You absolutely are. Eating well is part of your treatment.

coverage.how: Asks how eating has changed and what he manages on a typical day.
Explains steady weight helps him cope, keep strength, recover and stay on schedule.
Suggests plastic cutlery, cooler foods, sharp flavours and alternatives to red meat.
Asks about anti-sickness tablets, encourages taking them as prescribed and gives eating tips.
Suggests sips, sugar-free gum, moist foods, gentle brushing and the team's mouthwash.
Asks about deliberate restrictions and acknowledges his reason.
Explains all cells use glucose, diet does not starve the cancer, and weight loss is the real harm.
Lists energy and protein snacks and drinks, and offers supplement drinks between meals.
Gives hand washing, thorough cooking, use-by dates and avoiding unpasteurised products.
Lists temperature, shivers, feeling unwell, vomiting, frequent diarrhoea and mouth sores as helpline triggers.
Summarises the plan, checks understanding by teach-back and arranges weighing at the next cycle.

concern.how: He reveals he has cut out sugar and starch believing sugar feeds cancer; the dietitian validates the motive, explains the evidence and links his weakness to under-eating.

safety.point: Temperature, shivers, feeling suddenly unwell, not keeping fluids down, frequent diarrhoea or mouth sores means ringing the chemotherapy helpline at once.
Anti-sickness medicine taken as prescribed; the team can change it if it is not working.
A sore or ulcerated mouth should be reported to the team.

scripts.notes: The card gives no specific chemotherapy regimen; the advice is general UK oncology dietetic advice. Weighing at the next cycle is invented. The helpline is assumed to be on a chemotherapy alert card, as is standard in UK units.

turns.text: Hello, come in and have a seat. I'm one of the GPs. Before I go through your blood tests, could you tell me what you understood they were for, and whether anything has been worrying you?
You said you were checking for anaemia and something to do with my gut. I've been worried, honestly. I looked things up and frightened myself.
That's very understandable. What were you most worried they might show?
Something serious. Cancer, I suppose. I've felt so drained for months.

Thank you for telling me. The results don't point to cancer. There are two findings. First, your iron level is low and you're mildly anaemic, meaning fewer red blood cells carrying oxygen. That explains much of the tiredness.
Okay. And the second?

The second test looks for antibodies, proteins made by the immune system, and yours is positive for coeliac disease. Here the immune system reacts to gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye, and inflames the lining of the small bowel. That lining absorbs food, including iron, which is why the two results fit together.
Coeliac. I've heard of it. Is it serious?
It's common, around one person in every hundred, and it's very manageable. Once gluten is removed from the diet, the bowel usually heals and most people feel much better. How does that sound so far?
Better than I feared. So is it definite?

Not quite. It's usually confirmed by a camera test called an endoscopy: a thin flexible tube is passed through the mouth into the upper bowel, and tiny samples are taken to look at under a microscope. I'll refer you to the specialist gut team. Have you changed what you eat since the tests?
Actually, yes. I stopped eating bread a few days ago, after reading online.

That's a natural thing to do, and a few days shouldn't matter. But please go back to eating gluten every day, in more than one meal, until the camera test. If gluten is cut out early, the bowel starts healing and the test can look normal even though you have the condition.
So I've got to keep eating the thing that's making me ill?
For now, yes, and I know that's frustrating. A clear answer matters, because the treatment is lifelong. If symptoms become hard to bear, let me know.
Lifelong. What does the treatment involve?

It's a gluten-free diet, avoiding wheat, barley and rye, including hidden sources in sauces and processed foods. Once it's confirmed, I'll refer you to a dietitian, a food specialist, to help you plan meals. A national coeliac charity also has good guides.
And the iron?

I'll start iron tablets today. They can upset the stomach or cause constipation, and they turn stools dark, which is harmless. We'll recheck your blood in a few weeks to make sure the level is rising.
Okay. Actually, there's something else. My daughter's eight and she's always saying her tummy hurts. Have I given this to her?
I can hear that's really worrying you. Coeliac disease does run in families, so it's right to think of her. But it isn't anything you did, and tummy aches in children have lots of common causes.
But could she have it?

It's possible, and it's easy to check. Close relatives, like children, parents, brothers and sisters, can be offered a simple blood test. Book her an appointment and mention your diagnosis and her tummy aches. Please don't change her diet before she's tested.
That's a relief, that there's a test. I'll book her in.

Good. While you wait, please contact us sooner if you lose weight without trying, notice blood in your stools, have worsening tummy pain, or feel breathless or dizzy. For severe pain or heavy bleeding, go to A&E or call 999.
Right. Weight loss, blood, pain getting worse, breathless or dizzy.
Exactly. To make sure I've explained things well, could you tell me in your own words what happens next?
I keep eating gluten, take the iron tablets, wait for the camera test, see a dietitian if it's confirmed, and get my daughter tested.
That's spot on. The hospital will write to you with an appointment. If you haven't heard within a few weeks, ring the surgery and we'll chase it. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No, I think that's everything. Thank you for explaining it so clearly.

coverage.how: Asks what she understood the tests were for and what she feared before giving results.
Explains the low iron and the positive antibody test in plain words and links them.
Explains coeliac disease as an immune reaction to gluten inflaming the bowel lining; common and manageable.
Explains endoscopy with biopsies and refers to the specialist gut team.
Asks whether she has changed her diet and responds without criticism.
Tells her to keep eating gluten daily until the test and explains a falsely normal result.
Explains the lifelong gluten-free diet, dietitian referral and a charity for support.
Starts iron tablets, explains side effects including harmless dark stools and a repeat blood test.
Responds to her guilt about her daughter and explains blood testing for close relatives.
Gives red flags: weight loss, blood in stools, worsening pain, breathlessness or dizziness.
Asks her to summarise the plan and explains the hospital letter and how to chase it.

concern.how: She raises her daughter's tummy aches and her guilt; the doctor acknowledges the worry, says it is not her fault, and gives a clear route to testing.

safety.point: Keep eating gluten until the camera test so the result is not falsely normal.
Iron tablets turn stools dark, which is harmless.
Weight loss, blood in stools, worsening pain, breathlessness or dizziness need earlier contact; severe pain or heavy bleeding needs A&E or 999.

scripts.notes: The card gives no antibody level; the script calls the test simply positive. The advice to eat gluten in more than one meal a day before biopsy follows UK guidance. The child's test would be arranged through her own GP appointment; the script does not say who orders it.

turns.text: Hello, come on in. I'm one of the GPs. My colleague diagnosed gout in your big toe a few days ago. How is it now?
Much better, thanks. Last week I couldn't bear the bedsheet on it. Now I can get a shoe on, just about.
That's good to hear. How are you getting on with the colchicine tablets? Any side effects, like an upset stomach or diarrhoea?
Bit of a loose stomach the first day, nothing since.

Good. If diarrhoea comes back or you start vomiting, stop the tablets and let us know. For the remaining pain, rest the foot and raise it when you sit; a cool pack wrapped in a towel helps. Finish the colchicine as prescribed. Can I explain what gout is?
Please. I thought it was an old man's thing from too much port.

Lots of people think that. Your blood contains a waste product called uric acid. When the level is too high, it can form tiny sharp crystals in a joint, often the big toe, and the body reacts with sudden inflammation. That's why it went red, hot and painful.
Right. So how do I stop it happening again? I can't go through that every month.
That's what I'd like to help with. Can I ask about a few everyday things, with no wrong answers? What does a typical day's eating and drinking look like, including water?
I run a pub, so I'm on my feet all day. I grab a burger or a pie. Hardly any water. Most evenings I'll have four or five pints with the regulars.

Thanks for being honest; that helps. Beer and spirits raise uric acid most, along with sugary fizzy drinks. Large portions of red meat, offal like liver, and shellfish add to it too. Water helps your kidneys clear uric acid, so drink more through the day.
Here we go. I read online I've got to give up drinking completely. I can't do that. It's my business, and it's my social life.

I can see why that would feel impossible, and I'm not going to ask you to stop altogether. It's about cutting down. The general guidance is no more than 14 units a week, spread over several days, with some drink-free days. At the moment you're well above that.
Fourteen units. That's about two nights out for me.
It's a big change, so you don't need to get there overnight. What would feel realistic as a first step?
Maybe a couple of nights off a week. And on the other nights, two pints instead of five, then water.

That's a good start, and it's your plan, so it's more likely to stick. Weight matters too. Losing weight gradually, not with crash diets, which can trigger attacks, and staying active both lower uric acid and help your blood pressure. Would you like support from our health coach?
Maybe. I'll think about it. Do I need any tests?

Yes. Once the attack has fully settled, in a few weeks, I'd like a blood test for your uric acid level, plus kidney function, blood sugar and cholesterol, because gout often goes with heart and kidney risks.
And if it comes back anyway?

There's a daily tablet that gradually lowers uric acid and prevents most attacks. It can be considered even after one attack, and is usually recommended if attacks keep returning. We'll discuss it when your results are back.
Okay. Anything I should watch out for in the meantime?

Yes. If the joint becomes very hot, swollen and much more painful again, other joints are affected, or you get a fever or feel shivery and unwell, get seen the same day. That could be a joint infection, which needs urgent treatment. Out of hours, call 111.
Infection. I wouldn't have guessed that.
It's uncommon, but worth knowing. Could you tell me the main things you'll do?
Rest the foot, finish the tablets, more water, fewer pints and nights off, fewer burgers, and a blood test.
Spot on. And if the joint's hot and swollen and you've got a fever?
Get seen that day, or ring 111.
Perfect. Let's book the blood test in a few weeks and a review with me afterwards to go through the results. Is that all right?
Yes. Thanks, doc.
You're welcome. You've made a really sensible plan.

coverage.how: Asks how the toe is, how the colchicine is going and about diarrhoea.
Explains uric acid crystals forming in a joint and causing sudden inflammation.
Advises rest, raising the foot, a cool pack and finishing the colchicine.
Asks about a typical day's food, drink and water with no wrong answers.
Names beer, spirits, sugary drinks, red meat, offal and shellfish as raising uric acid.
Reassures him he need not stop altogether, gives the 14-unit guidance and lets him set a first step.
Explains gradual weight loss and activity, warns about crash diets and offers a health coach.
Plans uric acid, kidney, sugar and cholesterol tests once the attack has settled.
Explains a daily uric-acid-lowering tablet can be considered, especially with repeat attacks.
Gives same-day warning signs of a joint infection and the 111 route.
Checks understanding with a summary and books the blood test and review.

concern.how: He says he cannot give up drinking; the doctor rules out an all-or-nothing rule, gives the weekly guidance and lets him choose a realistic first step.

safety.point: Stop colchicine and report if diarrhoea returns or he vomits.
Crash diets can trigger attacks; weight loss should be gradual.
A very hot, swollen joint, other joints affected or fever needs same-day review for possible joint infection.

scripts.notes: The health coach is offered as a typical practice resource. The timing of the uric acid test, a few weeks after the attack settles, follows UK guidance. His weekly intake is not stated on the card; the script only says it is well above the guidance, which follows from four or five pints most evenings.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the doctors in the children's area, and I've just examined your son. Before anything else, I'm sorry you've had to wait four hours. That's far too long with a little boy who's hurt himself.
Four hours! He's exhausted, I'm exhausted, and people who came in after us went first. Nobody told us anything.

You're right to be angry, and not being kept informed makes it worse. Tonight several very sick children arrived by ambulance. Everyone is assessed on arrival and the most urgent are seen first, which is why some went ahead. That doesn't make your wait acceptable.
Fine. But it's not just the wait.
Please tell me. I'd like to hear what else has upset you.
That nurse. Asking how it happened, who was in the room, had he been hurt before. Like I'd hit him. I'm his mum. I love him.
That sounds really distressing.
I had social workers in my life when I was a kid. I know how it goes. One note on a computer and they're knocking on your door, taking him off me.

Thank you for telling me that. I can understand why those questions felt so frightening. Can I explain why they're asked? We ask them about every child who comes in with any injury, whoever the parent is. It's a routine way of keeping all children safe, not a judgement about you.
Every child?

Every single one. His injury fits exactly what you described, and I have no concerns at all about how you care for him. To be honest about records, tonight is written in his notes, and his GP and health visitor get a summary, as for every young child seen here. It will say it was an accidental fall and that you brought him in promptly.
So nobody's going to come round?
No. There's no reason for anyone to. You did exactly the right thing bringing him in.
Okay. Okay. Sorry for shouting.

Please don't apologise; it's been a long, worrying evening. Let me tell you about his examination. He's alert and talking normally, his pupils react well, he walks steadily, and there's just a small bruise on his forehead. He wasn't knocked out and he hasn't been sick.
So why no scan? I thought you'd want to check his brain.

I understand. Scans use radiation, so for children we only scan when there are warning signs, like being knocked out, repeated vomiting, a fit or something abnormal on examination. He has none, so the chance of anything serious is very low.
Right. What do I do when we get home?

Over the next few days he might have a mild headache, feel tired or be grumpier than usual. That settles by itself. Give children's paracetamol or ibuprofen as the packet directs, keep things quiet, avoid rough play, and keep him home from nursery until he's himself.
Can he go to sleep? I've heard you're meant to keep them awake.

He can sleep normally; that's an old myth. But keep a responsible adult with him for the first day and night, and check on him while he sleeps, to make sure he's breathing normally and stirs when you disturb him.
And what would mean bringing him back?

Come straight back or call 999 if he's hard to wake or unusually drowsy, vomits more than once, has a fit, has a worsening headache, has trouble walking, talking or seeing, has clear fluid from his nose or ears, or just isn't acting like himself.
That's a lot to remember.
It is, so I'll give you a leaflet listing all of it. Could you tell me the main signs you'd come back for?
If he's really sleepy or I can't wake him, keeps being sick, has a fit, his headache gets worse, or he's not himself.

That's exactly right. If you'd like to give feedback about the wait or the questions, the Patient Advice and Liaison Service, PALS, can take it or help you make a complaint. Their details are on the leaflet, and I'll pass your comments to the nurse in charge tonight.
I might. I just don't want another family feeling like I did.
That's worth hearing. Is there anything else you'd like to ask before you take him home?
No. Thank you. You've actually listened.
You're welcome. I hope he sleeps well, and you too.

coverage.how: Introduces himself or herself, names the four-hour wait and apologises without excuses.
Explains the ambulance arrivals and triage priority while saying the wait is still not acceptable.
Invites her to say what else upset her and listens without interrupting.
Explains that every injured child is asked how the injury happened, as routine child safety.
Says honestly what the record and the GP and health visitor summary say, and that there are no concerns.
Gives the normal examination findings and explains why no scan is needed.
Explains that mild headache, tiredness and irritability may occur and settle.
Advises pain relief, quiet rest, normal sleep and a responsible adult for the first day and night.
Lists the warning signs for returning or calling 999.
Explains PALS for feedback or a complaint and passes her comments on.
Asks her to repeat the warning signs and invites further questions.

concern.how: Her fear of being judged surfaces after the apology; the doctor explains the routine questions, states there are no concerns and is honest about what the record says.

safety.point: A responsible adult stays with him for the first day and night and checks him while he sleeps.
Drowsiness, repeated vomiting, a fit, worsening headache, problems walking, talking or seeing, clear fluid from nose or ears, or unusual behaviour need immediate return or 999.
Paracetamol or ibuprofen only as the packet directs.

scripts.notes: The card says the examination is normal; the script specifies no loss of consciousness and no vomiting, consistent with that. The summary to the GP and health visitor reflects routine practice for young children seen in emergency departments; local arrangements vary.

turns.text: Hello, nice to see you again. Last time we agreed your symptoms are due to the menopause, and you wanted to talk about treatment. Before we do, how are the symptoms affecting you at the moment?
Badly. I wake up soaked two or three times a night, I get flushes in meetings and lose my train of thought, and I'm snappy with my husband.
That sounds exhausting, on top of a busy job. If we could improve one thing first, what would it be?
Sleep. If I could sleep, I'd cope with the rest.
That makes sense. What do you already know, or what have you heard, about hormone replacement therapy, HRT?
To be honest, I'm scared of it. My best friend was diagnosed with breast cancer this spring. She's convinced her HRT caused it.
I'm so sorry about your friend. That's frightening, and it's natural it's made you wary. Can I explain how HRT works, then talk honestly about the cancer risk?
Please. I want the truth.

HRT replaces oestrogen, the hormone that falls at the menopause. Because you still have your womb, you'd also need a second hormone, a progestogen. Oestrogen on its own can thicken the womb lining, and the progestogen protects it.
So it's two hormones?

Usually, yes. Oestrogen can be a skin patch, a gel you rub on, or tablets. The progestogen can be a tablet, or a hormonal coil placed in the womb, which lasts for several years and many women find convenient.
And would it actually help?
For most women it works well. Flushes and night sweats usually improve within weeks, and sleep and mood often follow. It also helps keep bones strong, lowering the chance of fractures later.
But the cancer.

Let's talk about it. HRT with both hormones does slightly increase the chance of breast cancer. The extra risk is small, and it's linked to how long it's taken, so it's lower with shorter use. Being overweight or drinking alcohol regularly can raise the risk by a similar or larger amount. We'd review whether you still need it every year.
So my friend might be right?

Her HRT may have played a small part, but many women develop breast cancer without ever taking it, so nobody can say what caused hers. Whatever you decide, keep checking your breasts and go to your routine breast screening.
What about clots? My mum always said hormones give you clots.

Good question. Oestrogen tablets slightly raise the risk of a clot in the leg or lung. Patches and gel go through the skin and don't increase that risk in the same way, so many women choose them. You've no history of clots and you don't smoke, which also helps.
And if I don't want hormones at all?

That's absolutely fine. A talking therapy called cognitive behavioural therapy can help with flushes, sleep and mood. There are also some non-hormonal medicines that reduce flushes, although they're usually less effective than HRT. Cutting down caffeine and alcohol, and wearing layers, can help too.
If I did try HRT, what would it be like at first?

Some women get breast tenderness, bloating or headaches in the first few months, and irregular spotting is common early on. These usually settle. But bleeding that's heavy, carries on beyond the first few months, or starts again after it has settled should be checked, so let us know.
That's a lot to think about.
It is, and it's your decision. There's no rush. I can give you a leaflet and a decision guide to read with your husband, and we could talk again next week.
Actually, I think I'd like to try a patch. The sleep is ruining everything.

That's a reasonable choice. We'd start an oestrogen patch with a progestogen, and I'll go through the progestogen options with you now. Then I'd like to see you about three months after starting, to check how it's working and any side effects. Does that sound okay?
Yes. Three months.
Before you go, could you tell me what you'll look out for once you start?
Sore breasts or spotting early on are normal, but heavy bleeding or bleeding that carries on means I ring you. And I keep going to breast screening.
Exactly right. And if you change your mind at any point, just come back and we'll talk again.

coverage.how: Asks how symptoms affect sleep, work and home, and what she most wants to improve.
Asks what she already knows or has heard about HRT.
Explains oestrogen replacement and why a progestogen protects the womb lining.
Describes patch, gel and tablets, and the hormonal coil for the progestogen.
Explains relief of flushes, sleep and mood and protection of bone strength.
Gives an honest account of a small, duration-related breast cancer risk with context.
Explains that transdermal oestrogen avoids the clot risk of tablets.
Mentions cognitive behavioural therapy, non-hormonal medicines and lifestyle measures.
Explains early side effects and which bleeding must be reported.
Leaves the decision to her, offers a decision guide and time, and accepts her choice.
Agrees a review about three months after starting.

concern.how: She raises her friend's cancer early; the doctor acknowledges it, then answers with honest, proportionate risk information and breast awareness advice.

safety.point: Keep checking breasts and attend routine breast screening.
Oestrogen tablets slightly raise clot risk; patches and gel do not in the same way.
Heavy, persistent or returning bleeding on HRT must be reported.

scripts.notes: No figures for breast cancer risk are given, as the card has none; the comparison with weight and alcohol follows UK patient decision aids. The script leaves the choice of progestogen to a later part of the consultation.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the GPs, and I do the joint injections here. Could you confirm your full name and date of birth for me, please?
Margaret Ellis, born on the fourth of June.
Thank you. Do you have any allergies, to medicines, plasters or skin cleaners?
None that I know of.
Good. What's your understanding of why your physiotherapist suggested an injection, and what are you hoping it will do?
The tendons in my shoulder are inflamed. The exercises have helped a bit, but it still wakes me at night. I'm hoping it'll calm the pain so I can keep going.

That's exactly the idea. The injection contains a steroid, which reduces inflammation, usually mixed with a local anaesthetic to numb the area. I'd clean the skin, then inject into the space at the top of your shoulder where the tendons are irritated. It takes a minute or so and stings briefly.
How long would it work?

The anaesthetic may ease the pain within minutes but wears off after a few hours. The steroid usually works within a few days, and relief often lasts several weeks, sometimes months. Keep up your exercises: the injection eases the pain while the exercises strengthen the shoulder.
Are there side effects?

Some. A common one is a flare of pain for a day or two afterwards. Some people's face goes red and warm for a day. Less commonly, the skin where I inject becomes thinner or paler. And because you have diabetes, the steroid can raise your blood sugar for a few days.
I don't usually check my sugar. I'm only on tablets.

That's fine. If you have a meter, check a bit more often for a few days. If not, watch for feeling very thirsty, passing urine much more often, or feeling unusually tired, and ring us if that happens. For most people it settles without any change to their tablets.
What else?

There's one rare but serious risk, an infection in the shoulder. It affects very few people, but you should know the signs: the shoulder becoming increasingly hot, red, swollen and more painful after the first couple of days, or a fever and feeling unwell. If that happens, contact us the same day or call 111.
That's the bit that frightens me.
Can I ask what worries you most about it?
My husband had a stroke. I'm the one who gets him washed and dressed. If my arm were out of action, I don't know what we'd do.

That's a huge responsibility, and it's completely sensible to think about it. The infection risk is very low. A flare is more likely, and it lasts a day or two. Is there anyone who could help with his care for a couple of days afterwards?
My son lives nearby. He could come round in the mornings.
That sounds a good plan; perhaps book the injection for a day he's free. And if caring is hard generally, we can arrange a carer's assessment, which looks at extra support for you both.
I didn't know about that. And what if I decide not to have it?

That's entirely your choice. You could continue the physiotherapy for longer, use pain relief such as paracetamol, or simply wait, because this kind of shoulder pain often improves with time. The injection is an option, not a requirement.
And afterwards, can I use the arm?

Yes, gently. Avoid heavy lifting or strenuous use for a day or two, so please don't help your husband move on your own. Then gradually restart your exercises. Paracetamol and a cold pack can help with any flare.
Right. My son in the mornings, no lifting, watch my sugar.
Exactly. So, to recap: a possible flare, flushing, skin changes, a rise in blood sugar, and rarely infection. Do you have any other questions?
No, I think I understand. I'd like to go ahead.
Thank you. So I can be sure, could you tell me in your own words the warning signs of infection?
If it's getting hotter, redder, more swollen or more painful after a couple of days, or I get a temperature, I ring you that day.
That's right. So you're happy for me to go ahead with the injection into your right shoulder today?
Yes, I'm happy.
Thank you. I'll record your consent in your notes, and then we'll get you comfortable.

coverage.how: Confirms identity and allergies, then asks her understanding and hopes.
Explains steroid with local anaesthetic and how the injection is given.
Explains the onset and likely duration of relief and the role of exercises.
Explains flare, facial flushing and skin thinning or paleness.
Explains a temporary rise in blood sugar and how to watch for it with or without a meter.
Explains the rare infection risk with its signs and checks she can repeat them.
Describes more physiotherapy, paracetamol and waiting as alternatives.
Explores her caring role and plans help from her son and a carer's assessment.
Advises gentle use, no heavy lifting for a day or two, and a gradual return to exercises.
Recaps the risks, answers questions, confirms agreement and records verbal consent.

concern.how: Her fear about infection opens into her caring role; the doctor puts the risks in proportion and helps her arrange cover and support.

safety.point: Allergies are checked before the procedure.
Thirst, passing more urine or unusual tiredness after the steroid should prompt a call.
A hot, red, swollen, increasingly painful shoulder or fever needs same-day contact or 111.
No heavy lifting, including moving her husband alone, for a day or two.

scripts.notes: The patient's name and birthday are invented for the identity check. The card says the problem is irritated tendons; the script places the injection in the space at the top of the shoulder, the usual site for subacromial injection.

turns.text: Good morning. I'm one of the doctors on the ward team. We think you're ready to go home today. How are you feeling this morning, and do you feel ready?
Better than when I came in, that's for sure. Still coughing, and I'm wiped out just walking to the bathroom.

That's very common at this stage. You came in with pneumonia, an infection in your right lung. Your temperature has settled, your breathing is much better, and your blood tests are improving, so the infection is responding. You can finish the treatment safely at home.
So more tablets?

Yes, antibiotic tablets for a few more days. Take them at the times on the label until they're all gone, even if you feel better, so the infection doesn't come back. They can upset your stomach or loosen your stools. If you get a rash, stop them and get advice that day. If your face or lips swell or you can't breathe, call 999.
Right. And then I'll be back to normal?

It takes longer than people expect. The tiredness and cough can last several weeks, and some people take a few months to feel completely themselves. That's normal and doesn't mean the infection's come back.
I'd better take it easy, then.

For a while, yes. Rest when you need to, drink plenty of fluids, and try to eat regular meals, even small ones. Build up gradually: walking round the house at first, then outside, a little further each day.
Fair enough.
Can I ask about smoking? Your notes say you smoke.
Twenty a day, for forty years. Too late now, isn't it?

It's never too late. Stopping helps your lungs recover, lowers the chance of another chest infection, and protects your heart. The stop smoking service offers nicotine replacement or medicines with weekly support, which makes quitting far more likely. Shall I refer you?
Go on, then. I've been meaning to.

Great. Also, because you smoke and because of your age, we usually arrange a follow-up chest x-ray in about six weeks, to make sure the shadow from the infection has cleared and that nothing else is behind it. Your GP will organise it.
Nothing else behind it. You mean cancer?
It's a sensible check, and most of the time the x-ray is clear. I'm not expecting a problem; it's just the careful thing to do. How are things at home? Is anyone there with you?
Nobody. My wife died last year. It's just me now.
I'm very sorry. That must be hard, especially going home after being so unwell.
It's the nights. What if I get bad again in the small hours and can't reach the phone? Nobody would know.
Thank you for telling me; that's a really understandable fear. Is there anyone, family, a neighbour or a friend, who could check on you for the first few days?
My daughter's up north. I haven't wanted to worry her. There's a neighbour, Pat, who's kind.

It might help to tell your daughter, and ask Pat to look in daily for a while. Keep your phone by the bed. I'll also ask our discharge team about a personal alarm, which calls for help at the press of a button, and some short-term help at home.
An alarm would make me feel a lot better.

I'll arrange that before you leave. And if you're feeling low or lonely, your GP can help with that too. They can also offer the yearly flu jab and a one-off pneumonia vaccine, which help protect you.
I've never bothered before. I will now.

Now the important part. Call 999 if you're struggling to breathe, have chest pain, cough up blood, or become confused or very drowsy. If the fever comes back, your cough or phlegm gets worse, or you're not improving, contact your GP or 111 the same day.
Breathing, chest pain, blood or confusion, that's 999.
Exactly. Could you tell me the rest of the plan in your own words?
Finish the antibiotics, rest and eat, build up slowly, the stop smoking people, the x-ray in six weeks, the jabs, tell my daughter, and ask Pat to look in.
Perfect. A discharge letter goes to your GP today with all of this, including the x-ray, stop smoking referral and alarm. Any other questions?
No. Thanks, doctor. I feel a bit less on my own.

coverage.how: Asks how he feels and whether he feels ready to go home.
Explains pneumonia is improving and that treatment can finish at home.
Explains taking and completing the antibiotics, common side effects and allergy signs.
Explains that tiredness and cough can last weeks and recovery can take months.
Advises rest, fluids, regular meals and gradually building up activity.
Asks about smoking, explains the benefits of stopping and offers a referral.
Explains the follow-up chest x-ray in about six weeks and addresses his worry about it.
Asks about home, acknowledges his bereavement and plans checks, a phone by the bed and an alarm.
Mentions the yearly flu jab and the one-off pneumonia vaccine from his GP.
Lists 999 symptoms and same-day GP or 111 symptoms.
Asks him to summarise the plan and explains the discharge letter to his GP.

concern.how: An open question about home reveals he lives alone and fears the nights; the doctor acknowledges his loss and arranges contacts, an alarm and GP support for low mood.

safety.point: Stop the antibiotic for a rash; call 999 for facial or lip swelling or difficulty breathing.
Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, confusion or drowsiness need 999; returning fever or worsening cough need same-day GP or 111.
Follow-up chest x-ray in about six weeks to confirm the shadow has cleared.

scripts.notes: The antibiotic is not named. The personal alarm and short-term home help depend on local services and are offered to be explored, not promised.

turns.text: Hello, please come in. I'm one of the GPs. Your blood test results are back. Before I go through them, could you tell me why you understood the tests were done, and how you've been feeling generally?
It was my yearly diabetes check, I think. Then they asked me back for another one. I feel fine, apart from my knees.

That's right. The second test was to check the first result. Both tests, three months apart, show your kidneys aren't working as well as we'd expect. Your kidney function score, called eGFR, is 48. That's what we call chronic kidney disease, stage three. Chronic just means long-lasting.
Kidney disease. Oh dear.

I can see that's a shock. Can I explain what it means in practice? It's very common, especially in people over seventy with high blood pressure or diabetes. At this stage it usually causes no symptoms, and it tends to change slowly, often staying stable for many years. Your urine test was reassuring too, with no significant protein leaking through.
But it's going to get worse, isn't it?
Not necessarily. What makes you feel it will?
My brother had kidney trouble. He ended up on dialysis three times a week for years, and then he died. I watched all of it.
I'm so sorry. That must have been very hard to watch, and it's no wonder this result frightens you. Do you know what caused his kidney problems?
Not really. He was diabetic as well, and he never looked after himself.

I can't predict anyone's future exactly, but I can tell you honestly that most people with kidney function at your level never need dialysis. Your kidneys are still doing most of their work. The aim now is to protect them so they stay that way.
That's not what I expected. How do we protect them?

Mainly by keeping your blood pressure and diabetes well controlled, because both strain the kidneys over time. Your ramipril helps here by keeping your blood pressure down. This looks after your heart as well, which matters because kidney disease raises heart risk.
I've always taken my tablets.
That's really good. There's one thing I'd like to change. You mentioned your knees. Do you take ibuprofen for them?
Most days. I buy it at the supermarket.

Thank you for telling me. Ibuprofen and similar anti-inflammatory painkillers can reduce blood flow to the kidneys and harm them, especially alongside ramipril. I'd recommend stopping the tablets. Paracetamol is safer, and an anti-inflammatory gel rubbed onto the knee is fine, because very little reaches the blood. Gentle regular exercise and physiotherapy can help too.
Right. I had no idea.
Most people don't. That's why it's worth asking the pharmacist before buying any new medicines or remedies, and telling them you have kidney disease.
I will.

One more important thing. If you become unwell with vomiting, diarrhoea or a fever and can't keep fluids down, stop the ramipril and metformin for the time being. Restart them once you've been eating and drinking normally for a day or two. If you're no better within a day or two, contact us or call 111.
Stop them when I'm ill. That seems backwards.
It does sound odd, but when you're dehydrated those tablets can put extra strain on the kidneys or upset the body's balance. I'll give you a card with these sick day rules written down.
And how will you know if it's getting worse?
We'll check your blood and urine at least once a year, and more often if anything changes, so we'd spot any decline early and act on it. Could you tell me what you'll do differently from today?
No more ibuprofen tablets, paracetamol or the gel instead, ask the chemist before buying anything, keep taking my tablets, and stop those two if I'm being sick and can't drink.
That's exactly right. And when would you restart them?
When I've been eating and drinking properly again for a day or two.
Perfect. I'd like to see you in a few weeks to check your blood pressure and how the knees are on paracetamol. Does that suit you?
Yes. I feel much better than when you first said kidney disease.
I'm glad. Please come back sooner if you have any questions or worries at all.

coverage.how: Asks why she thought the tests were done and how she feels.
Gives the eGFR of 48 and names chronic kidney disease, stage three, explaining chronic.
Explains it is common, usually symptom-free and slow to change, with a reassuring urine test.
Explores her fear of dialysis and explains honestly that most people at this level never need it.
Explains controlling blood pressure and diabetes to protect kidneys and heart, including ramipril.
Asks about ibuprofen, explains the harm and offers paracetamol, topical gel and exercise.
Explains the sick day rules for ramipril and metformin and gives a card.
Advises asking a pharmacist before buying new medicines.
Explains blood and urine monitoring at least once a year.
Checks she can repeat the key changes and the restart rule, and agrees a review.

concern.how: She expects decline; an open question draws out her brother's dialysis, which is acknowledged before honest reassurance about her own outlook.

safety.point: Stop regular ibuprofen; use paracetamol or topical gel instead.
Ask a pharmacist before buying new medicines and mention kidney disease.
Sick day rules: pause ramipril and metformin when unable to keep fluids down; seek help if no better within a day or two.

scripts.notes: The card gives one eGFR value for two tests; the script treats both as 48. Stage three corresponds to stage 3a at this value. Topical NSAID gel is treated as acceptable for knee arthritis in this patient, in line with usual UK practice; a clinician may prefer to confirm this.

turns.text: Thanks for waiting. I've finished examining your daughter. Her chest is clear, her ears and throat show signs of a cold, there's no rash, and she's alert and responding well. This looks like a viral infection, a cold with a fever, which her body will fight off by itself. Antibiotics don't work on viruses, so she won't need them.
Okay. That's good. She felt so hot last night.
Before I go on, what worried you most, and what were you hoping we'd do today?
I just wanted someone to check it wasn't something serious. Meningitis, or her chest. You hear stories.
Of course. I specifically looked for signs of those, and there aren't any. Fever is actually the body's normal way of fighting infection. It isn't dangerous in itself, even at 38.5.
So I shouldn't try to bring it down?

You don't need to chase the number. Keep her comfortable in light clothing, don't wrap her up, and don't sponge her with cold water, as that just upsets her. Offer drinks often, a little at a time is fine, whether that's milk or water.
And the medicine?

Paracetamol or ibuprofen are for when she's miserable or distressed, not just because she's warm. Follow the dose for her age on the packet. Give one of them, and if she's still distressed before the next dose is due, you can try the other. Don't give both at the same time.
Okay. One at a time.

Exactly. Make sure she's drinking enough. Signs she's getting dry are fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth, no tears when she cries, or being unusually sleepy. If you notice those, contact us or 111 the same day.
Got it.

Now the most important part. Call 999 straight away if she has a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it, has a fit, is floppy or very hard to wake, is struggling to breathe, with grunting or her ribs sucking in, or her lips look blue.
A glass on the rash. I've heard of that.
Good. Also, if the fever lasts five days or more, she seems to be getting worse, or you're just worried, get her checked again. Trust your instinct; you know her best.
The thing is, I won't be there tonight. I'm on nights at the warehouse. My mum's having her.
I see. How do you feel about that?
Mum's brilliant with her, but her English isn't great. She wouldn't know the glass thing, and I'm not sure she'd ring 999 and explain herself.
Thank you for raising that; it's a very sensible worry. What language does your mum speak best?
Polish.

I'll look for our fever advice in Polish and print it, and if we haven't got it, I'll write the key signs down very simply. 999 and 111 can get a phone interpreter, so she just needs to say Polish and give the address. Could you show her the glass test before you leave?
Yes, I can do that. And she can call me at work. They let me keep my phone.
That's a good plan. Can I suggest writing the address clearly on paper by the phone, so she can read it out? Is anyone nearby who speaks English and could help?
My sister lives two streets away. I'll ask her to be on standby.
Excellent. So your mum has the leaflet, can phone you or your sister, and knows to call 999 for the danger signs. Could you tell me those danger signs, so I'm sure I've explained them clearly?
A rash that doesn't go when you press the glass, a fit, floppy or I can't wake her, struggling to breathe, or blue lips.
That's right. And when would you get her seen again, if it's not an emergency?
If she stops drinking or has dry nappies, if the fever goes on five days, or if she's getting worse, or I'm worried.
Perfect. Most children with a cold like this are much brighter within a few days. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No. I feel much better about tonight. Thank you.

coverage.how: Explains the normal examination and a viral cold that needs no antibiotics.
Asks what worried him most and what he hoped for.
Explains fever as a normal response that is not dangerous in itself.
Advises light clothing, no cold sponging and regular small drinks.
Explains paracetamol or ibuprofen for distress, by the packet, one at a time.
Lists signs of dehydration and the same-day route.
Lists the 999 signs: non-blanching rash, fit, floppiness, breathing difficulty and blue lips.
Advises review for fever of five days or more, worsening or parental worry.
Explores his concern about his mother and plans translated advice, interpreters, the address and his sister.
Asks him to repeat the danger signs and the reasons for a routine review.

concern.how: He mentions his night shift; the doctor asks how he feels, hears the language worry and builds a practical plan around it.

safety.point: Dehydration signs need same-day contact with the practice or 111.
Non-blanching rash, fit, floppiness or hard to wake, breathing difficulty or blue lips need 999.
Fever of five days or more, worsening, or parental worry need a review.
Telephone interpreters are available through 999 and 111.

scripts.notes: The script adds signs of a cold in the ears and throat, a benign finding consistent with the card. The advice on alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen follows UK guidance for persistent distress.

turns.text: Hello, I'm one of the emergency doctors looking after you. The nurse tells me you'd like to leave now. I'm not here to stop you, but could you give me a few minutes to talk it through first?
A few minutes, fine. But I'm going. The pain's gone, the tests were normal. I feel fine.
I'm really glad the pain's gone. Can I ask what's making you want to leave right now, before the second test?
I've just got things to do. I can't be stuck in here all afternoon.
That's fair; waiting around is frustrating. Is there something in particular this afternoon that's pressing?
Look, my lad finishes school at three. There's nobody else to get him. His mum's working abroad. I haven't even told anyone I'm here.
Thank you for telling me. That's a really important reason, and I completely understand wanting to be there for him. How old is he?
Seven. He'll be stood at the gate wondering where I am.
Of course you're worried. Let's see if we can sort that out together. But first, can I explain why we'd like you to stay for the second test, so you can decide with all the facts?
Go on.

Chest pain can come from lots of things, like muscles or indigestion, but sometimes it's the heart. Your heart tracing and first blood test this morning were normal, which is reassuring. But damage from a heart attack can take a few hours to show up in the blood, so one normal test doesn't rule it out.
So what's the second test for?

It measures troponin, a protein released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged. If the level rises between the first and second samples, it can show a heart problem the first test missed. That's why the timing matters, and yours is due in two hours.
And if I go anyway, what's the worst that happens?

Honestly, most people with a normal first test turn out to be fine. But if this were a heart attack, leaving now could mean missing treatment that protects your heart, and further problems could happen at home. Smoking adds to that risk. It isn't likely, but it is possible, and it can be serious.
I didn't think of it like that. But I still can't leave him at the gate.
No, and you shouldn't have to. Does his school have an after-school club, or could they keep him in the office for a while if you rang them?
They've got an after-school club till six. He's never been, but he'd like it. His mates go.
That could work well. And is there anyone who could collect him from there, in case the result takes longer?
My mate Dave could. His boy's in the same class.
Then shall we use the phone at the nurses' station to ring the school and Dave now? That way your son's safe, and you can stay for the result.
Yeah. Yeah, okay. That makes sense.
Good. Before you ring, I just want to check I've explained things properly. Can you tell me why we want the second test, and what could happen if you leave without it?
The first test can miss a heart attack. The second one checks if the level's gone up. If I go and it was my heart, I could miss the treatment and have more trouble at home.
That's exactly it. And what have you decided?
I'll stay, if the school and Dave can sort it.

Thank you. And to be clear, it is your decision. If anything changes and you feel you have to leave, tell us first. We'd give you advice and arrange for you to come back for the second test, and you can return at any time without anyone judging you.
Okay. Good to know.
Whatever happens, if the chest pain comes back, especially if it lasts more than a few minutes or comes with breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick, call 999 straight away. Don't drive yourself.
999, and don't drive. Got it.

If the second test is normal, we'll talk about going home and any follow-up, such as a heart clinic, and help with stopping smoking. If it's raised, we'll explain the treatment. I'll come back as soon as the result is in.
Thanks, doc. Sorry for being difficult.
