I don't like strangers in my house. I never have. And I don't see why it's needed. I've lived there for forty years.
That's a long time, and you know it better than anyone. Is it just having people in, or is there something else that bothers you?
It's private, that's all.

I understand. Can I explain why we suggest it? Here on the ward, the bed, toilet and floors are all designed for safety. At home they're different. A visit lets us see how you manage your stairs, toilet, bed and kitchen with your frame, and what would make them easier and safer.
And what would that involve?

It would be me and a physiotherapist. We'd take you home by hospital transport, and it usually takes about an hour. You'd show us how you do things, and we'd look at what might help, like rails or a raised toilet seat. Then you'd come back to the ward with us.
So I'd come back here afterwards?

Yes, the visit is to help plan your discharge, not the discharge itself. And it's your choice. You can say no. If you agree, you can stop it at any point, and you can tell us that some rooms are private and we won't go in.
And if I say no?

Then we'd still plan your discharge. We'd use what you tell us about your home, perhaps a relative's description or photographs, and we might arrange a visit after you've gone home instead. Saying no won't stop you going home.
Well. I don't know.
Is there something about the house itself that worries you?
Since my husband died, I've let things go. There's stuff everywhere, newspapers, boxes. It's not clean. If you see it, you'll decide I can't cope. You'll put me in a home.

Thank you for telling me. That must have been hard to say. I'll be honest with you. My job is to help people get home safely, and that's what we're planning for you. Where you live is your decision, and an untidy house is not a reason for a care home.
You can't promise that, though.

I can't promise what will happen in future, and I won't pretend to. But I can promise I'm not looking at whether your house is tidy. I'm looking at whether you can move safely with your frame, so you don't fall again.
So what would you do about the mess?

If boxes or papers are in the way of your frame, they could cause another fall. We'd talk about clearing a safe path, not clearing your house. Anything that's moved would be agreed with you first, and we can arrange help if you'd like it.
My niece offered to help sort it out. I said no, but maybe.
Would you like her with you on the visit? Some people find a familiar face helps.
Yes. She'd come. She's very sensible.
That would be lovely. So, just to check I've explained it clearly, could you tell me what the visit would involve?
You and the physio take me home for about an hour, I show you how I manage, I can keep rooms private, and I come back here. And it's not about the mess.
That's exactly right. And it's about stopping another fall. Would you like to go ahead?
All right. But I want the back bedroom kept private.
Of course. I'll write that down. I'll speak to your niece and find a day that suits her. And if you change your mind before then, or on the day, just tell me or the nurses. That's completely fine.
Thank you. You've been very patient.

Not at all. In the meantime, please keep using your frame and call the nurses whenever you get up at night, so you don't fall here either. If you feel dizzy, or you notice any new pain in your hip or legs, tell the nurses straight away.
I will. I don't want another fall.
Neither do I. I'll come back tomorrow with a date.
Lovely. And thank you for not judging me.

coverage.how: Acknowledges her reluctance and asks what worries her first.
Explains the purpose: stairs, toilet, bed and kitchen with her frame, and what would help.
Describes who comes, about an hour, transport and the return to the ward.
States it is her choice: she can say no, stop at any point, or keep rooms private.
Explains discharge planning continues using other information if she declines.
Says a care home is not the plan and an untidy house is not a reason, without promising the future.
Explains a safe path for the frame, with any changes agreed with her.
Offers her niece's presence on the visit.
Checks understanding, asks for her decision and says she can change her mind.

concern.how: A direct question about the house brings out the clutter and fear of a care home; the therapist answers honestly, refuses to over-promise, and reframes the visit around falls rather than tidiness.

safety.point: Use the frame and call the nurses when getting up at night to avoid a fall on the ward.
Dizziness or new hip or leg pain should be reported to the nurses straight away.

scripts.notes: The physiotherapist attending, hospital transport, the length of about an hour and the niece are the script's choices. The script assumes she has capacity to decide where she lives, which the card does not question.

turns.text: Hello, Mrs Ahmed. As you know, today is our last planned session. Before anything else, how do you feel things have gone since the visits began? What are you most proud of?
Walking to the shop, I think. At the start I couldn't get to the front door.

I remember. Let's look at your goals together. You wanted to wash and dress yourself without help, and you do. You wanted to make your own lunch, and you're making simple meals every day. And the shop: you walk there and back on your own. Those were all yours, and you've done every one.
It doesn't feel like that much when you say it.

It's a great deal. Six months ago, you needed help with all of it. Which is why, as we discussed, the regular visits will finish today. Our team's role is rehabilitation towards goals, and you've reached them.
I did ask whether they could carry on. Even once a month?
I know, and I'm glad you asked. Can I ask what you'll miss about the visits?
Oh, just the company, I suppose. Someone to talk to.
Tell me more about that.
My friends stopped calling after the stroke. I think they didn't know what to say. Your visit is often the only proper conversation I have all week.
That sounds very lonely. Thank you for telling me. How has your mood been, alongside that?
Low, if I'm honest. Some days I don't get dressed until the afternoon. I haven't told anyone.

I'm glad you've told me. Low mood is very common after a stroke, and it's treatable. I need to ask you something directly, and I ask everyone. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn't worth living?
No. Nothing like that. Just flat. Fed up.
Thank you for answering. If that ever changes, please contact your GP that day, or call one one one, or nine nine nine if you feel unsafe. Would you be willing to see your GP about your mood?
I could. I didn't think it was worth bothering them.

It's absolutely worth it. There's also talking therapy, which you can refer yourself to, or your GP can. And I'd like to think about company. There's a stroke survivors' group that meets locally, with people who understand what you've been through. How would that feel?
A bit nerve-racking. But I'd meet people like me.
Exactly. There are also local activities, like the library's craft afternoon or volunteering, when you feel ready. You used to work in a school office, didn't you?
Yes. I loved it. I've thought about volunteering, actually.

That's worth exploring. I'll give you details of the group and a volunteering centre. Now, if anything changes, if your walking or self-care gets harder, you can be referred back to us. Your GP can do that, and so can other services such as the stroke nurse.
So I'm not cut off completely.
Not at all. Ending the visits doesn't mean ending your support. One more important thing: do you remember the warning signs of another stroke?
Face dropping, arm weakness, speech going funny.
That's right. Face, arms, speech. If you notice any of those, even if they pass quickly, call nine nine nine straight away. Don't wait to see if they settle.
I won't.

So, to sum up. You've met your goals, and our regular visits end today. You'll see your GP about your mood and think about talking therapy. You'll try the stroke group, and look into volunteering. And you can be referred back if things change. Here are the team's contact details in writing.
Thank you. I'm sad, but I see why.
It's natural to feel sad. Could you tell me what you'll do first?
Ring the GP this week about my mood, and call the stroke group about the next meeting.
That's a great start. It's been a real pleasure working with you.
And you. Thank you for everything.

coverage.how: Asks how things have gone and what she is most proud of.
Names each achieved goal: washing and dressing, simple meals, the shop.
Explains the rehabilitation role and that regular visits end today.
Asks what she will miss and follows up on company.
Asks about mood directly and screens for thoughts of self-harm.
Offers GP review, talking therapy by self-referral, the stroke group and volunteering.
Explains re-referral via the GP or other services if things change.
Checks the warning signs of stroke and advises nine nine nine without waiting.
Summarises the plan and gives written contact details.

concern.how: Asking what she will miss reveals that the visits are her main company and that she has been low; the therapist asks directly about risk and links her to GP, therapy and social contact.

safety.point: Asks directly about thoughts of self-harm or that life is not worth living.
If thoughts of self-harm develop, contact the GP that day, one one one, or nine nine nine if unsafe.
Face, arm or speech symptoms, even brief, mean calling nine nine nine straight away.

scripts.notes: Her previous school office job, the library and volunteering centre are the script's choices. Who can re-refer to a community neurological team varies by area; the script names the GP and the stroke nurse.

turns.text: Hello, Mrs Brennan. Thank you for having me back. How are you today, and how have the stairs been since my last visit?
About the same. Slow. I go up once at night and stay there. My knees are worse in the cold. Have you heard about the stairlift?
I have, and I'm afraid it isn't the news we were hoping for. Is now a good time to talk about it?
Oh. Go on.

The engineer has surveyed your stairs, and a stairlift can't be fitted. Your staircase is too narrow for the rail and the seat, even a curved one, to fit safely. There wouldn't be room for you to sit and travel without catching the wall.
Oh.
I'm so sorry. I know you were looking forward to it.
I was. I'd told my sister it was coming. I thought that was the answer.
It's a real disappointment, and it's all right to feel that. Take your time.
So what now? I can't keep doing those stairs.
Before we talk about options, can I ask what you'd been hoping the stairlift would let you do?
Sleep in my own bed. Use my bathroom without worrying. And not be stuck upstairs or downstairs all day.

Thank you, that helps me think about what matters. There are a few alternatives. A second stair rail would let you use both hands, which makes the stairs safer. A through-floor lift is a small lift that goes up through the ceiling into a bedroom. Or we could move your bed downstairs, with a downstairs toilet or a commode.
A lift through the ceiling? Could I have that?

It might be possible, and I'll look into it. But I'll be honest: it's a major adaptation. It depends on whether there's space, usually in the front room and a bedroom above, and on funding, which often means a grant assessment. It usually takes months, not weeks.
Months. And downstairs means the front room, I suppose.
It could. How would you feel about sleeping downstairs?
I'd hate it. That bedroom was ours, my husband's and mine. Forty years. And the front room faces the street. The neighbours would see a bed through the window. Everyone would know.

That's completely understandable. Your bedroom holds a lot of memories, and you deserve privacy. If you ever chose a downstairs room, we can make it private: a curtain or blind on the window, a screen, and a bed that looks like a sofa during the day. But it would be your choice, not something we'd push.
I don't want to give up my room.

Then let's start with what keeps you there safely. I'll order the second rail, and I'll ask about the through-floor lift. Meanwhile, a commode downstairs could save you trips during the day. How does that sound?
The rail and the commode, yes. And ask about the lift.

I will. Until then, please take the stairs one step at a time, leading up with your stronger leg and down with your weaker one. Hold the rail, don't carry anything, and keep the landing light on at night.
Good leg up, bad leg down. My physio told me that once.
That's it. And if you fall, do you have a way of calling for help?
No. My sister rings me most mornings.
I'd like to arrange a pendant alarm, which you wear and press to call for help. If you fall and are hurt or can't get up, press it or call nine nine nine. Don't try to struggle up if you're hurt.
A pendant. Yes, that would ease my sister's mind.
Good. I'll phone you next week once I've heard about the rail and the lift. Could you tell me what we've agreed?
A second rail, a commode downstairs, a pendant alarm, and you'll ask about the lift. One step at a time, good leg up.
Perfect. I'm sorry again about the stairlift.
Not your fault, love. Thank you for being straight with me.

coverage.how: Asks how she is and how the stairs have been.
Gives a warning shot, then states the stairlift cannot be fitted and why.
Pauses, acknowledges disappointment and gives her time before solutions.
Asks what she hoped the stairlift would allow.
Explains a second rail, a through-floor lift, moving the bed downstairs and a commode.
States honestly the lift depends on space and funding and takes months.
Explores her feelings about sleeping downstairs and offers privacy measures, as her choice.
Advises one step at a time, good leg up, holding the rail, not carrying things, lighting.
Arranges a pendant alarm, advises what to do after a fall, and agrees a call next week.

concern.how: Asking how she would feel about sleeping downstairs draws out her bond with the bedroom and fear of neighbours seeing a bed; the therapist validates it, offers privacy, and builds the plan around keeping her upstairs.

safety.point: Stairs one step at a time, holding the rail, carrying nothing, landing light on at night.
After a fall with injury or inability to get up, press the pendant or call nine nine nine and do not struggle up.

scripts.notes: A second stair rail is assumed to be possible on this narrow staircase; the card does not say. Through-floor lift feasibility and the grant route are described generally. The pendant alarm and next-week call are the script's choices.

turns.text: Hello, Mr Clarke. Your GP asked me to visit about the burn on your hand and the numbness. How is the burn healing, and has anyone checked it?
The practice nurse dressed it last week. It's healing, she said. The blister's gone down.

I'm glad it's been seen. May I look? That's clean and healing well. Can I explain why this happened? The chemotherapy has affected the nerves in your hands and feet, so they don't send pain and heat signals properly. Normally you'd let go of a hot handle instantly. Now your hand doesn't warn you, so burns and cuts happen more easily and you notice them later.
That's exactly it. I didn't feel a thing until I saw the blister.

So we use your eyes instead of your fingers. In the kitchen, use oven gloves for anything that's been near heat, including pan handles. Turn handles inwards so you don't knock them. Look for steam or a glow rather than touching to test heat. And take extra care with knives, because you won't feel a slip.
I've always just grabbed things. Habit.

Most cooks do. In the bathroom, run the cold tap first, then add hot. Check the water with a bath thermometer or your elbow, if that still feels normally. A thermostatic valve, which stops the water getting too hot, can be fitted to the bath or shower.
My elbow's fine. It's just the hands and feet.

Good. Now, because you won't feel small injuries, check your hands and feet every day. Look at your palms, between your fingers, the soles and between your toes. A mirror helps for the soles. You're looking for marks, blisters, cuts or redness.
Every day? Even if nothing's happened?

Every day, because you might not know something's happened. If a wound shows spreading redness, swelling, pus, feels hot, or you get a fever, get it seen the same day by your GP, or call one one one. After chemotherapy, infections can need prompt treatment.
Right. I'll write that down.
Can I ask about your work? What does your job involve?
I'm a chef. Head chef, at a hotel. I'm due back next month.
That's a hot, busy kitchen. How are you feeling about going back?
Honestly? Terrified. If they find out I burnt myself at home, they'll say I'm a danger. I'll lose my job. I've been keeping my hands in my pockets when my manager calls round.

That sounds like a lot of worry to carry on your own. Thank you for telling me. Your job clearly matters to you. Losing feeling after chemotherapy is a recognised health condition, and employers have a duty to consider reasonable adjustments.
What does that mean, in a kitchen?

Occupational health, the workplace health service, can assess what you can safely do and advise your employer. A phased return, with shorter shifts at first, gives you time to adjust. Adjustments might include heat-resistant gloves or less time on the grill.
I don't want them knowing about the burn.

That's your choice. You don't have to tell them about the burn. What you share about your health is up to you. But telling occupational health about the numbness could protect you, because it lets them plan to keep you safe.
I suppose they're on my side, really.
They should be. One more thing: if the numbness gets worse, spreads, or you notice weakness or trouble walking, tell your cancer team. They'll want to know.
Is it likely to get worse?
For many people it improves slowly over time, but it varies. Your cancer team can tell you more. Can you tell me the main safety points we've talked about?
Gloves for anything hot, handles in, look don't touch. Cold tap first, elbow or thermometer. Check hands and feet every day. Redness, pus or fever, same day. Tell the cancer team if it's worse.
Perfect. And work?
Speak to occupational health about a phased return, and it's my choice what I tell them.
Exactly. I'll arrange the thermostatic valve and a bath thermometer, and I'll leave you a written summary. Shall I call you before you go back to work?
Please. That would help.
Good. Look after those hands.
I will. Thanks.

coverage.how: Asks about healing and whether it has been checked; looks at it.
Explains nerve damage removes heat and pain warnings, so injuries happen and go unnoticed.
Advises oven gloves, handles inwards, judging heat by sight, and care with knives.
Advises cold tap first, thermometer or elbow, and a thermostatic valve.
Advises daily checks of palms, fingers, soles and toes, with a mirror.
Names spreading redness, swelling, pus, heat or fever as same-day signs.
Asks about his work and responds to his fear of losing his job.
Explains occupational health, phased return and that disclosure is his choice.
Advises reporting worsening numbness or weakness to his cancer team.
Asks him to summarise the safety points and checks his understanding.

concern.how: Asking how he feels about going back brings out his fear of losing his job and hiding his hands; the therapist acknowledges it, explains reasonable adjustments, and respects his choice about disclosure.

safety.point: Signs of wound infection or fever need same-day review by the GP or one one one.
Run cold water first and test with a thermometer or a part with normal feeling.
Worsening or spreading numbness, weakness or trouble walking should be reported to the cancer team.

scripts.notes: Finding the burn clean and healing is invented and kept benign; the card says only that he burnt his palm. The hotel job and the employer's visits are the script's choice. Elbow sensation is assumed normal, as he says.

turns.text: Hello, Mr Shaw. I understand you'd like to talk about a wheelchair. Can you tell me what's led you to ask now, and what you hope it would change?
I just can't walk far any more. My GP said to ask you. I want to be able to get out without it being an ordeal.
Getting out matters to you. What does a typical day look like at the moment?
I get up late, potter around the house, watch telly. I used to do the shopping and take my nephew to football. I've stopped all that.
That's a lot to have lost. Living with pain for four years is exhausting, and I'm not going to dismiss what you're asking. Can I be honest about wheelchairs, and then we can work out what fits?
Go on.

If someone uses a wheelchair for all their mobility, their leg and back muscles weaken and their joints stiffen. Over time that often means more pain, not less. So I'd be cautious about a wheelchair replacing walking altogether. That's not the same as saying no.
But you don't understand. It's not just the pain.
Then help me understand. What else is going on?
Last month I was in the supermarket and my legs just went. I ended up on the floor in the middle of the aisle. People staring. I haven't been out on my own since.

That sounds frightening and humiliating. I'm sorry that happened. Can I ask some questions about it? When your legs gave way, did you have any new numbness, especially around your bottom or between your legs?
No. Nothing like that.
Any new weakness in your legs since, or any change in your bladder or bowels, like not feeling when you need to go, or leaking?
No. My GP asked me the same. He examined me after and said it all looked normal. He thought the pain just caught me.
Good, I'm glad he checked. That's reassuring. How has your confidence been since, and your mood?
Rubbish. I keep thinking it'll happen again. I don't sleep well. I feel useless.

That's a very understandable reaction. Fear of falling after a fall is common, and it can keep people at home even when their body could do more. The good news is it can be worked on. Our team's psychologist helps people with exactly this, and I can refer you. Would you be open to that?
Maybe. If it helps me get out.

That's the aim. Now, some options. One is a wheelchair for long distances only, like shopping centres or days out, while you keep walking around the house and for short trips. I can refer you to the wheelchair service for that.
That's what I actually want. Not to sit in it all day.

Good. Another is a walking aid with a seat, so you can stop and sit when you need to. And there's pacing: planning outings, shopping at quieter times, using a trolley to lean on, and resting before the pain builds.
A seat on a walker. That would have helped in the supermarket.
Exactly. Then we'd set graded goals, building up step by step. What would you most like to get back to?
Taking my nephew to football. Even just watching.

That's a great goal. We could plan towards it, perhaps with the walker and seat. Before we finish, the warning signs. If you get numbness around your bottom or between your legs, new weakness in both legs, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels, go to A&E the same day. Don't wait.
Same day. Right.

So the plan: a walker with a seat to try, a referral to the wheelchair service for long distances, pacing for outings, the psychologist for your fear of falling, and football as the goal. Does that sound fair?
Yes. More than I expected, honestly.
I'll see you in two weeks to see how the walker's going. Can you tell me the warning signs, so I know I've explained them clearly?
Numbness down below, both legs going weak, bladder or bowel problems. Straight to A&E.
Exactly. Thank you for telling me about the fall. It's changed what we're aiming for.
Thanks for listening.

coverage.how: Asks what led to the request and what he hopes it would change.
Asks about a typical day and notes the shopping and football he has stopped.
Acknowledges four years of pain and says the request will not be dismissed.
Explains weakness, stiffness and often more pain if a wheelchair replaces walking.
Explores the fall, screening for saddle numbness, weakness and bladder or bowel change.
Discusses a wheelchair for long distances, a walker with a seat, pacing and graded goals.
Asks about confidence and mood, and offers psychology support for fear of falling.
Explains cauda equina warning signs need A&E the same day.
Agrees the plan and arranges review in two weeks.

concern.how: An open question after his 'it's not just the pain' brings out the supermarket fall; the therapist screens for red flags, then names and offers help for his fear of falling.

safety.point: Asks about saddle numbness, leg weakness and bladder or bowel change after the fall.
Saddle numbness, weakness in both legs or bladder or bowel problems mean A&E the same day.

scripts.notes: The GP examining him after the fall and finding nothing new is invented and kept benign, so the fall is treated as pain-related. The two-week review, the team psychologist and the nephew are the script's choices. Wheelchair service referral routes vary by area.

turns.text: Hello, Mr Evans. Thank you for coming in. I'd like to go through last week's memory assessment. Overall, your attention, reasoning and problem-solving were good. The area that was affected was short-term memory, meaning holding on to new information, like a message or an appointment. That's common after a stroke. Does that fit with what you've noticed?
I suppose so. I forget things people tell me. I'm fine with things from years ago.
That's typical. How has it shown up day to day, with appointments, tablets or money?
I missed the dentist last month. And I paid the gas bill twice. The bank sorted it out.
Thank you for telling me. Before we go on, I know you've asked me not to tell your wife the results. I want to reassure you that I won't share your information without your consent.
Good. She rang you, didn't she?
She did, and I told her I couldn't discuss it without speaking to you first. Can I ask, gently, why you'd rather she didn't know?
Because I've always looked after things. The money, the house, her. If she finds out, she'll take over. She'll treat me like a child. I'll just be the patient.
That sounds like a real fear, of losing your place in the family. Thank you for being honest. That makes complete sense.
I'm not useless. I just forget things.

You're certainly not useless. Can I share one thought, without any pressure? People who involve their partner often find strategies work better, because there's someone to back them up. And sometimes partners worry more when they don't know. It's your decision either way.
She does worry. She's noticed things.

I'll also be honest about one thing. If I ever had serious concerns about your safety, for example with your tablets, I'd talk to you first about sharing information. I wouldn't go behind your back. Does that feel fair?
As long as you talk to me first.

Always. Now, strategies to keep you in charge. A diary or phone reminders for appointments, set as soon as you book. For bills, a routine: check them on the same day each week, and tick them off once paid. Direct debits can stop double payments.
Direct debits. That would have saved me the gas bill.

Exactly. For tablets, a weekly organiser can help, with a box for each day and time. Your pharmacist can advise whether your tablets are suitable for one. Have you ever missed a dose, or taken a dose twice?
I think I've missed a few. Once I wasn't sure, so I took it again.

That's important. If you're unsure whether you've taken a dose, don't take another. Check the patient leaflet, or ask your pharmacist. If you think you've taken too much, or you feel unwell, call one one one, or nine nine nine if you're seriously unwell.
I didn't know that. I thought it was safer to take it.
With some tablets a double dose can cause harm, which is why the organiser helps. You'd see at a glance whether the box is empty.
Right. I'll get one.
Good. I wonder whether a joint session might help, with your wife here. You'd decide beforehand exactly what we say and what we don't. You'd stay in charge.
So I could tell her about the strategies, but not the scores?
Exactly, whatever you choose. You could present it as your plan, which it is.
I'll think about it. Maybe if I'm the one explaining.
That sounds like a good way forward. If she phones again before then, what would you like me to say?
Tell her I'm working on things with you, and that I'll talk to her myself.
I'll say exactly that. Shall we meet again in two weeks, to see how the reminders and organiser are going? Could you tell me what we've agreed today?
Phone reminders, direct debits, a tablet organiser from the pharmacist, and never take a dose twice if I'm unsure. Maybe a joint session. And you'll tell her I'll talk to her.
That's it exactly. You've handled a difficult conversation really well.
Thanks. It's a relief to have a plan.

coverage.how: Explains short-term memory was affected while attention, reasoning and problem-solving were good.
Asks about appointments, tablets and money; he reports the dentist and gas bill.
Confirms no sharing without consent and explains what the wife was told.
Gently asks why, and reflects his fear of losing his role.
Explains the benefits of involving her and says it is his decision.
Says honestly that serious safety concerns would be discussed with him first.
Offers reminders, a bills routine, direct debits and a pharmacist-advised organiser.
Asks about missed and doubled doses and advises not to repeat an uncertain dose.
Offers a joint session in which he decides what is said.
Agrees what to tell his wife and arranges review in two weeks.

concern.how: A gentle question about why brings out his fear of being treated like a child and losing his role; the therapist reflects it and offers strategies and a joint session that keep him in charge.

safety.point: If unsure whether a dose was taken, do not take another; check the leaflet or ask the pharmacist.
Suspected overdose or feeling unwell: one one one, or nine nine nine if seriously unwell.

scripts.notes: The assessment profile, the missed dentist appointment and the double gas payment are invented and kept mild. Not repeating an uncertain dose is general advice; a pharmacist should confirm it for his specific medicines. The two-week review is the script's choice. The script assumes he has capacity.

turns.text: Good morning, please sit down. I'm the optometrist. Before I explain what I found, could you tell me how long this has been going on, when it's worst, and what you've tried?
On and off for over a year. Mornings are worst; my lashes crust and my eyes burn. I've tried supermarket drops, and once my doctor gave me antibiotic ointment.
Did the ointment help?
For a week or so. Then it all came back. That's why I'm here.
That helps. Do you get red cheeks or flushing, perhaps with hot drinks? Any dandruff or other skin problems? And do you wear contact lenses?
My cheeks do go red quite easily, and I get a flaky scalp in winter. No contact lenses.

Thank you, that fits. The edges of your eyelids are red, and the tiny oil glands just behind the lashes are blocked. Normally they release a thin oil that stops your tears drying out. When they clog, the lids get inflamed and the tears evaporate, which causes that burning, gritty feeling.
So it is an infection, then. I keep catching it.

It isn't an infection you've caught. It's called blepharitis, which simply means inflamed eyelids. It's very common and tends to be long-term. People whose skin flushes easily or who get a flaky scalp are more prone to it.
Oh. I did wonder. I thought it was because I wasn't washing properly.

I'm glad you said that, because many people worry about the same thing. This has nothing to do with being unclean; it's down to how your oil glands and skin behave. Cleaning the lids helps because it's part of the treatment, not because you've done anything wrong.
That's a relief, honestly. But can't you just give me stronger antibiotic drops to clear it for good?

I understand why you'd want that. But germs aren't the main problem here, so antibiotics only calm things briefly, as you found. Using them repeatedly also makes them less effective when you really need them. What works long-term is daily lid care.
Every day? What does that involve?

Two simple steps. First, warmth. Hold a clean flannel soaked in warm water over your closed eyes for about five to ten minutes, re-warming it as it cools. A reusable heated eye mask from the pharmacy also works. The warmth melts the thick oil in those glands.
And then?
Then gently massage the lids. With a clean fingertip, roll the upper lid down towards the lashes and the lower lid up, a few times each, to ease the softened oil out.
And the crusting on my lashes?

That's the second step: cleaning the lid edges once a day, ideally in the morning. Use cooled boiled water with a little baby shampoo on a cotton pad, wiping along the lash line, or ready-made lid wipes from the pharmacy.
Okay. And for the burning, is there anything?
Yes, lubricating drops, or artificial tears, which top up your tear film. Use them whenever your eyes feel gritty. If you use them often, choose preservative-free ones, as preservatives can irritate.
So if I do all this, how soon will it be gone?

Honestly, blepharitis can be controlled very well, but it usually doesn't go away completely. Most people notice a real improvement after a few weeks of regular care. If you stop, it often creeps back, so think of it like brushing your teeth.
Disappointing, but at least I know what it is.

Knowing helps. Some warning signs, though: if an eye becomes painful rather than gritty, your vision blurs and doesn't clear with blinking, light hurts, or the eye goes very red, contact us or another optometrist the same day, or call 111 if we're closed.
Painful, blurry, light hurting or very red. Same day.
That's right. Keep the compress warm, not hot, so you don't burn the skin. Your red cheeks may be rosacea, a skin condition that often goes with this; mention it to your GP.
I will. I've never had them looked at.
I'd like to see you in about six weeks to check the glands. Before you go, what will you do at home each day?
Warm flannel for five to ten minutes, massage, clean the lashes, and drops when they feel dry.
Perfect. You've done nothing wrong, and this should get a lot easier.
Thank you. I feel much better.

coverage.how: Asks duration, worst time of day and what she has tried, then whether the ointment helped.
Asks about flushing, dandruff, skin problems and contact lenses.
Describes the inflamed lid edges and blocked oil glands behind the lashes and what the oil does.
Names blepharitis and explains it is common, long-term and not caught from anyone.
Says directly that it has nothing to do with being unclean, and why cleaning still helps.
Explains that bacteria are not the main problem, antibiotics only calm it briefly and overuse has a cost.
Describes the warm flannel or heated mask for five to ten minutes, then lid massage towards the lashes.
Describes daily lid cleaning with diluted baby shampoo or pharmacy lid wipes.
Recommends lubricating drops as needed, preservative-free if used often.
States honestly that it is controlled rather than cured and improves over a few weeks.
Lists pain, blurred vision that does not clear, light sensitivity and marked redness as same-day signs.
Books a review in about six weeks and asks her to describe the home routine.

concern.how: She assumes a repeated infection and then admits she fears she is not washing properly; the optometrist removes the blame explicitly and explains why antibiotics will not give the lasting cure she hopes for.

safety.point: A painful eye, blurred vision that does not clear, light sensitivity or a very red eye needs same-day review, or 111 if closed.
Compresses should be warm, not hot, to avoid burning the eyelid skin.

scripts.notes: The card does not mention rosacea; the script suggests her flushing may be rosacea and that she mention it to her GP. Compress time of five to ten minutes and a review at about six weeks are the script's choices.

turns.text: Thanks for waiting. First, your reading glasses. Your eyes are focusing just as I'd expect at your age, and a pair of reading glasses will make small print much clearer. We'll choose them together shortly. There's also something on your photograph I'd like to show you.
Oh. Is something wrong?

I don't think anything is wrong, but I want to explain it properly. This is the photograph of the back of your right eye. Here's the nerve, here are the blood vessels, and just here, away from the centre, is this small darker patch.
I see it. What is it?

It's called a naevus, which is really a freckle inside the eye. It's a small cluster of the same pigment cells that make freckles on the skin. They're very common; we find them in lots of adults at routine tests, and most people never know they have one.
A freckle. My mum had a freckle on her back, and that turned out to be melanoma.
I'm so sorry about your mum. I can understand why that word worries you. May I ask how she is now?
She had it removed years ago and she's fine. But I panicked the moment you said freckle.

That's a natural reaction. Let me tell you why this one doesn't worry me. It's small, it's flat, the colour is even, and the scan, which shows the layers in cross-section, shows no fluid around it. Those are all the features we expect from a harmless naevus.
But could it turn into cancer?

I'll be honest with you. Very rarely, over many years, a naevus can change into a cancer called melanoma of the eye. For a freckle like yours, that chance is very low. Eye melanoma is also a separate condition from skin melanoma, so your mum's history doesn't mean this freckle is cancer.
So why tell me at all, if it's nothing?

Because the best way to be sure it stays harmless is to watch it. I've saved today's photograph and scan on your record. Next time, we take new ones and compare them side by side, looking for any growth or change.
When would that be?

I'd like to see you again in about six months for repeat photographs. If it looks exactly the same, we'll usually check it once a year at your routine eye test. Each time we look at its size, its edges, its colour, and whether there's any fluid.
Okay. Six months. Should I be feeling anything?
Have you noticed any flashes of light, a shadow in your vision, or anything looking blurred or bent recently?
No, nothing. I only came because I can't read the menu in restaurants.

That's what I'd expect; these freckles don't cause symptoms. But if you notice flashing lights, a shadow across your vision, new floaters, or straight lines looking wavy, especially in your right eye, please contact us promptly rather than waiting for your appointment. If that happens out of hours, call 111.
Flashes, a shadow, floaters, wavy lines. Right.

If we ever saw it grow, become thicker, develop orange pigment or have fluid leaking, we'd refer you to the hospital eye clinic, where specialists can look more closely. Yours has none of those features, so a referral isn't needed now.
And if it did change, could they do something?
Yes. That's exactly why we monitor: finding any change early gives the most options. But please keep it in proportion; most freckles like this simply stay the same for life.
That does make me feel better. My mum will ask me a thousand questions, though.
I can give you a written note with the name, naevus, and a copy of the photograph, so you can show her. It also says when your next check is. Would that help?
Yes, please.
Lovely. Just so I know I've explained it clearly, could you tell me in your own words what we found and what happens next?
A harmless-looking freckle in my right eye. You'll photograph it again in six months, then yearly if it hasn't changed. And I come back sooner if I get flashes, shadows or wavy lines.
Exactly right. Now, let's choose those reading glasses, so you can read the menu again.
Thank you. That's a weight off my mind.

coverage.how: Opens with the reading glasses result and returns to choosing them at the end.
Signposts a finding and walks her through the photograph on screen.
Explains a naevus as a freckle of pigment cells inside the eye, common in adults.
Lists small, flat, even colour and no fluid on the cross-section scan as reassuring.
Asks directly about flashes, shadows and blurred or distorted vision.
Acknowledges her mother's history, states the very low chance of change and that eye melanoma is separate from skin melanoma.
Explains that saved images allow side-by-side comparison for growth or change.
Agrees repeat photographs in about six months, then yearly if unchanged, naming size, edges, colour and fluid.
Lists flashes, a shadow, new floaters and wavy lines as reasons to contact the practice promptly.
Names growth, thickening, orange pigment or fluid as reasons for referral and says hers has none.
Offers a written note with a copy of the photograph and asks her to summarise the plan.

concern.how: The word freckle triggers her memory of her mother's melanoma; the optometrist asks about it, acknowledges the fear and answers honestly about the small risk and why monitoring protects her.

safety.point: Flashes, a shadow, new floaters or wavy lines mean contacting the practice promptly, or 111 out of hours.
Monitoring exists so that any change is found early, though most such freckles never change.

scripts.notes: The review plan of about six months, then yearly if unchanged, is a common community approach; a clinician should confirm it matches local guidance.

turns.text: Thank you for staying. This has been a shock. Before I explain, I'd like to hear what's on your mind.
He was here a year ago and you said he was fine. Now he's losing the sight in one eye. How did you miss it?
I can hear how upset and angry you are, and that's completely understandable. Please go on.
He trusted you. And now he can't see my face properly with that eye.
That must be hard to watch. Let me explain today's findings, then come back to last year; you deserve a straight answer on both.
Go on, then.

The macula is the small central part of the retina, the seeing layer at the back of the eye, which gives us our central vision for faces and reading. In your dad's left eye, abnormal blood vessels have grown under it and are leaking. That's wet macular degeneration, and it causes the wavy lines and the grey patch.
And last year?

Last year my colleague recorded small yellow deposits, an early, dry stage that's common at his age and often changes slowly. The wet form is different: it can develop within weeks, and his started about two weeks ago.
So you're saying nobody could have seen this coming.

The wet changes weren't there to be seen then; his vision was unchanged. What the record doesn't show is whether he was taught to check his eyes at home and come straight back if lines looked wavy. If he wasn't, he should have been, and I'm sorry. I'll look into it.
Thank you for being honest, at least.
When did he first mention anything to you?
About two weeks ago. He said door frames looked bent. I told him he was just tired.
That's a very normal thing to say. Tiredness is a far more common explanation, and you had no reason to think otherwise.
But if I'd brought him in then...
I understand, and it's clear how much you care. What matters now is that he's been seen and the referral goes today. Treatment works best started promptly, and that's what's happening.
Okay. What happens now, then?
I've made a fast-track referral to the hospital's macular clinic. He should normally be seen within two weeks. If nothing arrives within a week, ring us and we'll chase it.
And what will they do?

If they confirm it, the usual treatment is injections into the eye after numbing drops; most people feel pressure, not pain. They're repeated regularly at first, aiming to stop the leaking and prevent further loss. Some people regain a little sight, but I can't promise that.
Injections in his eye. He'll hate that. And his other eye?
His right eye has dry deposits but no wet changes, and its sight is good. Does he still drive, and how is he managing at home, including with his tablets?
He gave up driving last year. He lives alone, but I'm round most days. He's struggling with the small print on his tablets.
Good lighting and a magnifier help, and his pharmacist can print larger labels. The hospital can point him to sight loss support.
I'll ask about that.

With this grid, he covers one eye, looks at the centre dot and checks the lines are straight and complete, then the other eye, daily. New wavy lines, a blank patch or sudden blurring in his right eye means contacting us the same day.
Every day, one eye at a time. I'll do it with him.

Thank you. About last year: if you'd like to complain formally, I'll give you our complaints procedure in writing, and you can take it to the NHS if you're unhappy with our answer. I can also arrange a meeting with our practice manager to go through the records.
I'd like the meeting. I'm not looking to sue anyone. I just want to know he was looked after.
That's completely fair; I'll ask the manager to ring you this week. Before you go, what will you do over the next few days?
Wait for the hospital, ring you if nothing in a week, the grid every day, and the manager will call.
Exactly. If his right eye changes suddenly, contact us the same day, or call 111 out of hours. I'll ring your dad on Friday to check the appointment has come.
Thank you. I'm sorry I shouted.
No need to apologise. You were standing up for your dad.

coverage.how: Invites her to speak first, lets her continue and acknowledges her anger and distress.
Explains the macula, leaking abnormal vessels and the link to wavy lines and the grey patch.
Contrasts early dry deposits with the wet form, which can develop within weeks.
States what the record shows, admits it cannot show whether home-check advice was given, apologises if not and promises to look into it.
Explains the fast-track referral, being seen within two weeks, and ringing if nothing arrives within a week.
Describes injections after numbing drops, repeated at first, aiming to stop further loss without promising recovery.
Asks when he first mentioned it and normalises her tiredness explanation.
Reports the right eye, asks about driving and home, and offers practical help with small print.
Explains daily one-eye-at-a-time grid checks and same-day contact for changes.
Offers the written complaints procedure, the NHS route and a meeting with the practice manager.
Asks her to summarise the plan and promises a call to her father on Friday.

concern.how: After venting, she admits she told her father it was tiredness; the optometrist normalises that response, relieves her guilt and turns the focus to the prompt referral now under way.

safety.point: New wavy lines, a blank area or sudden blurring in the right eye needs same-day contact.
Out of hours, a sudden change should prompt a call to 111 rather than waiting.

scripts.notes: The card does not give the right eye's state or his driving; the script makes the right eye dry with deposits and good sight, and has him already stopped driving. The fast-track timescale of within two weeks reflects common UK pathways; a clinician should confirm the local standard.

turns.text: Hello, come in. I'm the optometrist. I've had a look at your eyes, but first tell me in your own words what's been happening, and whether it's both eyes.
Both eyes. Itchy, watery, red, and my eyelids are puffy in the morning. It's like this every summer, but this year it's worse.
That sounds miserable. Do you have hay fever, with sneezing or a runny nose, and any asthma or eczema?
Hay fever, yes, my nose is streaming. I had eczema as a child. No asthma.
Thank you. What have you used so far, drops or tablets, and how often?
Nothing for the hay fever this year. Just some drops from the supermarket.
Do you know what they were called, or what it said on the box?
Redness relief. They make your eyes white straight away. I've used them four or five times a day for about two weeks. I work in sales; I can't look like I've been crying.

I understand wanting to look fresh at work. Those drops narrow the blood vessels, so the redness fades for a few hours. When they wear off, the vessels widen again, often more than before. Used several times a day, they keep the eyes red, which is probably why they look worse now.
So I've been making it worse? Great.

You weren't to know; the box makes them sound helpful. My advice is to stop them now. The eyes may look a bit redder for a few days, then they should settle, especially once we treat the allergy properly.
Okay. So what is it, actually?

It's allergic conjunctivitis, an allergy affecting the thin clear skin over the white of the eye and inside the lids. Pollen lands on the eye and your body overreacts, releasing histamine, which causes the itching, watering and swelling. The good news is that the front of your eye is healthy, and your vision is normal.
That's a relief. How do I stop it?

Some simple things first. Wraparound sunglasses keep pollen out. Shower and wash your hair in the evening, and keep windows closed on high pollen days. Instead of rubbing, which makes it worse, hold a cool, clean flannel over your closed eyes.
I do rub them constantly. Okay. And drops?

There are drops called mast cell stabilisers, such as sodium cromoglicate, which you can buy from a pharmacy. They stop the allergic reaction starting, so they work best used regularly through the season, and they can take several days to reach full effect. Next year, start them a couple of weeks before your symptoms usually begin.
Several days? I need something now.

If they're not enough, stronger anti-allergy drops work within minutes, but need a prescription from your GP or an optometrist with extra prescribing training. Start the pharmacy drops today and come back if you're not improving.
Let's do that. How often do I use them?
Follow the leaflet, which usually means several times a day, every day, even on good days. That regular use is what keeps the reaction switched off.
And my contact lenses? I wear dailies.

Dailies are ideal, because each morning you start with a clean lens, free of pollen. Take the lenses out before using the drops, and wait at least fifteen minutes before putting them back, because preservatives can soak into lenses. On really bad days, glasses may be more comfortable.
That makes sense. Should I take a tablet as well?
Your nose is streaming too, so an antihistamine tablet could help both your nose and your eyes. There are non-drowsy ones; the pharmacist can help you choose one that suits you.
I'll ask on the way home.

There are some symptoms that aren't typical of allergy. If an eye becomes painful rather than itchy, light hurts, your vision goes blurred, only one eye is badly red, or there's thick sticky discharge, take your lenses out and be seen the same day, here or at eye casualty. If we're closed, call 111.
Pain, light, blurry vision, one eye, sticky. Lenses out and same day.
Perfect. So, what's your plan?
Stop the redness drops, buy the cromoglicate drops and use them regularly, take a tablet, sunglasses, lenses out before drops, and no rubbing.
Exactly. If it isn't clearly better in a week or two, come back and we'll consider the stronger prescription drops.
Thanks. I'll be back if I still look like I've been crying at work.

coverage.how: Asks her to describe the symptoms, which eyes, and about hay fever, asthma and eczema.
Asks what she has used, then the product type, frequency and duration.
Explains pollen, histamine and the allergic reaction, and that the cornea and vision are healthy.
Covers wraparound sunglasses, evening showers, closed windows, cool compresses and not rubbing.
Explains pharmacy mast cell stabiliser drops taking days to work and faster prescription drops if needed.
Agrees she starts the pharmacy drops today, used regularly as the leaflet says.
Advises lenses out before drops, waiting before reinsertion, and glasses on bad days.
Suggests a non-drowsy antihistamine tablet chosen with the pharmacist.
Explains rebound redness from the vessel-narrowing drops and advises stopping them.
Lists pain, light sensitivity, blurred vision, one very red eye and sticky discharge, with lenses out and same-day review.
Has her summarise the plan and agrees to return if not clearly better in a week or two.

concern.how: When asked exactly what she has used, she describes daily redness-relief drops used to look fresh at work; the optometrist explains the rebound effect kindly, removes any blame and gives a better plan.

safety.point: Pain, light sensitivity, blurred vision, one very red eye or sticky discharge means lenses out and same-day review, or 111 if closed.
If not clearly improving in a week or two, she should return for stronger prescription treatment.

scripts.notes: Product choices are generic: pharmacy sodium cromoglicate drops and faster-acting prescription anti-allergy drops. The advice to wait at least fifteen minutes before reinserting lenses follows common leaflet guidance for preserved drops; a clinician should confirm.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the optometrist. Thanks for coming straight in. Tell me exactly what you were doing when this happened.
Grinding a bracket in the garage. Something flicked up and it's felt scratchy ever since.
Were you hammering metal on metal at any point, or only grinding? And were you wearing goggles or safety glasses?
Just the grinder. No goggles; it was a quick job.

Thank you. Hammering fragments travel faster and can go deeper, so that matters. I can see a tiny piece of metal on the surface of the cornea, the clear front window of the eye, away from the centre. There's no sign it has gone deeper, and your vision is normal.
Can't I just leave it to work its way out?
It's best removed today. Metal on the eye rusts, which stains it and keeps it sore, and it can let infection in. It usually takes only a few minutes.
A few minutes of what, exactly?

First, numbing drops; they sting for a second, then the eye goes numb. You'll rest your chin and forehead on the microscope, like earlier, and look at a target with your other eye. I'll lift the fragment off with a very fine, sterile instrument while I watch through the microscope.
An instrument. You mean a needle.
It's a fine sterile tip, used very gently and from the side. I notice you've gone a bit quiet. How are you feeling about it?
Honestly? I fainted at a blood test once. The thought of something coming at my eye...

Thank you for telling me; that's very common. You'll be looking at the target, so you won't see it coming. We'll go slowly. If you need me to stop, just raise your hand and I'll stop straight away. And if you feel faint, we can lie your chair back first.
Raise my hand. Okay. Will it hurt?

With the numbing drops you shouldn't feel pain, perhaps a light touch. The removal usually takes less than a minute. When the drops wear off, after about twenty minutes, the eye may feel scratchy for a day or so.
And what could go wrong?

It's a common, safe procedure, but there are small risks. It leaves a tiny scratch, which usually heals in a day or two. Rarely there's slight scarring or infection, hence the antibiotic ointment. Sometimes a rust ring is left behind; if so, I'd send you to eye casualty the same day to have it cleared.
What if you can't get it out?

If it turns out to be deeper, nearer the centre or through the surface, or it doesn't lift off easily and safely, I'll stop and refer you the same day to the hospital eye casualty. I don't expect that, as it's right on the surface.
Okay.
So, are you happy for me to go ahead? It's absolutely fine to say no, or to ask more questions first.
No, let's get it done. As long as I can stop you.
You can, any time. Here come the drops; a quick sting. Now chin on the rest, eyes on the target.
Okay, I'm ready.
All done. You were very steady. It came off in one piece, with no rust mark left.
Is that it? I barely felt a thing.

That's it. Use the antibiotic ointment as labelled until the course is finished. Don't rub the eye while it's numb; you could scratch it without feeling it. It may feel gritty and water a little for a day or so, which is normal.
Can I drive home?
Your vision is clear, but the ointment blurs things for a while, so put the first dose in once you're home.
Fine.
If the eye gets more painful instead of less, your vision blurs, it goes very red, light hurts, or there's sticky discharge, come back the same day or go to eye casualty. Out of hours, call 111.
More pain, blurry, red, light, sticky. Got it.
About the goggles: I know a quick job feels too quick to bother. But safety glasses kept right by the grinder take seconds to put on, and cost far less than a week off work.
Yeah, point taken. I'll hang a pair on the bench.
Good plan. I'd like to check the eye the day after tomorrow. Can you tell me what you'll do until then?
Ointment as labelled, no rubbing, back the day after tomorrow, sooner if it's worse.
Perfect. See you then.

coverage.how: Asks what he was doing, specifically about hammering, and about goggles.
Explains the surface fragment on the cornea, no deeper damage, and why rust and infection make removal today sensible.
Describes numbing drops, chin and forehead rests, a fixation target and a fine sterile instrument.
Explains touch or pressure rather than pain, under a minute, and grittiness when the numbness wears off.
Lists a small surface scratch, rare scarring or infection, and a rust mark possibly needing a second visit.
Notices he has gone quiet, asks, hears the fainting history and agrees a raised hand as the stop signal.
Asks for consent and states that saying no or asking more is fine.
Explains same-day referral to eye casualty if it will not lift off safely.
Covers the antibiotic ointment as labelled, no rubbing while numb, grittiness and blurring from ointment.
Lists increasing pain, blurred vision, marked redness, light sensitivity and discharge as same-day signs.
Suggests keeping safety glasses by the grinder, framed around his time and work.
Books a check the day after tomorrow and asks him to repeat the plan.

concern.how: When the instrument is mentioned he goes quiet; the optometrist names it, he reveals the fainting episode, and the fear is managed with the fixation target, a stop signal and the option to recline.

safety.point: Increasing pain, blurred vision, marked redness, light sensitivity or discharge means returning or eye casualty the same day, or 111 out of hours.
Eye protection should be worn for grinding; a pair kept by the grinder removes the excuse of a quick job.

scripts.notes: The removal is described as straightforward, in one piece with no rust mark left; this is invented and benign. The numbness lasting about twenty minutes and a check the day after tomorrow are the script's choices.

turns.text: Hello again, come and sit down. How has the eye felt since I saw you, and have you managed to use the ointment as I showed you?
Much better, thanks. It stopped hurting after a couple of days, and it isn't blurry any more. I've used the ointment as it says on the label.

Brilliant. Today the vision in your left eye is back to normal, the same as the right. And when I put in the yellow dye and looked under the blue light, there was no staining at all. That dye sticks to any damaged area, so no stain means the surface has completely healed.
So that's it, I'm fixed?
The scratch has healed, yes, so you don't need to come back to our eye conditions service. I'll send a note to your GP saying you've been discharged.
Do I keep using the ointment?
Yes, please finish the course as written on the label, even though it feels fine. The new surface is still delicate, and finishing it protects against infection while it strengthens.
Okay.

There's one thing I'd like you to know about. Scratches from fingernails sometimes lead to something called recurrent erosion. The new surface layer hasn't fully stuck down yet, so it can come away again, usually first thing in the morning, when the eyelid pulls on a dry surface as you open your eye.
What would that feel like?
Very like the original scratch: sudden pain, watering and sensitivity to light on waking. It can happen weeks or even months later.
That doesn't sound fun.

It isn't, but we can lower the chance. I'd recommend a lubricating eye ointment, which you can buy at the pharmacy, at bedtime for a few weeks once the antibiotic course has finished. It keeps the surface slippery overnight, so the lid doesn't stick to it.
Fine. Actually, can I ask about my contact lenses? I'm flying out on Saturday for my sister's wedding, and I really want to wear them for the photos.

Of course, and what a lovely occasion. I'll be honest with you, because I want your eye to be well for the wedding. The surface has only just healed. A lens rubs on that new layer and reduces the oxygen reaching it, which raises the risk of the scratch reopening or of an infection. My advice is to wear your glasses for this trip.
Glasses in my sister's wedding photos? I've been planning this for months.

I understand it's disappointing. Photographers work around glasses all the time, and anti-reflection lenses help in photos. But think about the alternative: an infection abroad could spoil the whole trip, and it would be harder to get treated. I'd much rather you enjoyed every day of it.
I suppose you're right. When can I wear them again, then?

Once you've finished the antibiotic, and your eye has felt completely normal for about a week. Then start with a fresh pair, not the ones you were wearing before. If anything feels uncomfortable, take them out and call us.
Okay, fair enough. Glasses for the wedding.

Thank you. Now, about your little one's nails: keeping them short and filed, perhaps while she's asleep, helps a lot. Some parents use scratch mitts at night. And when you lift her close to your face, it helps to hold her hands.
I'll file them tonight. She's lethal.

If the eye suddenly becomes painful, red, watery or sensitive to light again, or your vision goes blurry, please be seen the same day, here or at eye casualty. If we're closed, call 111. And never put a contact lens into a sore eye.
And if it happens while I'm abroad?

Then don't wait until you get home. See a local eye doctor or go to the hospital there the same day; your travel insurance can help you find one. Take your lubricating ointment with you, and the letter I'll give you today describing the scratch.
That's helpful, thank you.
Just to check I've been clear, could you tell me what you're going to do now?
Finish the antibiotic, then the lubricating ointment at night for a few weeks. Glasses for the wedding. Lenses only after a normal week, a fresh pair. Same day if it hurts again, at home or abroad.
That's perfect. I'll write the letter now. Have a wonderful time at the wedding.
Thank you, I will.

coverage.how: Asks how the eye has felt and whether the ointment was used as labelled.
Reports normal vision and no staining with the yellow dye, explaining what that means.
States the scratch has healed and she is discharged, with a note to her GP.
Advises finishing the course as labelled to protect the new surface.
Explains the new layer may not have stuck down and can lift on waking, with the symptoms.
Recommends pharmacy lubricating ointment at bedtime for a few weeks after the antibiotic.
Explains the risk of lenses on newly healed surface, advises glasses for the wedding and when to restart.
Suggests short filed nails, mitts at night and holding the baby's hands near her face.
Lists sudden pain, redness, watering, light sensitivity and blurring as same-day signs.
Advises same-day local care abroad, using travel insurance, and carrying the letter and ointment.
Asks her to summarise the plan and closes warmly.

concern.how: She raises the wedding and her lenses; the optometrist acknowledges the disappointment, explains the risk honestly and offers practical ways to look good in glasses, and she accepts.

safety.point: Sudden pain, redness, watering, light sensitivity or blurred vision means same-day review, or 111 if closed, and no lenses in a sore eye.
If the eye becomes sore abroad she should be seen locally the same day, not wait until home.

scripts.notes: Restarting lenses after the antibiotic course and about a week of a completely normal eye, with a fresh pair, is a cautious choice; practice varies and a clinician should confirm. Night-time lubricating ointment for a few weeks is the script's recommendation.

turns.text: Good morning, please sit down. I'm the optometrist who runs this eye pressure service with the hospital. We do the same checks you had in clinic, closer to home. How do you feel about being moved here?
Honestly? Not great. Six years at the hospital, and now the high street. It feels like cost-cutting.
Thank you for being honest. That's a reasonable worry, and I'd like to answer it properly. First, could you tell me what you understand about your eyes, and what the hospital told you?
They said the pressure is high, but no glaucoma. They've never given me drops. I thought I had glaucoma waiting to happen.

That's partly right. You have ocular hypertension, which means the pressure inside your eyes is higher than average. Glaucoma is when the optic nerve, the cable from the eye to the brain, becomes damaged, often with loss of side vision. You have the raised pressure, but no damage.
So it could still turn into glaucoma.
It can in some people, which is why we keep checking. But many people with raised pressure never develop glaucoma, and regular checks spot any early change long before you'd notice it.
And today?

Today I measured your eye pressures, scanned your optic nerves to check the nerve fibres, and did the field test, which checks your side vision. I compared them with your hospital results, and everything is unchanged.
Unchanged. Good. But why can't they keep seeing me there?

I'll be straight with you. Hospital clinics are very busy, and the consultant needs those appointments for people whose sight is at risk and needs treatment. Your results have been stable for years, which is why you've moved. It's a sign your eyes are doing well, not that you matter less.
That's one way of putting it. But what if you miss something?

Fair question. I've had extra training for this service, and we use the same tests and standards agreed with the hospital consultants, who review our results. If anything changes, I can refer you straight back, quickly, without going through your GP.
Straight back. All right. My brother's the reason I worry, really.
Would you tell me about your brother?
He's four years older. Glaucoma, found late. He's lost most of his side vision and can't drive. I don't want that.

I'm sorry; that must have been hard to see, and it makes sense that you're anxious. The big difference is timing. Your brother's was found late. Yours is being watched closely, before any damage, which is how sight is protected.
Put like that, it does help.
Glaucoma does run in families, so your family history matters. Do you have children, or other brothers and sisters?
Two daughters, both in their forties, and a younger sister.

Then I'd encourage them all to have regular eye tests and tell their optometrist about you and your brother. Your sister, if she's over forty, can have free NHS eye tests because her brother has glaucoma.
I'll tell them. Is there anything I should watch out for?

Raised pressure usually causes no symptoms, which is why the checks matter. Very rarely, a different problem makes the pressure rise suddenly: a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes around lights, headache or feeling sick. That's an emergency; go to eye casualty or A&E straight away.
Painful red eye, haloes, feeling sick. Straight to A&E.
Exactly. And the checks only work if you come. If you miss one, we'll contact you to rebook, and if we can't reach you, we tell the hospital and your GP. Please ring if you can't make a date.
I've never missed one in six years.
That's brilliant, and it's partly why you're doing so well.
So when do I come back?
Your consultant has asked for checks once a year, so I'll book you for the same time next year, and you'll get a reminder. Are you happy to carry on with us?
Yes, I am. I came in ready for a fight, to be honest.
I'm glad we talked it through. If you notice any change in your sight between visits, ring us and we'll see you sooner. What will you take away from today?
My results are stable, you can send me straight back, my family should get tested, and I ring if my sight changes.
Perfect. See you next year.

coverage.how: Introduces the service and asks directly how he feels about the move.
Asks what he understands and what the hospital said.
Explains ocular hypertension, the optic nerve and that glaucoma means damage, which he does not have.
Lists pressures, nerve scan and field test compared with hospital results, all unchanged.
Explains hospital capacity for those needing treatment and frames the move as a sign of stability.
Describes extra training, agreed standards, consultant review and direct re-referral.
Asks about his brother and acknowledges what he witnessed.
Explains family risk, advises regular tests for daughters and sister, and the sister's free NHS test if over forty.
Describes the rare sudden pressure rise symptoms and that it is an emergency.
Explains rebooking, informing the hospital and GP, and asks him to ring rather than miss.
Books the yearly check and confirms he is happy to continue, with a summary.

concern.how: He opens with the cost-cutting suspicion and later names his brother; the optometrist answers the money worry honestly, acknowledges the brother's loss and shows that early monitoring is the difference.

safety.point: A painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes, headache or nausea is an emergency for eye casualty or A&E.
Any change in sight between visits means ringing to be seen sooner rather than waiting.

scripts.notes: The free NHS sight test for a sibling of someone with glaucoma applies to those aged forty or over in England; other UK nations differ. Acute pressure rise symptoms are mentioned as a rare, separate problem.

turns.text: Hi, thanks for waiting while I looked at the scan. Before I go through it, how is your vision affecting you day to day, at work and when you're driving at night?
At work I'm fine close up, wiring and that. Night driving's the worst: headlights have big streaks and halos. My glasses never seem quite right.
That's useful, thank you. Is it the same in both eyes?
The right's worse, I think.

That fits. The cornea is the clear dome at the front of your eye, like the glass over a watch face, and it does most of the focusing. Your scan shows it's thinner than normal and bulging forward into more of a cone shape, in both eyes, more on the right.
A cone? That doesn't sound good.

It explains your changing glasses and the streaky lights. It's called keratoconus. It usually starts in the teens, worsens through the twenties, then often settles later in adult life. Yours is at an early stage, and there's a lot we can do.
Keratoconus. I've actually read about that. Isn't that the one where you need a transplant and go blind?
I'm glad you asked rather than worrying on your own. What else did you read?
That your cornea can get so bad you need a donor one. I'm a trainee electrician. If I can't see, I lose my apprenticeship.

That's a frightening thing to read. Honestly, most people with keratoconus never need a transplant; only a minority do, usually when it's advanced. It very rarely causes blindness. And catching it early, as we have, means it can often be stopped from worsening.
Stopped how?
I'm referring you to the hospital eye clinic, to the cornea specialists. They'll repeat detailed scans to measure the shape and thickness of your cornea over time, to see whether it's still changing.
And if it is?

Then they'll usually offer cross-linking. After numbing drops, vitamin drops are put on the cornea and activated with ultraviolet light, which stiffens it so it stops bulging further. For most people it's one treatment. It won't reverse the change, but it can stop it getting worse.
So my eyes stay as they are. But they're blurry now.
Yes, and that's the other part. Specially fitted contact lenses, often rigid ones, give the eye a smooth new front surface, so many people see much better in them than in glasses.
Okay. That's better than I thought.
Can I ask you something? Do you rub your eyes much?
All the time. Hay fever. I really grind them, especially in the mornings.

That's really important. Hard rubbing is strongly linked to keratoconus getting worse, because it presses on a cornea that's already weak. Stopping is one of the most useful things you can do yourself, starting today.
But they itch like mad. What do I do instead?

Treat the itch properly. Pharmacy anti-allergy drops used regularly in the season help, and so can a hay fever tablet. A cold compress calms the itch. If you feel the urge, press gently with clean fingertips instead of rubbing. Your GP can help with the eczema too.
Cold flannel instead of rubbing. I'll try.

On driving: with your glasses, you meet the legal standard, so you can keep driving. If your vision gets worse, especially at night, come back for a check, and we'll tell you whether you need to inform the DVLA.
And work?

Plenty of people with keratoconus work in skilled trades, with glasses or lenses, and with treatment there's every reason to expect you'll carry on. It can run in families, so your brother and parents should have their eyes checked.
My little brother rubs his eyes too. I'll tell my mum.
Good idea. Can I check I've explained it well? What will you tell your mum tonight?

That my cornea's thin and bulging, it's called keratoconus, the hospital will check if it's changing, they can stop it with cross-linking, special lenses can help me see, and I've got to stop rubbing.

Spot on. The hospital letter should come in the next few weeks; if not, ring us. And if the sight in either eye ever drops suddenly, or an eye becomes painful and watery, contact us or eye casualty the same day.
Thanks. I came in for new glasses and I'm leaving with a plan.
That's how it should be. I'll see you after your hospital visit, too.

coverage.how: Asks about work, night driving and each eye.
Explains the cornea as the clear focusing dome and the scan showing thinning and a cone shape.
Names keratoconus, its usual course through the teens and twenties, and that his is early.
Asks what he has read, then corrects the transplant and blindness fears honestly.
Asks about rubbing and explains it presses on and worsens a weak cornea.
Suggests anti-allergy drops, tablets, cold compresses, gentle pressing and GP help.
Explains referral to the cornea specialists for repeat shape and thickness scans.
Explains cross-linking stiffens the cornea, is usually one-off, and halts rather than reverses.
Explains rigid lenses giving a smooth surface and that only a minority need transplants.
Confirms he meets the standard now and should be rechecked if sight worsens, with advice on the DVLA.
Reassures about skilled trades and suggests family members are checked.
Asks him to explain it as he would to his mother and agrees a hospital chase and review.

concern.how: On hearing the name he raises what he read about transplants, blindness and his apprenticeship; later he admits hard daily rubbing. Both are answered honestly, with the rubbing turned into the most useful action he can take.

safety.point: Hard eye rubbing worsens keratoconus and should stop from today.
A sudden drop in sight or a painful, watery eye needs same-day contact with the practice or eye casualty.

scripts.notes: Whether keratoconus must be reported to the DVLA depends on the case; the script defers that to a later check. The family check advice reflects a known familial tendency.

turns.text: Good news first: I've had a really clear look at the back of both eyes, and the retina and the optic nerves are healthy. Your pupils were quite small, which is why I used the drops. They widen the pupil, like opening a window, so I can see the whole retina.
That's a relief. Everything's very blurry close up, though, and the lights are so bright.
That's the drops working. Your pupils are wide open, so more light gets in than usual, which is why it's glaring. The drops also relax the focusing muscle a little, so close things are blurred.
How long does it last?
Usually around four to six hours, though for some people it lasts until the next morning. It wears off gradually by itself.
Right. Well, I'd better get going.
Before you do, how did you get here today, and what are your plans for the rest of the afternoon?
I drove. I need to pick up my grandson from school in an hour. My daughter's at work, and there's nobody else.

I can see that's important, and you're in a difficult spot. I do have to be honest: I'd advise you not to drive until your vision is back to normal. The glare and the blurring make it harder to judge things. Every driver has a legal responsibility to make sure their eyesight is fit to drive, so the decision is yours, but I'd be letting you down if I didn't say so.
But I can see, just about. And it's only ten minutes away.
I know, and many people feel they could manage. But near a school, children step out suddenly, and that's exactly when glare and slow focusing matter. I'd much rather we found another way.
Like what? I can't leave him standing at the gate.

Of course not. Let's think it through together. Could you ring the school and ask whether he can stay at the after-school club, just today? Is there another parent or grandparent who could take him home with theirs? Or a taxi from here to the school and back, and collect your car later?
The school does have an after-school club. And my neighbour's granddaughter is in the same class.
Either of those would work well. You're welcome to use our phone, and to sit in the waiting room while you sort it out.
Let me ring my neighbour first. She'll do it, I'm sure. What about my car?
It can stay in our car park until your eyes are clear, or until tomorrow. Your daughter could bring you back for it this evening.
Okay. What should I do for the rest of today?
Wear sunglasses outside; it'll be much more comfortable. Leave close work like reading or sewing if it's blurry; it won't harm your eyes, it's just frustrating. And try not to rub them.
Is there anything else I should know about these drops?

There's one rare reaction I always mention, so you know what to look for. In a very small number of people whose eyes are shaped a certain way, widening the pupil can make the pressure inside the eye rise suddenly. It's uncommon, I checked your eyes before using the drops, and I'm not expecting it.
That sounds scary. What would happen?
You'd know about it. The warning signs are a painful, red eye, blurred vision with haloes or rainbows around lights, a headache over the eye, and often feeling sick or being sick.
And what would I do?
