Treat it as an emergency, because it needs treatment quickly. During our opening hours, ring us straight away. Otherwise go to the hospital eye casualty or A&E, today or tonight, and tell them you had dilating drops. If you're unsure, call 111. Don't wait to see whether it settles.
Painful red eye, haloes, headache, feeling sick. Eye casualty or A&E, and tell them about the drops.
Exactly. And the plan for this afternoon?
My neighbour collects my grandson, I don't drive until my eyes are normal, sunglasses, no rubbing, and the car stays here until my daughter brings me back.
That's perfect. I'll write the warning signs on a card for you to keep. Next time, you might bring someone with you or come by bus, in case we need the drops again.
I will. Thank you for talking me out of it.
Thank you for listening. Let me get you the phone.

coverage.how: Opens with the healthy result and why small pupils needed the drops.
Explains wide pupils letting in more light and the relaxed focusing muscle.
Gives four to six hours, sometimes until the next morning.
Asks how she travelled and about her afternoon plans.
Advises against driving, explains glare and focusing risks near a school, and her legal duty.
Works through the after-school club, a neighbour and a taxi, and offers the phone and waiting room.
Advises sunglasses, avoiding blurry close work and not rubbing.
Explains the rare pressure rise in certain eye shapes calmly, noting she was checked first.
Lists painful red eye, haloes, headache and nausea or vomiting.
Gives the practice in hours, eye casualty or A&E otherwise, 111 if unsure, and to mention the drops.
Asks her to repeat the plan and offers a written card.

concern.how: She reveals the school pickup when asked about her plans; the optometrist acknowledges the pressure on her, is honest about driving, and solves the problem with her until she arranges her neighbour.

safety.point: She should not drive until her vision has returned to normal.
A painful red eye, haloes, headache or nausea after dilation are warning signs of a sudden pressure rise.
These need urgent care: the practice in hours, eye casualty or A&E otherwise, or 111 if unsure, mentioning the drops.

scripts.notes: The card does not say whether her drainage angles were checked; the script says she was assessed before the drops, which is usual practice. The effect lasting four to six hours is typical for routine dilating drops.

turns.text: Thanks for bringing him in; he did really well. Could you tell me what you've noticed, when it happens, and how long you've seen it?
His left eye drifts in towards his nose, mostly when he's tired or looking at a book. It started maybe three months ago. You really see it in photos.
That's helpful. Does it happen every day, and does he ever tilt his head or cover one eye?
Most evenings. He sometimes screws one eye up in the sun, that's all.
You mentioned your own squint. Can you tell me about it, and anyone else in the family with eye problems?
I had an operation when I was about six. My sister had glasses young too. A lazy eye, I think.

That's useful; squints and long sight often run in families. Today I found two things. First, he's long-sighted, so his eyes work extra hard to focus, especially close up. Second, his left eye turns in a little, and its sight looks slightly lower than the right.
Why would long sight make the eye turn in?

Focusing and turning the eyes inwards are linked. When a child works hard to focus, the eyes tend to turn in too, and in some children one eye overdoes it. That's a squint: the eyes not pointing the same way.
My mum says he'll grow out of it. Lots of babies' eyes wander.
She's right that babies' eyes can wander in the first few months. But at his age, a true squint usually doesn't go away by itself, and waiting can lose valuable time.
Time for what?

A child's sight is still developing until around seven or eight. If one eye turns, the brain starts ignoring its picture, and that eye's sight may never fully develop; that's a lazy eye. The earlier it's treated, the better the chance of good sight.
So what happens now?

I'm referring him to the hospital children's eye service. He'll see an orthoptist, who specialises in how the eyes work together, and usually an eye doctor. They'll use drops that relax his focusing to measure his long sight accurately.
And then?

Glasses are usually the first treatment. They do the focusing work for him, so in many children the eye straightens a lot, or completely, while wearing them. If the left eye's sight stays lower, they may suggest patching the stronger eye for part of the day.
Will he need an operation? I had one, and I still remember the hospital. I hated it.

I'm sorry; that sounds like a hard memory. I can't promise, because it depends on how he responds to glasses. But many children whose squint is linked to long sight are treated with glasses alone. If an operation were ever suggested, the team would explain everything and help you prepare him.
That's better than I feared.
And children's eye units work hard to make visits less frightening now.
Okay. He's three, though. How do I get glasses on him?

Choose frames with him, so they feel like his. Flexible frames with a soft band help them stay on. Put them on for something he enjoys, like a favourite programme, and praise him lots. If he takes them off, calmly pop them back. Most children settle within a week or two.
Favourite programme, lots of praise. He loves diggers; there's probably a digger frame somewhere.

I'm sure there is. While you're waiting, contact us or your GP straight away if the eye suddenly turns much more, the other eye starts turning, he says he sees double, or an eye becomes red or painful.
Okay.
And one more thing: if you ever notice a white or unusual glow in his pupil in a photo instead of the usual red eye, get him checked urgently, within a day or two. I saw nothing like that today.
A white glow in photos. Got it.
Can I check I've explained things clearly? What will you tell his mum and your mum tonight?

He's long-sighted, his left eye turns in and won't go away by itself. The hospital will check him, probably glasses, maybe patching, and an operation isn't certain. Ring if it gets worse, double vision or a white glow.
That's exactly right. The hospital letter should come in the next few weeks; if nothing arrives within a month, ring us and we'll chase it.
Thank you. That's much less scary than I expected.

coverage.how: Asks what he has seen, when, and for how long, plus head tilting or covering an eye.
Asks about his own operation and other family eye problems.
Explains long sight as extra focusing effort and the slight turn and reduced sight in the left eye.
Links focusing effort with the eyes turning in and defines a squint.
Explains the developing visual system, the brain ignoring the eye, lazy eye and the value of early treatment.
Acknowledges wandering in young babies but states a true squint at this age rarely goes away.
Explains referral to the children's eye service, the orthoptist and drops to measure long sight.
Explains glasses often straighten the eye and patching may follow for weaker sight.
Acknowledges his memory, avoids promises and explains many such squints need glasses alone.
Gives tips on choosing frames, a favourite programme, praise and calm consistency.
Lists a worsening or new turn, double vision, red or painful eye, and a white glow in photos.
Asks what he will tell the family, confirms it and gives the chase timescale.

concern.how: He first relays his mother's view that the boy will grow out of it, then raises his dread of an operation; the optometrist corrects the first gently and answers the second honestly, explaining that glasses alone often suffice.

safety.point: A sudden worse or new turn, double vision, or a red or painful eye means contacting the practice or GP straight away.
A white or unusual glow in the pupil in photos needs urgent review within a day or two.

scripts.notes: The card does not give the father's family history beyond his own squint; the script adds a sister with a childhood lazy eye. Nothing abnormal was seen today in the pupil reflex; the white glow advice is general safety-netting.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for waiting. I'm the pharmacist, and thank you for letting me look at her face. Before I explain, can you tell me how the sores started and how they've changed?
Three days ago it was a little red spot by her mouth. Then it went blistery, burst, and now it's this yellow crust. She keeps picking at it.
That's really helpful. Has she been scratching anywhere else, and has anyone at home or in her class had anything similar?
Not at home. A boy in her class had something on his chin last week, I think.
And is she herself otherwise? Eating, playing, no temperature, no change in how she's behaving?
Yes, she's fine in herself. Just this.

Good. What I can see is impetigo. It's a common infection on the surface of the skin, caused by bacteria that often get in through a tiny scratch. The golden crust is typical. It's only a small patch, and that's the kind I can treat here today.
Impetigo. Another mum at the school gate said that's what kids get from dirty houses.

I'm glad you told me, because that simply isn't true. Impetigo is very common in young children, in every kind of home. It spreads by touch, at school or nursery. It says nothing about how you look after her.
It's just me and her now. I've been worried the school will think I'm not coping.

That sounds like a lot to carry. You noticed it early and brought her straight in, which is exactly right. Schools see impetigo every term. Would it help if I wrote a short note saying she's been assessed and treated here?
Yes, it would, actually.

Then I'll do that. For treatment, I can supply an antiseptic cream called hydrogen peroxide cream, under the NHS Pharmacy First service. It's a 5-day course. You apply a thin layer to the sores, usually two or three times a day; the label will tell you exactly.
Do I put it straight on top of the crusts?

Soften the crusts first with a clean cloth and warm water, then pat dry and apply the cream. Wash your hands before and after, and use a fresh cloth each time. Don't scrub the crusts off; it should never hurt.
Right. And how do I stop it spreading? She's always touching her face.
Keep her nails short and remind her not to pick the sores. Give her her own towel and flannel, and wash those and her pillowcase on a hot wash. Plenty of hand washing for both of you.
What about school? I'm meant to be at work tomorrow.

This is the hard bit, I'm afraid. The guidance is that she stays off until the sores have crusted over and healed, or until 48 hours after starting an antibiotic, if she ends up needing one. With the cream alone, it's when they've healed. I know that's difficult with work.
So it could be a few days. Why not just give her an antibiotic, so she's back sooner?

It's a fair question. For a small patch like this, the antiseptic cream works well, and using antibiotics only when they're needed keeps them working for her in future. If it isn't clearing, an antibiotic cream is the next step, and I can review that.
Okay, that makes sense.

There are some warning signs too. If the sores spread despite the cream, she gets a temperature or seems unwell, or you see large blisters or redness and swelling around them, bring her back or see the GP the same day. Out of hours, call 111.
And if it's just slow?
If it's not clearly better by the end of the 5-day course, come back and we'll look again. And tell us if it keeps coming back after it has cleared.
Got it.
Can I check I've explained it clearly? Could you tell me how you'll use the cream and what would make you come back?

Soften the crusts, pat dry, thin layer of cream two or three times a day for the course, and wash my hands. Own towel, short nails. Back if it spreads, she gets a temperature or big blisters, or it's not better after the course.
Exactly right. Here's a leaflet, and I'll write the school note now. She'll be fine, and so will you.
Thank you. That's a weight off.

coverage.how: Asks how the sores began and changed, about scratching, and about similar sores at home or school.
Checks she is eating, playing and herself, with no temperature or change in behaviour.
Names impetigo and explains it as a surface skin infection from bacteria entering a small scratch.
Corrects the hygiene myth directly, says how common it is, and praises his early action.
Explains the hydrogen peroxide antiseptic cream supplied under Pharmacy First as a 5-day course.
Explains softening the crusts, patting dry, applying a thin layer and washing hands before and after.
Gives practical steps: short nails, no picking, own towel and flannel, hot washes and hand washing.
States the school guidance honestly, including the 48-hour rule if an antibiotic is started.
Explains antiseptic first for a small patch to keep antibiotics working, with an antibiotic cream as the next step.
Gives same-day warning signs and a review point, then uses teach-back.

concern.how: The father repeats the dirty-homes remark and then admits he fears being judged as a single father; the pharmacist corrects the myth, acknowledges his load and offers a school note.

safety.point: Spreading sores, fever, feeling unwell, large blisters or surrounding redness need same-day review, or 111 out of hours.
Return if not clearly better by the end of the course, or if it keeps recurring.
Hand washing before and after applying the cream, and no scrubbing of crusts.

scripts.notes: The examination finding of localised, non-bullous impetigo with three small lesions and no systemic features is on the card. The dosing frequency of two or three times daily follows standard UK guidance for hydrogen peroxide 1% cream; a clinician should confirm the wording against the current Pharmacy First protocol.

turns.text: Hi, I'm the pharmacist. Let's step over here where it's quieter. You mentioned hay fever. Tell me what's been happening, and what you've tried so far.
Sneezing all day, my nose runs and then blocks, and my eyes are itchy and streaming. It's been two weeks. I haven't tried anything yet, but my friend's given me some of her tablets.
Okay. Before we talk about those, do you have asthma, or ever get wheezy, tight-chested or short of breath at this time of year?
No, never had asthma.
Good. Do you take any regular medicines, or have any other health conditions?
Just the contraceptive pill. Nothing else.

Thanks; that's fine with hay fever treatments. So, hay fever is your immune system overreacting to pollen as if it were harmful. It releases chemicals such as histamine, and those cause the sneezing, the runny nose and the itchy eyes.
Right. So can I just take my friend's tablets? They're antihistamines.
I'd advise against it. Medicines are chosen for one person, and borrowing them means you don't really know what you're taking. Do you know what hers are?
She said they make her sleepy, so probably the old kind.

Then they're likely a drowsy antihistamine. Those affect the brain more, and can leave you groggy and slow the next morning, even if you don't feel sleepy. The newer non-drowsy ones work just as well for most people without that effect.
That's actually what happened last summer. I took something drowsy and felt like I was in a fog in my exams.
That must have been horrible. How did the exams go?
Badly. I keep thinking it was my own fault for being ill. I'm scared it'll happen again, and mine start in 10 days.

It wasn't your fault. Hay fever genuinely affects concentration, and that tablet made it worse. This year we can plan properly. It's also worth telling your school's exams officer that you have hay fever, in case they can help, for example with seating away from open windows.
I didn't know I could do that. So what should I take?

A non-drowsy antihistamine tablet, once a day. It works best taken every day through the season, not just on bad days. A small number of people still feel a little drowsy, so start today, and you'll know well before your first exam.
Okay. Will that sort out my nose too?

It helps the sneezing and running, but a blocked nose responds better to a steroid nose spray. It calms the swelling inside your nose. It takes several days of daily use to work fully, so starting now gives it time before the exams.
A steroid? Is that safe?

Yes. It's a low dose that acts mainly inside the nose. Let me show you: blow your nose, tilt your head slightly forward, put the nozzle just inside one nostril, aim it towards the outside, away from the middle, and sniff gently. Then the other side.
Head forward, aim outwards. Got it. And my eyes?

If they're still itchy with the tablet, antihistamine eye drops can help. Also wear sunglasses outside, shower and change your clothes after being out, keep windows closed, and put a little balm around your nostrils to trap pollen.
That's easy enough. When should I see a doctor?

If you get wheezing, chest tightness or breathlessness, see your GP promptly, because hay fever can trigger asthma, and if breathing is very difficult, call 999. Also see your GP if these treatments haven't helped after a couple of weeks.
Okay.
Just so I know I've explained it well, could you tell me how you'll use each one?
Non-drowsy tablet once a day, every day, starting today. Nose spray every day, head forward, aim outwards. Eye drops if I need them. And I'll talk to the exams officer.
Perfect. And no borrowed tablets. Good luck with your exams, and come back any time if you need us.
Thanks, I feel much better about it.

coverage.how: Asks about symptoms, duration and what she has tried, which brings out the friend's tablets.
Asks about asthma, wheeze and chest tightness, then regular medicines and conditions.
Explains hay fever as the immune system overreacting to pollen, with histamine causing the symptoms.
Advises against borrowed tablets and contrasts drowsy with non-drowsy antihistamines.
Asks how last year's exams went, removes the self-blame and suggests telling the exams officer.
Recommends a once-daily non-drowsy antihistamine taken every day, starting now to test tolerance.
Explains the steroid spray, its several-day onset and the head-forward, aim-outwards technique.
Suggests antihistamine eye drops and gives pollen avoidance measures.
Gives GP and 999 thresholds for breathing symptoms and for poor response.
Uses teach-back for each product and closes.

concern.how: Her experience of drowsy tablets surfaces when drowsiness is explained; the pharmacist asks about the exams, removes the self-blame and builds the plan around the exam date.

safety.point: Borrowed or drowsy antihistamines can cause next-day grogginess and should be avoided before exams.
Wheeze, chest tightness or breathlessness need prompt GP review, and severe breathing difficulty a 999 call.
Start the non-drowsy tablet early to check it does not cause drowsiness before an exam.

scripts.notes: The patient's combined pill is invented and benign; it does not interact with antihistamines or nasal steroids. Over-the-counter steroid nasal sprays are licensed from 18 years, which fits the card's age.

turns.text: I can see you're really fed up, and I'd like to sort this out properly. Would you come into our consultation room, so we can talk in private?
Fine. But this is the third pharmacy today. Nobody can tell me anything, and I've got one patch left.

Three pharmacies in one afternoon is exhausting, and I'm sorry. Let me be straight with you. Your patch is out of stock with all our usual suppliers, and they've given no date for more. It's a supply problem, not something your GP or the other pharmacies have got wrong.
So what am I supposed to do? Just go without?
No, we'll find you an option. First, when is your current patch due to be changed?
I put it on yesterday, so it lasts until about Sunday or Monday.
That gives us a few days, which helps. How have you been since starting HRT?
Like a different person. Sleeping, no more soaking sheets.
And before you started, what were things like?
Awful. Night sweats every night, flushes in front of a class. I nearly gave up teaching. And we've got an inspection next week. If it all comes back then, I don't know what I'll do.
That sounds really frightening, especially with an inspection coming. So this isn't a small inconvenience; it's about your work and your sleep, and I'll treat it that way.
Thank you. Everyone acts like it's just a few hot flushes.

Menopause symptoms can be disabling, and you deserve proper treatment. Can I reassure you on one thing? A short gap in HRT isn't harmful to your health. To be honest, though, symptoms can come back within days, and you might have some irregular bleeding.
Bleeding? That's all I need.
It can happen when the hormone levels drop, and it should settle. But if the bleeding is heavy, or carries on after you restart, tell your GP, because that should always be checked.
Okay. So what are the options?

There are three. I can keep checking other suppliers. Your GP can prescribe an equivalent patch from another manufacturer. Or, if no patch is available, a different form of HRT could be used, such as an oestrogen gel with a separate progestogen, or tablets.
But I'd need a new prescription, and getting a GP appointment takes weeks.

You shouldn't need an appointment for this. I'll phone your practice myself this afternoon and ask them to issue an alternative, explaining that it's urgent. I'll also check whether there's an official shortage protocol for your patch, which can let me supply an alternative without a new prescription.
Can you really do that?
Only if one is in place nationally, so I won't promise it. But I'll look straight away, and the GP route works either way.
And how will I know what's happening? I can't keep ringing round.

I'll call you by six this evening with an update. Let me check I have the right mobile number. If the practice issues something, I'll order it today and aim to have it ready before your patch is due to be changed.
Okay. That's more than anyone else has done.
If you do switch products, the new one may feel slightly different at first, so give it a few weeks, and tell your GP if your symptoms don't settle. Is there anything else worrying you?
No. I think I just needed someone to listen.
Can I check we're agreed? Could you tell me the plan back, in your own words?
You'll call my GP and check for a shortage protocol, ring me by six, and I keep this patch on until it's due. If I get heavy bleeding, or it carries on after I restart, I tell the GP.
That's it exactly. Here's our direct number; ask for me by name. And good luck with the inspection.
Thanks. And sorry I shouted earlier.
There's no need to apologise. You'd had a really difficult day.

coverage.how: Invites her into the private room and acknowledges her frustration and the three pharmacies before explaining.
Explains the supply problem honestly and says it is nobody's error.
Asks when the current patch is due to be changed and how she has been on HRT.
Asks about symptoms before treatment and recognises the effect on her work and sleep.
Reassures her that a short gap is not harmful while warning about returning symptoms and bleeding.
Sets out other suppliers, an equivalent patch, or another form of HRT.
Offers to phone the practice herself and to check for an official shortage protocol, without promising one.
Commits to a call by six with an update and confirms her mobile number.
Advises her to report heavy bleeding or bleeding that continues after restarting.
Uses teach-back and gives a direct number.

concern.how: When asked about life before HRT she reveals her fear for the inspection and of being dismissed; the pharmacist names the impact and validates that menopause symptoms can be disabling.

safety.point: A short gap in HRT is not harmful, though symptoms may return.
Heavy bleeding, or bleeding that persists after restarting, must be reported to the GP.
A new product may take a few weeks to settle; tell the GP if symptoms persist.

scripts.notes: The patch change day and the alternative forms are generic. Whether a serious shortage protocol exists for any particular product changes over time, so the script does not claim that one is in place.

turns.text: Good morning, I'm the pharmacist. You asked about ibuprofen tablets for your knees. Before I suggest anything, could you tell me about the pain and how it affects you?
Both knees ache, the right one worse. Stiff first thing, and by the end of a game of bowls I'm limping.
Has it been getting worse lately? And have you noticed any swelling, redness or heat, or the knee locking or giving way?
Slowly worse over the years. No redness. A bit puffy sometimes. It doesn't lock.
Thank you. You said paracetamol did nothing. How did you take it, and for how long?
A couple when it was bad, for a week or so. Waste of time.

That's honest, and it matches what we know: paracetamol on its own often helps knee arthritis very little, so you're not imagining it. Can I check your health? I can see you take ramipril and a statin. Any kidney problems, stomach ulcers, indigestion or bleeding?
Kidneys are fine as far as I know. I had an ulcer years ago, mind.

That's important, thank you. It's the main reason I wouldn't recommend ibuprofen tablets for you. At your age, with a past ulcer and on ramipril, they raise the risk of bleeding from the stomach, can strain the kidneys, and can push your blood pressure up.
My mate at the club takes them every day and he's fine.
He may be, and his health may be different from yours. They're reasonable for some people, but for you the risk is real, and taking them every day makes it higher.
So what, then? I'm not giving up bowls.
I wouldn't want you to. What does bowls mean to you?
Everything, since my wife died last year. It's the only time I see people. If my knees stop me, I'm just sat at home.
I'm so sorry about your wife. Then let's make this plan about keeping you playing. The first choice for knee arthritis is an anti-inflammatory gel, rubbed into the knees.
A gel? That's not real medicine.

It's a fair thought, but it's the same type of medicine as ibuprofen. Rubbed over the knee, it works in the joint, and much less reaches your stomach and kidneys. Knees are close to the skin, so it works well for many people.
Right. How do I use it?

Rub a small amount gently into each sore knee, usually three times a day; the pack will tell you. Wash your hands afterwards, and don't put it on broken skin or cover it tightly. Give it a week or two of regular use.
And that's it?

Not quite. Exercise is the other main treatment. Strengthening your thigh muscles takes pressure off the knees. Your GP can refer you to physiotherapy for a programme, and bowls itself keeps you moving.
So moving is good? I thought I was wearing them out.
No, staying active helps arthritis. A walking stick on bad days and comfortable cushioned shoes can help too. If the gel and exercise aren't enough, your GP can talk about other options.
Okay. Anything I should watch for?

Yes. If a knee becomes hot, red and very swollen, you can't put weight on it, or you feel feverish, get seen the same day or call 111. And if you ever pass black, sticky stools or vomit blood, call 999.
Right. I'll remember that.
Let's see how you get on. Could you pop back in about two weeks and tell me how the gel is going?
I can do that. I'm in for my prescriptions anyway.
Great. Just so I'm sure I've been clear, could you tell me the plan?
Gel rubbed in, three times a day, no ibuprofen tablets. Ask the GP about physio. Back in a fortnight. Seen the same day if a knee's hot and swollen, and black stools mean 999.
Spot on. Let's keep you on the green.

coverage.how: Asks how the pain affects him, its progression, and about swelling, redness, heat and locking.
Asks how he took paracetamol and says honestly that it often helps knee arthritis little.
Asks about kidney problems, ulcers, indigestion and bleeding, which brings out the past ulcer.
Links the oral ibuprofen risks to his age, past ulcer and ramipril.
Accepts that the friend may be fine and explains why his own risk is different.
Asks what bowls means to him and frames the plan around keeping him playing.
Recommends a topical anti-inflammatory gel, explains why it is safer, and explains how to use it.
Explains strengthening exercise, corrects the wearing-out belief and suggests asking the GP about physiotherapy.
Mentions a stick and cushioned shoes, and that the GP can discuss other options.
Gives same-day signs for a hot swollen knee and 999 signs of gastrointestinal bleeding.
Arranges a review in about two weeks and uses teach-back.

concern.how: His refusal to give up bowls is explored rather than argued with, revealing his bereavement and isolation; the plan is framed around keeping him playing, and his doubt about gels is answered.

safety.point: Oral ibuprofen is unsuitable given his age, previous ulcer and ramipril.
A hot, red, swollen knee, inability to bear weight or fever needs same-day review or 111.
Black stools or vomiting blood need a 999 call.

scripts.notes: The past stomach ulcer is in the hidden concern. The examination is not described; the history given is benign, with no red, hot joint. Topical NSAID frequency is given as usually three times daily, as for common ibuprofen gels; the pack should be followed.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the pharmacist who gives the vaccinations. Your daughter booked today, but I'd like to hear from you first. What do you know about the flu vaccine, and what's making you unsure?
She worries about me. But honestly, I had the jab last year and was in bed for a week after. I think it gave me flu.
A week in bed sounds miserable; no wonder you're hesitant. Can I explain what's in the vaccine?
Go on.

The injection contains no live virus, so it can't give you flu. Some people feel achy for a day or so afterwards, which is the immune system responding. But a week in bed sounds like a separate illness. Autumn is peak season for colds and other viruses, and the vaccine doesn't protect against those.
So it was just bad luck?
Most likely, yes. The vaccine also takes about two weeks to build protection, so catching something soon afterwards is a coincidence of timing.
I see. But I'm on a blood thinner for my heart. Should I have anything injected at all?

That's a sensible question. In fact, your heart rhythm problem, your diabetes and your age are exactly why it's offered to you. Flu can be far more serious for you: it can cause pneumonia, put strain on the heart, and upset your blood sugar.
I didn't know that.

The apixaban isn't a reason to avoid it. I'll use a fine needle into the muscle of your upper arm, then press firmly on the spot for a couple of minutes, without rubbing. You might get a small bruise, but bleeding is very unlikely.
And what will I feel afterwards?
Most commonly a sore arm, perhaps a little redness, and sometimes feeling tired or achy for a day or two. Paracetamol can help if needed. Serious reactions are rare.
How rare? What kind?

Very rarely, someone has a severe allergic reaction within minutes. I'm trained to recognise and treat it, and I have emergency medicine here in the room. Can I check a few things? Are you well today, with no fever?
I'm fine. A bit of a sniffle, that's all.
A sniffle without a fever is fine. Have you ever had a serious reaction to a vaccine, or a severe allergy to anything?
No, nothing like that. Just the week in bed.
Thank you. The decision is completely yours. You can have it today, think it over and come back, or decide not to have it. Nobody here will be cross either way.
My daughter might be.
She clearly cares about you. But it's your arm and your choice. Is there anything else you'd like to know before you decide?
No, you've explained it. I'll have it.
Thank you. So, to confirm, you're happy for me to give you the flu vaccine in your left arm today?
Yes. Left is fine.
Lovely. Afterwards I'll record which vaccine you had, its batch number and today's date, and the details will go to your GP practice so that your records are up to date.
All right. Then I can go?

Yes, after a short sit in the waiting area. If you have a temperature, or aches lasting more than a couple of days, or your arm becomes very swollen, hot or painful, ring us or call 111. If you have any trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a rash spreading fast, call 999.
Breathing trouble or a swollen face means 999. Got it.
Exactly. And what will you do if you just feel achy?
Rest, paracetamol, and ring you if it lasts more than a couple of days or the arm's bad.
Perfect. If you'd roll up your left sleeve, we'll do it now.

coverage.how: Asks what she knows and what makes her unsure, drawing out last year's illness.
Explains there is no live virus and offers seasonal viruses and timing as the likely explanation.
Links the offer to her heart rhythm problem, diabetes and age.
Explains a fine needle and firm pressure without rubbing because of apixaban.
Describes a sore arm and mild aches for a day or two, managed with paracetamol.
Explains the rare severe allergic reaction and that the pharmacist is trained and equipped.
Checks she is well without fever and asks about previous vaccine reactions and severe allergies.
States the choice is hers, including saying no, and asks for consent in plain words.
Explains recording the vaccine, batch and date and informing the GP practice.
Gives 111 and 999 thresholds and checks her understanding.

concern.how: Her belief that the vaccine caused flu and her fear about her heart and blood thinner surface in turn; each is acknowledged and answered with plain facts linked to her own conditions.

safety.point: Firm pressure without rubbing after injection because she takes apixaban.
Trained and equipped to manage the rare severe allergic reaction.
Breathing difficulty, face or throat swelling or a fast-spreading rash need a 999 call.

scripts.notes: No previous anaphylaxis, current fever or other contraindication is assumed, as the patient confirms in the script. Inactivated injected influenza vaccines are used for adults in this age group; a clinician should confirm the observation wording against the local service protocol.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the pharmacist. The hospital asked us to see you about your new medicines. First of all, how have you been since you got home?
Not bad. Tired, a bit shaky. They went through it all very fast, though. I've got a bag of boxes and no idea what's what.
That's really common after a heart attack; there's a lot to take in. What did you understand from the hospital?
That an artery was blocked, they put a stent in, and these stop it happening again.

That's right. Let's go through them box by box. Aspirin and ticagrelor both stop blood cells called platelets sticking together, so a clot can't form. Atorvastatin lowers cholesterol and protects the artery walls. Bisoprolol slows and protects your heart. Ramipril lowers blood pressure and helps the heart muscle recover.
And the spray?

The GTN spray is for chest pain; I'll come back to it. The most important two are aspirin and ticagrelor. Your stent is new, and for the next 12 months it needs both. If either is stopped early, a clot can form in the stent and cause another heart attack.
Both? Even for a few days?
Even for a few days. Why do you ask? Is something coming up?
I've a dental check-up next week. My brother was told to stop his blood thinners before the dentist, so I was going to stop these on Sunday.

I'm really glad you mentioned it. Please don't stop them. Check-ups and most dental treatment are done safely on these tablets. Tell your dentist about the heart attack and the stent, and show them your list. If they ever suggest stopping, they should speak to your heart team first.
Blimey. I'd have done it without asking anyone.

Lots of people would, which is why I'll write it on your medicine list. You may bruise more easily, and your gums may bleed a little when brushing; that's expected. But blood in your urine, black stools or bleeding that won't stop needs urgent advice.
Okay. Anything else they do?

Ticagrelor can make some people feel short of breath at first; tell your GP if that bothers you. Bisoprolol can cause tiredness or cold hands. Ramipril sometimes causes a dry cough. Atorvastatin can occasionally cause muscle aches; report any unexplained muscle pain.
Now the spray. When do I use it?

If you get chest pain, stop and sit down. Use one or two sprays under your tongue, then close your mouth. If the pain isn't gone after five minutes, use it again. If it's still there five minutes after the second dose, call 999 straight away. It can make you dizzy or give you a headache, which is why you sit.
Sit, spray, wait, spray again, then 999.
Exactly. Do you ever buy painkillers for aches and pains?
Ibuprofen sometimes, for my back.

Please avoid ibuprofen and similar anti-inflammatories, including those in some cold remedies. With your blood thinners they raise the bleeding risk, and they're hard on the heart and kidneys. Paracetamol is the safer choice. Always tell the pharmacist what you take before buying anything.
Right. What about work? I drive all day.

Driving is a big question after a heart attack, and the rules depend on what you drive. Please ask the cardiac rehabilitation team before you go back; they'll advise on driving, exercise and returning to work.
They've phoned already. I've got an appointment.

Good. Now supplies. The hospital has given you a few weeks' worth. Order repeats from your GP when you're down to about a week's worth, so you never run out. Your GP practice will also review these medicines with you.
Okay. That's a lot.
It is. Can I check the most important bits? What will you do about the dentist, and what will you do if you get chest pain?
Keep taking both blood thinners and tell the dentist about the stent. Chest pain: sit down, spray, wait five minutes, spray again, then 999 if it's still there.
That's exactly right. And how long do you take the ticagrelor?
12 months, unless the heart team says otherwise.
Perfect. Here's a written list with all of that on it. Ring me if anything is unclear.

coverage.how: Asks how he has been and what he understood from the hospital.
Names each medicine from the boxes and says in one plain sentence what it does.
Explains that both antiplatelets protect the stent for 12 months and that stopping early risks a clot.
Asks what is coming up, uncovers the dental plan and advises continuing and informing the dentist.
Covers bruising and bleeding to report, ticagrelor breathlessness, and the main effects of the others.
Gives the sit, spray, five-minute repeat and 999 plan for GTN, with dizziness and headache.
Asks about painkillers, advises avoiding ibuprofen and similar, and suggests paracetamol.
Refers driving and work questions to the cardiac rehabilitation team.
Explains ordering repeats when down to a week's supply and a GP medicines review.
Uses teach-back for the dental plan, GTN plan and ticagrelor duration, then gives a written list.

concern.how: His question about stopping for a few days is followed up, revealing the plan to stop both tablets before the dentist; the pharmacist advises against it and records the advice on his list.

safety.point: Do not stop aspirin or ticagrelor early, including before dental treatment, without the heart team.
Blood in the urine, black stools or bleeding that will not stop need urgent advice.
GTN: sit down, repeat after five minutes, and call 999 if pain persists five minutes after the second dose.
Avoid ibuprofen and similar anti-inflammatories with antiplatelets.

scripts.notes: The size of the hospital supply and the absence of current chest pain are invented and benign. The GTN instructions follow standard UK patient advice. Driving rules are deliberately referred to the cardiac team because they depend on licence group.

turns.text: Thanks for sitting still for those readings. Before I tell you the result, how are you feeling? Any headaches, chest pain, breathlessness or changes in your eyesight?
None of that. Fit as a fiddle. Go on, how bad is it?
Both readings were close to 158 over 96. The top number is the pressure when your heart pumps, and the bottom one is when it rests between beats. Both are higher than we'd like.
Ha. White coat nerves, that's all. You lot make me nervous.
That's a real thing, actually. Readings in a pharmacy or surgery can be higher than at home, so one visit isn't enough to diagnose high blood pressure. We need to confirm it first.
So how do you confirm it?

With an ambulatory monitor. It's a cuff on your arm connected to a small box on your belt. It measures your blood pressure regularly for 24 hours while you carry on as normal, overnight included. That gives a much truer picture.
Sounds a faff. Does it hurt?
It squeezes a bit, like today, and might wake you once or twice. You'd bring it back the next day. I can book you in this week if you like.
Go on, then. Thursday?
Thursday's fine. Can I ask, does anyone in your family have high blood pressure, heart disease or a stroke?
My dad had a stroke. He was 52. Never worked again. Couldn't even talk properly.
I'm so sorry. That must have been very hard to watch. Is that on your mind today?
Honestly, yes. I'm 47. Is that going to be me?

I can understand that fear. Your dad's stroke does raise your risk somewhat, and high blood pressure is a major cause of strokes. But you've found this early, while you feel well. If it's confirmed, treatment lowers the risk of stroke and heart attack considerably. Most people never feel high blood pressure, which is why checks matter.
So I'd be on tablets for life?
Not necessarily. That depends on the monitor results and on your GP. But whatever they show, there's a lot you can do yourself, starting now.
Like what?

Cutting down on salt, especially in ready meals and takeaways. Keeping alcohol within the recommended limits. Being active most days, even brisk walking. And the biggest one for your heart and arteries: stopping smoking.
I knew that was coming. I've tried before.

Most people need a few attempts, so that isn't failure. We run a stop smoking service here: regular support from me, plus nicotine patches or other products. People are much more likely to succeed with support than on their own. Would you like to start?
Maybe. Can I think about it until Thursday?
Of course; we'll talk about it when you collect the monitor. Your readings today and the monitor results will be sent to your GP, who will decide on the next steps with you.
Will I hear from them?
Yes, the surgery should contact you once they've seen the results. If you haven't heard within a couple of weeks, give them a ring.
Fine. Anything I should look out for in the meantime?
It's very unlikely, but if you get a sudden severe headache, chest pain, or signs of a stroke such as a drooping face, a weak arm or slurred speech, call 999 immediately.
Face, arm, speech. Like the adverts.
Exactly. Just so I know I've been clear, could you tell me what happens next?
Monitor on Thursday for a day and a night, results to my GP, think about stopping smoking, and 999 for stroke signs or bad chest pain.
Perfect. You've done the right thing coming in today.

coverage.how: Asks how he feels and about headache, chest pain, breathlessness and vision changes.
Gives the reading clearly and explains the top and bottom numbers.
Takes the white coat comment seriously and explains that clinic readings can run high and must be confirmed.
Offers and explains the 24-hour ambulatory monitor and books it.
Asks about family history and responds to his fear about his father's stroke.
Explains honestly why high blood pressure matters and that treatment lowers risk.
Discusses salt, alcohol, activity and smoking as steps to start now.
Offers the pharmacy stop smoking service and revisits it at collection.
Explains that results go to the GP, who will decide next steps, and what to do if he hears nothing.
Gives 999 symptoms and uses teach-back.

concern.how: His joke about white coat nerves is taken seriously, and the family history question brings out his father's stroke; the pharmacist names the fear and answers it with honest, hopeful facts.

safety.point: A single raised reading is confirmed with ambulatory monitoring before diagnosis.
Sudden severe headache, chest pain or stroke signs need a 999 call.
Contact the GP if no word arrives after a couple of weeks.

scripts.notes: He has no symptoms, as the script states. A reading close to 158/96 sits in the range where UK guidance offers ambulatory monitoring rather than urgent same-day referral.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the pharmacist. I'm sorry you're feeling so rough. Before I suggest anything, how often are you having diarrhoea and being sick, and how much are you managing to drink?
Diarrhoea maybe six times since yesterday. Sick three or four times, less this morning. I can keep sips of water down.
That's good; sips are the right approach. Do you feel dizzy when you stand up, is your mouth very dry, or are you passing much less urine than usual?
A bit lightheaded if I get up quickly. Not weeing as much, now you mention it.

Thank you. Most stomach bugs settle by themselves within a few days. The main risk is losing too much fluid, and that's what we need to manage. How have you been taking your usual tablets since you became ill?
I've been forcing them down. Twice they've come straight back up.
That sounds horrible. What made you keep going with them?
My doctor said never miss them. If I stop my blood pressure or diabetes tablets, I'll have a stroke, won't I? I'm on my own. It frightens me.
I can see why you've been so careful, and usually that's exactly right. But when you're losing fluid, the rules change for a few days. They're called sick day rules, and they're standard advice.
Sick day rules? Nobody told me.

When you're dehydrated, the kidneys get less blood. Ramipril and indapamide can lower your blood pressure further and strain the kidneys. Metformin can build up if the kidneys aren't working well, which can be dangerous. So it's safer to pause all three for now.
But my sugar will go sky high.

A few days without metformin is very unlikely to cause harm, especially while you're eating little, and pausing your blood pressure tablets briefly won't put you at risk of a stroke. Restart all three once you've been eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours.
So stop them, and start again a day or two after I'm eating properly.

Exactly, and I'll write that down for you. For fluids, I'd recommend oral rehydration sachets. Mix one with the amount of water on the packet, sip it slowly, and have more after each loose stool. They replace salts as well as water.
Can't I have something to stop the diarrhoea? It's awful.

As you've no blood and no fever, you could take loperamide for a short time. Take it as the packet says, and stop if you become constipated, your tummy swells, or you get a temperature. It won't cure the bug, it just slows things down, so the fluids are still the main thing.
All right. How long should this last?

Usually a few days. But if you can't keep any fluids down, you pass very little urine, feel confused or very drowsy, faint, see blood in your stools, or it isn't easing after a few days, contact your GP the same day or call 111.
And if it's really bad?
If you collapse, become very confused or have severe tummy pain, call 999.
Okay.
You said you're on your own. Is there someone who could check on you today and tomorrow?
My neighbour. She'd pop in if I asked.
Please do ask her. And stay at home until you've had no diarrhoea or vomiting for two days, so you don't pass it on, and wash your hands well.
I'll text her when I get home.
Lovely. Can you tell me the plan, so I know I've explained it clearly?

Stop the metformin, ramipril and water tablet for now, and restart after a day or two of eating and drinking normally. Sachets, and loperamide for a short time. GP or 111 if I can't keep fluids down, there's blood, or I'm hardly weeing.
That's exactly right. Here are the sachets, the loperamide and your written plan. I hope you feel better soon.
Thank you. That's a real relief.

coverage.how: Asks frequency of diarrhoea and vomiting and how much she is drinking.
Asks about postural dizziness, dry mouth and reduced urine.
Explains that most bugs settle in a few days and that fluid loss is the main risk.
Asks how she has been taking her tablets and why she persisted.
Explains reduced kidney blood flow, ramipril and indapamide effects and metformin build-up.
Advises pausing all three and restarting after 24 to 48 hours of normal eating and drinking.
Recommends oral rehydration sachets and explains how to make up and sip them.
Judges loperamide suitable without blood or fever, with short use and stop rules.
Lists same-day and 999 warning signs clearly.
Asks who can check on her, advises staying home and hand washing, and uses teach-back.

concern.how: Asking why she kept taking tablets that she vomited brings out her fear of a stroke and of being alone; the pharmacist validates her care, then explains why a brief pause is safe.

safety.point: Pause metformin, ramipril and indapamide while dehydrated and restart after 24 to 48 hours of normal eating and drinking.
Stop loperamide if constipated, the abdomen swells or a fever develops.
Unable to keep fluids down, very little urine, confusion, fainting or blood in the stools need same-day help or 111.
Collapse, marked confusion or severe abdominal pain need a 999 call.

scripts.notes: The stool and vomit frequencies and mild postural light-headedness are invented and consistent with mild dehydration suitable for self-care with close safety-netting. The neighbour is invented. The 48-hour exclusion is given in words as two days.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the pharmacist. You said you'd rather just use the moisturiser, and that's your choice, but I'd like to understand. What worries you about the steroid cream?
Steroids thin the skin. I've read about children getting hooked on them, and about steroid withdrawal.
Those are understandable worries; lots of parents have them. Have you seen anything happen to someone you know?
My sister. She used strong creams from abroad for years, on her face. Her skin's thin and marked now.

I'm sorry; that must have been upsetting to see, and it makes your caution reasonable. What happened to your sister came from very strong creams used for years without supervision. This is hydrocortisone 1%, the mildest type, used on small patches for a short time. Used like that, skin thinning is very unlikely.
So it's not the same thing?
Not the same strength, and not the same way of using it. How has he been sleeping?
Badly. He scratches till it bleeds and wakes up crying. None of us sleep. I feel terrible, like I'm letting him down.

You're clearly not letting him down; you're trying to protect him, which is why you're asking. The trouble is, once eczema is inflamed, the itch makes him scratch, scratching inflames it more, and moisturiser alone often can't break that cycle. The steroid calms the inflammation so the skin can heal.
How long would he need it?

Only while the patches are red, usually a week or two, then stop. Use it as the label says, on the red patches only, not on normal skin. For the amount, we use fingertip units: a line squeezed from the tip of an adult finger to the first crease covers an area about the size of two adult hands.
That's less than I imagined.

It is. Keep using the emollient every day, lots of it and often, even when the eczema has cleared, because it protects the skin. Smooth it on in the direction the hair grows. Leave a gap between the emollient and the steroid, so one doesn't dilute the other.
Okay. Anything else with the moisturiser?

One important safety point. Emollients soak into clothes and bedding, and fabric with emollient in it can catch fire easily. So keep him away from open flames and heaters, and wash his clothes and bedding often. That applies to paraffin-free ones too.
I never knew that.
Few people do. For the nights, keep his nails short, try cotton sleepsuits that cover the skin, keep the bedroom cool, and put the emollient on before bed. A soap substitute in the bath helps too.
We could try cotton pyjamas.

Good idea. Now, watch for infection. If the eczema becomes weepy, crusted or very sore, spreads quickly, or he has a temperature, see the GP that day. Clusters of small painful blisters or punched-out sores need urgent same-day help; call 111 if the surgery is closed.
Blisters means urgent. Right.
And if it isn't clearly better after a week or two of using both creams properly, or it keeps coming back, go back to your GP.
So you think I should use it.
I think it'll help him, and used this way it's safe. But you're his mum, and I want you to feel comfortable. What are you thinking now?
I'll try it. A week or so, small amounts, on the red bits.
That sounds very sensible. Would a written plan help, so you know which cream goes where?
Yes, please.
Here it is. Before you go, could you tell me how you'll use each cream?

Steroid only on the red patches, fingertip amounts, as the label says, and stop when it's settled. Moisturiser lots, every day. A gap between them. Away from flames. GP that day if it's weepy, and urgent if it's blistered.
Perfect. I hope you all get a good night's sleep soon.
Thank you. I feel much better about it.

coverage.how: Asks what worries her and whether she has seen problems in someone she knows.
Validates the worry and contrasts a mild short course with years of strong unsupervised creams.
Explains the itch-scratch cycle and why moisturiser alone may not settle a flare.
Explains red patches only, as labelled, fingertip units, and stopping when the flare settles.
Explains generous, frequent emollient use beyond the flare and a gap between the two creams.
Warns about emollient-soaked fabric catching fire, including paraffin-free products.
Asks about his sleep and the family, then gives night-time measures.
Gives same-day signs of infection and urgent signs of eczema herpeticum, with 111.
Agrees a return to the GP if not better after a week or two or if it recurs.
Asks what she now thinks, offers a written plan and uses teach-back for each cream.

concern.how: Asking whether she has seen harm brings out her sister's experience, and asking about sleep brings out her guilt; both are acknowledged before the explanation.

safety.point: Emollient in fabric is a fire risk; keep away from flames and heaters.
Weeping, crusted, painful or spreading eczema or fever needs same-day GP review; clustered painful blisters are urgent.
Mild steroid only on red patches, for a short time, as labelled.

scripts.notes: The treatment duration of usually a week or two reflects typical UK advice for a mild topical steroid in a flare; the prescription label governs. The bleeding from scratching is invented but common and benign.

turns.text: Thank you for letting me look. Can you tell me more about the pain and the rash, and whether you've had any rash on your face or near your eye?
It started as burning on my right side, like a scald, four days ago. Then the spots came up. Nothing on my face.
And do you feel unwell otherwise? Any fever, headache or problems with your eyesight?
No, just tired and sore.

Thank you. This is shingles. It's caused by the chickenpox virus. After you've had chickenpox, the virus stays asleep in a nerve for years, and later it can wake up and travel along that nerve to the skin. That's why the pain came first, and why the rash is a band on one side.
Shingles. My husband had it. He was in pain for months afterwards.
I'm sorry; that must make this worrying. Is that what's on your mind?
That, and the baby. I look after my granddaughter. Could I give it to her?

Let me take each in turn. First, the good news: your rash appeared within the last 72 hours, so I can supply antiviral tablets today. They help the rash heal faster and may ease the pain. They can't promise you won't have pain afterwards, but starting early gives the best chance.
Good. Is there anything I should know?
Do you take any other medicines, including anything you buy, and do you have any allergies or kidney problems?
Just a cholesterol tablet. No allergies, and my kidneys are fine.
Those are fine together. Take the tablets as the label says, spaced through the day, and finish the whole course even if you feel better. Drink plenty of water while you're taking them.
And the pain now?

Paracetamol regularly, as the packet says. Wear loose cotton clothes, keep the rash clean and dry, and if clothes rub, cover it loosely with a non-sticky dressing. Avoid sticky plasters on the blisters.
And the baby?

You can't give anyone shingles, but someone who has never had chickenpox can catch chickenpox from the fluid in your blisters. Babies less than a month old, pregnant women who haven't had chickenpox, and people with weak immune systems are most at risk.
She's only 3 weeks old.
Yes, so I'm sorry, but please don't look after her until all your blisters have crusted over. That's usually about a week. I know that's hard news.
My daughter's back at work. She relies on me. What do I tell her?

Tell her plainly that it's shingles and you're staying away from the baby until the blisters crust over, to keep her safe. Perhaps her partner or another relative could cover for a week. Would it help if I wrote a short note explaining it?
Yes. She'll take it better from you.

I'll do that. About your husband: some people do get nerve pain that carries on after the rash heals. If that happens, see your GP; there are specific nerve pain medicines that can help when ordinary painkillers don't.
That's reassuring.
If the rash spreads to your face, near your eye or all over your body, your vision changes, or you feel very unwell or confused, get help the same day from your GP, or call 111.
Face or eye, same day.
Exactly. And once you're better, ask your GP about the shingles vaccine; it lowers the chance of it coming back. Could you tell me the plan, so I know I've been clear?
Tablets for the full course, paracetamol, loose clothes. No looking after the baby until the blisters crust. GP or 111 if it reaches my face or eye. And ask about the vaccine.
Perfect. I'll write your daughter's note now.
Thank you, dear. That's a weight off my mind.

coverage.how: Asks about the pain, the rash, face or eye involvement and systemic symptoms.
Explains shingles as the reactivated chickenpox virus travelling along a nerve.
Explains the within-72-hours antiviral supply and what it can and cannot achieve.
Checks medicines, allergies and kidneys, then explains completing the course.
Advises paracetamol, loose clothing, keeping the rash clean and dry, and loose non-sticky cover.
Explains that blister fluid can cause chickenpox in non-immune people and names those most at risk.
Says clearly she must not look after the baby until all blisters crust, and helps plan what to tell her daughter.
Explains post-shingles nerve pain and that the GP has specific treatments.
Lists same-day signs: face, eye or widespread rash, vision change, feeling very unwell or confused.
Mentions asking the GP about the shingles vaccine and uses teach-back.

concern.how: The diagnosis prompts her memory of her husband, and an open question brings out the fear for the baby; the news about childcare is given kindly with a practical plan, and the husband's pain is answered later.

safety.point: Avoid the 3-week-old baby, pregnant women without chickenpox immunity and immunosuppressed people until all blisters crust over.
Rash on the face or near the eye, vision change, widespread rash or feeling very unwell or confused needs same-day help or 111.
Complete the antiviral course and drink plenty of water.

scripts.notes: The cholesterol tablet is invented and benign, with no relevant interaction with aciclovir or valaciclovir. The timing of shingles vaccination after an episode is left to the GP. Crusting usually takes about a week.

turns.text: Hello again, come in and have a seat. I've had a look at your X-ray report, and I'd like to go through it with you. First, though, how has the shoulder been since we met?
Not good. It's stiffer, if anything. And the nights are the worst part. I wake every time I roll onto it.
That sounds exhausting. What is it stopping you doing, at home and at work?
I can't do my bra up or reach my back pocket. At the salon, holding the hairdryer up is agony by the afternoon.
Thank you, that helps. So, the X-ray was normal. That means no arthritis, no fracture and nothing worrying in the bone, which is good news.
But then why can't I move it? If the X-ray's normal, surely nobody actually knows what's wrong.

I can see why it feels like that. An X-ray shows bone well, but not the soft lining around the joint, which is where your problem is. So the normal result is useful: it rules other things out and supports what I found.
So what is it, then?

It's called frozen shoulder. The joint sits inside a sort of bag, called the capsule. In frozen shoulder that lining becomes inflamed, then thickens and tightens, like a jumper shrinking in the wash. That's why every direction is limited. Does that make sense?
I've heard of it. Does it go away?

For most people, yes. It usually moves through three stages: a painful stage, a stiff stage, then a slow thaw as movement returns. To be honest, though, it often takes many months, sometimes more than a year.
That long? The doctor mentioned my diabetes. Is this my fault for not controlling it?
Not at all. Frozen shoulder is simply more common with diabetes, even when it's well controlled. Do mention it at your next diabetes review, though.
All right. So what can actually be done?

There are a few options. Pain relief, which your GP or pharmacist can advise on, helps you sleep and keep moving. Gentle exercise within comfort keeps the movement you have. And a steroid injection can ease pain during this painful phase.
Should I be stretching it hard to get it moving? My friend said to push through.

Right now, no. Forcing painful stretches irritates the lining and makes the pain worse. Try these instead. Lean on the table, let the arm hang and swing it in small circles. Then slide your hand forward along the table as far as is comfortable. Little and often.
That's easier than I thought. What about the nights?
Lie on your back or other side, with a pillow supporting the sore arm. For dressing, sore arm in first and out last. At work, could you rest the arm between clients for a while?
Maybe. But that's the thing. What if it never comes back properly? I've done hair for twenty years.
That sounds like a real worry. Is it your job you're most concerned about?
Yes. If I can't lift my arms, I can't work. I've been lying awake over it.

I'm glad you told me. Most people get most of their movement back, and many return to everything they did before. Some keep a little stiffness, but rarely enough to stop them working. And I can write a note for your employer about adapting your work.
That would help. And the injection, would I have that here?

We can arrange that with your GP, depending on what's offered locally. Meanwhile, if you get a fever, the shoulder becomes hot, red or swollen, you notice new weakness, or the pain becomes severe and constant, see a doctor promptly, or call 111 out of hours.
Hot, red, swollen, fever, weakness or constant severe pain. Got it.
Exactly. So: gentle exercises little and often, a pillow at night, a conversation about pain relief and the injection, and adapting work. What will you do this week?
The swinging and the table slide a few times a day, pillow at night, ask about pain relief, and see if the salon will let me take breaks.
Perfect. Let's book a review in three weeks to check your progress and talk about the injection again. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No, I feel better knowing what it is. Thank you.
You're welcome. It's a frustrating condition, but it does improve. I'll see you in three weeks.

coverage.how: Asks how the shoulder has been and what the night pain and stiffness stop her doing at work and home.
Explains that the X-ray rules out bony causes but cannot show the capsule, so it supports the clinical findings.
Names frozen shoulder and explains the inflamed, thickened, tight capsule with a plain analogy.
Describes the painful, stiff and thawing stages and is honest that it often takes many months or longer.
States the diabetes link without blame and suggests raising it at her diabetes review.
Covers pain relief via GP or pharmacist, gentle exercise and a steroid injection, and how the injection is accessed.
Advises against forced stretching and teaches pendulum and table-slide exercises, little and often.
Gives sleeping position with pillow support, dressing order and work adaptations.
Asks what worries her most and gives an honest, hopeful answer about recovery and work, with an offer of a letter.
Lists fever, hot red swollen joint, new weakness and severe constant pain as reasons for prompt medical review.
Summarises, asks her to say back the plan and books a review in three weeks.

concern.how: Her doubt about the normal X-ray is answered first; later her fear about never recovering and losing her job is invited, named and met with honest reassurance and practical work support.

safety.point: Fever, a hot, red or swollen shoulder, new arm weakness or severe constant pain needs prompt medical review, or 111 out of hours.
Forcing painful stretches in the painful phase is avoided because it aggravates the capsule.

scripts.notes: The card does not say where steroid injections are given; the script defers to the local pathway via GP or physiotherapy referral. The three-week review interval is the script's choice.

turns.text: Thanks for waiting while I wrote up my notes. Before I explain what I found, could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?
I start about eight, sit at the kitchen table with my laptop and usually just work through. Lunch at the desk, mostly. I finish around six.
So a long stretch looking down at the laptop. Do you take breaks or move around at all?
Not really. Making tea, maybe. Since I stopped commuting I barely leave the house on weekdays.

That's really common since people started working from home. So, my findings. The muscles in your neck and upper back are tight and tender, and the joints are a little stiff. Importantly, the tests of your nerves, your strength and the feeling in your arms were all normal.
That's good, I suppose. But what about the headaches?

The neck and head share nerves, so when the top of the neck is stiff and the muscles are tired, you can feel a dull headache, often at the back of the head. By late afternoon those muscles have held your head over a laptop all day.
So it's just my neck?
That's what the pattern suggests. You sound a little unsure, though. Is there something about the headaches that's worrying you?
Honestly, I looked it up. One site said daily headaches can mean a brain tumour. I haven't slept properly since.

Thank you for telling me; that must have been frightening. Headaches from a tumour are very rare, and usually come with other things: steadily worsening, waking you at night with vomiting, or weakness, confusion or changes in vision. Yours build through the day, ease overnight and fit what I found in your neck.
They do go when I sleep. And I've no other symptoms.

That's reassuring. I'll also give you clear warning signs. First, your set-up. A laptop on a table makes you look down all day. Could you raise the screen to eye level, on a stand or some books, and use a separate keyboard and mouse?
I've got an old keyboard somewhere. And the chair? Mine's a dining chair.

A chair that supports your lower back helps, and a cushion behind you will do for now. But here's the important part: there's no single perfect posture. Changing position often matters more than sitting the right way.
Really? I thought I had to sit up straight all the time.

Lots of people think that, but even a good posture held for hours gets uncomfortable. Your best posture is your next one. So I'd like you to get up every half an hour or so, even for a minute. Can I show you two exercises for those breaks?
Yes, please.

First, sit tall, gently tuck your chin in as if making a double chin, hold for a few seconds, and relax. Repeat a few times. Second, roll your shoulders back slowly and squeeze your shoulder blades together. Both should feel comfortable, not painful. How was that?
That feels nice, actually. Easier than I expected.
Good. General activity helps too. Could you fit in a walk at lunchtime, to replace the walking you used to do on your commute? And how have sleep and stress been, apart from this worry?
Work's busy. Year-end is stressful. A walk would probably help my head as well.

It often does. Now, the warning signs. If you ever get a sudden, very severe headache, a headache with a fever, a stiff neck or a rash, or with weakness, confusion or loss of vision, call 999 or go to A&E straight away.
Sudden and severe, or with fever, rash, weakness or vision problems. Right.
And see your GP if the headaches change pattern or get steadily worse, or if you develop pins and needles or weakness in your arms. Is that clear?
Yes. It's actually a relief to have a list.
Good. So what will you change this week?
Raise the laptop, use the keyboard, get up every half hour, do the two exercises and walk at lunch.
That's a great plan. Most people notice an improvement within a few weeks of changes like these. If you're not improving, you can book back in with us directly. Does that sound all right?
Yes. Thank you for taking the tumour thing seriously.
Of course. You were right to mention it. Take care.

coverage.how: Asks about her hours, set-up, breaks and movement before advising.
Explains stiff, tender neck muscles and joints and that nerve and strength tests were normal.
Explains the shared nerve supply and why the headache builds through the day.
Notices her uncertainty, asks about the worry and explains honestly why her pattern does not suggest a tumour.
Advises raising the screen, a separate keyboard and mouse, and back support.
Explains there is no single perfect posture and that changing position matters more.
Recommends breaks about every half hour and teaches chin tucks and shoulder rolls.
Suggests a lunchtime walk and asks about sleep and stress.
Gives emergency headache red flags and reasons to see the GP.
Agrees this week's changes and explains self-referral back if not improving.

concern.how: Her hesitation is picked up and she discloses the tumour fear; it is acknowledged, explained against her own benign pattern, and followed by a promise of clear warning signs.

safety.point: Sudden severe headache, headache with fever, stiff neck or rash, or with weakness, confusion or loss of vision needs 999 or A&E.
A change in headache pattern, worsening headaches, or arm pins and needles or weakness needs a GP review.

scripts.notes: The card states no warning features and a pattern that eases overnight; the script uses these to reassure. The working hours given by the patient are invented and benign.

turns.text: Good morning, I'm one of the physiotherapists. Please come in and sit down. I understand you've had a difficult time getting this appointment. How are things?
Difficult? I've been cancelled twice. Twice! A text the night before, both times. I've been sat at home with this ankle for a month and nobody cared.
Two cancellations at the last minute, and a month waiting with a stiff ankle. I can hear how frustrating that has been.
Frustrating doesn't cover it. I arranged lifts both times. My son took a day off work.
That makes it worse, because it affected your family too. I'm genuinely sorry. That isn't the service you should have had, and I apologise on behalf of the department.
So why did it happen?

I'll be honest with you. Several of our staff were off sick at the same time, and some clinics had to be cancelled at short notice. That's the reason, not an excuse. It shouldn't have fallen on you twice.
Well, at least you're not pretending it didn't happen.
If you'd like to raise it formally, you can contact the Patient Advice and Liaison Service, called PALS. I can give you their details. Raising a concern won't affect your treatment in any way.
I might. Let's just get on with the ankle.
Of course. Tell me about it now. How is the pain, and what happens with the swelling?
Not much pain, really. It's the stiffness. And by the evening it's puffed up like a balloon.
How are walking and stairs, and what have you been doing on your own since the boot came off?
I limp, especially first thing. Stairs one at a time. I've just been walking round the garden. I didn't know what else I was allowed to do.
That was sensible. Is there anything in particular you're working towards, or anything that's worrying you about it?
My daughter's getting married in seven weeks. I'm walking her down the aisle. And I keep thinking this wait has ruined it. That I'll be hobbling in front of everyone.
That's a really important day, and now I understand why the cancellations felt so serious. Can I tell you what I think?
Go on.

Stiffness and swelling after weeks in a boot are expected, because the joint and muscles tighten when they're not used. Starting physiotherapy a few weeks later than planned isn't ideal, but it very rarely causes permanent damage. Ankles like yours usually respond well, and you've already kept it moving in the garden.
So it's not ruined?

No, I don't believe it is. Let's start now. First, sit and draw circles and letters in the air with your foot, to loosen the joint. Second, hold the kitchen worktop and rise up onto your toes, then lower slowly. Third, stand on the injured leg for as long as you can, still holding on. Shall we try them?
The toes one is hard. But I can do it.
That's a good start. For the evening swelling, rest with the foot raised above hip level and do the foot circles. Walk little and often rather than one long walk.
And will I be walking normally by the wedding?

I can't promise a perfect walk, and I don't want to give you false hope. But seven weeks of regular exercise usually makes a big difference, and most people in your position walk comfortably by then. Practising walking slowly and evenly, the way you'll walk on the day, is a good goal.
I'll take that. I just want to get her there without limping.

That's what we'll work towards. One important thing: after time in a boot there's a small risk of a blood clot. If you get new pain, warmth or swelling in the calf, get urgent medical advice that day. If you're suddenly breathless or have chest pain, call 999.
Calf pain or swelling, breathless, chest pain. Right.

Exactly. Now, I don't want you waiting again. Before you leave, we'll book your next two appointments with me at reception, and I'll give you the department's direct number in case anything changes. Does that work?
Yes. And thank you. I came in ready for a fight.
I understand why. Let's go and sort those appointments out now, and I'll see you next week.

coverage.how: Opens with an invitation, lets him vent and reflects the impact back.
Apologises sincerely for the department without excuses.
Gives the honest reason, staff sickness, without blaming colleagues.
Explains PALS and that raising a concern will not affect his care.
Asks about pain, swelling, walking, stairs and what he has done himself.
Asks what he is working towards or worried about.
Explains that stiffness is expected and that a short delay rarely causes permanent damage.
Teaches range, calf-rise and balance exercises and advises elevation for swelling.
Is hopeful about the wedding but refuses to promise a perfect walk.
Explains clot warning signs and when to call 999.
Books his next two appointments before he leaves and gives a direct number.

concern.how: An open question draws out the wedding; the fear of permanent damage is answered with an honest explanation, and his goal is adopted as the rehabilitation target without false promises.

safety.point: New calf pain, warmth or swelling after immobilisation needs urgent same-day medical advice.
Sudden breathlessness or chest pain means calling 999.
Balance practice is done holding a stable surface.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination findings; the script assumes low pain, no signs of a clot and a fracture cleared for full weight-bearing, which a clinician should confirm. Two follow-up appointments is the script's choice.

turns.text: Hello again, and thank you for showing me round. How are you getting about at the moment, inside the house and outside?
Slowly. Indoors I'm fine, I just hold onto things as I go. Outside's harder. The hip's sore after a few minutes.
And what do you enjoy that the hip is making difficult?
The garden, mainly. And walking down to the pub on a Friday with my mates. I've stopped that.
That's a real loss. Your GP mentioned two near-falls in the garden. Can you tell me what happened?
Once I caught my foot on the step by the shed. The other time I turned round too quickly by the greenhouse. Grabbed the fence both times. Didn't hurt myself.

I'm glad you weren't hurt. When I watched you walk, I noticed you lean over to the left with each step and your steps are short. That's your body protecting the painful hip, but it also makes you less steady, especially when you turn.
I know what's coming. You're going to tell me to use a stick.
I'd like to talk about it, but it's your decision. You've said no before. Can I ask what puts you off?
My dad got a stick. Within a year he was in a home. I'm not ready for that. A stick says you're on the way out.

That must have been hard, and I can see why a stick carries that meaning for you. Your dad's stick didn't put him in the home, though; his health did. For many people, a stick is what keeps them independent.
Maybe. I still don't like the look of it.

That's fair. Here are the choices. With no aid, nothing changes, but the risk of a fall stays. A single stick is the lightest option and still lets you garden and get to the pub. A frame is the steadiest, but it's bulky, mostly for indoors, and I don't think you need one.
So you'd say a stick.

For you, I think a stick would help most. It takes some of your weight through your arm instead of the sore hip, so the hip hurts less and you're steadier. You hold it in your right hand, on the opposite side to the bad hip, and move it forward with your left leg.
The right hand? I'd have thought the same side.
Most people do, but the opposite side works better. May I adjust this one for you, so the handle is level with your wrist when your arm hangs down?
Go on, then. No promises.
That's the right height now. Try walking to the door: stick and left leg forward together, then the right. How does that feel?
Strange. But the hip's easier, I'll give you that.
Let's try the garden step. Going up, step up with the right leg first, then bring the stick and the left leg. Coming down, stick and left leg first, then the right.
Up with the good, down with the bad. My wife will remember that better than me.

That's exactly it. A few other things: keep the path by the shed clear, wear shoes that fasten rather than slippers, and have a light on when it's dark. And take your time turning; turn in a small circle rather than twisting.
The slippers will upset my wife. She bought them.
