Perhaps a pair with a closed back and a good grip, then. Remember, using the stick is your choice. What would you be willing to try?
I'll use it in the garden and down to the pub. Not in the house.

That's a great start, and we can talk about indoors next time. If you do fall, stay calm and check whether you're hurt. Only get up if you can do it safely, by rolling onto your knees and using a sturdy chair. If you can't get up or you've hurt yourself, call for help, and if it's serious, ring 999.
My wife's usually around. I'll keep the phone in my pocket.
Good idea. I'll visit again in two weeks to see how you're managing with the stick. Can you tell me the main points we agreed?
Stick in the right hand, garden and pub. Up with the good, down with the bad. Proper shoes. Phone in my pocket.
Perfect. And next Friday, I hope you get to the pub.

coverage.how: Asks how he gets about indoors and out and what the hip stops him enjoying.
Asks where and how the near-falls happened and whether he was hurt.
Describes his lean and short steps and links them to reduced steadiness.
Asks what puts him off and responds respectfully to his father's story.
Compares no aid, a stick and a frame for him.
Explains offloading through the arm and the opposite-hand rule.
Adjusts the stick to wrist height and teaches level walking and the garden step.
Advises on clear paths, fastened shoes, lighting and turning.
States it is his choice and accepts outdoor use as a start.
Explains how to get up safely after a fall and when to call for help or 999.
Arranges a review visit in two weeks and checks his understanding.

concern.how: Asked directly what puts him off, he links the stick to his father's decline; this is acknowledged and reframed as a tool for staying independent, without pressure.

safety.point: If he falls and cannot get up safely or is hurt, call for help, and 999 if serious.
Clear paths, fastened shoes, lighting and slow turning reduce fall risk.

scripts.notes: The card gives the lean to the left; the short steps are an added benign gait observation. The stick height rule and stair sequence are standard teaching; a clinician should confirm a stick is appropriate rather than a frame given two near-falls.

turns.text: Thank you for doing that test; I know it wasn't pleasant. When I laid you back with your head turned to the right, your spinning started and your eyes made a particular flickering movement. That pattern tells me you have something called benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
That's a mouthful. What does it mean?

It means short bursts of spinning brought on by moving your head. Your inner ear contains tiny crystals that normally stay put. Sometimes a few come loose and drift into a balance canal. When you lie down or look up, they roll, and your brain thinks you're spinning. Benign means it isn't dangerous.
Crystals? So it's nothing to do with my brain?

That's right. The spinning lasts less than a minute, it's triggered by certain positions, your hearing is normal, you have no other symptoms, and the test reproduced it exactly. That all points to the ear. You sound worried, though. What's on your mind?
My sister had a stroke last year. It started with dizziness. I've been lying awake thinking these are little strokes.

That's understandable after what happened to your sister, and I'm sorry. Stroke dizziness is usually constant, and comes with things like weakness, slurred speech or double vision. Yours comes and goes with position, and the test showed the classic ear pattern. I'm confident this is your inner ear.
That's a relief. Really. So can you fix it?

There's a treatment called a repositioning manoeuvre. I move your head and body through a series of positions, holding each for about a minute. It takes around ten minutes altogether. The aim is to roll those loose crystals out of the canal to a place where they cause no trouble.
Does it work?
It works well for most people, often after one or two treatments. A few need more sessions.
Will it make me dizzy again? I hate being sick. That's the bit I'm dreading.

Honestly, yes, you'll probably spin briefly in one or two positions as the crystals move. You might feel sick, but vomiting isn't common. I'll go slowly, keep a bowl nearby, and you can sit as long as you need afterwards. You may feel unsteady for a day or so.
All right. As long as I can stop.
You can stop at any time. Before we decide, I need to check it's suitable. Do you have any neck or back problems, any recent injury, or anything that stops you lying back or turning your head?
No, my neck's fine. A bit of a stiff back in the mornings, nothing more.
That's fine. You should also know the alternatives. This often settles on its own over weeks, so you could wait. There are also home exercises, though they tend to work more slowly.
I don't want to wait. It's affecting work. I can't reach the top cupboards at school.
That makes sense. So, would you like me to go ahead with the manoeuvre today, knowing you might feel dizzy and sick for a short time, and that you can ask me to stop at any point?
Yes. Let's do it.

Thank you. One important point first. If you ever get dizziness with weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision, a drooping face, trouble walking or a sudden severe headache, that isn't this condition. Call 999 straight away.
Weakness, speech, double vision, face, walking, headache. Call 999.
Exactly. Right, let's begin. Sit on the couch, turn your head to the right, and I'll lower you back. Keep your eyes open if you can, and squeeze my arm if you need me to stop.
Oh, it's spinning. It's passing now.
Well done, that's exactly what we expect. I'm turning your head slowly to the other side now. Then you'll roll onto your side, and finally I'll help you sit up.
That wasn't as bad as I thought. A bit queasy.
You did really well. Sit for a few minutes before you stand. For a couple of days, take care on stairs and getting out of bed. You don't need to sleep sitting up. Is someone driving you home?
My husband's in the waiting room.
Good. I'll see you next week to repeat the test, and repeat the manoeuvre if needed. What would you do if your symptoms changed?
If it's anything like weakness, slurred speech or double vision, ring 999. Otherwise, take care on stairs and come back next week.
Perfect. I hope you sleep better tonight.

coverage.how: Explains the positive test and describes the condition as loose inner-ear crystals.
Links brief positional spinning, normal hearing and no other symptoms to the ear rather than the brain.
Asks what is on her mind and responds to both the stroke fear and the fear of vomiting.
Describes the positions, holding times, total time and the aim of moving the crystals.
Explains that it often works after one or two treatments.
Explains brief spinning, nausea and unsteadiness for a day or so.
Screens for neck or back problems, injury or limits to lying back or turning.
Offers waiting and home exercises as alternatives.
Confirms she can stop at any time and asks for consent explicitly.
Lists stroke warning signs and tells her to call 999.
Gives stairs and getting-up advice and books a review to retest next week.

concern.how: Her worried tone is noticed and she names the stroke fear, which is answered by contrasting stroke dizziness with her pattern; the fear of being sick is met with honest, practical reassurance.

safety.point: Dizziness with weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision, facial droop, trouble walking or sudden severe headache needs 999.
Take care on stairs and getting out of bed for a couple of days, and do not drive home straight after treatment.

scripts.notes: The manoeuvre is described generically for a right-sided posterior canal presentation as the card implies. Holding times and total duration are approximate. No strict post-treatment restrictions are advised, in line with current practice; a clinician should confirm local advice on driving afterwards.

turns.text: Hello, may I sit down? I'm the ward physiotherapist. I hear you're going home tomorrow. How are you feeling about it?
Pleased. I miss my own bed. A bit nervous, I suppose. It's a big step.
It is. What do you think you'll find most difficult at home?
The stairs, probably. And just being on my own again.

That's natural. Can I say how well you've done? When you came in after the operation, you could barely stand. Now you're walking the corridor with your frame and you've managed the practice stairs. That's real progress.
The nurses made me work hard.

It shows. Let's go over the frame. Keep it close, step into it rather than walking behind it, and don't lean over it. And never pull yourself up on it, because it can tip. Push up from the chair arms, then hold the frame.
Push from the chair, then hold the frame. I remember.

Lovely. And the stairs: hold the rail with one hand and the stick in the other. Going up, good leg first, then the operated leg and the stick. Coming down, stick and operated leg first, then the good leg. Can you tell me which is which?
Up with the right, my good one. Down with the left and the stick.
Perfect. Now, your bedroom and toilet are both upstairs. What about at night? How will you get to the toilet?
Oh, I'll manage. I always do.
I'm sure you're very capable. A lot of people find the night the hardest part, though, especially when they're sleepy. Is anything about it worrying you?
Well, if I'm honest, yes. I'm frightened of falling in the dark. That's how I fell in the first place. But I haven't told my daughter.
Thank you for telling me. Can I ask why you haven't mentioned it to her?
She already thinks I should go into a home. If she knew, she'd have me in one by the weekend.

I understand. Staying in your own home matters, and our aim is to help you do that safely. Making night-times safer is exactly how we support that. Would you consider a commode beside your bed, so you don't have to walk to the toilet in the dark?
A commode. Well, I'd rather that than another fall.

I can arrange for one to be delivered before you get home. A plug-in night light would help too, and keep your frame within reach of the bed. Would you be happy for me to explain to your daughter that these are to keep you independent?
Yes, if you put it like that. She'll listen to you.
I'll speak to her this afternoon. Also, please keep to the movement advice on the leaflet from your surgical team, and carry on with your exercise sheet, as you've done here.
The sheet with the drawings. I've got it in my bag.

The carers will come in four times a day to help with washing, dressing and meals. The community therapy team will visit in the first few days to check your walking and stairs at home and move your exercises on.
And what if I fall anyway?

Keep a phone or a personal alarm on you all the time, even in the bathroom. If you fall, stay calm and check whether you're hurt. Don't try to get up if it hurts or you can't do it safely; press your alarm or call for help.
My daughter's been on about one of those pendant alarms. I'll say yes.

That's a good idea. Lastly, some warning signs. If you get pain or swelling in your calf, a red or leaking wound, a fever, or a sudden increase in pain in your hip, contact your GP or the ward urgently that day. If you're suddenly breathless or have chest pain, call 999.
Calf, wound, fever, hip pain, I ring. Breathless or chest pain, it's 999.
Exactly right. Could you tell me the main things you'll do at home?
Push up from the chair, not the frame. Up with the good. Commode and night light. Wear the alarm. And my exercises.
Wonderful. Do you have any other questions before tomorrow?
No. I feel much better about the nights now. Thank you.
You're very welcome. I'll come back this afternoon when your daughter visits.

coverage.how: Asks how she feels about going home and what she expects to be difficult.
Gives honest, specific praise for her progress since surgery.
Checks frame use: close, step into it, no leaning, never pull up on it.
Reviews the stairs sequence and asks her to say which leg leads.
Asks directly about the night and then invites any worry.
Offers a commode, night light and frame within reach, and arranges delivery.
Reminds her of the surgical movement leaflet and her exercise sheet.
Explains what the carers and community therapists will do.
Advises carrying a phone or alarm and what to do after a fall.
Lists clot, wound, infection and hip pain warning signs and when to call 999.
Asks her to summarise and invites questions.

concern.how: Her brushed-off answer about the night is gently challenged, she admits the fear and her reason for hiding it, and night-time aids are framed as protecting her independence, with an offer to explain this to her daughter.

safety.point: Never pull up on the frame; push up from the chair arms.
Carry a phone or alarm at all times and do not get up after a fall if it is unsafe.
Calf pain or swelling, wound redness or leakage, fever or a sudden rise in hip pain need urgent same-day contact; breathlessness or chest pain means 999.

scripts.notes: The card does not give the surgical approach or any hip precautions, so the script defers to the surgical team's leaflet. Commode delivery and community therapy timing depend on local services.

turns.text: Hi, come in. I'm the physiotherapist who'll be working with you through your rehab. It's two weeks since your operation, so first of all, how do you feel the knee is doing?
Good, honestly. The swelling's going down and I've ditched the crutches. I reckon I'm ahead of schedule.
That's a really good start, and the wound has healed well. What have you been told about the recovery plan so far?
Not much. Do the exercises, build it up. I'm aiming to be back for the last games of the season. Three months, right?
Okay. Tell me a bit more about why those games matter so much.
It's the end of my contract. If I'm not playing when they decide, I'm probably out. Football's all I've done since I was a kid.

So much more than a few games is riding on it. Thank you for telling me. I need to be honest with you, even though it isn't what you want to hear. Coming back to football in three months isn't realistic after this operation.
What? I've heard of people back way quicker than that.

I understand that's a shock. Most people need at least nine months before they're ready to play again. Your new ligament was made from a tendon, and over the coming months your body slowly turns it into a strong ligament. In the early months it's at its weakest, even though the knee feels good.
But if it feels fine?

That's the trap. Feeling fine isn't the same as being strong. People who go back too early have a much higher chance of injuring the ligament again, and a second operation means another long recovery. I want you to play for years, not just this season.
So I'm out for the season. Brilliant.
I can see how gutting that is. How are you feeling about it?
Sick. Honestly, I don't know who I am if I'm not playing. And without the contract I don't know what I'll do for money.
That's a lot to face, and it's normal to feel low about it. Have you got people around you to talk to? And if your mood stays low, please speak to your GP, because support is available.
My girlfriend, my dad. I haven't told the club anything yet.

It might help to involve the club's medical staff early. With your permission, I could send them a rehab plan, so they can see your commitment. Many players keep training alongside the team during rehab, going to matches and doing gym work, so they stay part of the squad.
That might actually help. They do like players who graft.

Let me explain the plan. First, we settle the swelling and get the knee fully straight and bending well. Then we build strength in the thigh and hip. Later we add running, jumping and changes of direction. You return to football when you pass strength and movement tests, not when a date arrives.
So if I smash the tests, I could be back quicker?

The tests guide us, but the graft still needs time, so we won't rush. What you can do now is plenty: the exercise bike, upper body work in the gym and your knee exercises. What you must avoid is running, twisting, kicking a ball or jumping until we say so.
No kicking a ball at all? Not even in the garden?

Not yet, I'm afraid. One awkward twist could undo the surgery. A few warning signs too: if you get calf pain or swelling, the wound becomes hot or red or starts leaking, you get a fever, or the knee gives way, get medical advice promptly. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain means 999.
Calf, wound, fever, giving way. And breathless or chest pain is 999.
Exactly. So, for the next few weeks, what goals shall we set?
Get it fully straight, bend it more, bike every day. And talk to the club physio this week.
Those are great goals. Can I check what you've understood about the timescale?
At least nine months, and only when I pass the tests. I don't like it, but I get it.
That's honest, and I respect it. I'll see you next week, and I'll write that summary for the club physio. Is there anything else on your mind?
No. Just glad you didn't fob me off.
You deserved the truth. See you next week.

coverage.how: Asks how the knee feels and what he understands of the plan.
Asks why the end-of-season games matter so much.
States clearly and kindly that three months is not realistic.
Explains graft maturation over months and the higher re-injury risk with early return.
Describes the stages of rehabilitation and criteria-based return to football.
Asks how he feels, normalises low mood and points to support via the GP.
Suggests involving the club's medical staff and staying involved with the squad.
Lists safe activity now and what to avoid until cleared.
Gives calf, wound, fever and giving-way warning signs, and 999 for sudden breathlessness or chest pain.
Agrees short-term goals, checks his understanding of the timescale and books next week.

concern.how: The contract emerges when he is asked why the timing matters; after the news, his fear for his identity and income is explored and met with emotional support and a plan to show the club his commitment.

safety.point: Early return to sport greatly increases the risk of re-rupture.
Persistent low mood should be raised with the GP.
Calf pain or swelling, wound changes, fever or giving way need prompt advice; sudden breathlessness or chest pain means 999.

scripts.notes: The card gives a tendon graft but not its source; the script stays generic. Exercise bike use at two weeks assumes enough knee bend, which a clinician should confirm.

turns.text: Thanks for letting me examine you. Your strength, reflexes and feeling in both legs are normal, and so is the feeling around your bottom. With pain going from your back down to your calf, this is what we call sciatica. It means a nerve in your lower back is irritated.
Sciatica. My dad had that. Does it mean a slipped disc?

Often a slightly bulging disc is the cause, yes. The good news is that most sciatica settles by itself over weeks to a few months. Staying as active as you can actually helps it recover faster than resting in bed.
I've been lying on the sofa most evenings. And the driving's killing me.

Long drives are tough with sciatica. Try to stop every hour or so, get out and walk for a few minutes, and adjust your seat so you're well supported. At night, lying on your side with a pillow between your knees often helps. And speak to your GP or pharmacist about pain relief that's right for you.
I'll try that. Is that everything, then?

Nearly. There's one important thing I tell everyone with back and leg pain. Very rarely, the bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spine, called the cauda equina, gets badly squeezed. That's called cauda equina syndrome. It's rare, but if it's caught early, surgery can prevent permanent damage to the bladder, bowel and legs.
That sounds frightening. How would I know?

These are the signs. Numbness or tingling around your bottom, genitals or inner thighs, the area that would touch a saddle. New trouble starting to pass urine, not feeling when you need to go, or leaking. Losing control of your bowels. Changes in sexual function. Or pain, numbness or weakness in both legs.
Okay. That's a lot.

It is, so I'll give you a card with them written down. The key thing is that if you notice any of them, go straight to A&E the same day. Don't wait for a GP appointment, and don't wait to see if it passes.
A&E for back pain, though? They'd think I was wasting their time.
Not at all. They would much rather see you and find nothing than see you too late. Is there anything else that might stop you going?
Well, I live alone. And I'm out on country lanes all day, miles from anywhere. I'd probably just think I'll see how it is tomorrow.

Thank you for being honest; that's exactly why I asked. Waiting until tomorrow is the one thing to avoid, because hours matter. If you're out on a route, stop and go to the nearest A&E, or call 111 if you're unsure where it is. If you can't get there safely, call 999. Would it help to tell someone close to you the signs too?
My sister, maybe. She'd nag me to go.
That's a good idea. Here's the card. Can you tell me, in your own words, what the warning signs are?
Numb around my backside or privates. Problems peeing, or not feeling it. Losing control of my bowels. Changes in, well, down there. Or both legs going.
That's exactly right. And what would you do?
A&E the same day. Not wait till tomorrow, even if I'm out on a route.
Perfect. Separately, if your leg pain becomes much worse, or you notice your foot catching or your leg feeling weak, contact the surgery that day so we can reassess you.
And if it's just not getting better?
I'll book a follow-up with me in two weeks. If you're struggling before then, you can call the surgery and ask for a call back from me.
Two weeks. Fine.
How are you feeling about everything we've talked about?
Better. I thought you'd just tell me to rest. Now I know what to watch for.
Good. Let's quickly recap the plan: keep moving, take breaks when driving, a pillow between your knees at night, and pain relief advice from your GP or pharmacist. And the warning signs?
Same-day A&E, keep the card in my wallet, and tell my sister.
Spot on. Most people recover well from sciatica, and I expect you will too.
Thanks. I'll see you in two weeks.

coverage.how: Explains normal neurological findings and names sciatica as an irritated nerve.
Explains the usual recovery over weeks to months and that activity helps.
Advises driving breaks, seat support, side-lying with a pillow and pain relief via GP or pharmacist.
Introduces cauda equina syndrome as rare and explains why early surgery matters.
Lists saddle numbness, bladder, bowel, sexual and bilateral leg symptoms plainly.
States same-day A&E without waiting for an appointment, even on a work route.
Asks what would stop him going and answers the time-wasting and living-alone barriers.
Gives a warning card and asks him to describe the signs and action in his own words.
Advises same-day contact for much worse leg pain, foot drop or weakness.
Books a review in two weeks and explains how to contact the service sooner.

concern.how: His worry about wasting A&E's time is corrected, and an open question uncovers living alone and rural driving; the plan is adapted to his routes and involves his sister.

safety.point: Cauda equina warning signs: saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms.
Any warning sign means A&E the same day, not a GP appointment.
Do not wait until tomorrow; 111 for directions, 999 if he cannot get there safely.
Much worse leg pain or new weakness needs same-day reassessment.

scripts.notes: The two-week review interval is the script's choice. The card states no warning signs and normal saddle sensation, which the script relies on.

turns.text: Thank you for letting me assess you. Before I explain what I found, how is the pain affecting you day to day, at work and at night?
Work's okay sitting down; I'm in an office. But stairs are awful, and getting out of the car. And turning over in bed wakes me every time.
That sounds exhausting, especially with a baby on the way. Are you managing to get back to sleep?
Eventually. I'm just tired all the time now.

What I found fits something called pelvic girdle pain. Your pelvis is a ring of joints. In pregnancy, hormones soften the ligaments and your posture changes, so the joints can move unevenly, which causes pain at the front and in the buttocks.
Is it common?
Very. Up to one in five pregnant women get it, so you're far from alone.
But is it hurting the baby? That's what I keep worrying about.
No. Pelvic girdle pain affects the joints of your pelvis, not your baby. It's painful for you, but it doesn't harm the baby, and it's reassuring that your baby is moving normally.
Okay. And the birth? I read online it means I'll need a caesarean.

I can see why that frightened you. Most women with pelvic girdle pain have a vaginal birth. What helps is planning positions that are comfortable for you, such as kneeling or lying on your side, and making sure the team knows. Was that the main worry?
That and the baby. I've been imagining all sorts.

Then I'm glad you asked. Now, everyday movements. When you get out of the car or bed, keep your knees together and swing both legs round at once. Take stairs one at a time. Sit down to put on trousers, socks and shoes, rather than standing on one leg.
Knees together. That makes sense.

In bed, a pillow between your knees helps, and when you turn, squeeze your knees together and roll. During the day, pace yourself: break jobs into smaller chunks, and rest before the pain builds up, not after.
I've been trying to get everything done before the baby comes.

That's very common, but pacing will let you do more overall. Let me show you some gentle exercises. First, draw your tummy in gently and breathe normally. Second, the pelvic floor: squeeze as if stopping wind, lift, hold, then relax fully. Third, lying on your side with your knees bent, lift your top knee a little.
Like that? It doesn't hurt.

Perfect. Do them little and often, and stop any that hurt. Keep active within comfort; swimming is often good, though avoid breaststroke legs if they hurt. A pelvic support belt helps many women, and if walking becomes very painful, crutches can take the strain.
A belt sounds good. Can I have one today?
Yes, I'll fit one before you go. Please also tell your midwife about the pain, so it's written into your birth plan, including the positions that are comfortable for you.
I see her next week. I'll mention it.

Good. Now some important warning signs, which aren't caused by your pelvic pain. If you have any bleeding, fluid leaking, regular tightenings, a fever, or your baby is moving less than usual, contact your maternity unit straight away, day or night. Don't wait until the next day.
Bleeding, fluid, tightenings, fever or fewer movements. Ring the maternity unit.
Exactly. And the good news is that for most women this pain improves after the birth. I'd like to see you again in two weeks to check the belt and progress the exercises. Does that suit you?
Yes. I feel so much better. I really thought something was wrong with the baby.
I'm glad we've cleared that up. Could you tell me what you'll do differently this week?
Knees together getting out of the car and bed, stairs one at a time, sit to dress, pillow at night, the exercises and the belt. And tell the midwife.
Brilliant, you've got it all. If the pain gets much worse before your appointment, ring us and we'll see you sooner.
I will. Thank you so much.

coverage.how: Asks about work, stairs, the car and sleep.
Explains the pelvic ring, hormonal and postural changes, and that it is common.
States clearly that it does not harm the baby.
Explores the caesarean worry and explains most women have a vaginal birth with planned positions.
Advises knees together, stairs one at a time and sitting to dress.
Advises a pillow between the knees, rolling with knees together and pacing.
Teaches tummy, pelvic floor and side-lying hip exercises and encourages activity within comfort.
Offers a support belt today and crutches if walking becomes very painful.
Asks her to tell her midwife so it is in the birth plan.
Lists obstetric warning signs needing urgent maternity unit contact.
Books a review in two weeks, explains improvement after birth and offers earlier contact.

concern.how: She raises fear for the baby and then the caesarean she read about; both are answered directly and early, before the practical advice.

safety.point: Bleeding, fluid leaking, regular tightenings, fever or reduced fetal movements need immediate maternity unit contact.
Stop any exercise that hurts and avoid breaststroke legs if painful.

scripts.notes: The prevalence of up to one in five is a commonly quoted NHS figure, said in words. Belt supply on the day depends on local stock. The two-week review is the script's choice.

turns.text: Hello, please come in. I'm one of the physiotherapists in the cardiac rehabilitation team. How have you been since you left hospital?
Okay, I suppose. Tired. I've mostly been sitting in my chair, watching telly.
What does a normal day look like at the moment? Are you getting out at all?
Not really. My wife walks the dog now. I used to do that every morning.
That's a big change. How do you feel about starting the exercise programme?
Honestly? I nearly didn't come. Isn't it dangerous to get my heart going after a heart attack?
That's one of the most common worries we hear, so I'm glad you've said it. What exactly are you afraid might happen?
That I'll push it and have another one. Every time I feel a twinge in my chest, I panic and sit down.

That sounds frightening, living with that every day. Here's the important part: regular exercise is one of the best things for your heart. It strengthens the heart, helps your blood pressure and cholesterol, and lowers the chance of another heart attack. Sitting still for weeks actually makes things harder.
But how do I know it's safe for me?

Before you start, we assess you, check your heart rate and blood pressure, and plan exercise just for you. The classes are supervised by trained staff the whole time, and they start gently. Nobody will push you beyond what's safe.
That's a relief. I thought it was going to be like a gym.
Not at all. To judge the right effort, use the talk test. You should feel a little breathless and warm, able to talk in sentences but not able to sing. If you can't speak comfortably, slow down.
Talk but not sing. I can remember that.
Also, always warm up gently at the start and cool down at the end. That gives your heart time to adjust and avoids sudden strain, and stopping suddenly can make you dizzy.
What about the twinges, though? How do I know if it's serious?

Good question. Anxiety often causes a fluttery chest, a racing heart or tight breathing, and it eases as you calm down. Muscle aches feel sore when you press or move. Chest pain that feels heavy or tight, like your heart attack, or spreads to your arm, neck or jaw, needs action.
And what do I do then?
Stop and sit down. Use your GTN spray exactly as your discharge leaflet explains. Can you tell me how you'd use it?
Under my tongue, sit down and wait. If it's no better, another spray, and if it's still there, ring an ambulance.
That's right. Follow your leaflet's timing, and if the pain isn't easing as it describes, call 999 straight away. Don't drive yourself to hospital.
I've had it in my pocket every day but never dared use it.

It's there to be used, and knowing what to do should help you feel more confident. Before the programme starts, could you begin some short walks? Perhaps join your wife with the dog, just to the end of the road and back, and add a little more each day if it feels comfortable.
The dog would love that. I've missed it.
It'll help your mood too. Many people feel anxious or low after a heart attack; it's very common. If it's affecting you, our team includes people you can talk to, and your GP can help as well.
I have been a bit down. I'll mention it on the course.
Please do. Shall we book your start date? The next programme begins on Monday week. Would that suit you?
Yes. My wife will be pleased I'm doing something.
Good. Just so I know I've explained things clearly, can you tell me the main points?
Exercise helps my heart. Classes are supervised. Talk but not sing. Warm up and cool down. The spray as the leaflet says, then 999. And start walking the dog.
Perfect. You've taken in a lot. I'll see you on Monday week.

coverage.how: Asks how he has been and what his days look like.
Asks how he feels about exercise and what exactly he fears.
Explains the heart, blood pressure, cholesterol and reduced risk benefits.
Explains the assessment, supervision and gentle, individual start.
Teaches the talk test.
Explains why warm-up and cool-down matter.
Contrasts anxiety, muscle ache and cardiac-type chest pain.
Asks him to describe his GTN use, confirms the leaflet and when to call 999.
Suggests short, gradually longer dog walks before the programme.
Normalises anxiety and low mood and names team and GP support.
Books a start date and asks him to summarise the main points.

concern.how: He voices the danger fear and is asked to name it exactly; the explanation of benefit and supervision follows, and his chest twinges are addressed with a clear way to tell anxiety from cardiac pain.

safety.point: Cardiac-type chest pain: stop, sit, use GTN as the leaflet says, and call 999 if it does not ease; do not drive to hospital.
Exercise at a talk-but-not-sing effort and slow down if unable to speak comfortably.
Heavy or tight chest pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw needs action.

scripts.notes: The GTN dosing interval is deliberately left to his discharge leaflet; the patient's own description is consistent with standard advice. Monday week as a start date is the script's choice. The card does not give his heart function; the script assumes he is suitable for the programme, as his referral implies.

turns.text: Hello, come in and take a seat. I'm one of the podiatrists, and I have your scan result here. Before I go through it, how have you been since the scan, and what have you understood so far?
Honestly, not great. I saw the report online. It says Morton's neuroma, and I don't really know what that means.
Thank you for telling me. We'll go through it properly together. First, can you remind me how the pain affects your days at school, your shoes and your sleep?
By lunchtime it's burning between my toes, like standing on a hot pebble. I take my shoe off under the desk. It wakes me sometimes, but mostly it's the days.
That sounds really wearing, especially on your feet with a class all day. What shoes do you usually wear for work?
Smart ones, fairly pointed, with a small heel. My trainers are fine, actually.

That's a useful clue. Between your third and fourth toes runs a small nerve to those toes. The scan shows it has become thickened and irritated, because the bones on either side keep squeezing it. That's what a Morton's neuroma is.
So it is a growth, then. I looked the word up.
What did you read about it?
That a neuroma is a nerve tumour. I've barely slept. My aunt had cancer, and I keep thinking I'll lose my toes, or I won't be able to teach.

I'm so sorry you've been carrying that all week. Let me be very clear: a Morton's neuroma is not a cancer. It doesn't spread anywhere, and it isn't a danger to your toes. The word sounds frightening, but it simply means thickened nerve tissue from repeated pressure.
Really? Not cancer at all?
Not at all. It's a common, harmless problem, and most people with it carry on working normally. How are you feeling, hearing that?
Massively relieved. I feel a bit silly now.

Not silly at all; that's exactly why we explain reports. Now, why does it burn? When you squeeze into a narrow shoe, the bones press together and pinch the nerve. A heel tips your weight forward onto that same spot. Standing all day adds to it, so by lunchtime the nerve is angry. Trainers avoid all of that.
That makes sense. So what can I do?

Shoes are the biggest step. Look for a wide, deep toe area, a low heel and a soft, cushioned sole. Smart trainers or a wide lace-up would be ideal. If you can, slip your shoes off and wiggle your toes during breaks.
I can manage that. Is there anything else?
Yes. I'd like to give you a padded insole with a small raise placed just behind the painful area. It gently spreads those bones apart and takes pressure off the nerve.
And if it doesn't work?

We'd give it a few months first. If it's still troublesome, a steroid injection around the nerve often settles the pain, though the effect may wear off. The last step is a surgeon's opinion. Surgery helps many people but usually leaves permanent numbness between those toes, so we keep it in reserve.
I'd rather avoid an operation.

Most people avoid it with the simpler measures. Meanwhile, paracetamol from the pharmacy, used as the packet directs, can help, and the pharmacist can say whether anti-inflammatories suit you. Rest the foot when you can, and avoid tight shoes.
Is there anything I should look out for?

Yes. If the numbness spreads to other toes, your foot or toes swell, or they turn pale, blue or very red, get in touch sooner rather than waiting. Those aren't typical of a neuroma, so we'd want to see you.
Okay. Numbness spreading, swelling, or the toes going pale, blue or red.
Exactly. Just so I know I've explained it well, could you tell me in your own words what's going on and what the plan is?
It's a squashed, thickened nerve, not cancer. Wider, flatter shoes, the insole, painkillers if I need them, and shoes off in breaks. If that doesn't help, maybe an injection.
That's spot on. I'd like to see you again in about eight weeks to check how the insole and shoes are working. Does that suit you?
Yes, half-term would be perfect. Thank you, I think I'll actually sleep tonight.
I'm glad. Take care, and do call us if anything changes before then.

coverage.how: Opens by asking how she has been since the scan and what she already understands.
Asks about work, shoes and sleep, and about her work footwear.
Explains the thickened, irritated nerve squeezed between the bones in plain words.
Asks what she read, states clearly it is not cancer and does not spread, and checks how she feels.
Links narrow, heeled shoes and standing to her burning pain, and to why trainers feel better.
Advises a wide, deep toe area, low heel, soft sole and shoes off in breaks.
Offers a padded insole with a raise and explains how it spreads the bones.
Outlines a steroid injection and then a surgical opinion, with the numbness trade-off.
Advises pharmacy pain relief as the packet directs, pharmacist advice on anti-inflammatories, and rest.
Names spreading numbness, swelling and colour change as reasons to call sooner.
Asks for teach-back and agrees a review in about eight weeks.

concern.how: She reveals she read neuroma as nerve tumour and fears cancer; the podiatrist asks what she read, answers the fear directly and checks the relief.

safety.point: Spreading numbness, swelling or colour change in the toes should prompt earlier contact.
Pain relief as the packet directs, with pharmacist advice before anti-inflammatories.
A Morton's neuroma is benign and does not spread.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination findings; the script assumes a typical history with work shoes as the trigger and no other abnormality.

turns.text: Good morning, I'm the podiatrist you'll be seeing today. Thanks for referring yourself. Can you tell me how long you've had the cracks in your heels, and how much they bother you?
Over a year now, but this winter they've got much worse. Sometimes they bleed into my tights, and by the end of a shift it hurts to walk.
That sounds painful, and awkward at work. How long are you on your feet each day?
Most of the shift, standing at the front desk. We wear smart slip-on shoes, open at the back.
That helps me understand. Lots of people try all sorts of things at home. What have you been doing to look after them?
I file them hard every night. And once, I'll be honest, I trimmed the edge off with a razor blade because it kept catching.
Thanks for being honest; that's really common. May I have a look at both heels now?
Of course.

Around both heels the skin is thick, dry and hard, almost like a rim. Hard skin can't stretch, so when your heel spreads as you stand, it splits. That's what these cracks are. A couple are fairly deep, but they're clean, and I can't see any sign of infection.
But why have I got them? I do moisturise sometimes.

Usually it's several things together. Open-backed shoes let the heel pad spread outwards with every step. Standing for long periods puts a lot of weight through the heel. Then winter, central heating and simply getting older all make the skin drier.
So it's the work shoes, mostly.

They're a big part. About the razor blade: it's very easy to cut too deep, and an open cut on the heel can let infection in. Please don't use blades again. Today I'll remove the hard skin safely with a sterile blade, and it shouldn't hurt.
That's fine, I won't do it again. What should I use at home?

Every evening, after a wash, dry your feet gently and rub a thick cream containing urea into the heels. Urea softens hard skin and holds moisture in. Keep it off the skin between your toes, though, because that area needs to stay dry.
Every evening, okay. And the file?

Gentle filing only, a few times a week, on dry skin, and stop when it feels smooth rather than raw. Wear shoes with a closed back where you can, and socks or closed slippers at home, so the heel is held together.
I'll ask my manager about the shoes. Can I ask you something else? It's probably silly.
Not at all. Please, go ahead.
My mum had type 2 diabetes, and she lost the feeling in her feet. I've been thinking these cracks mean I've got it as well. I've been too scared to ask anyone.

I'm really glad you asked, and it isn't silly. Cracked heels are very common, and most people with them don't have diabetes; your shoes and dry skin explain yours well. But having a parent with diabetes does raise your own chance, so it's sensible to check rather than worry.
How would I check?

Your GP can arrange a simple blood test that shows your average sugar level over the last few months. I'll write to them today about your family history. I've also tested the feeling in your feet, and it's normal, which is reassuring.
That's a relief. I'll book the blood test.

Good. One more important thing. If a crack becomes red and the redness spreads, or it feels hot, swollen or leaks pus, or you feel feverish or unwell, get advice that same day from your GP or by calling 111. An infected crack needs prompt treatment.
Spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, or feeling unwell. Same day.
Exactly. Could you talk me through your routine at home, so I know I've explained it clearly?
Wash and dry, urea cream on the heels every evening but not between my toes, gentle filing a few times a week, no blades, and closed-back shoes and socks.
Perfect. Let's see you again in four to six weeks to check how the skin has softened. Shall we book that now?
Yes, please. Thank you for not making me feel daft.
You're very welcome. I'll start on the hard skin now, so tell me if anything feels uncomfortable.

coverage.how: Asks duration, pain and the effect on work and walking.
Asks about home treatment and thanks her for disclosing the blade without criticism.
Explains the thick, dry rim of hard skin that splits because it cannot stretch, and reports normal feeling on testing.
Explains open-backed shoes, long standing and dry skin as causes.
Explains the infection risk of blades and offers safe reduction today.
Gives the evening urea cream routine, avoiding between the toes.
Advises gentle filing a few times a week and closed-back shoes and socks.
Answers the diabetes worry honestly and explains the GP blood test.
Lists spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus and feeling unwell as same-day signs.
Asks for teach-back and agrees a review in four to six weeks.

concern.how: She hesitantly raises her fear of diabetes; the podiatrist welcomes the question, gives an honest risk picture and a simple way to find out.

safety.point: Spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus or feeling unwell need same-day advice from the GP or 111.
Do not cut hard skin with blades because of infection risk.

scripts.notes: The script invents a benign finding: no infection in the fissures and normal protective sensation on testing. It also has the podiatrist write to the GP about family history, which a clinician should confirm is local practice.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for bringing him in. I've finished examining your son, and before I explain, I can see you're frustrated. What did you understand from the GP, and what's worrying you most?
The GP just said growing pains and sent us here. Two months he's been limping off the pitch. It doesn't feel like anyone's taking it seriously.
That's understandable, and I am taking it seriously. Tell me about the pain. When does it come on?
During training and afterwards, mostly. The next morning he's stiff for a bit, then he's fine.
Does it ever wake him at night, or hurt when he's resting?
No, never at night. He just limps after football.

That's helpful, and reassuring. When I examined him, the pain was right at the back of both heels, where the calf tendon attaches to the bone, and squeezing there was sore. There was no swelling or redness. That pattern fits a condition called Sever's disease.
Disease? That sounds worse than growing pains.

The name is misleading, I'm afraid. It isn't a disease in the usual sense. Children have a growth area at the back of the heel bone that's still developing. The calf tendon pulls on it, and with lots of running it becomes irritated and sore.
So it's not broken?
No. It's very common in active children during growth spurts, especially footballers. It isn't a fracture, and it settles completely once that growth area matures, usually in the early teens.
Shouldn't he have an X-ray, just to be sure?

It's a fair question. When the story and examination fit this picture so clearly, an X-ray doesn't usually add anything, and it means some radiation for no benefit. If things changed, we'd think again.
Right. The thing is, he's got an academy trial next month. If this ends his football, he'll be devastated.
I can hear how much this matters to you both. This won't end his football. Children with Sever's carry on playing; we just adjust how much. Let's plan around the trial together.
So he doesn't have to stop?
No. I'd cut back training for now, perhaps dropping one or two sessions a week, and use pain as the guide. Mild discomfort is fine, but if he's limping during or after, he's done too much.
Okay, we can do that. What else?

Cushioned heel raises in his boots and trainers take strain off the tendon. Gentle calf stretches every day help too. I'll show you both one now: hands on the wall, back leg straight, heel down, and hold.
He can do that before school.
Perfect. After football, an ice pack wrapped in a towel on the heels for a short while can ease it. If he needs it, children's paracetamol or ibuprofen, as the packet directs, is fine.
And the trial itself?

Rest well in the days before, wear the heel raises, and warm up properly. It would also help to tell the coach about the condition. Academy coaches see Sever's all the time, and it shouldn't count against him.
I didn't think of telling them. That's a relief, honestly.

Good. There are some signs that would need prompt medical review, though. If he has pain at night or at rest, any swelling or redness, a fever, or a limp that doesn't settle with rest, please see your GP promptly, or call 111 out of hours.
Night pain, swelling, redness, fever, or a limp that won't settle.
Exactly. Those don't fit Sever's, so we'd want him checked. Could you tell me what you'll do at home, so I know it's clear?
Fewer sessions, let the pain guide him, heel raises, stretches every day, ice afterwards, and talk to the coach.
That's it. Let's book a review in six weeks, after the trial. Do you have any other questions?
No, I think that covers it. Sorry if I came in a bit heated.
Not at all. You were looking out for him. Good luck to him at the trial.

coverage.how: Names his frustration, asks what the GP said and what worries him, and says it is being taken seriously.
Asks when the pain comes on, about night and rest pain, and limping.
Explains the tender tendon attachment and Sever's disease as irritation of the heel growth area.
States it is common, not a fracture and settles when the growth area matures.
Explains why an X-ray adds nothing when history and examination fit.
Advises dropping some sessions and using pain and limping as the guide.
Recommends heel raises and demonstrates a calf stretch.
Advises ice in a towel and children's pain relief as the packet directs.
Plans rest before the trial, heel raises, warm-up and telling the coach.
Lists night pain, swelling, redness, fever and a persistent limp as reasons for prompt review.
Checks what he will do at home, books a review in six weeks after the trial and invites questions.

concern.how: His fear that the trial and his son's football are at risk surfaces; the podiatrist acknowledges it and shows how the boy can keep playing.

safety.point: Night or rest pain, swelling, redness, fever or a limp that does not settle need prompt GP review or 111.
Pain relief only as the packet directs.

scripts.notes: The card gives the examination; the script adds no other findings. Settling in the early teens is the usual course and is stated generally.

turns.text: Hello, come on in. I've read your X-ray report. Before we talk about options, how is the bunion affecting your day, which shoes can you wear, and what would you like treatment to achieve?
It throbs by the evening, and the bump rubs in nearly everything. I live in one pair of trainers. Mostly I just want it to stop hurting.

That's really helpful, because pain is exactly what we'd aim to treat. Let me explain what's going on. A bunion is when the big toe joint gradually drifts out of line. The toe leans towards the others, and the joint pushes outwards, making that bony bump on the side.
Can it be pushed back without an operation?
I'm afraid not. Non-surgical options can ease the pain and the rubbing a great deal, but they won't straighten the toe. For many people, though, that's enough.
Okay. What are the non-surgical things?

Shoes come first. Look for a wide, deep toe area and soft uppers that don't press on the bump. Keep the heel low, and choose laces or straps, so your foot doesn't slide forward into the front of the shoe.
I've tried wider shoes. They still rub sometimes.

Then padding can help. I can give you gel or felt pads that sit over the bump and spread the pressure. You may see toe spacers and night splints advertised. Some people find them comfortable, but they don't correct the bone.
Good to know, I nearly bought a splint online. What about insoles?

From watching you walk, your foot rolls in a little, so an insole might take some strain off the joint, and it's worth trying. Painkillers from the pharmacy, taken as the packet directs, can also help on bad days.
And if none of that works?
Then surgery is an option. The surgeon cuts and realigns the bone to straighten the toe. It's done to relieve pain that hasn't settled with other measures, not to change how the foot looks.
My sister had it done. She was stuck at home for weeks.

That's a common experience, so let me be honest about recovery. You'd usually wear a special post-operative shoe for around six weeks. Driving would be limited, especially as it's your right foot. And swelling can take several months to settle fully.
That's what frightens me. I have my two grandchildren three days a week so my daughter can work. I couldn't let her down.
That's a big responsibility, and it's right to plan around it. Can you tell me what caring for them involves? Do you drive them?
Yes, school runs and nursery. And the little one still needs carrying.

Then right now, with pain you can partly manage, surgery would cost you a lot. One approach is to try shoes, padding and an insole first. If surgery does become necessary, it could be planned for a time when your daughter can arrange other childcare.
That feels more realistic. Could I still see a surgeon, just to ask questions?
Of course. I can refer you to an orthopaedic surgeon now, simply to discuss it, with no commitment, or we can wait and see how the simpler measures go. Which would you prefer?
I think I'll try the other things first. If it's no better, then refer me.
That sounds sensible. Let's review in a couple of months. Can you tell me what you'll try in the meantime?
Wider shoes with laces and a low heel, the pads, the insole, and painkillers when I need them. No splint.
Exactly. And if surgery comes up later, what would recovery look like?
About six weeks in a special shoe, limited driving, and months for the swelling. Planned around the children.

Perfect. One last thing. If the joint becomes hot, red and swollen, or a sore or blister appears over the bump, please contact us or your GP promptly. That can mean inflammation or infection that needs checking.
Hot, red, swollen, or a sore. Got it.
Thanks. I'll fit the padding now and take some measurements for the insole.
Thank you. I feel like I have a proper plan now.

coverage.how: Asks about her day, her shoes and what she wants treatment to achieve.
Explains the big toe joint drifting out of line with a bony bump.
States that non-surgical options ease pain but will not straighten the toe.
Advises a wide, deep toe area, soft uppers, a low heel and laces or straps.
Offers gel or felt padding and explains spacers and splints do not correct the bone.
Links a possible insole to how her foot moves, and advises pain relief as the packet directs.
Explains surgery as an option for persistent pain, not appearance.
Describes around six weeks in a post-operative shoe, limited driving and months of swelling.
Asks what caring involves and weighs the options against it.
Offers referral now or later, agrees a review and checks understanding twice.
Advises prompt contact for a hot, red, swollen joint or a sore over the bump.

concern.how: Her sister's recovery and her childcare role surface; the podiatrist explores what she does and plans any surgery around it.

safety.point: A hot, red, swollen joint or a sore over the bump needs prompt review.
Driving is limited after right foot surgery.

scripts.notes: The script invents a benign gait finding, mild rolling in of the foot, to justify trying an insole. The X-ray result is as on the card.

turns.text: Good afternoon, thanks for coming in. Today is about making sure you have everything you need to decide about the nail surgery. First, what do you understand about it, and what are you hoping it'll do?
You take the whole nail off and stop it growing back. I'm sick of it. It catches on my socks and hurts if anything touches it.
That's right, and that's exactly what it's for. I need to check a few health questions first. Do you have any medical problems apart from your blood pressure, and are you taking anything else?
No, just the blood pressure tablets. Not diabetic. Nothing else.
Any allergies? And have you ever had a bad reaction to a local anaesthetic, perhaps at the dentist?
No allergies. The dentist's injections have always been fine.

Good. Your circulation was good when we checked your pulses, which matters for healing. So, the procedure. First, I inject local anaesthetic at the base of the toe to numb it completely. The injection stings briefly, but after that you shouldn't feel pain, just some pressure.
And then?
Once it's numb, I remove the nail. Then I apply a chemical called phenol to the nail root, which stops the nail growing back. Then a dressing goes on, and you go home the same day.
So it's gone for good?
That's the aim. The nail bed heals into smooth, toughened skin, so there's nothing left to cut, catch or press. Most people are very pleased with the result.
What can go wrong?

The main risks are infection in the wound, and occasionally a small spike of nail growing back, which can be treated. Once the anaesthetic wears off after a few hours, the toe will ache, so you'd take your usual painkillers as the packet directs.
That doesn't sound too bad.

The part people underestimate is the aftercare. The chemical leaves a wound that weeps for a while. The dressing needs changing regularly, and it usually takes four to six weeks to heal fully. You'd need roomy shoes during that time.
Four to six weeks. Hmm.
You don't have to go ahead. The alternative is to carry on having the nail cut back here every few weeks, which is perfectly reasonable. It's your decision.
No, I want it done. It's just, well, it's nothing.
It sounds like something's on your mind. Could you tell me about home, and how you'd manage afterwards?
My wife has dementia. I'm her carer, and I can't leave her for long. I walk her to the shops every day. I don't know how I'd manage dressings and all that, but I don't like asking for help.
Thank you for telling me. Caring for her is a lot, and planning for it is part of doing this safely. Is there anyone who could sit with her on the day of the procedure?
My son could come over, and he'd drive me as well.

That's ideal, because you shouldn't drive with a numb foot. For the dressings, you can come here, and you're welcome to bring your wife with you. If that's hard, I can ask the district nurses to visit. Short walks to the shops should be fine in a roomy shoe after the first couple of days.
Bring her with me? I didn't know that was allowed.

Absolutely. We'll book short appointments at quieter times. Now, after surgery, call us promptly if redness spreads up the toe, the pain gets worse rather than better, it swells, there's pus, or you get a fever. Out of hours, call 111.
Redness spreading, worse pain, swelling, pus or a temperature.
Exactly. Can you tell me back what the procedure involves, the main risks and the aftercare?
An injection to numb it, the nail off, and a chemical so it doesn't regrow. Risk of infection or a bit regrowing. Dressings here, with my wife, for four to six weeks, and my son drives me.
That's spot on. And remember, you can change your mind at any time, even on the day. Would you like to sign the consent form now, or take it home to think about?
I'll sign it now. I've wanted this for years.
Then let's do that, and we'll find a date that suits your son.

coverage.how: Asks what he understands and what he hopes for.
Confirms history, medicines, allergies and previous local anaesthetic reactions.
Explains the anaesthetic injection, nail removal and phenol to the root.
Explains the permanent benefit and the smooth, toughened nail bed.
Explains infection, a regrowing spike and pain after the anaesthetic wears off.
Describes weeping wound, regular dressings and four to six weeks to heal.
Offers continued nail cutting in clinic as a reasonable alternative.
Notices his hesitation and asks about home and managing afterwards.
Agrees his son sits with his wife and drives, clinic dressings with his wife welcome, or district nurses.
Lists spreading redness, worse pain, swelling, pus or fever, and 111 out of hours.
Checks understanding, states he can change his mind and offers the form now or later.

concern.how: His hesitation is noticed and invited; he reveals his caring role and pride, and the podiatrist plans practical support.

safety.point: Spreading redness, worsening pain, swelling, pus or fever after surgery need a prompt call, or 111 out of hours.
He should not drive home with a numb foot.
Pain relief as the packet directs once the anaesthetic wears off.

scripts.notes: The script assumes the clinic offers dressing appointments at which a carer can accompany the patient and can request district nurse visits; a clinician should confirm this is locally realistic.

turns.text: Good morning. Before anything else, congratulations. The ulcer under your foot has fully healed, and that's down to a lot of hard work from you. How are you feeling about being discharged today?
Pleased about the foot, of course. But I wasn't expecting to be let go so soon, to be honest.

That's understandable after so long. Discharge from this clinic doesn't mean your care ends. It means it moves to the community foot protection service, a podiatry team who specialise in feet like yours, closer to home.
So the foot's sorted, then?

It's healed, which is great news. But I must be honest with you. The new skin over an old ulcer is thinner and more fragile than normal skin, and ulcers often come back, particularly in the first year. That's why the next stage matters so much.
That's what I'm scared of. This team saved my foot. I could ring you any time. Out there, who do I call? It could come back and nobody would notice.

I really understand that. You've been coming here every week, and we know you well. Leaving that can feel like losing a safety net. So let's make sure you leave with a new one, and with a clear way back to us if you need it.
Okay. That would help.
Let's start with why checking matters. Because the feeling in your feet is reduced, you won't feel pain the way most people do. You didn't feel the ulcer forming last time, did you?
No. My wife spotted blood on my sock.

Exactly. So your eyes have to do the job that pain normally would. Every day, look over both feet, including underneath and between the toes. A mirror on the floor helps, or ask your wife to check under the ball of the foot.
We can do that before bed.

That's a good time. Next, your specialist shoes and insoles are your best protection. Wear them for every bit of walking, indoors as well as out, even to the kitchen. It only takes a few steps in the wrong shoes to damage fragile skin.
Even indoors? I usually wear slippers.

Even indoors. Slippers don't protect that skin enough. Moisturise your feet daily, but not between the toes. And please leave any hard skin and your nails to the podiatry team. Don't cut or file them yourself, or use corn plasters.
Fair enough. How often will the community team see me?

Usually every month or two, and more often if there's any concern. They'll write to you with your first appointment, and I'll send them a full summary today, so they'll know your history before they meet you.
And if something happens in between?

This is the important part. I'm giving you this card with our rapid-access number. If you notice any new break in the skin, a blister, blood on your sock, redness, swelling or warmth in the foot, call that same day. Don't wait for an appointment. You can still come straight back to us.
Same day, even for a small blister?

Yes, even a small one; it's much easier to deal with early. And if you feel unwell, feverish or shivery, with a hot, swollen or painful foot, go to the emergency department straight away, or call 999 if you're very unwell. That can be a serious infection.
Emergency department if I feel unwell with a hot foot. Right.
Could you tell me what you'll do each day, and when you'd call?

Check both feet every night with my wife, special shoes all the time, even indoors, moisturise but not between the toes, no cutting. Ring the number the same day for any break, blister, blood, redness, swelling or warmth.
That's exactly right. How are you feeling now about leaving?
Better. Knowing I can still ring you makes a big difference.
You can, and you should. You've done brilliantly, and the community team will be there with you. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
Can I still go fishing with my grandson?
Of course, in your specialist shoes, and check your feet when you get home, especially after a long day on the bank.
I will. Thank you, all of you, really.

coverage.how: Congratulates him and asks how he feels about discharge.
Explains care is moving to the community foot protection service, not ending.
States the healed skin is fragile and ulcers often return, especially in the first year.
Links reduced feeling to missing the first ulcer, so his eyes must replace pain.
Describes daily checks with a mirror or his wife, underneath and between the toes.
Stresses specialist shoes for every step, indoors and out, not slippers.
Advises daily moisturising, not between the toes, and leaving hard skin and nails to podiatry.
Explains review every month or two and the letter and summary to the community team.
Gives the rapid-access card and the same-day signs.
Explains going to the emergency department, or 999, if unwell with a hot, swollen foot.
Acknowledges his fear, checks understanding and asks how he now feels about leaving.
Supports fishing with his grandson in specialist shoes, with a foot check afterwards.

concern.how: He voices fear of losing the team; the podiatrist acknowledges it, provides a rapid route back and checks how he feels at the end.

safety.point: Any new break, blister, blood on the sock, redness, swelling or warmth means calling the rapid-access number the same day.
Feeling unwell with a hot, swollen foot means the emergency department, or 999 if very unwell.
No home cutting of nails or hard skin and no corn plasters.

scripts.notes: Review interval of every month or two reflects usual UK practice for a high-risk foot after a healed ulcer; local services may set a shorter interval.

turns.text: Hello, please take a seat. Your scan result is back. Before I go through it, could you tell me what you've noticed about your foot lately, and what you were hoping for from today?
It aches on the inside of my ankle, and the foot looks flatter than the other one. I was hoping you'd give me some insoles and that would be that.
Thank you. I'm afraid the result shows a little more than insoles alone can fix, although it is very treatable. Is it all right if I explain it now?
Oh. Yes, go on.

There's a tendon called tibialis posterior that runs behind the bone on the inside of your ankle and holds up the arch of your foot, a bit like a guy rope on a tent. The scan shows it's worn and thickened. The good news is that it isn't torn.
Worn? Is that why the foot's dropping?

Exactly. When that tendon weakens, the arch gradually sinks and the heel tilts outwards. It's also why you couldn't rise onto tiptoe on that side earlier, because that tendon does much of the work of lifting the heel.
Will it fix itself if I leave it?
I'll be honest with you. Left untreated, this tends to slowly get worse. But when it's treated early, as yours is being, most people do well and the pain settles.
My mother had a foot like this. She ended up in a wheelchair. Is that what's going to happen to me?
That must have been very hard to watch, and I can see why this frightens you. Can I ask what happened with her foot?
She just put up with it. She never saw anyone, and it got worse and worse until she stopped walking.

Thank you for telling me. Without knowing her details, I can't say exactly what she had. What I can say is that you're being treated early, and that makes a real difference. Most people in your position stay walking and active. I don't expect a wheelchair to be your future.
That's a relief. So what's the plan?

Three things. First, a supportive insole to hold up the arch and take strain off the tendon. Second, if it's very sore, a supportive ankle brace for a period. Third, and most important, a strengthening programme that builds up gradually, starting with gentle exercises I'll show you today.
How long until it's better?
Months rather than weeks, I'm afraid. Tendons recover slowly. It's important to keep the exercises going even once it feels better, because that's what stops it coming back.
Can I still walk the dog?

Yes, but for now keep the walks shorter and on flatter ground, and break up long periods of standing. Wear supportive lace-up shoes with a firm heel, rather than flat, soft shoes. Keep active, just at a level the tendon can cope with.
Will I need an operation in the end?
Surgery is only considered if this treatment doesn't work, and most people avoid it. We're not there, and I hope we won't be.
Okay. That's better than I feared when you said it was more than insoles.

One important safety point. If the pain suddenly gets much worse, the swelling increases, or the foot changes shape quickly, please contact us promptly rather than waiting for your review. That could mean the tendon has worsened, and we'd want to see you sooner.
Sudden worse pain, more swelling, or the shape changing quickly. Understood.
Could you tell me in your own words what's happening and what the plan is?

The tendon holding up my arch is worn but not torn. An insole, maybe a brace, exercises that I keep doing, shorter walks for now, and proper shoes. It can be treated, and I'm unlikely to end up like Mum.
That's exactly it. Let's arrange a review in six weeks to see how the tendon is responding. Does that work for you?
Yes. Thank you for being straight with me.
Of course. You've done exactly the right thing by coming early.

coverage.how: Asks what she has noticed and what she hoped today would bring.
Warns the result is more than insoles can fix and asks permission to explain.
Explains the worn, thickened but untorn tendon that holds the arch.
Explains the sinking arch, the heel tilting outwards and the failed tiptoe.
States it tends to worsen untreated but does well when treated early.
Sets out the insole, a brace if needed and graded strengthening.
Explains months of recovery and continuing exercises.
Advises shorter, flatter walks, breaking up standing and supportive lace-up shoes.
Asks about her mother before answering, then gives an honest, hopeful answer.
Explains surgery only if treatment fails, which most avoid.
Names sudden worse pain, more swelling or rapid change of shape as reasons to call.
Asks for teach-back and arranges a review in six weeks.

concern.how: She links her foot to her mother's wheelchair; the podiatrist asks about her mother first and answers honestly without false certainty.

safety.point: Sudden worsening pain, more swelling or a rapid change of foot shape need prompt contact.

scripts.notes: The script states that the heel tilts outwards as the arch falls, which is typical, and assumes no other scan findings.

turns.text: Right, that's all done. Let me explain what I found. You have a blister on the back of your right heel, about the size of a thumbnail. I let the fluid out with a sterile needle and left the skin on top in place, because it acts as a natural plaster. Then I covered it with a sterile dressing.
Thanks. It's only a blister, though, isn't it? I didn't even feel it.

That's exactly why we take it seriously. Diabetes has reduced the feeling in your feet, so you didn't notice it forming. Diabetes can also slow healing and make infection more likely. On a foot like yours, a small blister can turn into an ulcer if it isn't looked after.
I see. What do I need to do with it?

Keep the dressing clean and dry. If it gets wet or comes loose, replace it with one of these sterile dressings I'm giving you. Wash your hands first, don't touch the wound itself, and don't peel off the loose skin. Otherwise, leave it alone until I see you.
Can I have a shower?
Yes, but keep that foot out of the water, or use a waterproof cover. Now, the boots. Please don't wear them at all until the heel has healed.
None at all?
None at all. You need soft, roomy footwear that doesn't press on the back of the heel. I'll give you a special dressing shoe today that keeps pressure off it, and you can wear that indoors and out.
Right. That's fine.
Every day, look at the dressing and the skin around it. Can you see the back of your heel easily?
Not really. My knees aren't what they were.
Then a mirror on the floor can help, or someone at home could look. Is there anyone who could?
My daughter pops in most days. She'd check it.

That's ideal. Here's what you're both looking for: redness around the blister, especially if it spreads, warmth, swelling, pus or fluid coming through the dressing, a bad smell, or pain that's getting worse.
Redness, warmth, swelling, pus, a smell, more pain.
Exactly. And remember, because your feeling is reduced, you might not feel much pain even if it's infected. So what you and your daughter see matters more than what you feel.
That's a bit worrying.

It's sensible to know. If you notice any of those, call this clinic the same day. If it's the evening or the weekend, call 111. And if you feel very unwell, with a fever, shivering or confusion, call 999.
Got it. Can I ask something? I've got a charity walk in ten days with my grandson. I've raised quite a bit for it. I was planning to wear those boots, because they're nearly broken in now.

That sounds like a lovely thing to do together, and I understand you don't want to let him or your sponsors down. I'll be honest, though: wearing those boots again so soon would be a real risk to that heel.
So I can't do it?

I'm not saying that yet. It depends on how well it heals. If it's healed, you might manage in different, well-fitting shoes that you've already worn safely, perhaps with some padding. But if it's still open, a long walk could turn it into an ulcer.
Hmm. My old walking shoes never gave me any trouble.
Then those are worth considering. Let's decide together nearer the time, once we see how it's healing. Could the walk be shortened if needed?
Probably. They're quite flexible, and my grandson would understand.
Good. I'd like to see you again in three days. Before you go, could you tell me what you'll look for and what you'll do?
Keep it dry, no boots, and my daughter checks it every day. Redness, warmth, swelling, pus, a smell or more pain, I ring you the same day, or 111 out of hours, and 999 if I'm really unwell.
That's perfect. And bring your old walking shoes to the review, so I can check them.
Will do. Thanks for not just saying no.

coverage.how: Explains the thumbnail-sized blister, draining with the roof left on and the sterile dressing.
Explains reduced feeling, slower healing, infection risk and the risk of an ulcer.
Advises clean, dry dressing, how to replace it and keeping it dry in the shower.
Advises no boots and provides a dressing shoe that keeps pressure off the heel.
Asks him to check daily and arranges a mirror or his daughter.
Lists spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, smell and worsening pain.
Explains that pain may not warn him, so what is seen matters more.
Gives same-day clinic call, 111 out of hours and 999 if very unwell.
Responds to the charity walk honestly and agrees to decide nearer the time.
Books a review in three days, checks understanding by teach-back and asks him to bring his old walking shoes.

concern.how: He reveals the charity walk in the same boots; the podiatrist respects it, explains the risk and keeps the decision open.

safety.point: Signs of infection mean a same-day clinic call, 111 out of hours, or 999 if very unwell.
Reduced feeling means pain may not warn of infection.
No wearing of the new boots until healed.

scripts.notes: The card says the blister was drained and dressed; the script specifies aseptic aspiration with the roof left intact and provision of an offloading dressing shoe, both usual UK practice for a neuropathic foot.

turns.text: Hi, come in and have a seat. You've told me your toes have been sore for a few weeks. Can you tell me how they feel, when they're worst, and how they're affecting your studies and sleep?
They itch and burn, and they've gone this red-purple colour. It's worst in the evening, when I'm sitting at my desk. Some nights the itching keeps me awake.
That sounds miserable, especially when you're trying to study. Having looked at your toes, I'm confident these are chilblains. Have you heard of them?
My nan used to talk about them. I thought only old people got them.

Lots of people think that, but they're common in young people too. Chilblains happen when the tiny blood vessels in the skin react badly to cold. They tighten in the cold, and then if the skin warms up too quickly, they leak a little fluid into the tissue. That causes the swelling, itching and burning.
Is it damaging my toes?
It's very unlikely. Chilblains usually settle within a few weeks, and they rarely cause any lasting damage. The key is stopping new ones forming. Can I ask how you keep warm at home?
It's a shared house. It's quite cold, and a bit damp.
And when your feet are cold, how do you warm them up?
Honestly, I put them against the radiator at night. Or I take a hot water bottle to bed. We can't afford to have the heating on much, so I've been a bit embarrassed to say.

Thank you for telling me. Lots of students are in the same position, so please don't feel embarrassed; it actually helps me give you better advice. Warming cold feet quickly, on a radiator or with a hot water bottle, is one of the main things that sets chilblains off.
Oh no. So I've been making it worse.

Without knowing, yes, but it's easy to change. Cold, numb feet also can't sense heat well, so there's a risk of burns too. Instead, warm your feet gradually, with socks and a blanket, and let them come up to temperature slowly.
But how, if the house is freezing?

Keep your whole body warm, not just your feet, because being cold anywhere makes the vessels in your toes tighten. Wear layers, thick wool or thermal socks, and warm slippers or shoes with room for your toes. Get up and move around regularly, rather than sitting still for hours.
I could do that. And the itching?
Try hard not to scratch, because broken skin can become infected. A soothing lotion from the pharmacy, such as calamine or witch hazel, can ease the itch.
Okay, I'll get some.
About the heating: have you spoken to the student support service at your university? Many have hardship funds, and they can also advise you on raising the damp with your landlord.
I didn't know they did that. I'll look into it.

Please do; that's what they're there for. Now, a few things would mean seeing your GP. If the skin breaks, looks infected, with spreading redness, pus or more pain, or if a chilblain doesn't heal, see your GP. And if your fingers go white or blue in the cold, mention it, as that can be a related circulation problem worth checking.
So broken or infected skin, not healing, or my fingers changing colour.
Exactly. Just to make sure I've explained things clearly, could you tell me what you'll do differently from tonight?
No radiator or hot water bottle. Warm my feet slowly with socks and a blanket, wear layers, and keep moving. Calamine for the itch, no scratching, and speak to student support about the heating.
That's perfect. With those changes, I'd expect these to settle over the next few weeks. Do you have any questions?
Could they come back next winter?
They can, so start the warm socks and layers as soon as the weather turns cold. Prevention is much easier than treatment.
Thanks. That makes me feel a lot better.
You're welcome. Look after yourself, and come back if you're worried.

coverage.how: Asks how the toes feel, when they are worst and the effect on study and sleep.
Explains small vessels reacting to cold and then rapid warming.
Reassures that chilblains are common in young people, settle in weeks and rarely cause damage.
Asks how she keeps warm and how she warms her feet.
Explains that rapid warming sets chilblains off and risks burns.
