Advises whole-body warmth, layers, thick socks, roomy warm footwear and movement.
Advises not scratching and a pharmacy soothing lotion.
Suggests the university student support service and hardship funds.
Advises GP review for broken, infected or non-healing skin or fingers changing colour.
Asks her to explain what she will do differently tonight and invites questions.
Explains chilblains can recur and that starting warm socks and layers early prevents them.

concern.how: She admits the cold house and radiator warming; the podiatrist removes the shame, uses it to target the advice and points her to help with costs.

safety.point: Broken, infected or non-healing skin, or fingers changing colour in the cold, need a GP review.
Warming numb feet on a radiator or hot water bottle risks burns.

scripts.notes: The card gives the diagnosis; the script assumes no features suggesting another cause and gives only general, non-prescribing advice.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the podiatrist who saw your father this morning. Thank you for coming in. I can see you're upset, and I'd like to hear what you have to say.
Upset? I'm furious. He was here two weeks ago having his nails cut, and now the nurse finds an ulcer. How did nobody see it? Isn't that the whole point of coming here?
I can hear how angry and worried you are, and that's completely understandable. Please, go on.
He's diabetic, his circulation's poor, and everyone knows feet like his need watching. We trusted you.
Thank you for telling me. What have you been told so far, and what's worrying you most right now?
Only that there's an ulcer on his little toe. My uncle lost a toe like this. That's all I can think about.

That's frightening, especially after what happened to your uncle. Let me tell you what I found. The ulcer is on the side of his left little toe. It's small and shallow, and there are no signs of infection spreading into the foot.
So it's not as bad as I thought?

It's not as bad as it could be, but it does need close care. Today I cleaned and dressed it, and I've made an urgent referral to the hospital diabetic foot team. They'll also check his circulation properly.
And what about the appointment two weeks ago? Was it missed?

I'm truly sorry this has happened, and for the worry it's caused you both. I honestly don't know yet whether anything was there at that visit; ulcers can develop quickly. I don't want to guess. What I will do is review the notes from that appointment and look into it properly.
Good, because I want answers.

You deserve them, and your concerns will be taken seriously. If you'd like to make a formal complaint, you can contact the Patient Advice and Liaison Service. They help families raise concerns and can guide you through the complaints process. I'll give you their details before you go.
Thank you. Sorry, I know it's not you personally. I just feel awful. I live two hours away. I should have checked his feet myself.

Please don't blame yourself. Living that far away, you couldn't check his feet every day, and that's what his care team, including us, is there for. What matters now is that the ulcer has been found and is being treated quickly.
But will he lose the toe?

I can't promise, but I can be honest. The ulcer is small, it's been found early, and there's no sign of spreading infection, which are all good signs. The main challenge is his circulation. Poor blood flow means less oxygen reaches the wound, so it heals more slowly. That's why we'll monitor it so closely.
So it'll take a while to heal.
It may take weeks, yes. That's why the dressing reviews and the hospital team matter so much.
What should we be looking out for?

If you or anyone at home notices redness spreading, swelling, pus, a bad smell, the toe turning darker or black, or your father becoming feverish, confused or unwell, call us the same day, or 111 out of hours. If he seems very unwell, call 999.
Spreading redness, swelling, pus, a smell, a darker toe, or him being unwell.
Exactly. Would you like me to keep you updated? I'd need your father's agreement first.
Yes, please. He'll say yes. Could you ring me after the hospital appointment?
I'll ask him now and record his answer and your number in his notes. Then I'll call you after the hospital team has seen him. The district nurse will continue the dressings at home in between.
And when will you see him again?
I'll see him for a dressing review in three days, unless the hospital team takes over his care first. Either way, I'll let you know.
Okay. Thank you for listening. I came in ready for a fight.
You came in worried for your dad, as anyone would. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
No. Just look after him.
We will. I'll go and speak to him about the updates now.

coverage.how: Invites her to speak, lets her continue and acknowledges her anger and worry.
Asks what she has been told and what worries her most.
Explains the small, shallow ulcer with no spreading infection.
Explains cleaning and dressing, and the urgent referral including a circulation check.
Says sorry for the distress and declines to guess the cause before the notes are reviewed.
Commits to reviewing the earlier appointment and taking her concerns seriously.
Explains how to complain through the Patient Advice and Liaison Service.
Responds to her guilt and gives an honest answer about the toe.
Explains how poor blood flow slows healing and why monitoring is close.
Lists spreading redness, swelling, pus, smell, darkening, fever or confusion, with same day, 111 and 999.
Seeks her father's consent for updates and arranges a dressing review in three days.

concern.how: Her guilt about living far away and fear of amputation like her uncle surface; the podiatrist removes blame and answers honestly.

safety.point: Spreading redness, swelling, pus, smell, a darkening toe, fever, confusion or feeling unwell need same-day contact, 111 out of hours, or 999 if very unwell.
Urgent referral to the hospital diabetic foot team with a circulation check.

scripts.notes: The script refers to the uncle, the patient's brother, as the daughter would. Dressing review in three days and continued district nurse dressings are assumed local arrangements. UK guidance expects referral of a diabetic foot ulcer to the specialist team within one working day.

turns.text: Hello, I'm Sam, one of the radiographers on your machine. Have you got a few minutes before you go? How are you finding the treatment so far?
The treatment itself is fine, it's quick. But my skin's gone pink and it itches, especially at night.
Thank you for telling me. When did you first notice it, and is it anywhere other than the treated breast?
A few days ago, towards my armpit too. I've stopped my deodorant and moisturiser, because a friend said creams make burns worse.
We'll come back to that. May I look at the skin? Seeing it helps me give you the right advice.
Yes, of course.
Thank you. The skin is evenly pink, like mild sunburn, and dry, but it isn't broken, blistered or weeping, and nothing looks infected. That's what I'd expect at this stage.
So it is a burn, then? That's not supposed to happen, is it?

It isn't a burn in the sense of something going wrong. Skin renews itself all the time, and radiotherapy slows that down in the treated area, so it becomes pink, dry and itchy. Most people get a reaction like this.
Will it keep getting worse?
It often gets a little stronger towards the end of the course and for a week or two afterwards, because the effect builds up. Then it settles, and the redness fades over a few weeks.
And will it scar? My friend's sister had marks for ages.

A reaction like yours usually heals without scarring, though the skin may stay a shade darker for a while. Now, your friend's advice. You can keep using your usual moisturiser and deodorant while the skin is unbroken.
Really? I thought anything on the skin would make it worse.
That used to be the advice, but it has changed. A plain, unperfumed moisturiser, smoothed on gently, keeps the skin supple and eases the itch. If your deodorant ever stings, stop it then.
Yes. That's a relief, actually. Is there anything else I should be doing?

Wash with lukewarm water and a mild soap, and pat dry rather than rubbing. Wear loose, soft clothing and a soft bra without wiring. And keep the area covered and out of the sun, during treatment and for a good while after.
Fine. I mostly wear soft things anyway.
Good. Can I ask about your day? Is there anything you do regularly that you're worried about having to stop?
Well, yes. I swim every morning. It's when I see my friends. I assumed I'd have to give it up, and honestly, that's what's been getting me down.

I can see that matters a lot to you. The good news is that you can usually keep swimming while the skin is unbroken. Chlorine dries the skin, so rinse with fresh water afterwards, pat dry, and moisturise.
So I don't have to stop?
Not now. But if the skin breaks, blisters or weeps, stop swimming until it has healed, because broken skin can pick up an infection. Can you live with that?
Yes, definitely. What about a herbal cream my neighbour recommended?
Please check with us before putting anything new on the skin, including herbal or perfumed creams and talc. Avoid heat pads and ice packs on the area, and don't wet shave or wax under that arm.
All right. And if it does get worse, what then?

Tell us if the skin breaks, blisters or weeps, if pain is increasing, or if the area becomes hot and swollen. If you feel feverish, ring the helpline on your appointment card the same day; it's answered at any time.
I've got the card in my bag.
Perfect. Just so I know I've explained it clearly, could you tell me what you're going to do from today?
Moisturiser and deodorant are fine while the skin's unbroken. Gentle washing, loose clothes, no sun. Keep swimming but rinse after, and stop if it breaks. Ring if it blisters, weeps, or I'm feverish.
That's exactly right. I'll look at your skin again at the end of this week, or sooner if you're worried. Anything else on your mind?
No, that's everything. Thank you, I feel much better.

coverage.how: Asks how treatment is going, when the skin changed and where.
Asks permission to look, says why, and describes the even pinkness and unbroken skin plainly.
Explains the reaction as expected and why radiotherapy affects skin renewal.
Explains the reaction may peak at the end and shortly after the course, then settle, and answers the scarring question honestly.
Corrects the friend's advice kindly: usual moisturiser and deodorant while skin is unbroken.
Gives washing, patting dry, loose clothing and sun avoidance advice.
Asks about her routine and what she fears giving up.
Says swimming can continue with rinsing and moisturising, and stops if the skin breaks.
Lists products and practices to avoid without asking the team.
Lists what to report and how to contact the department at any time.
Teach-back, then agrees the next skin check at the end of the week.

concern.how: She reveals that losing her morning swim is what upsets her; the radiographer acknowledges it and shows how she can keep swimming safely.

safety.point: Keep the treated area out of the sun.
Stop swimming if the skin breaks, blisters or weeps, because of infection risk.
Report broken or weeping skin, increasing pain, heat or swelling; feeling feverish needs a same-day call.

scripts.notes: The card gives no skin findings; the script invents a benign mild, even erythema with intact skin and no infection. Skin care advice follows current UK radiographer guidance (moisturiser and deodorant allowed on intact skin; swimming allowed while skin intact). The helpline answered at any time is assumed; confirm local arrangements.

turns.text: Hello, I'm Alex, one of the radiographers. I'll be doing your planning scan today. Before we start, could you tell me what you've been told about the scan and the marks?
The doctor said I'd have a scan to plan the treatment. Then the nurse mentioned tattoos. I don't want them. Can't you just use a pen?
Thank you for telling me now, before anything's done. We can definitely talk about a pen. First, may I explain what today is actually for, so the rest makes sense?
Go on.

This scan isn't to look for cancer. It's a map. You'll lie on your back on a firm couch, with your arms resting above your head on a support. The scanner takes pictures of your chest for a few minutes, and the team use them to design treatment that targets the chest wall and protects your heart and lungs.
So why do I need marks at all?

Because you'll be treated over several weeks, and you need to lie in exactly the same position every time. The marks give us fixed points on your skin to line up with the lasers in the treatment room. Then we take a quick image to check before treating.
And the tattoos are what, exactly?
Each one is a tiny dot, about the size of a freckle, made with a fine needle and a drop of ink. It feels like a quick scratch. I won't pretend otherwise, though: they're permanent.
That's the problem.
Would you tell me what makes you reluctant? I'd like to understand before I say anything else.
I've lost my breast. Every time I look in the mirror I see the scar. I don't want more marks reminding me of all this, and I'll see them in a swimsuit for the rest of my life.

That makes complete sense. The surgery has already changed your body a great deal, and you didn't have much choice about that. Wanting to protect your body from any more change is entirely reasonable.
So do I have to have them?
No, you don't. Our department can use pen marks instead. We draw small marks and cover each one with a clear film dressing, like a thin, see-through sticker, so they don't wash off.
That sounds much better.

It suits many people, but I should be honest about the drawbacks. The dressings need to stay on for the whole course. You can shower, but gently, with no scrubbing or long soaks in the bath, and the skin underneath can get itchy. If a mark fades, we redraw it, which can mean a little extra time on the couch.
What about swimming?
Long swims tend to lift the dressings, so you might need to pause swimming during the course. Some people find the dressings more of a nuisance than they expected; others hardly notice them.
Would the treatment be less accurate with pen?
No. Whichever you choose, we line you up carefully and check your position with images before every treatment. The choice is yours, and either way you get the same treatment.
Then I'd like the pen marks, please.
Of course. If the dressings become a real nuisance, you can change your mind and have the dots at any point. Is anything else worrying you about the scan itself?
Will anyone see me undressed?

Only me and one colleague, who'll help position you. You'll be covered with a gown or a sheet whenever we're not adjusting your position, and you can ask us to stop at any time. Would you still like to go ahead with the scan today?
Yes, I would.
Thank you. I'm writing in your record now that you've chosen pen marks with clear dressings, not tattoos, so the treatment team know before your first appointment and nobody asks you again.
And if I've got questions later?

Ring the radiotherapy number on your appointment letter, or ask any radiographer when you come in. If a dressing comes off at home, don't redraw the mark yourself. Let us know, and we'll check and replace it before your next treatment. Shall we recap what we've agreed?
Pen marks under stickers, keep them on, gentle showers, ring you if one comes off. And the scan is today.
Exactly. Let's get you comfortable on the couch, and I'll talk you through each step.

coverage.how: Introduces self and asks what she has been told about the scan and marks.
Explains the planning scan as a map, the position and the purpose.
Explains that marks line her up identically every day with the room lasers.
Describes freckle-sized dots, a scratch sensation, and says plainly they are permanent.
Asks what makes her reluctant before arguing.
Acknowledges how much the surgery has changed her body.
Offers pen marks under clear film dressings.
Explains dressings stay on, gentle showering, itch, redrawing and swimming.
Says the choice is hers, imaging checks either way, and she can change her mind.
Asks whether she still wants the planning scan today.
Records the decision and gives the contact route and what to do if a dressing comes off.

concern.how: She explains that permanent marks would keep reminding her of the mastectomy; the radiographer validates it and offers the alternative without pressure.

safety.point: Her position is checked with images before every treatment, whichever marks she chooses.
She can ask to stop at any time during the scan.
If a dressing comes off, do not redraw the mark at home; tell the department so it is checked and replaced.

scripts.notes: The card states that the department offers pen marks under clear film dressings. Practice varies between UK centres; some use surface guidance with no marks. Dressing care advice is general.

turns.text: Hello, I'm Jo, one of the mammographers. I'll be taking your extra pictures this morning. Before we do anything, how have you been since the letter came?
Honestly? Awful. I've hardly slept. I just need to know, have I got cancer?

I can hear how frightening this has been, and I'm sorry you've had such a hard few days. I can't answer that yet, but I can explain what's happening. What did the letter say, and what did you take it to mean?
That they'd seen something and wanted me back. I assumed it means they've found a lump.

That's a very common thing to assume. Being recalled means the doctors reading your screening pictures saw an area in your right breast they'd like a clearer look at. It isn't a diagnosis. Often it's normal breast tissue overlapping, or something harmless such as a cyst, which is a small sac of fluid.
So why couldn't they tell from the first pictures?

Screening pictures are taken from standard angles, to check a lot of women quickly. Sometimes an area just needs a different angle or a magnified view. Most women who are recalled are found not to have cancer. I can't promise you're one of them, but it's important you know that.
Most. But some do.
Some do, yes, and I won't pretend otherwise. You seem to have been thinking about this a great deal. Can I ask whether anyone in your family has had breast problems?
My mum. She died of breast cancer when I was fifteen. And now my daughter's at university, and all I can think is that she'll lose her mum the same way.

Thank you for telling me. That's an enormous thing to carry into this room, and of course the letter brought it all back. It makes complete sense that you're expecting the worst. I'll make sure the doctor knows about your mum today.
Does that make it more likely?

Having a close relative with breast cancer can raise a woman's risk, and that deserves a proper conversation. The doctor can talk it through and, if it's appropriate, refer you to a family history service. But your mum's illness doesn't tell us what this area is.
Okay. So what happens now?

First, I'll take some more mammogram views of the right breast, possibly magnified. It's the same squeeze as before, for a few seconds each time. Then a doctor may do an ultrasound scan, which uses sound waves and a little gel on the skin. Many women need nothing more than that.
And if they need more?

Sometimes the doctor recommends a needle test, called a biopsy, to take a tiny sample of tissue under local anaesthetic. If so, they'll explain exactly why and what it involves, and ask for your agreement first. Nothing happens without you saying yes.
When would I know?

The doctor usually talks to you about what the pictures show before you leave today. If a needle test is done, those results take about a week, and you'd come back to discuss them in person. I don't want to promise more than that.
A week. I don't know how I'll cope.
That's understandable. Who do you have around you at the moment?
My husband. But I haven't told him. I didn't want to worry him.

That's a kind instinct, but it means you've been carrying this on your own. Many women find sharing it helps. Would you like someone with you later today, or at any results appointment? You'd be very welcome to bring him.
Maybe. I'll ring him after this.

Good. There's also a breast care nurse in clinic today. She's specially trained to support women through this, and she can sit with you after your pictures and give you her direct number for any questions afterwards.
I'd like that.

I'll arrange it. One more thing, whatever today shows. If you ever notice a new lump, a change in shape, puckering of the skin or a change in the nipple, see your GP promptly rather than waiting for your next screening.
I will. I didn't know you could be recalled with nothing wrong.
Many people don't. How are you feeling now? Would you like a minute, or are you ready for me to take the pictures?
A bit calmer. I'm ready. Let's get it done.
Thank you. I'll explain each step as we go, and you can ask me to pause at any time.

coverage.how: Introduces self and asks how she has been since the letter.
Asks what the letter said and what she took it to mean.
Explains recall as a request for a clearer look, not a diagnosis, with common benign causes.
Says most recalled women do not have cancer, without promising, and admits some do.
Asks about family history, acknowledges her mother's death, and addresses the risk question honestly.
Describes further views, possible ultrasound.
Explains a biopsy would be explained by the doctor and needs her agreement.
Says the doctor usually discusses imaging today and biopsy results take about a week.
Asks about support and invites her husband to today or a results visit.
Offers the breast care nurse and her direct number.
Advises reporting new breast changes to the GP whatever the result.
Checks how she feels and whether she is ready before imaging.

concern.how: Asked about family history, she reveals her mother's death and fear for her daughter; the radiographer acknowledges it, tells the doctor, and separates family risk from today's finding.

safety.point: No promise that the result is benign; most recalls are not cancer but some are.
A biopsy only happens after explanation and her agreement.
Report any new breast change to the GP promptly whatever today shows.

scripts.notes: Clinic arrangements are those given on the card. Family history referral is offered only if appropriate, as in current UK practice.

turns.text: Good morning, I'm Priya, one of the radiographers who'll be treating you. Before your first treatment, I'd like to go through the preparation with you. What did you make of the leaflet we sent?
To be honest, not much. Full bladder, empty bowel, lots of times and amounts. I got muddled.

You're not the only one, so let's keep it simple. The prostate sits just below the bladder and in front of the back passage. When your bladder is comfortably full, it pushes part of the bowel up and away from the area we're treating, so less healthy tissue gets radiation.
Right. And the empty bowel?

If the back passage is full of wind or stool, it can push the prostate slightly out of place. An empty bowel helps the prostate sit in the same position every day, so the treatment reaches the same spot each time.
Makes sense when you put it like that.

So, the routine. Empty your bladder, drink three cups of water, then wait 30 minutes before treatment. Try not to empty your bladder again during that time. We'll tell you each day when to start drinking.
Three cups, then 30 minutes.
Exactly. I noticed you said you haven't drunk anything this morning. Can I ask why?
I didn't want to need the toilet halfway through.
That's understandable. Is there anything in particular that worries you about that?
Well, since all this started, I leak a bit sometimes. If I'm full, I'm frightened I'll wet myself on the couch, in front of all you young people.

Thank you for telling me; I know that isn't easy to say. It's very common with prostate problems, and nobody here will think twice about it. You can wear a pad during treatment, and we'll put a protective sheet on the couch. If anything happens, we'll sort it out quietly.
That would help a lot, actually.

And the treatment itself only takes a few minutes once you're lined up. We watch you on cameras the whole time and can hear you. If you really can't hold on, just tell us, and we'll stop and help you.
So I won't be stuck there.

Never. Now, for your bowel. Try to eat regular meals, drink plenty through the day, and open your bowels before you come in if you can. If you become constipated or get diarrhoea, tell us, because we can help with both.
My wife says I should cut out vegetables. Is that right?
Please don't make big changes without talking to us first. Some people find it helps to cut down on foods that cause a lot of wind, such as beans or fizzy drinks. But keep eating a balanced diet.
Right. Anything else I should look out for?

Later in the course, many men need to pass urine more often or more urgently, or feel a burning when they go. Tell us if that happens. If you see blood in your urine or have a temperature, ring the department straight away. If you can't pass urine at all, that's urgent: go to the emergency department.
I'll remember that.
Just so I know I've explained it clearly, could you tell me the routine in your own words?
Go to the toilet, drink three cups of water, wait 30 minutes, don't go again. Open my bowels before if I can. And wear a pad if I want.
Perfect. And what would you report to us?
Going a lot or burning, constipation or the runs. Blood or a temperature, ring straight away.
And if you can't pass urine at all?
Straight to the emergency department.

Exactly. Now, about today. As you haven't had anything to drink, shall we start the routine now? Empty your bladder, have the three cups, and we'll treat you once the 30 minutes are up. I'll find you a pad and a sheet.
Yes, let's do that. Sorry to hold you up.
No need to apologise. It's much better to sort it out on the first day. Do you have any other questions before you start drinking?
No. I feel a lot better about it now.

coverage.how: Welcomes him and asks what he made of the leaflet.
Explains how a full bladder moves bowel away from the treated area.
Explains how an empty bowel keeps the prostate in a constant position.
Gives the routine in order: empty, three cups, wait 30 minutes.
Asks why he did not drink and what worries him.
Normalises leaking and offers a pad and protective sheet discreetly.
Explains treatment is short, he is watched, and staff will stop if he cannot hold on.
Gives bowel advice and asks him to report constipation or diarrhoea.
Explains frequency, urgency and burning, and urgent symptoms.
Teach-back of the routine and what to report.
Agrees to start the routine now and treat after 30 minutes.

concern.how: He admits he leaks and fears wetting himself; the radiographer normalises it and offers a pad, a sheet and the reassurance that they will stop.

safety.point: Staff watch him throughout and will stop treatment if he cannot hold on.
Blood in the urine or a temperature: ring the department straight away.
Unable to pass urine at all: go to the emergency department.

scripts.notes: The drinking routine is the department's own, as given on the card; UK centres vary. Diet advice is general and avoids specific restrictions.

turns.text: Hello, come in and have a seat. I'm Chris, the radiographer who runs this review clinic. How are your mouth and throat this week?
Sore. Really sore. Like a bad sore throat that won't go, and my tongue stings.
I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. How are eating and drinking going?
Drinking's all right. Eating's hard. I'm having a bit of soup, but I'm not finishing meals.
Thank you. And how are you taking the painkillers you were given last week? And what are you using to clean your mouth?
I take them when it gets unbearable, maybe once a day. And I use my mint mouthwash, the strong stuff, to keep it clean.

That's helpful to know. First, the soreness. Radiotherapy affects the lining of the mouth and throat, which normally renews itself quickly. Around this point in treatment it often becomes red and raw. It's expected, and it usually settles over several weeks after treatment finishes.
So it's not something going wrong.

No, it's the treatment affecting that area, but we can make it much more bearable. Painkillers work best taken regularly, as prescribed, rather than waiting until the pain is unbearable. Once pain is severe, it's much harder to bring down. The nurse can also help you time your doses so they're working when you eat.
I'd rather not take them all the time.
Can you tell me what worries you about taking them?
My brother hurt his back and ended up hooked on painkillers for years. I'm not going down that road. I'd rather not eat.

I can understand that, after seeing what your brother went through, and it's a sensible thing to ask about. Painkillers used for a short time, for a soreness that will heal, and checked by the team, are much less likely to cause that kind of problem. And not eating would weaken you during treatment, which is a real risk too.
So you won't just leave me on them?

No. We'll review them every week while you're on treatment, and once your mouth heals, the team will reduce them gradually and stop them. You won't be left on them. If you notice drowsiness or constipation, tell us, because both can be managed.
All right. I'll try taking them properly.

Thank you. Now, the mint mouthwash. I'd ask you to stop using it. Strong mouthwashes often contain alcohol and flavourings, which sting raw skin and dry the mouth out. Instead, rinse with a weak salt water mix, or we can prescribe a gentle, soothing mouthwash.
But I need to keep it clean.

You do, and you're right to think about it. Use a soft toothbrush, a child's one is ideal, with a mild toothpaste, gently, twice a day, and rinse after every meal. Sip water often and keep your lips moist. Avoid smoking and alcohol, as both make soreness worse.
What about food? I'm getting fed up with soup.

Softer, moist foods are usually easiest, such as scrambled egg, porridge, mashed potato with gravy, or yoghurt. Avoid spicy, salty, acidic or rough foods for now. I'd also like the dietitian to see you this week; they can suggest nourishing drinks and keep an eye on your weight. Is that all right?
Yes, please. I think I've lost a bit.

We'll weigh you before you leave. There are also a few warning signs. If you can't swallow fluids or your tablets, if you get a temperature or feel shivery, or if your mouth bleeds and won't stop, contact the department the same day. Don't wait for clinic.
Same day. Got it.
The helpline number on your treatment card is answered at night too. Could you tell me what you're going to do from today, so I know I've been clear?

Take the painkillers regularly, ask about timing them for meals, stop the mint mouthwash and use salt water or the one you give me. Soft brush, soft food, see the dietitian. And ring if I can't swallow, get a temperature or it bleeds.
That's exactly right. I'll ask the doctor to prescribe the soothing mouthwash today, and I'll see you here again next week.
Thanks. I didn't realise I was making it harder for myself.
You were trying to do the right thing, and you've told me what matters to you. Is there anything else bothering you?
No, that's it. Thank you.

coverage.how: Asks about the mouth and throat and about eating and drinking.
Asks how he takes the painkillers and what he cleans his mouth with.
Explains mucositis in plain words as expected and settling after treatment.
Explains regular dosing works better than waiting for severe pain.
Asks what worries him and answers the dependence fear honestly.
Explains weekly review, gradual reduction and side effects to report.
Advises stopping the alcohol mouthwash and offers salt water or a prescribed one.
Gives soft brush, rinsing, moisture and avoidance advice.
Suggests soft foods, offers the dietitian and weighs him.
Gives same-day warning signs and the helpline.
Teach-back, then confirms the prescription and next review.

concern.how: He reveals his brother's dependence on painkillers; the radiographer acknowledges it, explains why short supervised use is different, and promises review and reduction.

safety.point: Report drowsiness or constipation from painkillers.
Unable to swallow fluids or tablets, a temperature or bleeding that will not stop: contact the department the same day.

scripts.notes: The card does not name the painkiller; the script keeps it general. The dependence answer is deliberately cautious: lower risk with short supervised use, not no risk. The helpline answered at night is assumed; confirm locally.

turns.text: Hello, I'm Dana, one of the CT radiographers. Before your scan I'd like to explain a couple of medicines we may give you, and ask a few safety questions. Is now all right?
Yes, fine. The cardiologist mentioned something about slowing my heart down.

That's right. This scan takes pictures of the arteries that supply your heart muscle. Because the heart is moving all the time, a slower, steady beat gives much sharper pictures, rather like a camera catching someone walking instead of running.
And mine's too fast?

A little. Your heart rate today is 78 beats a minute, and we aim for below 65 for the clearest images. Under our department's patient group direction, which allows trained radiographers to give it, I can offer you a tablet that slows the heart for a few hours.
What sort of tablet?

It's called a beta-blocker. It calms the effect of adrenaline on the heart. You'd take it now, and we'd check your heart rate before the scan. Then, just before the pictures, we give a spray under your tongue, which widens the heart arteries for a short time so we can see them properly.
Okay.
Before I give you either, I need to ask some safety questions. Do you have asthma, or any breathing problem treated with inhalers?
No, nothing like that.
Do you ever get dizzy or faint, or have you been told your blood pressure is low?
Not low. But I'll tell you something. Years ago I was on a blood pressure tablet and I stopped it, because it made me feel faint and sluggish. And I've got to drive home after this.
I'm glad you told me; that's important. Do you remember what it was, or how long you took it for?
No idea of the name. A few weeks. I felt like I was wading through mud.

That sounds unpleasant, and I understand why you're wary. This is different, because it's a single dose rather than a daily tablet, and its effect wears off over the day. I'll check your heart rate and blood pressure before the scan, and if either is too low, we won't give the spray.
And the driving?

After the scan, you'll stay with us for 20 minutes so we can check you feel well. Most people feel fine, but some feel tired or light-headed. Please don't drive until you feel completely normal. If someone could collect you today, that would be the safest choice.
My wife could come, I suppose. I'll ring her.
Thank you. There's one more question, and I ask every man. Have you taken any tablets for erection problems, such as sildenafil, in the last two days?
No. Why does that matter?

Because those tablets and the spray both widen blood vessels. Together they can drop blood pressure dangerously low, so we never give the spray if someone has taken one recently. Thank you for answering.
What else might I notice?
The spray often causes a headache, or a flushed, light-headed feeling, for a few minutes. The tablet can make you feel a little tired. Both usually pass quickly. Do you have any questions so far?
What if I say no to the tablet?

That's your choice, and it's completely fine to refuse. We'd still try the scan, but with a faster heart rate the pictures may be blurred, and sometimes the scan then can't answer the cardiologist's question, which might mean another test.
I see. If it's one tablet and my wife's driving, I'll take it.
Thank you. At any point today, if you get chest pain, feel short of breath or feel faint, tell us straight away, whether you're in the waiting area or on the scanner.
I will.
So, to check we're agreed, could you tell me what's going to happen next?
I take the tablet now, and you check my heart rate. The spray just before the scan. Then I wait 20 minutes, and my wife drives me home.
Exactly. And if you feel unwell at home, or the headache lasts into the evening, contact your GP or ring 111. For chest pain, call 999. I'll get the tablet for you now.

coverage.how: Explains why a slow, steady heartbeat gives sharp pictures, with a camera comparison.
Gives his rate of 78 and the target below 65.
Explains the beta-blocker tablet and the spray under the tongue and their timing.
Asks about asthma, dizziness or low blood pressure, and erection tablets in the last two days.
Explains the interaction plainly and thanks him without embarrassment.
Asks about the old tablet and explains how a single dose differs, with pre-scan checks.
Explains headache, flushing, light-headedness and tiredness.
Explains the 20-minute observation and advises not driving until normal, ideally with a lift.
Makes refusal acceptable and explains the effect on image quality.
Tells him to report chest pain, breathlessness or faintness during and after the visit.
Confirms his choice and asks him to say what will happen next.

concern.how: He reveals a past bad reaction to a blood pressure tablet and worry about driving; the radiographer explores it, explains the single dose and checks, and plans a lift home.

safety.point: Heart rate and blood pressure are checked before the spray, which is withheld if either is too low.
Do not drive until feeling completely normal; a lift home is safest.
The spray is never given after recent erection tablets because of a dangerous drop in blood pressure.
Report chest pain, breathlessness or faintness at once.
Unwell at home: GP or 111; chest pain: 999.

scripts.notes: The script assumes he has no asthma, no low blood pressure and no recent erection tablets. The checklist shown is shortened; a full departmental checklist also covers heart block and other medicines. The heart rate target and observation time are those on the card; local protocols vary.

turns.text: Well done, that's your last treatment finished. You've worked really hard over these weeks. How are you feeling today?
Relieved, I suppose. But mostly tired. I thought I'd feel better by now.
That's a very common feeling on the last day, so let's talk it through. How's the tiredness, and how are your bowels and bladder at the moment?
I'm exhausted by the afternoon. My bowels are loose, three or four times a day, and I'm up at night to pass water.
Thank you. Any blood, pain or stinging when you pass water?
A little stinging sometimes. No blood.

That all fits with the treatment. It may surprise you, but side effects often carry on, or even get a little worse, for a week or two after the last treatment, because radiotherapy keeps working for a while. After that, they should gradually improve.
Worse? Oh dear.

A little, for some people, and then better. The tiredness can last longer, often several weeks. Rest when you need to, but keep up some gentle activity too, such as a short walk most days, because that actually helps tiredness improve over time.
That's the problem, really. In two weeks I've promised to look after my grandchildren on my own. My daughter's going away. I don't want to let her down.
That's clearly important to you. Can I ask how old they are, and what looking after them involves?
Four and seven. School runs, cooking, bath time, the lot.

That's a lot for anyone, let alone just after radiotherapy. I can't predict exactly how you'll feel by then. It might be wise to talk to your daughter now about a back-up, perhaps someone to share the school runs. Would that be possible?
Her husband's mother could help, I suppose. I just hate asking.

It isn't letting her down; it's planning sensibly. You may well feel up to it, and if so, wonderful. Now, while your bowel settles, drink plenty of fluids to replace what you're losing, and stick to plain foods. Cutting back on spicy and very high-fibre foods for now can help.
I've been living on toast.

Toast is fine, but try to add other plain foods too, such as rice, pasta, chicken or eggs, so you're getting enough nourishment. If the diarrhoea isn't settling, we can give you medicine for it, so do ask.
Okay. And what happens now? Do I just stop coming?

Your follow-up is an appointment with the oncology team in about six weeks. They'll ask how you're recovering, check on any side effects and talk about your future check-ups. The letter will come in the post.
Six weeks seems a long time.

It can feel that way, so you don't need to wait if you're worried. Contact us if the diarrhoea is more than you can manage, if you see blood, if passing water becomes painful, if you have a temperature, or if you feel dizzy or very thirsty, which can mean you're getting dehydrated. The number on your card is answered day and night.
Good. That's reassuring.

I should also mention longer-term effects. Most people recover well, but a few notice bowel or bladder changes months or even years later. If anything new starts, tell your GP or the team and mention your radiotherapy. And do keep using the vaginal dilator as we discussed; it helps keep the tissues healthy after pelvic treatment.
I've got the leaflet. I'll keep it up.

Thank you. Support doesn't stop today, either. There's the cancer information centre here, and local groups and charities that help people after treatment, with tiredness, money worries or just someone to talk to. Would you like their details?
Yes, please. My neighbour mentioned a group.
I'll print them for you. Before you go, have you got the department's number with you?
On my card, here.
Great. Could you tell me what you'll do over the next few weeks, so I know I've explained it clearly?

Expect it to get a bit worse before it's better. Rest, but keep walking. Plain food and plenty to drink. Ring if there's blood, pain passing water, a temperature, or I'm getting dried out. Clinic in six weeks. And ask about help with the grandchildren.
Perfect. It's been a pleasure treating you. Take care of yourself, and do ring if you're worried.

coverage.how: Congratulates her and asks how she feels.
Asks about tiredness, bowels and bladder, including blood or pain.
Explains side effects may continue or worsen briefly before improving.
Explains lasting fatigue and advises rest with gentle daily activity.
Asks about her plans and helps her think of a back-up without taking over.
Advises fluids and plain foods and offers anti-diarrhoeal help.
Explains the six-week oncology follow-up and what it covers.
Lists reasons to call before then, including dehydration, and the 24-hour number.
Mentions late bowel or bladder changes honestly and vaginal dilator use.
Offers the information centre and local support.
Checks she has the number and asks for a teach-back.

concern.how: She reveals the promise to look after her grandchildren; the radiographer explores what it involves and helps her plan a back-up without guilt.

safety.point: Side effects may worsen for a week or two after treatment.
Contact the team for unmanageable diarrhoea, blood, painful urination, temperature or signs of dehydration.
Report any new bowel or bladder change in future and mention the radiotherapy.

scripts.notes: Dilator advice, the 24-hour number and the absence of blood are on the card. The mild stinging and bowel frequency described by the patient are benign and consistent with the card.

turns.text: Thank you for waiting. I'm Ben, the radiographer in charge of your machine today. First, I'm sorry you've been kept waiting so long. I'm afraid I have to tell you that we can't treat you today.
You're joking. An hour I've sat out there. An hour! And now you tell me?

You're right to be annoyed. The machine developed a fault this morning. The engineers are working on it, but they don't expect it to be safe to use again today. We kept hoping it would be fixed quickly, and we should have told you sooner.
Can't you put me on another one?
I asked about that first. The other machines are fully booked today, and moving your treatment to a different machine needs checks that can't be done this afternoon.
This is ridiculous. You people never tell anyone anything.
I understand. It's frustrating, especially when you've made the effort to get here. Please tell me how you're feeling about it.
Furious. And scared, if I'm honest.
Thank you for saying that. What worries you most about missing today?
I read online that gaps in radiotherapy make it less effective. So that's it, isn't it? This has ruined my chances.

That's an important question, and what you read is true: the team does take gaps seriously, especially for lung treatment. That's exactly why there's a plan for this. The aim is to make up the missed treatment so the whole course still finishes in the planned time.
Make it up how?

The doctors have arranged an extra treatment for you this Saturday. With that, you'll receive the full course within the planned time, which is how the team protect its effect. If you'd like to talk it over with your doctor, I can arrange that too.
Saturday? I can't get here on a Saturday.
Can you tell me what makes it difficult?
I've been coming by taxi. My son drives me sometimes, but he works weekends. Today's taxi cost a fortune, and I've got nothing to show for it.

I'm sorry. That's a real problem, and paying for a wasted journey must sting. A few things might help. Hospital patient transport may be available if you qualify, and you may be able to claim back travel costs through the NHS travel costs scheme, depending on your income.
Nobody told me about that.

Then I'm glad we're talking about it. Some cancer charities also offer travel grants. Would you like me to refer you to our support team today? They can help with the forms and try to book transport for Saturday.
Yes. I suppose so.
I'll do that before you leave. I'll also ask whether the department can help with today's taxi, although I can't promise.
Well, that would be something.

So, your next treatment is tomorrow at your usual time, on your usual machine, and then the extra one on Saturday. We'll ring you this evening if anything changes. How are you feeling in yourself? Any new symptoms?
Same as last week. A bit of a cough. Tired.

That's expected at this stage. But if your breathing gets worse, you cough up blood, you get chest pain or you have a high temperature, don't wait for tomorrow. Ring the number on your card, which is answered day and night. If you're very breathless or have chest pain, call 999.
Right.
I also want you to know you can give feedback about today. The Patient Advice and Liaison Service can take a complaint or a comment, and I'll report what happened myself as well.
Maybe. I'll think about it. I know it's not your fault.
Thank you. Just so we're both clear, could you tell me the plan?
Tomorrow as usual, an extra one on Saturday, and the support team sorts out transport. Ring you if my breathing's worse, I cough up blood or I get a temperature.
That's it exactly. Thank you for being so patient with me, and I'm sorry again about today.

coverage.how: Apologises and gives the news in the first turn.
Explains the fault simply, admits the delay in updating him, and why another machine is not possible.
Acknowledges frustration and invites his feelings without defending.
Asks what worries him most.
Confirms that gaps matter, especially for lung cancer, and that there is a plan.
Explains the extra Saturday treatment keeps the course within the planned time.
Asks what makes Saturday difficult.
Explains patient transport, the travel costs scheme and charity grants, and refers him.
Confirms tomorrow's treatment and asks about symptoms.
Lists urgent symptoms and when to call 999.
Offers PALS and says the incident will be reported.
Asks for a teach-back of the plan.

concern.how: Asked what worries him, he fears the gap ruined his treatment and then reveals the transport cost; both are answered with honesty and practical help.

safety.point: Worse breathing, coughing up blood, chest pain or high temperature: ring the 24-hour number; severe breathlessness or chest pain: 999.

scripts.notes: The make-up plan is the card's. UK guidance treats lung cancer gaps as important and compensates within the planned overall time, as described. Cough and tiredness are invented and benign. Transport and travel cost help depend on eligibility, which the script states.

turns.text: Hello again, I'm Kim, the radiographer who did your scan. I want to explain properly what happened to your arm, and then check it again before you go. Is that all right?
Yes. It's really tight. What went wrong?

When we injected the dye for your scan, some of it leaked out of the vein into the tissue around the inside of your elbow, instead of travelling along the vein. That's why it's swollen and tight. I'm very sorry. It's uncomfortable, and it isn't what you expected.
Did someone put the needle in wrong?

We checked the cannula, the little plastic tube, with a salt water flush before the scan, and it was working. Leaks like this are a known complication. They can happen even when the cannula is placed correctly, because the injection is quite fast and veins can be delicate.
Right.

Can I check your arm again now? I'm looking at the swelling, the colour of your hand and how your fingers move. Can you wiggle your fingers and make a fist for me? Does your hand feel normal when I touch it?
Yes. It feels normal. My fingers are fine.
Good. Your fingers are warm and pink, you can move them normally, and the feeling is normal. Is the pain getting worse, better or staying the same?
About the same. Sort of aching.

Thank you. The radiologist, the doctor who reports scans, has examined your arm and is happy for you to go home. Usually the body absorbs the fluid over the next day or two, and the swelling goes down without any lasting harm.
So it'll just go away?

In most cases, yes. Until then, keep your arm raised on a cushion when you're sitting, ideally above the level of your heart. Our leaflet explains how to use a cold pack, so please follow that. You can take paracetamol if you need it, as the packet says.
The problem is tomorrow. I'm a hairdresser. I've got clients booked all day, and if I cancel, I don't get paid.

I'm sorry, that's a real worry. Holding scissors and a hairdryer up for hours could make it ache more. I'd suggest seeing how it feels in the morning. If it's still very swollen or sore, a lighter day might be wiser. Is there any way to spread your clients out?
Maybe. I'll speak to the salon. But is my arm damaged?

From everything we've checked, there's no sign of damage. Serious problems are rare, but I want you to know what to watch for. If the pain gets worse instead of better, if the skin blisters or changes colour, if your hand goes numb or tingly, or if your hand feels weak, you need to be seen urgently.
Where would I go?

During the day, ring this department on the number on the leaflet, and we'll see you straight away. Out of hours, go to the emergency department and take the leaflet, so they know what happened. If you're not sure, call 111.
Okay. Should I complain about this?

That's absolutely your right. I've already recorded what happened in your notes and on our incident system, so the department reviews it. If you'd like to raise a concern, the Patient Advice and Liaison Service can help, and their details are on the leaflet.
I'll think about it. At least you've been honest with me.
Thank you. Someone from the department will also phone you tomorrow to check on your arm. Is your mobile the best number?
Yes, it's on my form.
We'll use that. Is there a time of day that suits you, given you might be working?
Lunchtime would be best.
I'll note that. Your scan results go to your doctor as usual. Do you have any other questions?
No, that's fine.
Then, just to make sure I've been clear, could you tell me what you'll do tonight and what you'll look out for?

Keep the arm up, use the cold pack like the leaflet says, paracetamol if I need it. If it gets more painful, blisters, changes colour, or my hand goes numb or weak, I ring you, or go to the emergency department at night.
That's exactly right. Here's the leaflet with everything written down. And again, I'm sorry this happened.

coverage.how: Introduces self and explains the leak plainly.
Apologises and explains it is a known complication even with a working cannula.
Checks swelling, colour, movement and sensation aloud, and asks about pain.
States that the radiologist has examined the arm and is happy for discharge.
Explains absorption over a day or two and the swelling settling.
Advises elevation, the leaflet's cold pack advice and paracetamol.
Discusses her work honestly and suggests a lighter day if needed.
Lists the urgent warning signs.
Explains the daytime route, the emergency department out of hours, and 111.
Says it is recorded as an incident and arranges tomorrow's phone call.
Explains PALS and where their details are.
Teach-back and hands over the leaflet.

concern.how: She reveals her work and lost income and asks whether her arm is damaged and whether to complain; each is answered honestly and practically.

safety.point: Increasing pain, blistering, colour change, numbness, tingling or weakness needs urgent review.
Daytime: ring the department; out of hours: emergency department with the leaflet, or 111 if unsure.

scripts.notes: The pre-scan saline flush is invented and is standard practice. Cold pack use is left to the department's leaflet because UK local policies differ. Findings are those on the card.

turns.text: Hello, I'm Sarah, the sonographer who'll be doing the scan. And hello to you too, little one. Before we start, what have you been told about today?
Just that because she was breech, they want to check her hips. The doctor said they seemed fine when she was born, so I don't really understand why.

That's a very fair question. Babies who lie bottom first in the womb have a slightly higher chance of a hip that isn't settled properly in its socket. The check after birth is done by hand, and it can't pick up every small problem, so we use a scan to look more closely, even when the hips felt normal.
What are you actually looking for?

The hip is a ball and socket joint. At this age, much of it is still soft gristle, which shows up well on ultrasound. I'm checking that the ball sits deeply in the socket, and that the socket is a good shape.
Is it safe? Does it use X-rays?

No X-rays at all. Ultrasound uses sound waves, like the scans you had in pregnancy, and it doesn't hurt. Some babies grumble because the gel feels a bit cool, or because they don't like lying on their side.
What do I need to do?

I'll ask you to take off her nappy and lay her on her side on the couch, on a warm towel. I'll put gel on her hip and move a small probe over it, then turn her onto the other side. It usually takes about ten to fifteen minutes.
She hates being undressed.
Many babies do. You can stay right by her head and talk to her. If she's hungry, feeding her just before, or even during the scan, often keeps babies calm. A dummy helps some babies too.
I'll feed her. Sorry, I'm just nervous.
Please don't apologise. Can you tell me what's worrying you most?
My aunt had hip problems from when she was a baby, and she limped her whole life. I keep seeing these pictures of babies in harnesses. And I keep thinking it's my fault she was breech.
Thank you for telling me. You've been carrying a lot. First, being breech isn't anything you did or didn't do. It happens in many pregnancies, and there was nothing you could have done to change it.
Really?

Really. And most scans done for this reason are normal. Things are also very different from when your aunt was little. Now, when a problem is found early, treatment works well, and most children go on to walk and run completely normally.
And if it isn't normal?

Sometimes a hip just needs a repeat scan a few weeks later, as it matures. If treatment is needed, the baby usually wears a soft harness that holds the legs bent up and apart, so the socket grows around the ball. The specialist team fit it and look after you both, and it usually works well.
Would she be in pain in it?
No, babies get used to it quickly, and you can still cuddle and feed her. But let's not get ahead of ourselves; let's see what the scan shows.
When will I know?
In this clinic, I'll tell you the result at the end of the scan, and a letter goes to your GP. If anything needs following up, the specialist team will contact you with an appointment.
Oh, that's good. I thought I'd be waiting for weeks.

Not today. One more thing for her hips, whatever the result. If you swaddle her, keep it loose around the hips, so her legs can bend up and fall outwards, like a frog's. Wrapping her tightly with her legs held straight together isn't good for growing hips.
I didn't know that. My mum swaddles her really tightly.
It's a very common habit, and an easy one to change. Snug around the chest is fine, but loose around the legs. Could you tell me what we've talked about, so I know I've explained it well?

The scan checks the ball is in the socket. No X-rays, doesn't hurt, and I can feed her during it. It's probably normal, and if not, a harness usually works. Loose swaddling round the legs. And you'll tell me today.
That's perfect. Have you any other questions before we start?
No. I feel much better. Let's do it.

coverage.how: Greets mother and baby and asks what she has been told.
Explains the breech risk and the limits of the newborn hand check.
Explains the ball and socket and what the scan checks.
Says it uses sound waves, no X-rays, and does not hurt.
Describes undressing, lying on each side, gel, probe and duration.
Suggests feeding before or during and a dummy.
Asks what worries her most and addresses her guilt.
Says most scans are normal and explains repeat scan or treatment.
Explains the harness simply and that babies tolerate it.
Explains the result is given at the end of the scan with a letter to the GP.
Gives hip-healthy swaddling advice.
Teach-back and invites questions.

concern.how: She reveals her aunt's limp and her guilt about the breech position; the sonographer removes the guilt and explains how early treatment differs today.

safety.point: Any abnormal result is followed up by the specialist team with an appointment.
Swaddle loosely around the hips so the legs can bend up and out.

scripts.notes: The result-sharing arrangement is on the card. Scan duration of ten to fifteen minutes is typical but varies. No scan findings are given or assumed.

turns.text: Hello, thank you for coming in. I'm the speech and language therapist who saw your son. Before I go through the results, what do you already know about the assessment, and what are you hoping to hear today?
Not much, really. The school said he needed testing. I suppose I'm hoping you'll say he's just a bit behind.
That's a natural hope. What do you notice at home, when he talks or when you ask him to do things? And what has his teacher said?
If I say get your shoes, coat and bag, he comes back with just the shoes. His teacher says he looks lost when she gives instructions.
That matches what I saw. He finds it harder than most children his age to understand longer sentences and to put his ideas into words. We call this developmental language disorder, or DLD for short.
Disorder. That sounds serious.

I understand why the word worries you. It means language is harder for him to learn, without another cause such as hearing loss. It isn't a measure of his intelligence; he solved my picture puzzles easily.
So he's not slow?
No. He's a bright boy whose language needs more support. It's actually quite common. On average there are about two children with it in every classroom, so he's far from alone.
Will he grow out of it?

I want to be honest with you. DLD usually continues into adult life in some form, but the right support makes a real difference to how he copes, at school and with friends. Many people with DLD do very well; they learn ways around it.
Lifelong. I didn't expect that.

It's a lot to take in. Day to day, it mainly shows in two ways. With long instructions, he catches the first part and loses the rest. And when he tells a story or explains what happened, he struggles to get things in order.
That's him exactly. Can I ask you something? Is it my fault?
What makes you think it might be?
I work long shifts. When he was little I let him watch videos on the tablet for hours just so I could cope. I keep thinking if I'd talked to him more, this wouldn't have happened.

Thank you for telling me; I can hear you've been carrying that. DLD isn't caused by parenting, by screens, or by speaking more than one language at home. It comes from how a child's brain develops language. You didn't cause this.
I've felt so guilty.
That's understandable. But what I see is a mother who noticed, came along, and wants to help. That matters far more now.
So what happens next?

There are three parts. First, a block of weekly therapy sessions here, working on understanding and on telling stories. Second, a written report for school. Third, strategies for his teacher, like giving instructions in short chunks and using pictures.
And at home? What can I do?

Three simple things this week. Give one instruction at a time and ask him to tell it back to you. Use pictures or a quick sketch for the day's plan. And when he tells you about school, ask what happened first, then what happened next.
I can do that. But he already says he's stupid.

That's hard to hear. What will you tell him about today? You might say: your brain is great at lots of things, and words are a bit tricky, so we're getting help to make them easier. It puts the problem in the words, not in him.
He'd like the bit about his brain being great.
Good. Just so I know I've explained it clearly, could you tell me in your own words what DLD is?
It means language is harder for him to learn. It's not because he's slow and it's not because of me. It probably won't go away, but help makes it better.

That's exactly right. If you have questions before therapy starts, ring the clinic number on your letter during office hours. And if he seems very unhappy, or stops wanting to go to school, tell me or his GP early.
When will I hear from you?
Let's book a review in a few weeks, once therapy has started, to see how home and school are going. Is there anything else you'd like to ask today?
No. Thank you. I feel lighter, actually.

coverage.how: Opens by asking what she knows and what she hopes to hear.
Asks what she notices at home and what the teacher has said.
Names developmental language disorder and explains it as difficulty understanding and using language.
States it is not a measure of intelligence and not caused by parenting, screens or two languages.
Says it is common, usually lifelong, and that support changes how he copes.
Gives long instructions and story-telling as everyday examples.
Asks what lies behind the guilt, answers with facts about cause, and affirms her.
Sets out therapy block, school report and teacher strategies.
Gives three home strategies for this week.
Asks about the boy's view of himself and offers honest, positive words.
Checks understanding with teach-back, gives clinic contact and books a review.

concern.how: She asks if it is her fault; the therapist asks why, hears about the tablet videos, and explains clearly that screens and parenting do not cause DLD.

safety.point: If he becomes very unhappy or stops wanting to go to school, she should tell the therapist or GP early.

scripts.notes: The card gives no assessment detail; the script adds benign findings: difficulty with long sentences and narrative, with non-verbal puzzles solved easily. The prevalence statement of about two children per classroom reflects the commonly quoted figure of around seven per cent.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for having me in your home. I'm the speech and language therapist from the stroke team. You asked for some practical advice before going back to work, so let's start with you. How has your speech been recently?
Better than it was. On a good morning I sound almost normal. By the evening, or if I'm in a hurry, the words go mushy.
So it's best when you're fresh and worst when you're tired or rushing. What does your job involve day to day, and what worries you most?
I'm on the counter at a building society. Customers all day, some phone calls, explaining savings accounts. The phone worries me most, because they can't see my face.

That makes sense. Can I explain what's happening? The stroke has weakened the muscles you use for speech: your lips, your tongue and the back of your mouth. That's called dysarthria. The words are all there in your head; it's getting the muscles to shape them that's harder.
So it's not my brain going?
No, your language is fine. When you're tired, those weaker muscles tire faster, and when you rush, they can't keep up, so the sounds blur together.
That's exactly what happens. What can I actually do?

Three things. Slow down a little, slower than feels natural. Pause between phrases, which gives your muscles a moment to reset. And make the key words clear: names, amounts and dates. On the phone, it also helps to say, let me just repeat that to be sure.
Slower feels strange, like I'm talking to a child.
To you it feels slow, but to the listener it usually sounds calm and confident. Shall we try it? Tell me how you'd explain an account to a customer.
This account pays interest every month, and you can take money out at any time. That felt slow.
It was very clear, and it sounded professional. Are you keeping up your daily exercises?
Honestly, I've let them slip. They're boring.
That's very common. What about ten minutes after breakfast, rather than a long session? Short and daily works better than long and occasional.
Ten minutes I can manage.
Good. Fatigue is a big part of this after a stroke. Try to plan short breaks, and do the hardest speaking tasks, like phone calls, earlier in the day while you're fresher.
That makes sense. The thing is, last week in a shop a woman asked me if I'd been drinking. I was mortified. What if customers at work think that?
I'm so sorry; that must have really hurt. It was an unfair guess. What she heard was tired muscles after a stroke, not you, and your speech is easy to understand most of the time.
But I can't explain that to everyone.

No, and you don't have to. Some people find it helps to tell colleagues in one sentence, something like: I had a small stroke, and my speech can slur when I'm tired. Others prefer to say nothing. It's entirely your choice.
I think I'd tell my manager and the two people I work with most.

That sounds sensible. Your employer can also make reasonable adjustments, such as a quieter desk, phased hours, or fewer phone calls at first. Your manager or occupational health can help arrange that.
I didn't know I could ask for that.

You can. One more important thing. If your speech suddenly gets worse, or you have new weakness, numbness or a drooping face, that could be another stroke. Call 999 straight away; don't wait to see if it passes.
Even if it only lasts a few minutes?
Yes, even if it settles. Brief symptoms still need urgent checking. The ordinary end-of-day slurring that you already recognise is different; that's tiredness.
Okay. Sudden and new, call 999.
Exactly. So what will you try first?
Ten minutes of exercises after breakfast, slowing down and pausing, and doing my phone calls in the morning. And I'll ask my manager about a quieter desk.
That's a great plan. I'll ring you after your first two weeks back to see how it's going, and we can adjust things then. Does that suit you?
Yes. Thank you. I feel much more ready now.

coverage.how: Asks about her speech recently and summarises when it is best and worst.
Asks what the job involves and which speaking tasks worry her.
Explains dysarthria as weak speech muscles and why tiredness and rushing blur sounds.
Gives slowing, pausing and clear key words, with a phone check-back phrase.
Rehearses an account explanation with her and gives positive feedback.
Asks about the exercises and agrees ten minutes daily after breakfast.
Advises breaks and doing phone calls earlier in the day.
Responds kindly to the drinking comment and reframes it.
Offers a one-sentence explanation for colleagues and leaves the choice with her.
Mentions reasonable adjustments: quieter desk, phased hours, fewer calls.
Gives the stroke warning signs and 999, including symptoms that settle.
Asks what she will try first and agrees a call after two weeks at work.

concern.how: She describes being asked if she had been drinking; the therapist acknowledges the hurt, reframes it and offers a simple way to explain, leaving disclosure to her.

safety.point: Sudden worse speech, new weakness, numbness or facial droop may be a stroke: call 999 at once.
Symptoms that settle within minutes still need urgent checking.

scripts.notes: The card gives no exercise programme; the script assumes she already has daily speech exercises from earlier therapy, which is typical for community stroke care.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the speech and language therapist on the stroke unit. I assessed your mother's swallowing this morning. I understand you're unhappy with how things have gone, and I'd like to hear it from you first.
Unhappy? She's been here since Friday and nobody gave her so much as a cup of tea. I asked every nurse and they just said wait for the swallow person. Where were you?
You're right to be angry, and I'm sorry. Your mother waited all weekend for an assessment because there was no therapy cover, and that's not good enough for her or for you. Please, go on.
She kept asking me for water, and I had to say no. Do you know what that feels like?
It must have been awful, sitting with her and not being able to give her a drink. Thank you for following the advice; I know how hard that was. Can I explain why the nurses said no?
Go on, then.

When someone is admitted with a stroke, the nurses do a short swallow screen, a simple test with sips of water. If the person coughs, or their voice sounds wet, the swallow may not be safe yet. Then the rule is nothing by mouth until a full assessment.
It's only water. What harm could it do?

After a stroke, the muscles that close off the airway can be weak or slow. Water or food can then slip into the lungs instead of the stomach. That can cause a serious chest infection called aspiration pneumonia, which is a real danger after a stroke.
So you're saying it's because she's old.
No. The rule is the same for every patient who fails the screen, whatever their age. A young patient would have been kept nil by mouth too.
That's not what it felt like. It felt like she's eighty-four and nobody cares whether she eats.

I can hear that's what's hurt most. I won't pretend the weekend went well, but her age wasn't why she waited; the gap in our cover was. She's had fluids through the drip to keep her hydrated, and from today the team will keep a close eye on how much she's eating.
And what did you find this morning?

Good news, actually. Her swallow is much better than on Friday. She can start soft, bite-sized food, like fish in sauce, mashed potato or a soft omelette, and normal drinks. She needs to sit fully upright and have someone with her while she eats.
Someone with her? Why?

Supervision means a person sitting beside her, reminding her to take small mouthfuls, go slowly, and finish each one before the next. If you'd like to, you can do that at visiting times. I can show you how at lunchtime.
I'd like that. I've been feeling useless.
You're anything but. Here's what to look out for. If she coughs or splutters when eating or drinking, her voice sounds gurgly or wet, or she seems breathless, stop and tell a nurse straight away.
Cough, wet voice, breathless. Tell a nurse.

That's it. You mentioned asking about a complaint. You're entitled to, and I'd support it if you feel your mother was let down. The Patient Advice and Liaison Service, PALS, can help you by phone or in person, and the ward manager can see you today.
Will it make things worse for her? I don't want anyone taking it out on her.
No. A complaint won't affect her care in any way. It helps us fix gaps like this weekend's. I'll also report the delay myself.
Right. Thank you for saying that.
Can I check I've been clear? Could you tell me the plan for her eating and drinking?
Soft food in small pieces, normal drinks, sitting right up, someone with her. And if she coughs or sounds wet, tell a nurse.
Exactly right. I'll see her again tomorrow morning and update you afterwards, by phone or here, whichever you prefer.
Phone is fine. I'm sorry I shouted.
Please don't apologise. You were standing up for your mother, and you had good reason. Shall I come back at lunchtime to show you how to help her?
Yes, please. Twelve o'clock?
Twelve is perfect. I'll meet you at her bedside.
Thank you.

coverage.how: Introduces self, invites her to speak and lets her continue.
Apologises for the weekend wait and says it was not good enough.
Explains the water swallow screen and the nil by mouth rule until full assessment.
Explains aspiration into the lungs and aspiration pneumonia.
States the drip kept her hydrated and that intake will now be monitored.
Gives the results: soft, bite-sized food and normal drinks, upright and supervised.
Explains what supervision involves and offers to show her at lunchtime.
Says honestly that the rule applies at any age and the cause was the cover gap.
Supports a complaint, names PALS and the ward manager, and says care will not be affected.
Lists coughing, wet voice and breathlessness as signs to report at once.
Uses teach-back and agrees an update after tomorrow's review.

concern.how: She suggests her mother was neglected for being old; the therapist answers directly that the rule is age-blind and the delay was a cover gap, then supports her complaint.

safety.point: Coughing, spluttering, a wet voice or breathlessness at meals must be reported to a nurse at once.
Failed swallow screens mean nothing by mouth until full assessment because of aspiration pneumonia risk.

scripts.notes: Example foods for soft and bite-sized are the script's choice. The card states there was no weekend therapy cover; national stroke guidance expects specialist swallow assessment promptly, which is why the apology is unreserved. Medicines while nil by mouth are not discussed and would be managed by the medical team.

turns.text: Hello again, and thank you for letting me in. It's been a few weeks since my last visit, so first of all, how have eating and drinking been?
Not bad, really. The soft food is fine, and I'm drinking tea and water without any coughing.
That's really good progress. You mentioned on the phone that tablets are harder. Can you tell me exactly what happens when you take them?
The little ones go down. But the big white one and the capsule feel like they stick halfway. I have to keep swallowing, and I get panicky.
That sounds frightening. Lots of people find tablets harder than food after a stroke. Can I ask, and there's no wrong answer, have you been missing any tablets, or taking them differently?
Well. I haven't taken those two for about a week. I didn't want to choke. Please don't tell me off.
I'm not going to tell you off. You were scared and did what felt safe, and I'm glad you've told me. Do you know what those two are for?
One's the blood thinner, I think. The other's for my cholesterol.

Thank you. I need to be honest with you, because it matters. After a stroke, those medicines help to prevent another one. Stopping them without advice, especially the blood thinner, can raise that risk. So let's sort this out today.
Oh dear. Could I just crush them into my yoghurt?

Please don't crush tablets or open capsules unless a pharmacist has said it's safe. Some are made to release slowly or to protect your stomach, and crushing can change how they work or make them unsafe.
I didn't know that.
Most people don't. The good news is there are often alternatives. Your pharmacist or GP may be able to switch to a liquid, a smaller tablet, or a different medicine that does the same job.
So I might not need the big ones at all?

Possibly. That's their decision, but it's often possible. Meanwhile, can I show you a safer way to take the small ones? Sit right up in a chair, not leaning back. Take a sip of water first to wet your mouth, then one tablet, then another sip.
One at a time. I've been doing them all together.
That's very common, and one at a time is much easier. Shall we try with one of your small ones now?
There. That went down fine.
Well done. Now, about the two you've missed. I'd like your GP to know today. Shall I ring the surgery before I leave, or would you prefer to call your pharmacist yourself?
Could you ring the surgery? I'd get flustered.
Of course. I'll explain what's happened and ask them to review your tablets today. Would you like your daughter to know, so she can help?
I've been hiding it from her. She worries.
It's entirely your choice. She might be relieved to help, though, for example by collecting a new prescription. I could be there when you tell her, if that's easier.
I'll tell her myself when she rings tonight.

That sounds like a good plan. One more important thing. If a tablet or food ever blocks your throat so you can't breathe, speak or cough, that's choking, and someone must call 999. If you develop a cough, a temperature or breathlessness, contact your GP or call 111 the same day; it could be a chest infection.
Can't breathe or speak, 999. Cough or temperature, GP or 111.
Exactly. And if you're ever unsure about a tablet, please don't skip it quietly; ring the pharmacist. Can you tell me what we've agreed?
I don't crush anything, I take tablets one at a time sitting up, you ring the GP today, and I tell my daughter tonight.
That's perfect. I'll ring you tomorrow to hear what the GP has decided, and I'll visit again next week. Is there anything else worrying you?
No. I feel much better for telling you.

coverage.how: Asks how eating and drinking have been.
Asks her to describe exactly what happens with her tablets.
Asks non-judgementally about missed or changed medicines and reassures her.
Explains that stopping stroke-prevention medicines raises the risk of another stroke.
Advises against crushing tablets or opening capsules without pharmacist advice, with reasons.
Explains that the pharmacist or GP may offer a liquid, smaller tablet or alternative.
Teaches upright posture, a sip first, one tablet at a time, then practises.
Agrees the therapist will ring the GP surgery today for a review.
Asks about involving her daughter and leaves the choice with her.
Explains choking and 999, and chest infection signs with same-day GP or 111.
Uses teach-back, arranges a call tomorrow and a visit next week.

concern.how: A gentle, no-blame question lets her admit stopping two tablets; the therapist thanks her, explains the risk calmly and arranges a same-day GP review.

safety.point: Stopping a blood thinner or cholesterol tablet after stroke without advice raises the risk of another stroke.
Do not crush tablets or open capsules without pharmacist advice.
