Choking means calling 999; cough, temperature or breathlessness means same-day GP or 111.

scripts.notes: The card does not name her medicines; the script has her identify a blood thinner and a cholesterol tablet as the two missed, both typical after stroke. The therapist watches her swallow one small tablet, which assumes her swallow is safe for thin drinks, as the card states.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the speech and language therapist in the voice clinic. Thank you for coming in. Before we talk about choices, could you tell me what you understand about why your voice has changed?
The surgeon said a nerve to my voice box got bruised during the operation. One side isn't moving. That's about all I took in.
That's a good summary. How is your voice affecting your work and everyday life?
Badly. I run a small business, mostly on the phone. By lunchtime I'm almost whispering, and customers keep asking me to repeat things.
That sounds exhausting. Do drinks ever make you cough or splutter?
Sometimes with water, if I gulp it.

Thank you; we'll come back to that. Your voice comes from two vocal folds that meet in the middle and vibrate. On your left side the nerve isn't working properly, so that fold isn't moving. The two can't close fully, air leaks through, and your voice sounds weak and breathy and tires quickly.
Will it come back?
Often, yes. A bruised nerve frequently recovers over several months. But I can't promise that it will, or exactly when, and I'd rather be honest than give you false hope.
So what are the options?

The first is voice therapy with me. We'd work on breathing support, exercises to help the moving fold close the gap, and ways to use your voice without straining. It can make your voice stronger and less tiring, though it can't make the nerve recover faster.
How long before it helps?

Most people notice some change within a few weeks of daily practice. The second option is an injection by the surgeons. They put a soft filler into the weak fold to bulk it up, so the folds meet better. It often improves the voice quickly, but the effect usually wears off over a few months.
Quickly is what I need. Is there a permanent fix?

There is an operation, but it's usually only considered if the nerve hasn't recovered after many months, because the voice often gets better on its own. Can I ask what matters most to you in deciding?
Honestly, speed. If I lose customers, I lose the business. I'll take whatever's fastest, even if it's not the best.
That's a real pressure, and I'm glad you've said it. Wanting speed is completely fair. Can we look at the other things too, so that whatever you choose, you choose it knowing everything?
All right.

The injection is a small procedure, and because it's temporary, you might need it again. Therapy takes a little longer, but it builds skills that help whatever the nerve does. Many people actually have both. How does that sound?
Both? I didn't know I could.
Yes. You can start therapy now and still ask the surgeons about the injection, and you can change your mind later. Nothing you decide today closes the door on anything else.
Then I think I'd like both. And maybe some tips for the phone this week.

Definitely. Use a headset so you're not hunched over, sip water between calls, and book your longest calls for the morning, when your voice is fresher. With drinks, sip slowly rather than gulping, and I'll check your swallow properly at your first session.
Okay.
If you start choking on drinks, get chest infections with a fever and cough, or notice noisy or difficult breathing, get medical advice promptly. Call 111, or 999 if you're struggling to breathe.
Noisy breathing. That sounds serious.

It's unlikely with only one side affected, but it's important to know. So, to sum up: you'd like to start voice therapy, and I'll write to the surgeons today asking them to discuss the injection with you. Is that right?
Yes. And the phone tips this week.
Exactly. I'll book your first therapy session within the next couple of weeks. Can you tell me what you'll do if drinking becomes difficult?
Sip slowly, don't gulp. If I'm choking or getting chest infections, call 111, and 999 if I can't breathe.
Perfect. Thank you for being so clear about what you need.
Thank you. I feel I've got a plan now.

coverage.how: Asks what she understands about the voice change.
Asks about the effect on work and life, and about coughing on drinks.
Explains how a non-moving fold lets air leak and makes the voice weak and breathy.
Says recovery over several months is common but cannot be promised.
Describes voice therapy, its benefits and that it cannot speed nerve recovery.
Describes the filler injection and that its effect usually wears off.
Explains that permanent surgery is considered only after many months without recovery.
Asks what matters most to her.
Validates speed and sets out the trade-offs of each option neutrally.
Explains options can be combined and the decision changed later.
Advises a headset, sips of water between calls and long calls in the morning.
Gives choking, chest infection and noisy breathing as reasons for 111 or 999.
Summarises therapy plus a letter about the injection, and books the first session.

concern.how: She says she wants the fastest option to protect her business; the therapist accepts this as fair and makes sure she knows the trade-offs, leading to a combined plan.

safety.point: Choking on drinks, chest infections or noisy, difficult breathing need prompt medical advice: 111, or 999 if struggling to breathe.
Sip drinks slowly rather than gulping until the swallow is assessed.

scripts.notes: The card does not say whether her swallow has been assessed; the script plans an assessment at the first therapy session given her occasional cough on water. Timescales for nerve recovery and for injection effect are kept general.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm the speech and language therapist who recommended the swallow X-ray. Before I explain anything, what do you already know about the test, and how do you feel about it?
Not much. My wife said it's an X-ray while I eat. I'll be honest, I'm not keen.

Thank you for being honest; we'll talk that through. Let me explain why I suggested it. You've had two chest infections this year, and you've been coughing at meals. With Parkinson's, the swallow can become slower, and small amounts can go down into the lungs, which can cause infections.
Can't you just watch me eat?
I have, and it told me a lot. But food can sometimes go the wrong way without any cough at all. The X-ray lets us see inside, as it happens.
What actually happens?

You sit in a chair, side on to the X-ray machine. I'll give you small amounts of a drink, a soft food and perhaps a biscuit, each mixed with a white liquid called barium that shows up on X-ray. You swallow as normal, and we watch a moving picture on a screen.
Who's there?

Me and a radiographer, who runs the machine. The whole appointment takes about half an hour, but the X-ray is only switched on for a few minutes altogether. If you want to stop at any point, just say so and we stop.
And the radiation? I've had a few X-rays already.

It's a fair question. The dose is small, roughly the same as the natural radiation we all get from everyday life over a few months. We only switch the machine on while you swallow. For you, the benefit of finding out why the infections keep happening is much greater than that risk.
What will it show?

Whether food or drink is going into your airway, which textures are safest, and whether simple changes help, like tucking your chin down or taking smaller sips. Often we can find a strategy there and then that makes your swallow safer.
That's what worries me, though. I think you'll tell me I can't eat any more and put a tube in. I'd rather not know.
That's a big fear, and I'm glad you've told me. Can I ask what you've heard about tubes?
A man in my Parkinson's group had one. He hated it. I love my food. I'm not giving it up.
I understand. The most common result is that we find ways to keep you eating more safely, like a change of texture or a technique. A tube is never decided on the day, and it isn't the usual outcome.
But if it came to that?
Any decision about eating would be made with you, not for you. Even if there were some risk, you could choose to keep eating, knowing that risk, and we'd help you make it as safe as possible.
So I'd still have a say.

Always. And it's your choice whether to have the test at all. If you decide not to, I'll still support you with advice from what I can see at mealtimes, but we'd be guessing more about why the infections keep happening.
Put like that, I think I'd rather know.

That's entirely your decision. On the day, eat normally beforehand, take your Parkinson's tablets at your usual times, and bring your glasses and dentures if you wear them, so we see how you really eat.
I wear a top denture. And my tablets as usual?
Yes, keep to your usual times, so your swallow is as it normally is. And if you develop a fever, a cough or breathlessness before then, see your GP or call 111; don't wait for the test.
Right.
Could you tell me in your own words what the test involves and what happens afterwards?
I swallow food and drink with barium while you film it on X-ray. Only a few minutes of X-ray, a small dose. Then you tell me what's safest, and nothing changes without me agreeing.
That's exactly right. So, are you happy to go ahead next week?
Yes. I'll come. Can my wife be there?
She's very welcome to come with you, and on the day we'll see whether she can watch the screen. I'll send you a letter with the time.
Thank you. I feel better about it.

coverage.how: Asks what he knows and how he feels.
Links the test to his two chest infections, coughing at meals and silent aspiration.
Explains seating, the barium-mixed foods and drinks and the moving image.
Names the radiographer, gives the length and says he can stop at any time.
Puts the radiation dose in proportion and weighs it against the benefit.
Explains what the study shows, including strategies tried during it.
Asks about his fear of tubes and answers with the usual outcomes.
States decisions about eating are made with him, including choosing to eat with known risk.
Says the test is his choice and explains what happens if he declines.
Advises normal eating, usual Parkinson's medicines, glasses and dentures.
Advises GP or 111 for fever, cough or breathlessness before the test.
Uses teach-back and confirms he agrees to go ahead.

concern.how: He says he would rather not know because he fears a tube; the therapist explores the source, explains usual outcomes and that he keeps a say, and he chooses to proceed.

safety.point: Fever, cough or breathlessness before the test needs the GP or 111, not waiting for the appointment.
Parkinson's medicines should be taken at the usual times.

scripts.notes: The radiation comparison is kept general: a videofluoroscopy dose is commonly described as equivalent to weeks to a few months of natural background radiation. Test items such as a biscuit are the script's choice. Whether his wife may watch the screen depends on local radiation rules, so the therapist does not promise it.

turns.text: Hello, come in. This is our last session in this block, and he's playing next door with my colleague for a few minutes. Before we talk, how do you feel about it being the last one, and what have you noticed at home?
Mixed, honestly. At home he's chatting away. His granny understood everything on the phone last week, which never used to happen.

That's lovely to hear, and it matches what I see. When he started, he had three goals: saying k and g sounds instead of t and d, saying s clearly at the start of words, and being understood by people who don't know him. He's met all three. Today he named every picture correctly.
He's worked so hard.
He has, and so have you. You did the practice every week, even when he was tired. That's a big part of why he's done so well.
Thank you. So this is really it?

Yes. I'm recommending discharge today because he's reached his goals, his speech is clear to strangers, and his school has no concerns. Discharge means regular sessions stop, but it doesn't mean you can't come back.

I know it sounds silly, but I'm scared. Last year, before all this, some boys at school called him a baby because of how he talked. He cried every morning. What if he slips back and it all starts again?
That doesn't sound silly at all. Watching your child go through that is painful, and of course you want to protect him. Thank you for telling me.
So could he slip back?

Honestly, it's unusual once the sounds are secure, as his are. Small slips can happen when he's tired, excited or talking very fast, like a t creeping back in. That's normal and usually corrects itself. A real setback would be strangers struggling to understand him again over several weeks.
What should I do to stop that?

No more formal practice; he's earned a rest from that. Just keep talking, reading together and playing word games. If you hear a slip, say the word back correctly, like, oh, a cat, rather than asking him to say it again.
Just say it back correctly. Okay. And the teasing?
Has anything happened recently?
No, not this year. But I worry.

If it ever does, speak to his teacher straight away; schools take this seriously and have anti-bullying policies. And if he seems very unhappy or doesn't want to go to school, talk to the school and to your GP. You know him best.
And if I'm worried about his speech later on?
You can re-refer him yourself; you don't need to go through the GP. Ring the number on the discharge letter, or ask the school to refer him. Because he's known to us, we'll look at it quickly.
That's a relief. What will the letter say?
It'll summarise his goals, his progress, and that he's been discharged, with advice for home and school. You'll get a copy, and so will your GP and, with your agreement, his school.
Yes, the school should have it.
Good. Can I check I've explained things well? What will you do if you notice a slip?
Say the word back correctly and not make a fuss. And if strangers can't understand him again for a few weeks, ring you.
Exactly. And if any teasing starts?
Tell his teacher straight away, and the GP if he's really unhappy.
Perfect. Shall we bring him in? I'd love him to hear how proud we are of him.
Yes, he'll love that. He's been asking about his certificate.
Then let's give it to him. Hello! Come and sit with Mum. You've finished all your speech sessions, and you talk so clearly now. Here's your certificate. What will you tell your teacher?
He says he'll tell her he's a talking champion.
You certainly are. Well done, both of you. And remember, the number's on the letter if you ever need us.
Thank you so much for everything.

coverage.how: Asks how she feels about the last session and what she notices at home.
Lists his three goals and states each has been met.
Praises the boy's effort and her weekly practice.
Gives the reasons for discharge and explains what it means.
Acknowledges her fear about stopping and answers her question about slipping back.
Says relapse is unusual, describes small slips and what a real setback looks like.
Advises talking, reading and word games, and modelling the correct word.
Asks about recent teasing and advises speaking to the teacher, and the GP if he is unhappy.
Explains self-referral by phone or through the school.
Describes the discharge letter and who receives copies.
Uses teach-back, then brings in her son and ends with his certificate.

concern.how: She reveals last year's teasing and fear of relapse; the therapist validates it, checks for current teasing and gives clear steps if it recurs.

safety.point: If he becomes very unhappy or does not want to go to school, she should talk to the school and the GP.
Strangers struggling to understand him over several weeks is the sign to re-refer.

scripts.notes: The card does not state his goals; the script gives typical speech sound goals: correcting fronting of k and g, clear s at the start of words, and intelligibility to strangers.

turns.text: Hello, come in and have a seat. It's good to see you. Before we talk about today's swallow study, how have you been eating and drinking, and what were you hoping to hear today?
Not bad. Soft stuff, lots of gravy. I was hoping you'd tell me I'm back to normal. The cancer's gone, so I thought the rest would follow.
That's a very natural hope. Would you like anyone with you while we go through it?
No, I'm fine on my own. My wife's in the car.
All right. I'll be honest with you: the results are mixed. There's good news, and some news that may be disappointing. Is it okay if I start with the good news?
Go on.

Your swallow is safe for what you're eating now. Soft, moist food and drinks go down the right way, with nothing going into your airway. That's a really good result, and it's thanks to all the work you've put in.
And the disappointing part?

Your swallow is weaker than before your treatment. Hard or dry food, like crusty bread or tough meat, is still difficult, and from what I saw today, I don't think that's likely to come back fully to how it was.
Never?
Some people do keep improving slowly, so I won't say never. But I don't want to give you false hope. It's likely you'll always need to be careful with very dry or tough food.
Right.
Take your time. There's no rush.
It's just, I thought I'd beaten it. Why does it stay like this when the cancer's gone?

You did beat the cancer, and that's the most important thing. Radiotherapy works by damaging cancer cells, but it also affects the healthy muscles nearby. Over time they can become stiff and tight, a bit like scar tissue, so they don't squeeze as strongly.
I see. That's hard to hear.
It is. How are you feeling about it?
Gutted, honestly. My son's getting married soon. I'd pictured eating the whole wedding meal, and going out for a steak with my mates. That was going to be my proof that I'd won.
That makes complete sense. Those meals mean far more than food. Can we think about how to make them still feel like celebrations?
I suppose so.

For the wedding, you could ask the venue in advance for a softer version of the main course, perhaps slow-cooked meat with extra sauce. Many venues are happy to do that. With your mates, a slow-cooked dish or fish with plenty of sauce, and a sip of drink with each mouthful, can let you enjoy it with them.
So I'd still be at the table, just with more gravy.

Exactly, and nobody needs to know unless you tell them. It's also important to keep doing your swallowing exercises. They help stop the muscles getting stiffer over time, so they protect what you've got.
I'd stopped them, to be honest. I thought I was done.
Lots of people do. Would you start again, every day? I'll go through them with you before you leave. How's your mouth, by the way? Is it still dry? And how's your mood been?
Very dry. And I've been a bit low.

Thank you for telling me. Dry mouth can be eased with sprays, gels and sipping water, and we can advise on those. For your mood, our team has a psychologist, and there's a support group for people after head and neck cancer. Would either help?
Maybe the group. And I'll try the sprays.

I'll arrange both. Please contact us if you lose weight without trying, if food starts sticking more, or if you cough at meals or get a chest infection. Those can be signs that things are changing, and we'd want to see you sooner.
Weight, sticking, coughing, chest infections. Ring you.

That's it. So, your swallow is safe for soft, moist food, it's unlikely to fully return for hard or dry food, you'll restart the exercises, and I'll refer you to the group. I'll see you again in a few months, or sooner if needed. How does that sound?
Fair. Not what I wanted, but fair. And I'll ring the venue about the wedding meal.
That's a great idea. I hope it's a wonderful day.

coverage.how: Asks about eating and drinking and what he hoped to hear.
Offers someone to be present and warns that the results are mixed.
Gives the good news that his swallow is safe for his current diet.
States plainly that hard, dry food is unlikely to return fully, without false hope.
Explains radiotherapy stiffening healthy swallowing muscles, like scar tissue.
Allows a pause and asks how he feels before going on.
Draws out what the wedding and steak meal mean to him.
Suggests asking the venue for a softer dish, sauces and sips with mouthfuls.
Explains exercises protect against further stiffening and asks him to restart.
Asks about dry mouth and mood and offers sprays, a psychologist and a support group.
Lists weight loss, sticking food, coughing at meals and chest infections as reasons to call.
Summarises the results and plan and agrees a review in a few months.

concern.how: He reveals the wedding meal and steak were his proof of beating cancer; the therapist acknowledges the meaning and makes practical plans so he can still share those meals.

safety.point: Unplanned weight loss, food sticking more, coughing at meals or chest infections need contact with the team.

scripts.notes: The card gives the study result in general terms; the script adds that nothing entered his airway on soft, moist food, consistent with the card's safe result. The presence of a psychologist and support group in the head and neck team is assumed, as is common in UK centres.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming back, and for letting me watch her feed. Before I tell you what I saw, how have feeds been going at home, and what's worrying you most?

She drinks well, but she coughs and splutters nearly every feed, worst at night when she's really hungry. Milk comes out of her nose sometimes. I lie awake listening to her breathing. I'm terrified she'll choke.

That sounds really stressful, especially at night. What I saw today was that the milk was coming too fast for her. With the fast-flow teat she gulped, couldn't keep up, and spluttered. Babies born early can take a while to coordinate sucking, swallowing and breathing.
So is something wrong with her?
Nothing worrying. Her weight is on track, and the paediatrician found no other problem. With the slower teat she managed much better: far fewer coughs, and she settled nicely.
So I just change the teat?
That's part of it. The plan is a slower-flow teat, holding her more upright, and paced feeding. Shall I show you how pacing works?
Yes, please.

Hold her fairly upright, and keep the bottle more level, not tipped right up, so the milk just fills the teat. Let her suck for a few gulps, then tip the bottle down slightly so she can pause and breathe, then let her start again. You follow her lead.
Like this? She's stopping.
Exactly like that; she's taking a breath. You're doing it well. How confident do you feel trying it at home?
Fairly. It's slower than I expected, but she seems much calmer. I'll keep practising.
Good. Can I ask, has anything else been added to her feeds, or changed, since we last met?
Well. My mum said to put baby rice in the bottle to thicken it. She did that with me. I started a couple of days ago. I didn't tell anyone.

Thank you for telling me; I'm really glad you did. Your mum was trying to help, and it was common advice years ago. But please stop adding baby rice to her bottles. Babies this young aren't ready for solid food, it can upset her tummy, and it changes how the milk flows. If thickening were ever needed, we'd tell you exactly what to use.
My mum will be upset.
That's understandable; she loves her granddaughter. You could tell her the feeding team has given you a new plan. I'm happy to write it down so you can show her.
That would help.
Now, some important safety advice. Call 999 if she goes blue or grey around the lips, has pauses in her breathing, or seems floppy or very hard to wake.
Blue or grey, pauses in breathing, floppy. 999.
Yes. Some things need advice the same day from your GP or 111: fewer wet nappies, fast or noisy breathing, a temperature, or refusing feeds.
And the milk from her nose?
A little milk coming out of her nose, or brought up after feeds, can be normal, especially when she gulps. If she's comfortable and gaining weight, that isn't an emergency.
That's good to know.
Can you tell me what you'll do differently at home, and when you'd get help?
Slower teat, hold her upright, pace the feed. No baby rice. If she goes blue or stops breathing, 999. Fewer wet nappies, fast breathing, a temperature or not feeding, GP or 111 that day.

That's perfect. I'll see you again in a few weeks to check how she's doing and to watch another feed. Please bring the bottles and teats you use at home. If you're worried before then, ring the clinic during working hours.
Thank you. I feel calmer.
You're doing a great job. She's lucky to have such an attentive dad. I'll write that plan for your mum before you go.
Thanks. She'll come round.

coverage.how: Asks how feeds are going and what worries him most.
Explains the fast flow and gulping seen today, and why early babies may find coordination harder.
Acknowledges his stress and gives the reassuring weight and paediatric findings.
Sets out slower teat, upright position and paced feeding.
Demonstrates pacing, coaches him as he tries it and checks his confidence.
Asks openly whether anything has been added or changed.
Asks him to stop the baby rice and explains why.
Acknowledges his mother's good intentions and offers a written plan to show her.
Gives 999 signs: blue or grey colour, breathing pauses, floppiness.
Gives same-day GP or 111 signs: fewer wet nappies, fast breathing, temperature, refusing feeds.
Explains a little milk from the nose or brought up can be normal.
Uses teach-back and arranges a review in a few weeks.

concern.how: Asked openly about changes, he admits adding baby rice on his mother's advice; the therapist thanks him, explains why to stop and helps him handle his mother.

safety.point: Blue or grey colour, pauses in breathing, floppiness or being hard to wake mean calling 999.
Fewer wet nappies, fast or noisy breathing, a temperature or refusing feeds need same-day GP or 111.
Do not add baby rice or thickener to bottles unless a professional advises it.

scripts.notes: The card gives no detail of the feed seen; the script follows the card: gulping on a fast-flow teat, settling with a slower teat and pacing. UK advice is not to add baby rice or cereal to bottles.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the speech and language therapist in the voice clinic. Thanks for coming. Could you tell me what you were told at the ear, nose and throat clinic, and how you feel about it?
They put a camera up my nose and said there's no growth, just tight muscles. Some dysphonia thing. I don't know, to be honest.
Okay, we'll go through it together. First, how is your voice affecting you at work and at home?
I'm a supervisor in a warehouse. It's loud, forklifts everywhere, so I shout all day. By the evening I sound like gravel and my throat aches. My grandkids say I sound like a bear.

That sounds tiring. What you've got is called muscle tension dysphonia. Dysphonia just means a voice problem. When the muscles around your voice box work too hard, often from shouting or strain, they squeeze too tightly, and the voice sounds rough and tires quickly.
So it's just strain?

Yes. The camera let the doctors look directly at your vocal folds, the two bands in your voice box that make sound. They saw no growth or lump, and the folds moved normally. That's why they're confident it's muscle tension, not anything more serious.
My brother had throat cancer. It started with a hoarse voice, just like this. He died two years ago. How can a little camera see everything?
I'm so sorry about your brother. No wonder this has frightened you. Can you tell me a bit more about what happened with him?
He ignored it for ages. By the time he went to the doctor, it had spread. I keep thinking I'm next.
That's a heavy thing to carry, and getting checked was exactly the right thing to do. Unlike your brother, you've been seen early, by specialists, and they looked closely.
But can they be sure?

I'll be honest: no test is perfect. But a camera examination by the ear, nose and throat team is the standard way to check for this, and it's very good at spotting growths on the vocal folds. If your voice got worse despite therapy, or new symptoms appeared, we'd ask them to look again.
So I'm not just being fobbed off.
No. I'll also keep an eye on your voice at every session, and if I'm concerned, I'll contact them directly.
Okay. That helps. So what's therapy, then?

Usually a few sessions with me. We'd work on relaxing the tight muscles, breathing so your voice is supported, and ways to be heard without straining. You'd practise short exercises every day between sessions.
And at work? I can't stop shouting.

A few practical things. Rather than shouting across the warehouse, walk over, or use a hand signal or a radio. Sip water through the day. And when your voice is tired, rest it at breaks rather than chatting over the noise.
A radio. We have those, actually. I just never use them.
That could make a big difference. Can I ask about smoking? It's something I ask everyone with a voice problem.
About ten a day. I know, I know.

No lecture. Smoke irritates and dries the vocal folds, so stopping would help your voice, and it would lower your cancer risk too. Would you like support to stop? There's a free local service with medicines or patches, and people are much more likely to succeed with help.
After my brother, I've been thinking about it. Yes, go on.

I'll refer you today. One more important thing. See your GP promptly if you get pain in your throat or ear, difficulty swallowing, a lump in your neck, or cough up blood, or if your hoarseness gets worse despite therapy. Those would mean a further check.
Pain, swallowing, a lump, blood, or getting worse. GP.
Exactly. Can you tell me in your own words what's causing your voice problem, and what we're going to do?
Tight muscles from shouting, not a growth. Therapy to relax them, use the radio, drink water, and get help to stop smoking.
That's spot on. I'll book your first session for next week, and I'll send the stop smoking referral today. How are you feeling now?
Better. I came in expecting the worst. Thanks for listening about my brother.
Thank you for telling me. I'll see you next week.

coverage.how: Asks what he was told and how he feels.
Asks how his voice affects work and home.
Explains muscle tension dysphonia in everyday words.
Explains the camera saw no growth and normal movement, hence the team's confidence.
Expresses sympathy about his brother and explores the fear.
Admits no test is perfect and says what would prompt another look.
Describes therapy: relaxing muscles, breath support and daily exercises.
Advises walking over, using a radio or hand signals, water and voice rest.
Asks about smoking without lecturing and offers a stop smoking referral.
Lists pain, swallowing difficulty, neck lump, coughing blood and worsening hoarseness.
Uses teach-back and books the first session for next week.

concern.how: He reveals his brother's death and doubts the camera; the therapist explores it, answers honestly about the test's limits and gives clear reasons for re-examination.

safety.point: Throat or ear pain, difficulty swallowing, a neck lump, coughing blood or worsening hoarseness despite therapy mean prompt GP review.
Stopping smoking lowers cancer risk and helps the voice.

scripts.notes: The card says the camera found no growth; the script adds that the vocal folds moved normally, consistent with muscle tension dysphonia. The number of cigarettes is the script's choice and is said in words.

turns.text: Good morning. I'm the vet who examined Misty yesterday. Before I go through the result, what have you been noticing at home, and what did you understand about why we took blood?
She eats like a horse but she's skin and bone. She's sick now and then, and she yowls at night. You mentioned her thyroid.

Yes, and what you describe fits. Her thyroid hormone level is raised. The thyroid is a small gland in the neck that sets the body's pace. Too much hormone makes everything run too fast, so she burns food faster than she eats it and feels restless.
That explains the hunger. And the lump you felt?
That's the enlarged gland. In cats this is almost always a non-cancerous growth of thyroid tissue. A cancerous cause does happen, but it's rare.
My neighbour said thyroid trouble means cancer. I've been dreading this all night.
I'm sorry you've had such a worrying night. I can't be completely certain, but by far the likeliest cause is a benign growth, and it's very treatable. Does that help?
It does. But does she need treating? She seems lively enough.

She does. Her heart was racing when I examined her, because the hormone drives it. Untreated, that strains the heart and can raise her blood pressure, which can damage the eyes and kidneys. So treatment protects her, even though she seems bright.
What are the choices?

There are four. First, daily tablets: they work well and can start today, but they're lifelong and need regular blood checks. Second, a prescription low-iodine diet, which only works if she eats nothing else at all.
She steals the dog's food, so that's unlikely.
Then the diet may be hard. Third, surgery to remove the affected gland. It can cure her, but it needs an anaesthetic, which is riskier while her heart is racing, so we'd settle her on tablets first.
And the fourth? I read something about radiation.

Radioactive iodine: a single injection at a specialist centre. It usually cures the condition without an anaesthetic. The drawbacks are the cost and the time she'd be away. What have you heard about it?
That she'd be shut away for weeks, and afterwards she'd be dangerous to my grandchildren. They come every weekend.

That's a fair worry. She'd stay at the centre while the radioactivity falls, usually a week or more, depending on the centre. Then, for a short while, you'd limit cuddles and keep children and anyone pregnant away from her and her litter. The centre gives exact rules. After that, she's completely safe.
So it's not forever, then.

No, it's temporary. One more point, whatever you choose: an overactive thyroid pushes extra blood through the kidneys, which can hide kidney disease. Once it's controlled, kidney values sometimes rise, so we recheck them after treatment starts.
So fixing one thing might uncover another?

Sometimes. Her kidney results are normal at the moment, which is reassuring, but we'll keep an eye on them. My suggestion is to start tablets today while you think about the longer term. That doesn't commit you to anything else.
Sounds sensible. How do I get tablets into her? She's a wriggler.

Try hiding each one in a little soft food, or I'll show you how to place it at the back of her mouth. Give them at the same times each day, wash your hands afterwards, and keep them well away from the grandchildren.
What should I watch for?

Ring us promptly if she stops eating, vomits more, becomes very quiet, scratches her face sore, or her gums or the whites of her eyes look yellow. Those can be side effects. If she's ever breathless or collapses, that's an emergency, day or night.
Right. And when do we come back?
In about three weeks for a blood test to check her hormone level and kidneys, and I'll listen to her heart again. Could you tell me the main points, so I know I've explained it clearly?
Probably not cancer, she needs treating for her heart's sake, tablets now, ring if she's off her food, yellow or scratching, and bloods in three weeks, kidneys too.
Spot on. And the radioactive iodine?
Some time away, then a short spell keeping the grandchildren back. I'll think about it.
Exactly. I'll give you a leaflet on all four options, and we can talk again at the recheck. Any other questions?
No, that's much clearer. Thank you.

coverage.how: Opens by asking what he has noticed and what he understood about the blood test.
Explains the gland as the body's pace-setter and links excess hormone to weight loss, hunger and restlessness.
States the usual benign cause and that a cancerous cause is rare, without false certainty.
Links the racing heart to strain and blood pressure damage, so treatment is needed even though she seems well.
Names all four options in turn: tablets, low-iodine diet, surgery and radioactive iodine.
Gives one advantage and one drawback for each option in plain words.
Asks what he has heard and answers honestly about the stay and the short period of precautions.
Explains that thyroid control can unmask kidney disease and that kidney bloods will be rechecked.
Suggests tablets now without commitment and explains how to give them.
Lists side effects to report promptly and an emergency for breathlessness or collapse.
Agrees a three-week recheck, asks him to summarise including the radioactive iodine points, and gives a leaflet on the options.

concern.how: His fear of cancer surfaces early and is met with an honest, reassuring explanation; his worry about weeks away and the grandchildren is invited and answered with the real, temporary precautions.

safety.point: Untreated, an overactive thyroid strains the heart and can raise blood pressure, damaging the eyes and kidneys.
After radioactive iodine, close contact with children and pregnant people is limited for a short time, following the centre's rules.
Controlling the thyroid can unmask kidney disease, so kidney bloods are rechecked after treatment starts.
Loss of appetite, more vomiting, lethargy, facial scratching or yellow gums are reported promptly; breathlessness or collapse is an emergency.

scripts.notes: The card does not give the exact hormone result, the treatment centre's stay or the recheck interval. The script uses a three-week recheck, a typical UK interval after starting tablets, and says the radioactive iodine stay is usually a week or more and varies by centre. Tablet handling advice is general; no dose is given.

turns.text: Hello, and hello, Bruno. While we do his booster, I'd like to talk about the hot weather coming. How does he cope on walks, and when it's warm?
He pants a lot and snores like a train, but that's Frenchies, isn't it? It's quite cute really.
Lots of owners think so. Has he ever really struggled?
Last summer he flopped down on a walk and I had to carry him home. He was gasping.

That must have been frightening. Flat-faced dogs have narrow nostrils, a long soft palate and often a narrow windpipe, so air has to squeeze through. Dogs cool down mainly by panting, so he can't lose heat well. The snoring is the sound of that narrowing, not just a breed quirk.
Oh. I didn't realise snoring meant anything.

It's a useful clue. In hot weather he can overheat quickly. That's heatstroke, when his body temperature climbs so high that his organs start to fail. It can become life-threatening within minutes rather than hours.
Minutes? That's scary, with the heatwave next week.

It is, so let's plan. Walk him only early in the morning or late in the evening, keep walks short and gentle, and press the back of your hand on the pavement. If it's too hot for your hand, it's too hot for his paws.
What about at home?
Plenty of shade and fresh water, a cool tiled floor or a cooling mat, and a fan nearby. Avoid conservatories, caravans and cars, which heat up very fast, even with a window open.
About cars, I should say something. Last summer I left him for a few minutes while I paid for petrol.

Thank you for telling me; plenty of people have done the same without realising. But even a few minutes in a parked car can be dangerous for him, so please never leave him, not even briefly. Is that something you can plan around?
Yes. I feel awful now.
You're asking the right questions now, and that's what matters. You mentioned a festival at the weekend?
On the seafront. Crowds, music. I'd planned to take him.
Honestly, during a heatwave I'd advise against it. Crowds, little shade, hot sand and pavements, and noise would all push his breathing hard. Could someone look after him at home in a cool room?
My sister could. He'd hate missing out, though.
He'll be far happier cool on the sofa. Now, the warning signs of heatstroke: very heavy, noisy breathing, lots of drooling, a dark red tongue or gums, wobbling, vomiting, or collapse.
And if I see those?

Act straight away. Move him somewhere cool and shaded, pour plenty of cool water over him, and keep him in a breeze. Then ring us and bring him in, cooling him on the way. Don't wait to see if he improves.
Cool him first, then come in. Got it.

Exactly. Longer term, his breathing could be assessed properly. Some dogs like Bruno benefit from surgery to widen the nostrils and shorten the soft palate, which can make a big difference to their comfort.
I'd never heard of that. Would it hurt him?

It's done under anaesthetic with pain relief, and we'd talk through the risks first, since anaesthesia needs extra care in these breeds. Something you can start now is his weight. He's a little overweight today, and extra fat around his neck and chest makes breathing harder, especially in the heat.
I do give him a lot of treats.
Swap some for pieces of his own food, and we'll weigh him again in a month. Even a small loss will help him cope. Shall we also book a separate appointment to discuss his breathing?
Yes, please, after the heatwave.
Good idea. So, just to check, what will you do this week?
Walk him early or late and short, check the pavement, shade and water, no car, no festival. If he's struggling, cool water, a breeze and ring you.
Perfect. And if it's after hours, our phone line will direct you to the emergency vet. Any other questions?
No. Thank you for not making me feel stupid.
Not at all. Have a cool, quiet week, Bruno.

coverage.how: Asks how he copes on walks and in warmth, then draws out last summer's collapse.
Explains the narrow airway anatomy and panting, and reframes snoring as a sign of narrowing.
Defines heatstroke and stresses that it can become life-threatening within minutes.
Advises early or late, short, gentle walks and the hand test on the pavement.
Advises shade, water, cool floors or mats, a fan, and avoiding conservatories, caravans and cars.
Raises the festival and advises honestly against it, offering an alternative.
Thanks her for disclosing the car, does not judge, and is clear it is never safe.
Lists the warning signs from the card in plain words.
Gives the first-aid sequence: shade, plenty of cool water, breeze, ring and come in, cooling on the way.
Mentions assessment and airway surgery, with the extra anaesthetic care these breeds need.
Links his extra weight to harder breathing in heat and agrees swapping treats and a weigh-in.
Asks her to say what she will do this week and adds the out-of-hours route.

concern.how: Her belief that snoring is cute is corrected gently with an explanation; her embarrassed admission about the car is welcomed without blame and turned into a clear rule.

safety.point: Heatstroke can become life-threatening within minutes in a flat-faced dog.
Never leave him in a parked car, even for a few minutes.
Cool him first with plenty of cool water and a breeze, then ring and come straight in, cooling on the way.
Out of hours, the practice line directs her to the emergency vet.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination findings. The script assumes a typical brachycephalic airway and mentions nostril widening and soft palate shortening as the usual UK surgical options; a clinician may wish to confirm the wording.

turns.text: Thank you for coming in. I'm the vet who treated Rocky last night. I can see you're upset about the bill, and I'd like to hear everything before I say anything.
Upset? Six hundred and forty pounds! Nobody told me it would cost that. I feel completely ripped off.
That's a lot of money to be faced with. Please go on; I'm listening.
It was midnight, he was screaming in pain, someone pushed a form at me, and now this. I'm on my own with two kids. I can't just find that.
Thank you for telling me. Before we talk about the bill, how is Rocky this morning?
He's fine, actually. Bouncing around and wanting breakfast.

That's really good to hear, and it fits with how he was when I checked him early this morning. He came in vomiting with a very painful tummy, so I gave pain relief and anti-sickness medicine, and kept him on a drip because he'd lost a lot of fluid.
And the X-rays? They found nothing. Why should I pay for nothing?

That's a fair question. With a painful abdomen and repeated vomiting, the biggest worry is a blockage, such as something he'd swallowed, which can be fatal if it's missed and needs surgery. The X-rays ruled that out, so we could treat him with medicine instead of an operation.
So it wasn't for nothing, then.

No. A normal X-ray was the answer we needed. About the cost: our record shows an estimate of four hundred to seven hundred pounds was given, and the consent form was signed. I'm not saying that to catch you out.
Maybe someone said a number. I honestly don't remember. I'd have signed anything.
That's completely understandable. Making decisions at midnight, frightened for your dog, is incredibly hard, and I'm sorry the total came as such a shock this morning.
Can you at least tell me what it's all for?
Of course. Roughly, it's the out-of-hours examination, the X-rays, the overnight stay on the drip with nursing, and the medicines. I'll print the itemised bill so you can go through it at home.
Fine. But I still can't pay it all today.
Let's look at what's possible. Do you have pet insurance?
No. I cancelled it last year to save money.

Then our office manager can talk to you about paying in instalments. I can't promise a discount, as that isn't my decision, but I'll ask her to see you today. Some animal charities also help owners on certain benefits, and she can tell you about those.
That would help. I just need time to pay it.
Then I'll ask her to agree a written plan with you before you leave today. What else would help you most right now?
Knowing I can complain, if I still want to.

You're entitled to. You can write to the practice manager, and if you're not satisfied with the reply, there's an independent veterinary mediation service she can tell you about. It won't affect Rocky's care in any way.
Good. Now, what do I do with him at home?
For the next two days, give small, bland meals, little and often, and make sure he always has water. Give the anti-sickness tablets as labelled, and keep exercise to gentle lead walks.
He'll hate the gentle bit.
Just for a couple of days. Please bring him straight back, or ring the out-of-hours line, if the vomiting returns, he won't eat, his tummy seems painful again, or he goes quiet and flat.
Vomiting, not eating, painful, or quiet. Right.
Exactly. Could you tell me what you'll do at home, so I know I've been clear?
Small bland meals, water, tablets, short walks, and back straight away if he's sick or off-colour.
That's it. I'm sorry last night was so stressful. I'll take you to the office manager now to sort out the plan.
Thanks. I'm glad he's all right, at least.

coverage.how: Names her upset, says he will listen first, and invites her to go on.
Asks how Rocky is before the money and confirms his progress.
Explains the pain relief, anti-sickness medicine and drip and why each was given.
Explains that the X-rays were to rule out a blockage needing surgery, so normal was useful.
States what the record shows without accusing her, and says so explicitly.
Acknowledges how hard a midnight decision is and apologises for the shock of the total.
Breaks the bill into its main parts and offers the itemised bill.
Asks about insurance and offers instalments and charities without promising a discount.
Explains writing to the practice manager and independent mediation, with care unaffected.
Gives two days of bland meals, water, medication and gentle walks.
Lists the return signs and checks she can repeat them.
Asks what would help her most and agrees a written payment plan with the office manager before she leaves.

concern.how: Her money worries and feeling rushed are heard in full and acknowledged before the record is mentioned; her doubt about the X-rays is answered by what they ruled out, and practical payment help follows.

safety.point: Return at once if vomiting returns, he will not eat, his abdomen is painful again or he becomes quiet.

scripts.notes: The card gives the treatments and the figures. The itemised parts of the bill, the instalment option and the charity help are the script's general choices; the independent mediation service reflects the UK veterinary complaints route. Anti-sickness tablets at home are assumed, since the card mentions the medication but not its form.

turns.text: Hello, come in, both of you. How has Bramble's arthritis been affecting his day-to-day life?
He's stiff first thing, slow on the stairs, and he won't jump into the car any more. I have to lift him.
That must be hard for you both. What have you tried so far?
Shorter walks, and a joint supplement from the pet shop. Not much difference.
Apart from the supplement, have you given him any other medicines at home, including anything from your own cupboard?
Well, on his bad days, half of one of my ibuprofen. He seems brighter after.

Thank you for telling me; it's really important I know. Ibuprofen is made for people, and dogs handle it very badly. Even small amounts can cause stomach ulcers, bleeding and kidney damage, so please don't give him any more. You were trying to help him, and I understand why.
I had no idea. Have I hurt him?
His blood tests last week were normal, which is reassuring. Has he had any vomiting, black stools or a poor appetite?
No, nothing like that.
Good. Arthritis is wear and inflammation in the joints, here in his hips and elbows. We can't cure it, but we can usually control the pain well, so he's comfortable.
So, the tablets you mentioned.
Yes, an anti-inflammatory painkiller made for dogs. It calms the inflammation that causes the pain. Give it every day with food, because food helps protect his stomach.
Can I start tonight?

Not quite. Because he's had ibuprofen recently, we need a gap of several days first. Two anti-inflammatories close together greatly increase the risk to his stomach. I'll write down the date to start.
Okay. What about side effects?
Most dogs do very well. Watch for vomiting, diarrhoea, black or tarry stools, or going off his food. If any of those happen, stop the tablets and ring us that day.
Right. Can I ask you something honestly? My last dog went on strong painkillers, and he was put to sleep soon after. Is this the beginning of the end?
I'm glad you asked. No. Many dogs take these painkillers for years, and they often become more active, not less. Starting them now is about giving him good years, not counting down.
That's a relief. I've been dreading it.

Other things help too. Keeping him lean takes pressure off his joints. Two or three short walks a day are better than one long one. Non-slip rugs on hard floors, a ramp for the car and a warm, padded bed all make a difference.
A ramp would save my back as well.
Definitely. To see whether the tablets are working, keep a simple diary: good days, bad days, and how he manages the stairs and the car. That tells us more than one visit can.
I can do that. But what if he has a really bad day?
Please don't reach for your own tablets. Ring us, and we can see him or adjust the plan. If he can't stand, or cries out in pain, ring straight away, day or night.
Understood. No more of mine.
Thank you. And because he'll be on this long term, we'll check him regularly and repeat his blood tests, to make sure his kidneys and liver stay healthy.
How often is that?
I'd like to see him a few weeks after he starts, then usually every few months, with blood tests at least once or twice a year. Could you tell me the plan, so I know I've been clear?
No more ibuprofen, wait for the start date, then the tablet every day with food. Stop and ring if he's sick, has diarrhoea, black poo or won't eat.
That's exactly right. And the other changes?
Keep him slim, little walks, rugs, a ramp and a comfy bed. And the diary.
Perfect. Let's book his recheck before you go. Is there anything else on your mind?
No, thank you. I feel much better about it.

coverage.how: Asks how arthritis affects his daily life and what has been tried.
Asks directly about any medicines at home, including the owner's own.
Explains arthritis as joint wear and inflammation that cannot be cured but can be controlled.
Explains the drug calms inflammation and is given daily with food to protect the stomach.
Lists the side effects and says to stop and ring the same day.
Explains why ibuprofen harms dogs, checks for signs, and credits his intention.
Explains the gap of several days and why combining anti-inflammatories is risky.
Answers directly that painkillers here are about good years, not the end.
Covers weight, short regular walks, rugs, a ramp and a padded bed.
Explains regular checks and kidney and liver blood tests on long-term treatment.
Asks him to keep a diary of good and bad days, stairs and the car, to judge the response.
Gives a bad-day plan: ring rather than use his own tablets, and ring straight away if the dog cannot stand or cries out.
Asks for a summary and books the recheck.

concern.how: A direct question about home medicines draws out the ibuprofen, which is handled without blame; later he voices his fear that painkillers mean the end, and it is answered plainly.

safety.point: Human ibuprofen is dangerous for dogs and must not be given again.
A gap of several days is needed after ibuprofen before the dog's anti-inflammatory is started.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, black stools or loss of appetite mean stopping the tablets and ringing the same day.
On a bad day he rings rather than giving his own tablets; inability to stand or crying out in pain means ringing straight away.

scripts.notes: The card does not say when the last ibuprofen was given or whether the dog has signs of harm; the script assumes no gut signs and normal bloods, as the card gives. The gap before starting is given as several days, without a fixed figure, since it depends on the drug chosen and the vet's judgement. The recheck schedule is typical UK practice.

turns.text: Hello, I'm the vet looking after Max today. Could you tell me what you've seen since he swallowed the sock, and how he's been today?
He was fine at first. Then last night he started vomiting, again and again, and he won't eat or drink much.

Thank you, that's really helpful. I've looked at his X-ray. It shows a pattern in the small intestine that strongly suggests something is stuck, very likely the sock. When the gut is blocked, nothing can pass, and the bowel wall can lose its blood supply and tear.
Can't you just make him sick, or wait for it to come out?

Making him sick now could do harm, because the sock has moved beyond the stomach. And waiting is risky, because a blockage like this rarely clears by itself and can become life-threatening. That's why I recommend an operation today.
Oh no. What does the operation involve?

Under a general anaesthetic, we open his tummy, find the sock, and remove it through a small cut in the bowel, then stitch it closed. If a section of bowel is badly damaged, we may need to remove it and join the healthy ends.
When would you do it?
This afternoon. His blood tests show he's a little dehydrated, so first he'll go on a drip to correct that, and he'll have pain relief straight away, so he's comfortable while we prepare.
And the anaesthetic? My last dog died under anaesthetic.
I'm so sorry. That must make today very frightening. Can you tell me what happened then?
He was old, he had a heart problem, they said. He just never woke up.

That sounds awful. Max is young and his heart sounds healthy, which lowers his risk, though no anaesthetic is completely risk-free. A nurse will monitor his breathing, heart, oxygen and blood pressure throughout, and he'll be on a drip.
Okay. What else could go wrong?

I'll be honest. The main risks are infection, the wound breaking down, and, most seriously, leakage from where the bowel was stitched, usually in the first few days. We'll watch for fever, pain, vomiting or him going flat, and act quickly.
How much will this be?

The estimate is eighteen hundred to two and a half thousand pounds. That covers the anaesthetic, surgery, medicines and his hospital stay. It may be higher if we need to remove bowel or he needs to stay longer, and we'd ring you before going over.
That's a lot.
It is. Is Max insured, and is there anyone you'd like to call before you decide?
He is insured. I'll ring my husband after, but he'll say yes.
Good. Our office can help with the insurance claim. Are you happy for me to go ahead?
Yes. Just get it out.
So you're agreeing to an anaesthetic, opening his abdomen, removing the sock, and removing damaged bowel if needed. Is there anything you'd like to ask before you sign?
No, I understand. Will you tell me how it goes?
Yes. I'll ring you as soon as he's in recovery, probably early this evening, and a nurse will call again before bedtime. Is this mobile number best?
Yes. And when he comes home, what then?
He'll usually stay in for a couple of days. At home he'll wear a cone collar to protect the wound, have small, soft meals little and often, and short lead walks only until his stitches are checked.
Okay. Sorry, I'm a mess. My son's in tears at home. He left the sock on the floor.
Please tell him it isn't his fault. Young Labradors swallow socks all the time; it's one of the most common things we remove. And you did exactly the right thing bringing Max in.
He'll be so relieved to hear that.
Just so I'm sure I've explained it well, could you tell me what's happening today?
An operation to take the sock out, maybe some bowel. The main danger is leaking, and you'll ring me after.
Exactly right. Please sign here, and if you think of anything, ring the desk.
Thank you. Please look after him.

coverage.how: Asks what she has seen since the sock and how he is today.
Explains the X-ray pattern and why a blockage can damage the bowel.
Explains why inducing vomiting or waiting is unsafe now.
Describes the operation, including possible removal of damaged bowel.
Asks about her last dog, then explains his lower risk and the monitoring.
Names infection, wound breakdown and leakage, and the signs to be watched.
Gives the estimate, what it covers and what could raise it, with a call before going over.
Checks insurance and whether she wants to call anyone.
Restates exactly what she is agreeing to, invites questions and checks understanding.
Agrees a call after recovery and a nurse's call before bedtime.
Tells her the child is not to blame and that sock removal is common.
Explains the drip for his dehydration and immediate pain relief before surgery.
Explains a short stay, then a cone collar, small soft meals and restricted lead walks at home.

concern.how: Her fear of anaesthetic death is explored before reassurance is offered; her son's guilt surfaces near the end and is answered directly with a message he can be given.

safety.point: Inducing vomiting or waiting is unsafe once a blockage has moved beyond the stomach.
Leakage from the bowel repair is the most serious risk, watched for over the first few days.

scripts.notes: The card gives no examination findings; the script assumes a young dog with a healthy heart on auscultation and mentions an enterotomy or resection as the usual UK approach. The update times are the script's choice.

turns.text: Hello. Oscar's ready to go home, and he's doing well. How are you feeling about taking him home, and what do you understand about why he blocked?
Nervous, honestly. I know he couldn't wee, and someone mentioned crystals.

That's right. Male cats have a very narrow tube draining the bladder. Crystals, tiny gritty particles in the urine, mixed with inflammation and formed a plug. We cleared it under anaesthetic, and the catheter kept the tube open while his bladder recovered.
And now he's weeing properly?
Yes, normally since the catheter came out. He's going home with pain relief, a liquid you can give by mouth or on a little food. Give it exactly as the label says, finish the course, then stop.
Easy enough. What about the food?

The prescription urinary diet helps dissolve these crystals and stops new ones forming. It must be his only food, so no treats or other cat food. He's been eating it here, so you can switch straight over at home.
He's fussy, but he's eating it?
He is, especially the wet version. Wet food is better, because more water means more dilute urine. A water fountain and several bowls around the flat will help him drink more too.
I'll get a fountain. Someone told me stress causes this. Is that true?
Stress can play a real part in bladder problems in cats. Has anything changed at home recently?
My new flatmate moved in with her dog a month ago. Is it the dog's fault?

It's not about blame, but a new dog is a big change for a cat. Give Oscar a dog-free room with his food, water and litter tray, plus high shelves and hiding places. Ideally, have more than one tray, in quiet spots.
He's started sleeping on top of the wardrobe, actually.
That tells us he wants height and safety, so make that spot comfy. Now, the important part. He could block again, and the risk is highest in the first few days.
That's what scares me. I work twelve-hour shifts.

Then let's plan for it. A blocked cat can become dangerously ill within a day or so, so we need to catch it early. The signs are straining with little or no urine, crying in the tray, going in and out repeatedly, licking his rear end, vomiting or hiding.
And if I see that?
Bring him in immediately, day or night. Don't wait until the morning. Out of hours, our phone line will direct you to the emergency vet.
But I won't see it while I'm at work.
Could someone check on him during your shifts this week? Your flatmate, perhaps?
She works from home most days. I could ask her.
That would be ideal. Ask her to check he's passing urine in the tray. A light-coloured clumping litter makes it easier to see, and check the tray yourself before and after each shift.
That's doable. When do you want to see him again?
In about a week, for a check and a urine test. Sooner if you're worried at all.
What will the test show?
Whether the crystals are clearing, and whether his urine is dilute enough. Many cats stay on this diet long term to keep crystals from coming back, and we'll decide that together.
Long term? Fine, if it keeps him out of here.
Before you go, could you tell me what you'd watch for, and what you'd do?
Straining, crying, little or no wee, licking or being sick, and I bring him straight in, even at night.
Exactly. And at home?
Only his special food, more water, a fountain, a dog-free room, and my flatmate checks the tray.
Perfect. Here's his medication and the discharge sheet. Our number is on it, and out of hours it will put you through to the emergency vet. You're going to do brilliantly.

coverage.how: Asks how she feels about going home and what she understands about the blockage.
Explains the narrow male urethra, crystals and inflammation forming a plug, and the catheter.
Explains giving the liquid pain relief as labelled and stopping at the end of the course.
Explains the diet dissolves crystals, must be the only food, and that he can switch straight over.
Recommends wet food, a water fountain and several bowls.
Asks about changes at home, avoids blame, and advises a dog-free room, trays, shelves and hiding places.
States that reblocking can happen, especially in the first few days.
Lists the warning signs and says he must be seen immediately, day or night.
Plans checks by the flatmate during shifts and tray checks before and after work.
Agrees a recheck in about a week with a urine test.
Explains the test shows crystal clearance and urine strength, and that the diet may be long term.
Hands over the discharge sheet and explains the practice number and out-of-hours route.
Asks her to repeat the warning signs, the action and the home plan.

concern.how: Her question about stress is welcomed and her worry about the flatmate's dog is reframed from blame to changes; her fear of missing a reblock during long shifts is answered with a practical checking plan.

safety.point: He could block again, with the highest risk in the first few days.
Straining with little or no urine, crying in the tray, licking his rear end, vomiting or hiding are the warning signs.
Any warning sign means being seen immediately, day or night, without waiting for morning.
The discharge sheet carries the practice number, which connects to the emergency vet out of hours.

scripts.notes: The card gives no drug name or dose; the script says only to give the pain relief as labelled. The one-week recheck with a urine test is the script's choice and is typical of UK practice. The card does not name the crystal type, so the script describes the diet in general terms.

turns.text: Hello. Kaiser's waking up nicely from the sedation. Before I show you the X-rays, could you tell me what you've noticed, and what you were hoping I'd say today?
He limps after a long walk and he's slow getting up. I was hoping it's a sprain. We'd planned to start agility in the spring.
Thank you. I'm afraid the X-rays show something more than a sprain, and it's not what you were hoping for. Is it all right if I go through it now?
Go on.

This is his pelvis. The hip is a ball and socket. In a healthy hip, the ball sits deep in the cup. In Kaiser's, both sockets are shallow and the joints are loose. This is called hip dysplasia. It's a developmental problem, and it's partly inherited.
Both sides? So he's got bad hips. At his age.
Yes. I can see that's a shock. Take a moment.
I just don't understand. He's a puppy.
It's very hard to hear. What's going through your mind?
That I paid a fortune for a dog that's broken. I'm wondering about sending him back to the breeder.

That's an understandable reaction. You could certainly contact the breeder; they'll need to know, as it affects their breeding. For advice on your rights, Citizens Advice can help. But whatever you decide, Kaiser isn't broken.
What do you mean?
There's no arthritis yet. Arthritis will probably develop over time, but many dogs with hip dysplasia live long, active, comfortable lives with the right management.
What does management mean?

Keeping him lean is the biggest thing. Then controlled exercise, regular lead walks rather than chasing balls, building muscle with physiotherapy or hydrotherapy, and pain relief when he needs it. I'd also like to refer him to an orthopaedic specialist to discuss whether surgery could help.
Surgery? What sort?
That's for the specialist, as the options depend on his age and his hips. Some procedures are best done while dogs are young, so referring him sooner rather than later makes sense.
And agility? That's the whole reason I got a shepherd.
I'll be honest: jumping and sharp turns would put a lot of strain on those hips, so I don't advise agility. Scent work, gentle swimming and long lead walks would give him a job without the pounding.
Scent work. He does love sniffing. But how long should his walks be? We do over an hour, twice a day.
For now, several shorter lead walks are kinder than two long ones, building up slowly. Avoid stairs where you can, put rugs on slippery floors, and lift him in and out of the car or use a ramp.
That's a big change for both of us.
It is, but it protects his hips. We'll also weigh him at every visit, because even a little extra weight puts more strain on those joints.
He's always hungry, so I'll need to watch that.
He'd be brilliant at scent work, by the way. One more thing: because the condition is partly inherited, I'd strongly advise that he isn't used for breeding, so it isn't passed on.
I wasn't planning to. Fair enough.

Watch for signs that his pain isn't controlled: limping more, stiffness after rest, reluctance to walk or climb stairs, bunny-hopping with both back legs, or being grumpy when touched. If you see those, ring us.
Bunny-hopping. I think he does that already.
That's useful to know, and it fits. If it gets worse, we'd act sooner. He may be sleepy tonight after the sedation, so keep him quiet. Could you tell me what you've taken from today?
Bad hips on both sides, arthritis later, but he can still have a good life. Keep him slim, shorter walks, no agility, a referral, and ring if he's sore.
Exactly. Would you like me to go ahead with the referral?
Yes. And I'll speak to the breeder, but I'm keeping him.
I'm glad. I'll send the referral today with the X-rays. Any questions before you take him home?
Not right now. Thank you for being straight with me.

coverage.how: Asks what he has noticed and what he hoped to hear.
Warns that the X-rays show more than a sprain and asks permission to continue.
Uses the X-ray to explain the shallow sockets and loose joints, and that it is developmental and partly inherited.
Explains arthritis is likely but many dogs live active, comfortable lives.
Pauses after the news and asks what is going through his mind.
Covers weight, controlled exercise, physiotherapy or hydrotherapy, pain relief and specialist referral.
Advises against agility honestly and offers scent work, swimming and lead walks.
Responds to the breeder idea without judgement, suggests contacting the breeder and Citizens Advice.
Advises against breeding because the condition is partly inherited.
Lists signs of uncontrolled pain and says to ring.
Replaces long walks with several shorter lead walks and advises on stairs, floors and the car.
Explains he will be weighed at every visit because extra weight strains the hips.
Asks for his summary and agrees the referral as the next step.

concern.how: An open question after the pause lets him voice that the dog feels broken and that he might return him; this is answered without judgement and reframed with what the dog can still have.

safety.point: More limping, stiffness, reluctance to walk, bunny-hopping or pain on touch mean ringing the practice.
He may be sleepy after sedation and should be kept quiet tonight.

scripts.notes: The card gives no hip scores or laxity measurements. The script avoids naming specific surgical procedures and leaves the choice to the specialist, as options depend on age and joint changes. The sedation aftercare advice is general.

turns.text: Pip's done really well. How are you feeling, and what do you know about why chocolate is dangerous for dogs?
Shaken. I just know it's poisonous. I feel like a terrible owner.

That's understandable, but this was an accident, and you got him here quickly, which was exactly right. Chocolate contains a substance called theobromine, a stimulant a bit like caffeine. Dogs break it down very slowly, so it builds up in their bodies. Dark chocolate has the most.
It was a big bar of dark chocolate, too.
Yes. The injection I gave made him sick, and he brought up a large amount. Because that happened within about an hour of him eating it, much of it was never absorbed, which greatly reduces the risk.
So he's safe now?
He's bright, and his heart rate is normal, which is very good. But I have to be honest: some may already have been absorbed, so he needs watching closely for the next day.
What's normal, then?
He may be tired after the injection, and his tummy may be a little upset, perhaps with soft stools. That's expected and should settle.
And what isn't normal?
Ring us at once if he vomits repeatedly, becomes restless or can't settle, pants heavily, his heart seems to race, or he trembles, wobbles or has a seizure. Don't wait to see if it passes.
And if it's the middle of the night? I'm worried he'll get ill again while we're asleep.
That's a real worry, so here's what to do. After hours, ring our usual number, and it will put you through to the emergency vet. Save it in your phone now, and keep your car keys handy.
Okay. The trouble is, we've got a party tonight.
Then put Pip in a quiet room away from the noise and guests, with water and his bed. Excitement can make his heart race, and guests might slip him food.
I'll put him in my bedroom. Should I feed him?
A small, plain meal later is fine if he's hungry. Check on him regularly through the evening, and before you go to bed, so you'd notice any change.
My son left the chocolate on the coffee table. I really told him off.

Teenagers forget, and so do adults; this happens in lots of homes. The fix is a household rule: chocolate goes in high cupboards, never on low tables, in bags or in coat pockets. Remind your guests tonight as well.
Good idea. Are there other things like this?

Yes. Grapes, raisins and sultanas can damage the kidneys, even in small amounts, so watch the fruitcake and mince pies. Sugar-free gum and sweets often contain a sweetener that's very dangerous for dogs. Onions and garlic are harmful too.
I'd no idea about the gum.
Many people don't. If he ever eats something you're unsure about, ring straight away rather than waiting. Could you tell me the warning signs that mean you should ring tonight?
Being sick again and again, restless, panting, a racing heart, shaking, wobbly or a fit.
Exactly right. And who do you ring if it's the middle of the night?
Our usual number, and it puts me through to the emergency vet.
That's it. The emergency service is at the animal hospital across town, so if you need it, set off as soon as they say so. With the party, will someone be able to drive you tonight?
My husband isn't drinking. He can drive us if we need to.
Good. And please ring us tomorrow morning with an update, even if he's completely fine. It helps us close the loop.
I will. First thing.
Perfect. You've done everything right today. I hope the party goes well, and that Pip sleeps through it.

coverage.how: Asks how she feels and what she knows about chocolate and dogs.
Explains theobromine as a slow-cleared stimulant and that dark chocolate is worst.
Explains the injection, the large amount brought up, and why early vomiting cuts the risk.
States honestly that some may have been absorbed and he needs a day of close watching.
Describes tiredness and a mildly upset stomach as expected.
Lists the warning signs from the card and says to ring at once.
Explains the usual number connects to the emergency vet and to save it.
Advises a quiet room away from the party, water and a plain meal, and regular checks.
Removes blame from her and her son and gives a household rule for storing chocolate.
Lists grapes, raisins, sultanas, sugar-free sweeteners, onions and garlic.
Explains where the out-of-hours hospital is and checks someone sober can drive tonight.
Asks for a call tomorrow morning even if he is fine.
Asks her to repeat the warning signs and the night-time number.

concern.how: Her guilt is answered in the first explanation and again when she mentions her son; her fear of the night is met with a concrete plan for reaching the emergency vet.

safety.point: Some chocolate may already have been absorbed, so he needs close watching for the next day.
Repeated vomiting, restlessness, panting, a racing heart, trembling, wobbliness or a seizure mean ringing at once.
After hours, the practice number connects to the emergency vet.
Grapes, raisins, sultanas, sugar-free sweeteners, onions and garlic are also dangerous to dogs.

scripts.notes: The card does not give the dog's weight or the exact amount, so the script makes no dose calculation. It does not add activated charcoal, which the card does not mention. The timescale of watching for the next day is the script's general advice.

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. Toby's result is back. Before I explain it, what do you understand about the test, and what's worrying you most?
You put a needle in the lump. I've hardly slept. I'm convinced it's cancer.
I'm sorry you've had such a worrying couple of days. The good news is that the sample showed only fat cells. That fits a lipoma, which is a harmless fatty lump.
Harmless? Are you sure?

A lipoma is a soft collection of normal fat under the skin. They're very common in older Labradors. They usually grow slowly or not at all, and they don't spread. His hasn't changed in a month, which fits.
My last vet said that about my old dog's lump. Months later it was cancer, and she died.
I'm so sorry. That must make this so much harder. Can you tell me what happened?
They said it was nothing and to leave it. By the time they took it out, it had spread.
That's a terrible experience, and it makes complete sense that you're frightened. I can't know the details of that case, but I can be honest about this one.
Go on.

A needle sample is a good test, but it only collects cells from part of a lump, so occasionally it can miss something. I'd be more concerned if it grew quickly, became firm or fixed, or changed in any way. Right now, none of that is happening.
Then why not just take it out and be sure?

That's a completely reasonable option. Removing it means the whole lump can be examined under the microscope, which gives a definite answer. The downsides are an anaesthetic, a wound to heal, and the cost.
And if we leave it?

Monitoring avoids surgery, and many lipomas never cause problems. The downside is living with some uncertainty, which I know is hard for you. Anaesthetic risk for a fit dog his age is low, though never zero, and we'd do blood tests first.
What would you do?
Based on this result, I'd usually suggest monitoring. But your peace of mind matters, and removing it is a sensible choice too. The decision is yours, and I'll support either.
I think I'd like to try watching it, if you'll take it seriously.
I will. Measure it once a month with a tape measure, across the same direction each time, and take a photo with a coin beside it. Write down the date and the size.
Once a month. I can do that.
Bring him back sooner if it grows quickly, becomes hard or fixed, turns red, sore or open, or if you find any new lumps. And let us know if he seems unwell in himself.
And if I still can't stop worrying?
Then tell me. I'll check it again in three months, and at any point we can take a small piece for testing, called a biopsy, or simply remove it. You won't be brushed off.
And if another lump turns up, will you just say it's fat as well?
No. Every new lump gets checked and sampled in its own right, because we can't tell what a lump is just by feeling it. A lipoma now doesn't mean the next one is the same.
Thank you. That's what I needed to hear.
Could you tell me what we've agreed, so I know it's clear?
It's most likely a harmless fatty lump. I'll measure and photograph it monthly, come back sooner if it grows, hardens, goes red or there are new lumps, and see you in three months.
Perfect. And if you change your mind about removing it?
I ring you, and we book it.
Exactly. I'll note today's measurement on his record, so we have a starting point.
That makes me feel much better.

coverage.how: Asks what she understands about the test and what worries her most.
Gives the result plainly: only fat cells, fitting a harmless fatty lump.
Explains what a lipoma is and its usual slow, non-spreading behaviour.
Explains a needle sample can miss part of a lump and lists the changes that would raise concern.
Invites the story of her last dog and acknowledges it without criticising the other vet.
Sets out removal and monitoring with the benefits and downsides of each, including the anaesthetic.
