Recommends monitoring while calling removal reasonable and leaving the decision to her.
Explains monthly measurement, a photograph with a coin, and written records.
Lists the changes that mean an earlier visit.
Agrees a three-month recheck and offers biopsy or removal at any point.
Explains that every new lump is checked and sampled in its own right.
Asks her to summarise and confirms her decision and how to change it.

concern.how: Her fear surfaces at once; the story of her previous dog is invited and acknowledged without blame, and her wish for removal is treated as reasonable, with a monitoring plan that takes her seriously.

safety.point: Rapid growth, hardening, fixing, redness, soreness or new lumps mean an earlier visit.
Every new lump is checked and sampled rather than assumed to be another lipoma.
A baseline measurement is recorded today so that change can be judged.

scripts.notes: The card gives no exact measurement or dog's blood results. The three-month recheck and monthly home measurement are the script's choices and are typical of UK practice for a stable lipoma.

turns.text: Luna's health check looks great. You mentioned you had some questions. What have you heard, and what's worrying you most?
I'm pregnant, and my mum says cats cause miscarriages and I've got to rehome her before the baby comes. I'm frightened.

Congratulations, and thank you for asking rather than worrying alone. I think your mum's thinking of toxoplasmosis. It's an infection caused by a tiny parasite. Most people who catch it feel fine, but catching it for the first time in pregnancy can harm the baby.
So she's right?

Partly. People catch it more often from undercooked meat, unwashed vegetables or soil than from their own cat. Cats only pass it in their droppings for a short time, usually after they first catch it, and fresh droppings take at least a day to become infectious.
So the litter tray is the risk?
That's the main link with cats. Ideally someone else empties it every day. If you have to do it, wear disposable gloves, empty it daily and wash your hands well afterwards.
My partner can do it. He'd better.

Good. Wear gloves for gardening too, because cats use flower beds. Wash fruit and vegetables well, cook meat until it's steaming hot all the way through, and wash your hands and boards after handling raw meat.
Should Luna be tested?
It isn't usually helpful. A blood test shows whether a cat has met the parasite at some point, not whether she's passing it now. The hygiene steps protect you either way.
What about me? Should I have a test?
That's a really good question for your midwife or GP. They can advise about your own health and any testing. I'd mention Luna at your next appointment.
Okay. But my partner keeps saying she has to go.

He and your mum clearly want to protect you and the baby, and that's understandable. But with simple precautions, the risk from a healthy cat is very low, and most families keep their cats safely through pregnancy. Rehoming isn't necessary for this.
Could I show him what you've said?
Of course. I'll give you a leaflet you can share at home. Is there anything else worrying you?
Will she hurt the baby? People say cats smother babies.

That's a common fear. Cats don't set out to harm babies, but they do like warm places, so keep her out of the cot and the nursery when you can't supervise. And never leave the baby alone with any pet.
How do I get her ready?

Make changes gradually, before the baby comes. Move her bed or tray to their new spots now, let her explore the nursery, and play recordings of baby sounds quietly. Keep a quiet space that's just hers, so she doesn't feel pushed out.
That sounds manageable. Will she act differently, though?

She might. Cats notice change, so she may hide more, want more attention, or occasionally go outside her tray. If that happens, or she seems unwell, bring her in, because stress can affect a cat's health.
Good to know.

For hygiene, keep her tray and food bowls out of the kitchen and away from the baby's room. And keep her flea and worm treatment and her health checks up to date, which keeps parasites out of the house.
She's due her worming soon, actually.
Perfect, we can sort that today. Before you go, could you tell me what you'll take home to your partner and your mum?

Luna can stay. Someone else does the tray daily, or I use gloves and wash my hands. Cook meat well, wash veg, gloves for gardening. No test for her, ask the midwife about me. And keep her out of the cot.
That's spot on. Here's the leaflet. Congratulations again, and do ring if anything else comes up.
Thank you. I feel so much better.

coverage.how: Asks what she has heard and what worries her most.
Explains toxoplasmosis as a parasite infection, mild in most people but harmful in a first infection in pregnancy.
Explains undercooked meat, unwashed vegetables and soil are commoner sources than a pet cat.
Advises someone else empties the tray daily, otherwise gloves, daily emptying and hand washing.
Advises gardening gloves, washing produce, cooking meat through and kitchen hygiene.
Explains a cat blood test shows past exposure, not current shedding.
Directs questions about her own testing to her midwife or GP.
Acknowledges the family's protective intent and explains rehoming is not necessary.
Advises gradual changes, nursery exploration, a quiet space, keeping out of the cot and supervision.
Recommends keeping flea and worm treatment and health checks up to date.
Explains she may hide, seek attention or soil outside the tray, and to bring her in if so.
Advises keeping the tray and bowls out of the kitchen and away from the baby's room.
Offers a leaflet to share and asks for her summary.

concern.how: Her fear for the baby and the family pressure to rehome surface at once and are answered with facts and precautions; her later worry about the cat and the newborn is answered with practical safety steps.

safety.point: Someone else should empty the tray daily; otherwise gloves, daily emptying and hand washing.
Gloves for gardening, washed fruit and vegetables, and meat cooked through reduce the risk.
Questions about her own health and testing go to her midwife or GP.
Keep the cat out of the cot and never leave the baby alone with a pet.
Behaviour change or illness in the cat after the changes at home means bringing her in.

scripts.notes: The card does not say whether the cat hunts or eats raw food; the script treats her as a healthy cat on a normal diet. The timing of egg infectivity is described only as at least a day, which matches mainstream UK advice for emptying the tray daily.
